Three weeks is right; budget around £4,000 per person with a hire car, mixing state-park camping and motels, before flights.

adventures.title: Pamir Highway
adventures.description: The Pamir Highway (M41) from Osh in Kyrgyzstan to Dushanbe in Tajikistan is the second-highest highway in the world, crossing the Pamir plateau at elevations consistently above 4,000 m through some of the emptiest landscape in Asia. Yak herders, Soviet-era infrastructure, and the deep blue of Karakul Lake at 3,900 m alongside the Chinese border provide the backdrop for what cyclists and motorcyclists rate among the world's greatest road adventures.

adventures.title: Silk Road Journey
adventures.description: The ancient Silk Road from Xi'an to Istanbul traces 7,000 km of trade routes through China's Gobi Desert, Central Asian steppes, Persian caravanserais, and Anatolian highlands. By a combination of train, bus, and shared taxi, the journey moves through Dunhuang's Mogao Caves, Uzbekistan's Registan Square, Turkmenistan's Gates of Hell, and Iranian bazaars where saffron and pistachios overflow in technicolour piles.

adventures.title: Japan Pilgrimage Shikoku 88
adventures.description: The Shikoku Henro is a 1,200 km walking pilgrimage circling the island of Shikoku, visiting 88 Buddhist temples associated with the monk Kūkai (Kōbō Daishi). Pilgrims walk in white robes carrying a wooden staff, believed to embody the spirit of Kōbō Daishi himself. The route takes 30–60 days depending on pace and includes mountain sections, coastal paths, and city temple visits. The culture of osetai — gifts of food and money given to pilgrims — is extraordinary.

adventures.title: Trans-Siberian Railway
adventures.description: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway on earth — 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok, crossing 8 time zones, the Ural Mountains, the vast Western Siberian plain, Lake Baikal (the world's deepest lake), and the Russian Far East over 7 days in one continuous run or 3 weeks with stops. The Mongolian branch via Ulaanbaatar and Beijing adds the Gobi Desert crossing and the most dramatic scenery. Bring books, vodka, and patience.

adventures.title: Amazon River Journey
adventures.description: Travelling the Amazon from Iquitos in Peru to Belém on the Atlantic coast of Brazil — 3,700 km on slow cargo boats and jungle lodges — is among the most immersive journeys on earth. Pink river dolphins surface alongside the boat, sloths hang from cecropia trees at the waterline, caimans glow in headtorch light, and the scale of the forest — 5.5 million sq km — reduces everything else to perspective. The slow boat from Leticia to Manaus takes 5–7 days; hammock space is cheap.

adventures.title: Skeleton Coast Expedition
adventures.description: The Skeleton Coast of Namibia runs 500 km of fog-shrouded Atlantic desert coastline from the Kunene River to Swakopmund, one of the most inhospitable and eerily beautiful landscapes on earth. Shipwrecks rust in the dunes, Cape fur seals crowd rocky points in their tens of thousands, and desert-adapted lions and elephants survive in this extreme environment. Access to the northern zone requires permits or a fly-in safari; the southern section is reachable by 4WD.

adventures.title: Spitsbergen Polar Bear Safari
adventures.description: Svalbard at 78° North is the world's most accessible Arctic wilderness — a high-Arctic archipelago of glaciers, polar bears, walrus, and Arctic foxes reachable by scheduled flight from Tromsø. Summer brings the midnight sun and boat expeditions into drift ice where polar bears hunt. Winter brings the blue twilight of polar night and the northern lights. Armed guide requirement means most access is via guided expedition.

adventures.title: Ethiopian Simien Mountains Trek
adventures.description: The Simien Mountains of northern Ethiopia are an eroded basalt plateau dissected into dramatic table mountains, with escarpments dropping 1,500 m to the Sudanese lowlands. The park is one of the last habitats for the Gelada baboon — troops of 1,000 graze the cliff-edge meadows — as well as the Ethiopian wolf and Walia ibex. The 5-day circuit from Sankaber to Ras Dashen, Ethiopia's highest peak at 4,550 m, combines serious altitude with extraordinary wildlife.

adventures.title: Kyrgyzstan Horse Trekking
adventures.description: Kyrgyzstan's Tian Shan mountains offer horse trekking through high-altitude jailoos (summer pastures) where nomadic herding families still move their flocks between valleys seasonally. Routes from Karakol into the Terskey Alatau ranges or from Naryn into the Song Kul plateau cross high passes above 4,000 m, reach ice-cold alpine lakes, and end each night in a yurt with fermented mare's milk and mutton. No technical riding experience needed; the horses know the terrain.

adventures.title: Via Francigena Italy
adventures.description: The Via Francigena is the ancient pilgrim road from Canterbury to Rome — 1,000 km of the Italian section alone runs from the Gran San Bernardo Pass through Tuscany and Lazio to St Peter's Basilica. The route passes through Siena's Piazza del Campo, the Crete Senesi lunar landscape, the medieval towers of San Gimignano, and thermal baths at Bagno Vignoni. This is gentle cultural walking at its finest, staying in abbeys and agriturismo.

adventures.title: Svalbard Ski Touring
adventures.description:
At 78° north, ski touring out of Longyearbyen in April hits the high-Arctic sweet spot: the sun is back after four months of polar night, the snowpack is still deep-winter dry, and by late month it never sets at all. Tours head into the glaciated valleys of Nordenskiöld Land or go boat-supported along the fjords, linking peaks like Trollsteinen and long glacier draws where the only other tracks belong to reindeer and ptarmigan.

The non-negotiable variable is polar bears: outside Longyearbyen every group must carry a rifle and flare pistol, which in practice means travelling with an armed guide unless you hold the permits yourself. Temperatures of -15 to -25°C with wind demand full expedition layering even under blue sky.

Budget around £5,500 for a guided week including snowmobile or boat support and Longyearbyen lodging; flights via Oslo or Tromsø land you two hours from the skin track. No visa is needed — Svalbard sits outside Schengen despite Norwegian administration.

adventures.title: Quebrada Humahuaca Cultural Trek
adventures.description:
The Quebrada de Humahuaca runs 155 km north from Jujuy towards the Bolivian altiplano, a UNESCO-listed canyon that has carried people and trade between the Andes and the lowlands for 10,000 years. Base yourself in the villages strung along Route 9: Purmamarca beneath the Cerro de los Siete Colores (Hill of Seven Colours), Tilcara with its restored pre-Inca hilltop fortress, and Humahuaca itself, from where a dirt road climbs to 4,350 m for the Serranía de Hornocal — the "fourteen-colour mountain" whose zigzag strata at sunset are the region's single best sight.

Day walks link cactus-studded ridgelines, adobe chapels and the blinding white Salinas Grandes salt flat over the Cuesta de Lipán pass; the rough detour to cliff-hung Iruya deserves an overnight. Altitude is the catch — the valley floor sits at 2,000-3,000 m and the viewpoints top 4,000 m, so acclimatise in Tilcara before pushing higher.

Buses and shared remises make this an easy independent trip; £1,200 covers a comfortable week of guesthouses and empanadas. Come April to September for dry, cloudless days; summer brings afternoon storms and landslides on the side roads. Time it for Humahuaca's February carnival and colour takes over completely.
highlights: Cerro de los Siete Colores at Purmamarca

adventures.title: Morocco Sahara Camel Trek
adventures.description:
Erg Chigaga is the Sahara that Morocco keeps quiet: some 40 km of unbroken dunes rising to around 100 m, reachable only by camel, foot or 4x4 across the stony hamada beyond M'Hamid, where the tarmac ends. The classic trip walks in over three days with a camel string carrying camp — you ride when you tire — arriving as the low sun sets the dune sea glowing orange, then pink, then deep violet before the stars switch on with no light pollution for a hundred kilometres.

Nights are spent in Berber camel-hair tents with tagine cooked over embers; the silence between the drumming is total. It is a different proposition from Erg Chebbi at Merzouga, where day-trippers arrive by coach — out here you may see no other group at all.

October to April is the season: summer temperatures pass 45°C and most camps close. Winter days are warm but nights drop near freezing, so pack a proper insulating layer. Count on roughly £400 for five days from a Marrakech pickup — a long day's drive over the Tizi n'Tichka pass and down the kasbah-lined Drâa valley gets you to M'Hamid.

adventures.title: Corsica Sea Kayak
adventures.description: Paddling the 1,000 km coastline of Corsica by sea kayak takes 6–8 weeks and reveals the island's true character — cliffs inaccessible from land, hidden sea caves echoing with swell, turquoise coves with transparent water, and wild camping on beaches shared only with loggerhead turtles. The west coast is rougher and more dramatic; the east coast is calmer and more agricultural. Winds from the Mistral and Libeccio can pin you in a cove for days.

imageAttribution.artist: Michael Clarke (michael clarke stuff on Flickr) https://www.flickr.com/people/mi

adventures.title: Wrangell-St. Elias Packraft
adventures.description:
Wrangell-St. Elias is the largest national park in the United States — six Yellowstones would fit inside it — and almost none of it has trails. A packraft expedition out of McCarthy is the classic way in: walk onto the Root Glacier past the ghost mines of Kennecott, cross the moraine of Donoho Basin, then inflate the boat and let the silty, fast Kennicott and Nizina rivers carry you down towards the Chitina. Ice cliffs, canyon walls and grizzly prints on every gravel bar; a fortnight can pass without seeing another party.

This is genuinely self-supported wilderness — no huts, no phone signal, weather and water levels judged for yourself. Cold water is the hazard that catches people: glacial rivers run at 2–4°C and braid unpredictably, so a drysuit and honest Class II-III judgement matter more than fitness.

Access is simple by Alaskan standards: drive the McCarthy Road from Chitina or fly in, base at McCarthy, and build a loop to match ability. Guided trips with all gear run about £5,000 for two weeks; June to August offers 18-hour daylight, with early summer giving the lowest water.

imageAttribution.artist:
National Park Service, Alaska Region

NPS photo by Neal Herbert

adventures.title: Tierra del Fuego Kayak
adventures.description: Paddling the Beagle Channel and the inner fjords of Tierra del Fuego is one of the most remote sea kayak expeditions available outside of polar regions — conditions include tidal races, glacial calving, williwaw squalls that can reach 100 km/h with zero warning, and water cold enough to kill in minutes. The reward is the Darwin Range in winter light, Magellanic penguins on shore, and the knowledge that Fitzroy and Darwin passed these same channels.

adventures.title: Aosta Valley Via Ferrata Circuit
adventures.description:
Courmayeur sits directly beneath the Italian face of Mont Blanc, and its via ferrata and protected routes put you on airy rock with the biggest wall in the Alps filling the sky. The centrepiece is the ferrata up Mont Chétif, the 2,343 m pyramid standing guard over the town: ladders and cable up steep rock to a summit ridge with the Brenva face, the Grandes Jorasses and the Val Veny glaciers arranged in front of you like a relief map. Around it a week fills easily — cabled scrambles and balcony paths above Val Ferret and Val Veny, a rest-day ride up the Skyway Monte Bianco cable car to 3,466 m, and long rifugio lunches of polenta and Fontina.

Be honest about what a ferrata week demands: a proper energy-absorbing lanyard set, helmet and gloves are mandatory, and afternoon thunderstorms build fast against the massif in July and August — a cable route is the last place to meet lightning, so climb early and be down by two.

June to September is the season, once the winter's cables have been re-checked. Around £2,200 covers a week of valley guesthouses, lifts and a couple of guided days; Geneva and Turin are both under two hours away.

adventures.title: Rinjani Summit Trek
adventures.description:
Rinjani, the 3,726 m volcano that dominates Lombok, packs more drama into three days than treks three times its length. From Sembalun the trail climbs through savannah grass to the crater rim at 2,639 m, where the ground drops away into a caldera holding the turquoise lake of Segara Anak and the smoking young cone of Barujari. The summit push leaves camp about 2 a.m.: the final ridge is two steps up, one slide back in volcanic scree, and then the dawn detonates — Bali's Agung to the west, Sumbawa's Tambora to the east, and the crater lake 2,000 m below your boots.

Descending into the caldera earns you a soak in the lakeside hot springs before the long haul out to Senaru through cloud forest alive with ebony leaf monkeys.

Book a licensed trek organiser in Sembalun or Senaru — porters carry camp and cook astonishing food off two gas rings — and check the park is actually open: Rinjani closes each rainy season (roughly January to March) and after significant seismic activity. April to October is the window; about £600 buys a good three-day package. Bring genuine warm kit — rim camps are windy and near freezing before dawn.

adventures.title: Yellowstone Winter Snowshoe
adventures.description: Visiting Yellowstone in winter transforms the world's first national park into a silent, steam-filled landscape of geysers erupting through snow, bison standing in thermal hot spots to keep warm, and wolves hunting elk across snow-covered valleys. Snowshoe access to the interior is by snowcoach from West Yellowstone; the Old Faithful area, Mammoth Hot Springs terraces, and Lamar Valley wolf watching are the key experiences. The park is almost entirely yours.

adventures.title: Bhutan Snowman Trek
adventures.description:
The Snowman is the trek the others measure themselves against: roughly 320 km across the roof of Bhutan from the Paro valley past Jomolhari to the lost high valleys of Lunana and out towards Bumthang, crossing eleven passes over 4,500 m — several above 5,000 m — in about a month of walking. Fewer people finish it in a year than summit Everest, mostly because snow can close the passes in either direction and there is no road, no airstrip and no realistic rescue between Laya and the far side of Lunana.

The reward is the Himalaya with nobody in it: camps beneath the unclimbed 7,570 m bulk of Gangkhar Puensum, yak herders moving whole households over 5,000 m saddles, and villages like Thanza where visitors are still an event.

Late September to mid-October is the only sensible window — earlier is monsoon mud, later risks the passes shutting for winter. Bhutan requires a licensed operator plus the Sustainable Development Fee (currently US$100 per day) on top of trek costs, which is why a full Snowman runs around £12,000. Train for it like an expedition: weeks of consecutive 6-8 hour days at altitude, with weather that can erase the schedule.
highlights: Lunana villages of Thanza and Chozo

adventures.title: Kimberley Coast Expedition
adventures.description: The Kimberley coast of Western Australia is one of the most remote and dramatic coastlines on earth — 2,500 km of sandstone gorges, waterfalls that flow direct into the sea in the wet season, Aboriginal rock art sites accessible only by boat, and saltwater crocodiles on every beach. Expedition yachts or small cruise vessels navigate the horizontal waterfalls (a tidal hydraulic unlike anything else on the planet) and the Montgomery Reef tidal emergence.

adventures.title: Balkans Mountain Traverse
adventures.description:
The Via Dinarica White Trail threads the spine of the Dinaric Alps for around 1,300 km, from the Slovenian karst down through Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Kosovo, Albania and North Macedonia, finishing on Korab, the 2,764 m summit shared by the last two. It is less a waymarked trail than an idea stitched together from shepherd paths, old supply routes and fresh GPS tracks — which is exactly its appeal.

The middle third is the treasure: Bosnia's Sutjeska National Park, where Maglić rises above the Perućica primeval forest; the limestone wilderness of Durmitor and the 1,300 m-deep Tara canyon; then the savage grey teeth of the Prokletije on the Montenegro-Albania-Kosovo borders. Expect route-finding, sparse resupply, and hospitality that will wreck your schedule — mountain huts and village households across the former Yugoslavia treat a passing hiker as an occasion.

Walk it in one push over about two months from mid-June, once the high snowfields clear, or section-hike the highlights in a fortnight. Carry navigation you trust and cash in several currencies, and stay on recorded tracks in Bosnia, where some ridgelines still carry marked minefields. Around £4,000 covers a frugal full traverse.
highlights: Maglić and the Perućica primeval forest

adventures.title: Papua New Guinea Kokoda Track
adventures.description: The Kokoda Track is a 96 km mountain trail across the Owen Stanley Range of Papua New Guinea, following the route of the 1942 Second World War campaign where Australian forces fought to halt the Japanese advance. The terrain — steep, jungle-clad ridges in intense tropical heat and humidity — is relentless. The track is as much a pilgrimage of military history as it is an adventure; every village has a war story, and porters carry both your pack and the oral history.

adventures.title: Namibia Desert Trek
adventures.description:
The Naukluft massif rises like a fortress from the gravel plains on the eastern edge of the Namib — the world's oldest desert — and its multi-day trail is one of Africa's toughest and least known. The full circuit run by Namibia Wildlife Resorts covers about 120 km in eight days (a four-day version exists), dropping in and out of dolomite kloofs where fixed chains assist the scrambles, past black pools that hold water year-round, and up onto plateaux where gemsbok and Hartmann's mountain zebra watch you pass. Nights are in simple stone shelters; you carry everything, and the marked water points are the trail's one mercy.

Pair it with dawn at Sossusvlei, ninety minutes away, where the dead camel thorn trees of Deadvlei stand black against 300 m apricot dunes — the desert's two personalities, dolomite and sand, in a single week.

The trail opens only in the cooler months (March to the third week of October) and group sizes are capped, so book ahead through NWR. It is hot even then, and the kit check exists because people have come badly unstuck here. Around £1,800 covers park fees, trail permits, nights at Sesriem and a hire 4x4 — there is no public transport within 100 km.

adventures.title: Cotswold Way End-to-End
adventures.description: The Cotswold Way is 164 km from Chipping Campden to Bath along the western escarpment of the Cotswolds, passing honey-stone villages built from local oolitic limestone, Iron Age hill forts, beech-wood ridge paths, and the spectacular Cleeve Hill and Haresfield Beacon. It is quintessential English long-distance walking — gentle enough for beginners, varied enough to satisfy experienced walkers, and finishable with a Roman bath and a gin and tonic.

adventures.title: Atacama Salt Flats Cycling
adventures.description: Cycling from San Pedro de Atacama through the Salar de Atacama — the world's driest desert and largest lithium deposit — to the Bolivian salt flats of Uyuni combines dramatic desert scenery with extreme altitude. The route crosses geysers at dawn, flamingo lagoons tinted pink at sunset, and the infinite white mirror of the Uyuni salt flat. Roads are rough; altitude from 3,500–5,000 m demands acclimatisation. Winds in the afternoon are fierce.

adventures.title: Outer Hebrides Cycling
adventures.description: The Hebridean Way runs 300 km from Vatersay in the south to the Butt of Lewis in the north, cycling the string of islands connected by causeways through the wildest Atlantic seascape in Europe. The Western Isles have 6,000 years of human history layered under the surface — Callanish Standing Stones, Dun Carloway broch, and the black houses of Arnol — and beaches of white shell sand and turquoise water that would pass for the Caribbean if the temperature were 20° warmer.

adventures.title: Iceland Winter Ice Cave
adventures.description: The crystal blue ice caves that form each winter inside the Vatnajökull glacier in southeast Iceland are one of nature's most extraordinary interiors — curved walls of ancient glacial ice in every shade of blue, from pale aquamarine to deep cobalt, with black volcanic ash layers recording past eruptions. Caves form between October and March and are guided-access only. Combine with the Jökulsárlón glacial lagoon where icebergs float silently to the black sand Diamond Beach.

adventures.title: Elburz Mountains Ski Tour
adventures.description:
The Alborz wall north of Tehran hides one of skiing's great secrets: reliably deep, dry continental powder on 4,000 m mountains, ninety minutes from a capital of nine million. Dizin, Iran's largest resort, has lifts to about 3,600 m and off-piste bowls that would be tracked out in minutes in the Alps and stay untouched here for days. Touring objectives stack up along the range — Tochal directly above Tehran's northern suburbs, big open lines in the Shemshak backcountry — and over it all stands Damavand, at 5,610 m the highest volcano in Asia, whose south-side ski descent is a two-to-three-day crampons-and-skins project from the village of Polour.

The riddle to solve is logistics, not snow: most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance and rules for independent travel change, so most skiers come through an Iranian mountain agency that handles permits, transport and the Damavand huts. Persian hospitality does the rest — expect to drink a great deal of tea.

December to March is peak snowpack at the resorts; April brings the spring corn window on Damavand. About £2,500 covers ten days with guiding, Dizin passes and Tehran transfers.

adventures.title: Australian Outback Walk
adventures.description: The Larapinta Trail runs 230 km along the backbone of the West MacDonnell Ranges from Alice Springs to Mount Sonder, through ancient quartzite ranges, red gorges, and desert waterholes where black-footed rock wallabies come to drink at dusk. The trail is dry — carry 6 litres minimum between water caches — and remote. Walking in June–August brings mild days and cold nights; April–May and September–October offer wildflower colour. Aboriginal Arrernte country requires cultural awareness.

adventures.title: Socotra Island Trekking
adventures.description: Socotra Island in the Arabian Sea is the Galápagos of the Indian Ocean — 37% of its plant species are found nowhere else on earth, including the extraordinary Dragon Blood Tree with its umbrella canopy, the frankincense trees, and the bottle-shaped Desert Rose. The island has basic tourism infrastructure and requires a Yemeni visa (current access via flights from Abu Dhabi). Trekking the interior plateau and coastal dunes is the way to experience the alien vegetation.

adventures.title: Tour de Mont Blanc Running
adventures.description:
Running the Tour du Mont Blanc compresses the hikers' fortnight into five huge days: 170 km and roughly 10,000 m of climbing around the entire massif through France, Italy and Switzerland, on the same trails the UTMB race covers in a single night and day. Stages of 30-40 km link Chamonix, Les Contamines, Courmayeur, Rifugio Bonatti's balcony above Val Ferret and Champex-Lac, over cols — Bonhomme, Seigne, Grand Ferret — that each rearrange the massif's geometry behind you.

Nothing is technical; everything is relentless. The trick that catches fit road runners is the descending — 10,000 m of quad-shredding downhill is what ends attempts, so train on descents and carry poles.

Rifugio and gîte nights mean you run with a five-kilo vest rather than a pack, but beds must be booked months ahead for July and August. Early September is the connoisseur's slot: the UTMB circus has just left, the larches are turning gold and the refuges stay open into the third week. Around £2,000 covers half-board huts and valley transfers. Carry UTMB-style mandatory kit — waterproofs, warm layer, foil blanket — because 2,500 m cols manufacture their own weather in any month.

adventures.title: Wadi Rum Desert Traverse
adventures.description: Wadi Rum is the largest wadi in Jordan — a valley of red and orange sandstone rising in monumental jebels (mountains) over a vast flat desert floor, where Lawrence of Arabia camped and where the Martian landscape draws film crews from around the world. A 5-day trek crosses the interior on foot with a Bedouin guide, sleeping in black goat-hair tents and waking to silence. The rock climbing at Jebel Rum is world-class; the sunsets are simply impossible.

adventures.title: Azores Multi-Island Trek
adventures.description: Trek across several of the nine Azores islands — volcanic mid-Atlantic outposts with twin craters, steaming fumaroles, whale-watching, and whale shark diving all within a few kilometres of each other. Sao Miguel's Sete Cidades caldera is a 5 km double crater lake walk; Pico Island's volcano (2,351 m, Portugal's highest summit) takes 7-8 hours return. Faial and Flores offer sea cliff walking and waterfalls. The islands are less than 2 hours from Lisbon; whale watching season runs April to October when sperm whales, fin whales, and blue whales pass through.

adventures.title: Iditarod Trail Dog Sled
adventures.description: The Iditarod Trail — 1,600 km from Anchorage to Nome across Alaska's frozen interior — is best known as the world's toughest sled dog race, but the trail is also accessible for supported expeditions and ski touring from Knik to Skwentna in the southern sections. Mushing even a short distance with a 12-dog team through boreal forest and tundra silence is a transport experience unlike any other on earth. The Yukon Quest route from Fairbanks is the alternative.

adventures.title: Via Alpina Red Trail Traverse
adventures.description:
The Via Alpina Red Trail is the full Alpine crossing: 161 stages and roughly 2,500 km from Trieste on the Adriatic to Monaco on the Mediterranean, staying in the mountains the whole way through all eight Alpine countries — Slovenia, Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland, Italy, France and Monaco. It was stitched together from existing waymarked paths, which means every night ends at a hut, gasthof or village inn, and no stage needs ropes or glacier travel — just legs, weather sense and about three months.

The trail's genius is its variety: karst plateaux above Trieste, the limestone giants of the Julian Alps, weeks of Austrian grass ridges and the Allgäu, the granite perimeter of Mont Blanc, and a final descent through the Maritime Alps where the vegetation slides from larch to olive as the sea appears.

Most walkers take a full June-to-September season for the whole line, or bite off national sections in two-week blocks. Huts remove the camping weight penalty but the cost adds up — budget around £8,000 for a full traverse at half-board rates, and book Swiss and Mont Blanc-area huts ahead in August. Snowfields linger on the highest cols into early July, so carry light spikes early in the season.
highlights: Julian Alps and Triglav National Park
Maritime Alps descent to the sea

adventures.title: Lost Coast Trail
adventures.description: The Lost Coast of northern California is one of the few sections of the US Pacific Coast inaccessible by road — the terrain was too steep and the population too sparse for Highway 1 to penetrate. The 35 km King Range trail runs between Mattole Beach and Shelter Cove along a coastline of tidal rocks, sea stacks, black sand beaches, and old-growth Douglas fir forest. Timing is critical — the tidal flats impassable at high tide. Plan around the tidal tables.

adventures.title: Pyrenees Haute Route
adventures.description:
The Pyrenean Haute Route shadows the France-Spain frontier for some 800 km from Hendaye on the Atlantic to Banyuls-sur-Mer on the Mediterranean, taking the highest sensible line the whole way — above the GR10 and GR11, and often above the paths altogether. Forty days of walking cross the range's best theatre: the 1,500 m limestone amphitheatre of the Cirque de Gavarnie with France's highest waterfall streaming down it, the granite needles of the Aiguilles d'Ansabère, Monte Perdido above the Ordesa canyon, and an optional side-trip to Aneto, at 3,404 m the roof of the Pyrenees, whose shrinking glacier still asks for crampons in early summer.

The HRP is a route, not a trail: waymarks come and go, several stages are pathless boulder-hopping, and storms build violently on summer afternoons, so confident navigation is the entry fee. Staffed refuges and unstaffed cabanes cover perhaps half the nights; a bivouac kit covers the rest.

July to September is the season — earlier, snow chokes the high cols. Count on £4,500 for the full traverse, including refuge half-board where available, resupply in valley villages, and the ceremonial swim in the Mediterranean that ends it.

adventures.title: Nanda Devi Sanctuary Trek
adventures.description:
Nanda Devi, at 7,816 m the highest peak standing entirely within India, rises from a sanctuary ringed by a barrier of mountains — a dozen of them over 6,400 m — that defeated mountaineers for half a century until Shipton and Tilman forced the Rishi Gorge in 1934. The inner sanctuary has been closed to all visitors since 1983 to let a battered ecosystem recover, and that closure is what makes the region extraordinary today: blue sheep, musk deer and snow leopard numbers have rebounded in the core zone.

What you can do is trek the sanctuary's rim on a strictly permitted quota route from Lata village — the ancient approach — climbing through birch and rhododendron to the meadows of Lata Kharak and on towards Dharansi Pass at about 4,250 m, where the great twin-summited wall of Nanda Devi finally reveals itself across the forbidden gorge. It remains one of the steepest, most demanding approaches in the Himalaya, and Lata keeps a living relationship with the goddess Nanda.

Permits are limited and arranged through the forest department with guides hired from Lata itself — expect paperwork and fees that support the village. May-June and September-October dodge monsoon and snow; around £6,000 buys the full staffed, expedition-style trek.

adventures.title: Bolivia Altiplano Salt Flat Trek
adventures.description: Crossing the Salar de Uyuni — 10,582 sq km of perfectly flat salt at 3,656 m — on foot over three days is one of the most disorientating experiences in travel: no horizon, no shadow, no depth, just white. The edge effects of the salt flat's geometric polygon cracks, the Isla Incahuasi cactus island in the middle, and the mirror effect after light rain transform the landscape repeatedly. Nights camping on the salt under the Milky Way at altitude are unforgettable.

adventures.title: Easter Island Discovery
adventures.description:
Rapa Nui (Easter Island) is the loneliest inhabited place on earth — 3,500 km of Pacific between it and the Chilean coast — and nearly nine hundred moai still stand, lie and wait across its 163 sq km. Walking is the way to take it in: over four or five days you can circuit the island's coast and volcanoes on foot, from the fifteen re-erected giants of Ahu Tongariki catching first light to Rano Raraku, the quarry-volcano where almost four hundred unfinished statues lean out of the grass exactly where the carvers downed tools. The clifftop village of Orongo, perched between the Rano Kau crater and 300 m sea cliffs, tells the later story of the Birdman cult that replaced the statue religion.

Anakena's palm-backed beach makes the one soft afternoon; the rest is windswept grassland, wild horses and surf hammering black lava shores.

Flights from Santiago — about five hours — are the only way in, and the national park ticket (around US$80, valid ten days) is checked at the main sites; Rano Raraku and Orongo admit you once each. November to April brings the warmest, most settled weather. Around £3,000 covers a week with guesthouse lodging and a guide for the key sites; book flights early — they are the trip's real cost.

adventures.title: Nepal Mustang Kingdom Trek
adventures.description: The Upper Mustang — the ancient kingdom of Lo on the Tibetan plateau north of Annapurna — was opened to trekking only in 1992 and remains heavily restricted (USD 500 permit for 10 days). The landscape is a high-altitude desert of wind-eroded red cliffs, centuries-old cave monasteries, whitewashed villages where Tibetan Buddhism survives in its pre-Chinese form, and the walled capital of Lo Manthang. The restricted permit keeps it genuinely remote.

adventures.title: Fiji Multi-Island Surf Trip
adventures.description:
Fiji built its surf legend on one wave: Cloudbreak, the left that detonates over a shallow reef pass a few kilometres out from Tavarua, routinely ranked among the best — and heaviest — waves on earth. Since exclusive access ended in 2010, anyone with a boat can paddle out, which does not mean anyone should: at size it is an expert's wave that ends trips on the coral. The honest brilliance of Fiji is the spread around it: Restaurants' mechanical freight-train left off Tavarua (shallow, perfect, still not for beginners), Namotu Left's longer, friendlier walls, Wilkes and Swimming Pools for rippable rights, and Mamanuca island resorts running daily boat shuttles to whichever pass is working.

May to October is prime: Southern Ocean groundswells arrive groomed by south-east trades and the reefs go from playful to serious overnight when a big pulse lands. Water sits around 26°C — boardshorts and a rash top, plus reef booties for the shallow ends of the tide.

Base on Namotu or Tavarua (book many months out) or more cheaply at Nadi-side surf camps with boat access. Evenings dissolve into kava sessions where the line-up hierarchy evaporates. Two weeks with daily boats runs about £5,000.
highlights: Boat shuttles to empty reef passes

adventures.title: Masoala Peninsula Trek
adventures.description: The Masoala Peninsula in northeast Madagascar is the largest primary rainforest reserve in Madagascar and the richest biodiversity hotspot in the Indian Ocean — home to 11 lemur species, the helmet vanga, red ruffed lemurs, and the iridescent comet moth. Getting there involves a boat from Maroantsetra; moving through the park involves local guides and basic forest camps. The peninsula's bay-side beaches are among the most isolated in the Indian Ocean.

adventures.title: Traverse of the Angels
adventures.description:
The Apuan Alps are the strangest mountains in Italy: a compact chain rising between the Ligurian Sea and the Serchio valley, where the marble quarries that supplied Michelangelo have sliced whole flanks into blinding white geometry. A week's hut-to-hut traverse strings the drama together — the rock towers around Monte Procinto (whose 1893 via ferrata is Italy's oldest), Pania della Croce, the "Queen of the Apuans", with the sea filling half the horizon from its summit, and Monte Pisanino, at 1,946 m the range's highest point, above the quarry basins of Carrara.

The walking is far harder than the modest altitudes suggest: paths cut across steep karst, several classic stages carry cabled sections where a via ferrata set is sensible, and water is scarce on the crests — the limestone drinks every stream. Rifugi such as Carrara, Donegani, Rossi and Forte dei Marmi space the nights well.

May-June and September-October are ideal; high summer is hot and hazy, though sea breezes take the edge off. Come by train — Carrara and the Versilia towns sit on the Pisa-Genoa line — and budget around £1,500 for a week of half-board huts, with a detour into the Fantiscritti quarry galleries and lardo di Colonnata eaten in the village that invented it.

adventures.title: Ganges Source Trek
adventures.description:
The walk from Gangotri to Gaumukh is only 18 km, but it carries more meaning per step than almost any trail in the Himalaya: this is the sacred source of the Ganges, where the Bhagirathi bursts milky and freezing from the ice cave at the snout of the Gangotri Glacier at 3,900 m. Sadhus walk it barefoot, pilgrims bottle the water, and above it all the granite spear of Shivling (6,543 m) and the triple-crowned Bhagirathi peaks stand like the temple architecture the whole valley imitates.

Push one day further, steeply up the moraine, to Tapovan at 4,463 m — the meadow directly beneath Shivling where a handful of ascetics live in stone huts. Camping there, with dawn light crawling down the west face, is the trek's true summit.

The trail sits inside Gangotri National Park, which caps daily visitor numbers: arrange the permit in Uttarkashi or online before driving up. The glacier itself is in visible retreat — locals will point out where the snout stood a generation ago. May-June and September-October avoid both monsoon washouts and winter closure (road and temple shut around Diwali). About £1,200 covers permits, a guide-cook team for the Tapovan night and transport from Rishikesh, itself a spectacular day-and-a-half's drive.

adventures.title: Trollfjord Kayak Norway
adventures.description: Trollfjord is perhaps the most dramatic fjord in Norway — 2 km long and barely 100 m wide, enclosed by vertical walls of gabbro rising 1,000 m on each side, accessible only by boat. Kayaking into Trollfjord at dusk, when the rock walls reflect in still water and sea eagles patrol the cliff tops, is one of the defining fjord experiences in Scandinavia. The base is Svolvær in the Lofoten Islands; week-long circumnavigation of Austvågøya island is the full circuit.

adventures.title: Canyonlands Canyoneering
adventures.description:
Southern Utah's slickrock country is the world capital of canyoneering, and a week split between Moab and Escalante samples its whole grammar. Around Moab, classics like Granary Canyon and the Medieval Chamber — finishing with a free-hanging 30 m rappel beside Morning Glory Bridge — teach the craft: anchors, rope work, downclimbs, the way Navajo sandstone rewards friction and punishes hurry. Then the Grand Staircase-Escalante backroads deliver the pure slots: Peek-a-Boo and Spooky's corkscrew narrows, linked as a loop that squeezes to shoulder width, and Zebra's pink-striped corridor, all reached off the washboard Hole-in-the-Rock Road with a topo map and good judgement.

The variable that kills people here is flash flooding: a storm cell fifty kilometres away can send a wall of brown water down a slot under blue sky. Check the forecast for the whole drainage, not the trailhead, and stay out when in doubt.

March-May and September-November bring workable temperatures; summer cooks, and winter ices the potholes. Permits are free and self-issued for most Escalante slots. Around £1,800 covers a hire 4x4, camping and a two-day guided course in Moab to calibrate your rope skills before going self-sufficient.
highlights: Morning Glory Bridge rappel near Moab

adventures.title: Greenland Icesheet Traverse
adventures.description:
Crossing the Greenland ice sheet is the classic apprenticeship for polar expeditions, and a monster in its own right: roughly 560 km on skis from Point 660 above Kangerlussuaq to the east-coast fjords near Isortoq, hauling 60-70 kg pulks for three to four weeks over ice up to three kilometres thick. The first week climbs through the crevassed margin onto the plateau; then comes the long middle — a horizon of nothing, sastrugi hammered to concrete by katabatic winds, temperatures below -30°C, and the strange mental weather of total whiteness. You navigate by compass bearing and GPS because there is nothing else to steer by.

Nansen made the first crossing in 1888, travelling west from the east coast, and modern teams keep his logic where they can: technical glacier work done early and the prevailing wind at their backs.

Expect to train seriously — months of tyre-dragging — and to join a guided team unless you hold real polar experience: Greenland requires expedition permits, insurance and approved communications for the ice sheet. April and May balance daylight, cold and stable snow. Around £15,000 covers guiding, freight, permits and the boat or helicopter connection on the east coast.

adventures.title: Copper Canyon Trekking
adventures.description: The Copper Canyon (Barrancas del Cobre) in Chihuahua, Mexico, is a network of six canyons deeper and broader than the Grand Canyon — up to 1,879 m deep and 150 km wide — carved by six rivers draining the Sierra Tarahumara. The Tarahumara (Rarámuri) people have lived in cave dwellings and scattered ranchos across the canyon for millennia and are famous for long-distance barefoot running. The Chepe train from Los Mochis to Chihuahua City is the iconic journey.

imageAttribution.artist: Comisión Mexicana de Filmaciones from México D. F., mÉXICO

adventures.title: Kungsleden Southern Section
adventures.description:
The Kungsleden's southernmost section, 78 km from Hemavan to Ammarnäs through the Vindelfjällen Nature Reserve — one of Europe's largest protected areas — is the quiet end of Sweden's King's Trail. While the crowds head north for Abisko and Kebnekaise, five days here cross open fell plateaux and the glacier-carved trench of Syterskalet beneath Norra Storfjället's 1,768 m summits, on boardwalks over cloudberry bogs and bridges over rivers running tea-brown with peat. Golden eagles work the thermals, and Vindelfjällen shelters brown bear, lynx and one of Scandinavia's healthiest arctic fox populations.

STF huts space the days evenly — Viterskalet, Syter, Tärnasjö, Serve, Aigert — selling basic provisions and firing lakeside saunas, so with a sheet liner and card payment you can walk hut-to-hut with a light pack. The Tärnasjön section, threading wooden bridges across an archipelago of lake islands, is the stretch nobody forgets.

July to September is the season: earlier, the fells still hold snowfields; late August adds blueberries and subtracts mosquitoes. Both trailheads have bus links and Hemavan has an airport. Around £1,400 covers huts, hut food and the celebration dinner in Ammarnäs.

adventures.title: Whitsundays Sailing
adventures.description: The Whitsundays in Queensland — 74 islands in the Coral Sea, half of them national park, accessible only by boat — are among the world's finest bareboat charter destinations. Whitehaven Beach with its 98%-pure silica sand and the Hill Inlet colour-shifting tidal pool are the icons; the snorkelling at Bait Reef and Hardy Reef delivers turtles, reef sharks, and dense coral gardens. A bareboat charter for 4–6 people makes the mathematics work out better than a resort.

adventures.title: Stikine River Raft
adventures.description:
The Stikine is the great wild river of northwest British Columbia, and floating its lower reach from Telegraph Creek to Wrangell, Alaska is one of North America's finest self-supported river expeditions: about 260 km of swift Class I-II water through a corridor where the Coast Mountains stand straight out of the river. Upstream — and emphatically not on the itinerary — lies the Grand Canyon of the Stikine, a 70 km Class V+ chasm run only by elite kayak teams; you can peer into it near Telegraph Creek before launching below.

The float piles up rewards daily: a side-trip to the Great Glacier's berg-dotted lagoon, a soak at Chief Shakes Hot Springs, black bears and moose on the gravel bars, and bald eagles at densities that stop feeling remarkable. Tides govern the final day across the delta to Wrangell.

June to August gives long daylight and workable water, but the river runs cold and fast with snowmelt, so drysuits and solid group rescue skills are non-negotiable, and the trip suits experienced wilderness paddlers rather than experts only. Logistics are half the expedition — ferry or flight to Wrangell, road shuttle to Telegraph Creek, customs at both ends; around £5,000 covers a guided descent.
highlights: Grand Canyon of the Stikine overlook
Bears and moose on the gravel bars

adventures.title: Atlas Mountains Trek
adventures.description: Jebel Toubkal (4,167 m) is the highest peak in North Africa and in the Atlas Mountains south of Marrakech. The 2-day ascent from Imlil via the Toubkal Refuge is straightforward in summer; winter conditions with ice and snow make crampons and ice axe necessary. Combine the summit with a 5-day circuit of the Toubkal massif via the Azzaden Valley and Tizi n'Ouanoums pass, sleeping in traditional Berber gîtes and eating tagine with mountain herbs.

adventures.title: Kinabalu Summit Climb
adventures.description:
Mount Kinabalu is the granite colossus of Borneo — at 4,095 m the highest mountain in Malaysia — and one of the planet's great botanical staircases: the trail from Timpohon Gate climbs from hill forest through cloud forest dripping with orchids and pitcher plants to a bare granite summit plateau that feels borrowed from another planet. Kinabalu Park, Malaysia's first UNESCO World Heritage site, protects thousands of plant species, including nine Nepenthes pitcher plants found on the mountain and, in the surrounding lowlands, the parasitic Rafflesia — the world's largest single flower — if your timing is lucky.

The climb is a regulated two-day affair: about 6 km and 1,400 m of ascent to the Laban Rata huts at 3,270 m, then a 2.30 a.m. start up rope-assisted slabs to Low's Peak for a dawn that throws the mountain's shadow across half of Sabah. The altitude bites harder than the distance suggests, so walk in slowly and hydrate.

Climber numbers are capped and packages (permit, compulsory guide, hut and meals) sell out months ahead — book early, especially around holidays. March to August is statistically driest, with afternoon cloud standard year-round. Around £800 covers the climb package and Kota Kinabalu transfers.

adventures.title: Perito Moreno Glacier Trek
adventures.description: The Perito Moreno glacier in Los Glaciares National Park is one of the few glaciers in the world that is not retreating — it advances at 2 m per day and periodically creates an ice dam across the Brazo Rico channel, which then breaks spectacularly. Ice trekking on the glacier surface with crampons takes you across a blue-white world of seracs, moulins, and crevasses that calve into the turquoise lake with thunder. The catwalks opposite offer free viewing; the ice trek is the upgrade.

adventures.title: Sahara Erg Chebbi Run
adventures.description: A 250 km multi-stage running race through the Moroccan Sahara — the Marathon des Sables format — carries each runner's food and equipment on their back for 6 days through the Erg Chebbi dunes, rocky hamadas, dry riverbeds, and oasis palmeries. Each stage between 20 km and 80 km (the 'long stage') must be completed before dark. Over 1,000 runners from 40+ countries share a profound experience of physical and mental challenge in one of the world's most beautiful landscapes.

adventures.title: Senja Island Norway Hiking
adventures.description:
Senja is what Lofoten was before the crowds found it — Norway's second-largest island, its outer coast a sawblade of granite dropping straight into the Norwegian Sea, its inner side all quiet farms and birch forest. The classic outing is Segla (639 m): two hours of steep, honest climbing from Fjordgård to a summit fin that overhangs Mefjorden. For the photograph everyone actually wants — Segla itself, seen side-on across the ridge — climb neighbouring Hesten instead and arrive for the midnight sun, which keeps the light golden from roughly 20 May to late July.

Base yourself in the fishing villages of Mefjordvær or Husøy and tick off Husfjellet's ridge walk, the Tungeneset walkway over wave-smashed rock, and Ånderdalen National Park's pine bogs on weather days — and weather days will come, because Senja's forecast changes hourly and sea fog can erase a summit in minutes. Carry full waterproofs even under blue sky.

Getting there is the catch: fly to Tromsø, then it is a 2.5-hour drive or the summer-only ferry to Botnhamn. A hire car is effectively mandatory — buses are sparse — and Norwegian prices mean the £2,000 budget goes on self-catering cabins, not restaurants.

adventures.title: Flores Island Hiking
adventures.description: Flores in eastern Indonesia is the gateway to Komodo National Park and the home of Mount Kelimutu — three crater lakes that change colour independently between turquoise, black, and deep red depending on volcanic chemistry. The lake colours shift seasonally; dawn visits catch the mist lifting from the caldera. Walking the Bajawa plateau reveals traditional Ngada villages with conical men's houses and shrine ancestor poles; the road from Labuan Bajo to Ende passes extraordinary volcanic scenery.

adventures.title: Lofoten Islands Winter Hike
adventures.description:
Lofoten in winter is the Arctic with the drama turned up: granite walls rising straight from black water, red rorbu cabins glowing under snow, and — on clear nights between November and March — the aurora overhead. This is not a summit-bagging season. Sensible winter hiking sticks to lower objectives: the beach walks at Haukland and Uttakleiv, the coastal path to Kvalvika Bay, and viewpoints like Offersøykammen — with microspikes on your boots, because every popular trail turns to polished ice. Svolværgeita's twin horns, the climb that defines Svolvær's skyline, is a roped, guided affair at any time of year and doubly so in winter.

The variable that catches people out is daylight: the sun barely clears the horizon in December and early January, giving a workable window of four to five hours — plan hikes for midday and aurora hunts for night. Weather swings from calm to storm-force within the hour, and the E10 road can close.

Fly to Bodø or Evenes, hire a car with studded tyres, and base in Svolvær, Henningsvær or Reine. This is also skrei season — the winter cod migration that built these villages — so eat accordingly. Around £2,500 covers a week of cabins, car and food.

adventures.title: Otter Trail South Africa
adventures.description: The Otter Trail is South Africa's oldest and most oversubscribed hiking trail — 42 km along the Garden Route coastline from Storms River Mouth to Nature's Valley, crossing 11 rivers (some requiring swimming) through dense indigenous coastal forest of Outeniqua yellowwood and milkwood trees. Cape clawless otters, Knysna loeries, and dolphins surfing the shore swell are the companions. Permit bookings open 12 months in advance and close within hours.

adventures.title: Xinjiang Wilderness Traverse
adventures.description: The Kanas Lake region in northern Xinjiang, on the border of Russia, Mongolia, and Kazakhstan, contains some of the most pristine and least-visited boreal wilderness in Asia — Mongolian-style steppe, Siberian taiga forest, and the deep blue of Kanas Lake, which local Tuvan herders believe contains a sea monster. Trekking from Hemu village through the forests and over the passes requires Chinese permits and a guide; autumn colour in late September is extraordinary.

adventures.title: El Caminito del Rey
adventures.description: El Caminito del Rey (The King's Little Path) is a 7.7 km walkway pinned along the vertical walls of the Málaga gorges of El Chorro — originally built for hydroelectric workers in 1905 and restored in 2015 after years of closure following fatal accidents. The route traverses two gorges — Desfiladero de los Gaitanes and Desfiladero de Gaitanejo — on a 1 m-wide pathway with sheer drops below and the rock face inches from your shoulder. Book online; it sells out.

adventures.title: Leh to Manali Motorcycle
adventures.description:
The Leh–Manali Highway is 428 km of high-altitude theatre: five passes including Tanglang La at 5,328 m — signposted for decades as the world's second-highest motorable road, a claim newer Ladakhi roads have overtaken without making the ride through it any less breathless. From Leh you climb through Upshi and the moonscape of the More Plains, camp at Sarchu (4,290 m) on the Himachal border, hairpin down the 21 bends of the Gata Loops, and finally drop into the green shock of the Kullu Valley.

The variable that catches riders out is altitude, not the road surface. Sleeping at Sarchu with an unacclimatised body is miserable and occasionally dangerous — spend two or three nights in Leh first, or ride south-to-north and gain height gradually. The season is roughly mid-June to early October; outside it, snow closes everything.

Hire a Royal Enfield in Leh or Manali (about £15–20 a day), carry cash, a puncture kit and spare fuel — pumps are 365 km apart at the worst gap — and expect snowmelt stream crossings that deepen after midday sun. Around £1,800 covers a week with bike hire, fuel, tent camps and dhaba food, excluding flights.

adventures.title: Aeolian Islands Sea Kayak
adventures.description: The seven Aeolian Islands north of Sicily — Lipari, Vulcano, Stromboli, Salina, Filicudi, Alicudi, and Panarea — form an active volcanic archipelago accessible by sea kayak from Milazzo. Paddling between islands takes advantage of the thermal winds and the reliable summer calm to cross channels up to 22 km. Stromboli's permanent eruption (every 15–20 minutes) is best viewed from the sea at night; Vulcano's fumarole beach is a sulphurous natural spa.

adventures.title: Torres del Paine Circuit
adventures.description:
The O Circuit is the full lap of the Paine massif — about 130 km over eight to ten days, folding the classic W into a bigger loop around the mountain's rarely photographed northern side. The back half is the reason to come: quiet trails through southern beech forest past Lago Dickson, the Los Perros glacier, and then the crux — John Gardner Pass (1,200 m), where you crest a rise and the entire Grey Glacier unrolls beneath you, a white highway pouring out of the Southern Patagonian Ice Field. Condors ride the thermals overhead most days.

Patagonian weather is the serious variable: winds regularly exceed 100 km/h at the pass, and rangers close it outright in bad conditions, so build a spare day into your itinerary. The circuit runs anticlockwise only, with a daily quota on the back side.

Book campsites months ahead — they are split across CONAF and two private operators, and high-season pitches (December–February) sell out embarrassingly fast. Refugios and serviced camps with meals exist at most stops, so you can trade money for pack weight. Around £2,800 covers ten days with camps, some refugio meals and the Puerto Natales logistics, excluding flights.

adventures.title: Sahel Overland
adventures.description: The West African Sahel — the semi-arid transition zone from the Sahara to the savannas — stretches 5,400 km from Senegal to Chad and has been traversed by overlanders since the 1960s trans-Africa rallies. By 4WD from Dakar across Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and into Nigeria, the route passes Dogon cliff villages, Fulani cattle camps, and the ancient mud mosques of Djenné. Logistics are complex; political situations change; this is for experienced overland travellers.

adventures.title: British Columbia Coast Trek
adventures.description:
The North Coast Trail is the wilder sibling of the West Coast Trail: 43 km along the top of Vancouver Island from Shushartie Bay to Nissen Bight, where it joins the Cape Scott trail network for the walk out to San Josef Bay. There is no road at the start — a water taxi from Port Hardy drops you at Shushartie and leaves — and what follows is genuinely hard travel: bottomless mud, root ladders, rope-assisted descents, cable-car river crossings, and long stretches of boulder and sand beach walked to tide timing. Miss a tide window at a headland and you wait.

The reward is the rawest coast in British Columbia: sea stacks off Cape Sutil (the island's northernmost point), wolf tracks on morning sand, black bears grazing the beach sedge at a distance, humpbacks blowing offshore. Carry a tide table and know how to read it — it is the single variable that wrecks schedules.

Every camp needs bear-safe food storage (canisters or the fixed caches), and everything you own should live in dry bags. Allow five to seven days, budget about £1,800 including the water taxi in and the shuttle back from the San Josef trailhead, and treat the forecast as fiction.

adventures.title: Nepal Kanchenjunga Trek
adventures.description: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m), the world's third-highest mountain, is the most remote and least-visited of Nepal's 8,000 m peaks — a 3-week trek just to reach its base camps. The north and south base camp circuit passes through intact rhododendron and bamboo forest still harbouring red pandas and snow leopards, through Tibetan-influenced villages at the Taplejung headwaters, and to the stupendous Yalung Glacier viewpoint beneath the south face. Restricted area permit required.

adventures.title: Wind River High Route
adventures.description: The Wind River High Route in Wyoming is a 100 km off-trail traverse of the Wind River Range — the most continuous wilderness in the lower 48 states — from Big Sandy Lodge to Elkhart Park, staying above 3,000 m throughout and crossing 10 passes without a maintained trail. Navigation by map and compass, boulder-hopping on persistent talus, and fishing for cutthroat trout in untouched alpine lakes make this the definitive American wilderness experience.

adventures.title: Okinawa Island Diving
adventures.description: Okinawa's Kerama Islands, 35 km west of Naha, are considered one of Japan's finest dive destinations — visibility regularly exceeds 30 m, coral coverage is among the highest in Japan, and hammerhead sharks gather at Yonaguni Island's rocky seamounts from December to April. The underwater ruins at Yonaguni — rectangular stone formations at 25 m debated as natural or ancient — add an archaeological dimension unique in world diving. Manta rays at Ishigaki's Manta Scramble are reliable from spring.

adventures.title: Sub-Antarctic Islands Voyage
adventures.description: The sub-Antarctic islands south of New Zealand — Auckland, Campbell, Antipodes, Bounty, and Snares — are among the least-visited places on earth and the most important seabird and marine mammal breeding grounds in the Southern Hemisphere. A permit expedition vessel visit lands by Zodiac on island coastlines thick with Hooker's sea lions, southern elephant seals, wandering albatrosses with 3 m wingspans, and yellow-eyed penguins. New Zealand permits are heavily restricted.

adventures.title: Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route
adventures.description: The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route traverses the Northern Japan Alps from Toyama on the Sea of Japan to Nagano in the interior, crossing at 2,450 m through the Tateyama mountain complex by a succession of cable cars, trolley buses, and ropeways — with a section on foot across the caldera at Murodo. In late April to May, the route cuts through snow walls up to 20 m high. Mount Tateyama (3,015 m) is one of Japan's three holy mountains.

adventures.title: Carpathian Bear Country Trek
adventures.description: The Romanian Carpathians have the highest density of brown bears in Europe — an estimated 6,000 animals in the mountain forests of Transylvania and Moldavia. Trekking the 1,500 km Via Carpatica long trail from Slovakia through Poland and Ukraine into Romania follows the ridge of the Carpathian arc through bear, wolf, and lynx territory on trails that are still largely unmarked and require navigation. Village guesthouses, forest ranger huts, and wild camping are the accommodation.

adventures.title: Raja Ampat Liveaboard Diving
adventures.description:
Raja Ampat sits at the absolute centre of the Coral Triangle: more recorded fish species (1,400+) and a larger share of the world's hard corals (around 75% of known species) than anywhere else on earth. A liveaboard is the way to reach the spread-out sites. In the Dampier Strait, Cape Kri holds the world record for fish species counted on a single dive, mantas queue at the cleaning stations of Manta Sandy, and pygmy seahorses hide in the sea fans of Mioskon. South at Misool, soft-coral walls drop into blue water patrolled by oceanic mantas, and epaulette 'walking' sharks shuffle across the reef on night dives.

Current is the variable that catches people: the fish life exists because water moves, and sites like Blue Magic can start ripping mid-dive. Bring a reef hook, an SMB you can deploy in open water, and honest self-assessment — 50 logged dives is a sensible minimum.

The season is October to April (Misool itineraries pause for mid-year swell). Above water, climb the Piaynemo lookout for the karst-islet panorama on all the postcards. Liveaboards run £2,500–5,000 for 7–10 nights out of Sorong, plus the marine park tag and internal flights.

adventures.title: Iceland Volcanic Interior Trek
adventures.description: The Highlands of Iceland — accessible only in summer when the F-roads open — are the emptiest landscape in Europe. The Fjallabak Reserve and Sprengisandur highland route cross black lava plateaus, active geothermal areas, and the vast Hofsjökull and Langjökull ice caps. The interior has no huts in some sections; navigation across featureless lava desert requires GPS. This is the Iceland no tourist bus reaches.

adventures.title: Spain Picos de Europa
adventures.description: The Picos de Europa are a compact limestone massif on the northern coast of Spain — only 40 km from the Bay of Biscay coast, rising to 2,648 m at Torre Cerredo. The famous Cares Gorge walk (24 km, mostly flat, carved into the canyon wall) is the accessible classic; the high mountain circuits from Fuente Dé cable car deliver scrambling on karst limestone with chamois and griffon vultures. The towns of Potes and Cangas de Onís are charming bases.

adventures.title: GR11 Pyrenean Traverse
adventures.description: The GR11 traverses the entire Spanish side of the Pyrenees from Cabo Higuer on the Bay of Biscay to Cap de Creus on the Mediterranean — 800 km through the Spanish national parks of Ordesa, Aigüestortes, and Cadí, staying almost entirely in Spain rather than the mixed-country approach of the Haute Route. The GR11 is well-marked, well-serviced with refugios, and follows the valley floors and passes in approximately equal measure. A classic European long trail.
highlights: Mediterranean finish at Cap de Creus

adventures.title: Okhotsk Sea Ice Walk
adventures.description: The drift ice of the Sea of Okhotsk reaches the coast of Hokkaido near Abashiri and Shiretoko Peninsula each winter — the southernmost drift ice in the Northern Hemisphere — and walking on it in late February to March with icebreaker cruise access is a uniquely Japanese experience. The Shiretoko Peninsula, UNESCO World Heritage, extends into the ice floes and hosts Steller's sea eagles, white-tailed eagles, and the rare Blakiston's fish owl in the forest behind the ice.

adventures.title: Spiti Valley Trek
adventures.description: The Spiti Valley in Himachal Pradesh is India's most dramatic high-altitude desert — a cold, arid, Tibetan-plateau landscape of white Himalayan peaks, ancient mud-brick monasteries (Key Gompa, Tabo, Dhankar), and the Pin River gorge. The Pin-Parvati Pass crossing at 5,319 m connects the green Kullu Valley with the desert Spiti in a dramatic 10-day trek through both environments. Altitude, remoteness, and cultural immersion combine to make this an exceptional Himalayan journey.

adventures.title: Fiordland Packrafting
adventures.description: Packrafting the remote river valleys of Fiordland National Park in New Zealand — inflating a 2.5 kg raft to cross the Dusky Sound, float the Arthur River, or descend the Seaforth to the sea — opens up wilderness that is physically inaccessible by foot or boat alone. Fiordland receives up to 8 m of rain per year; the rivers flood rapidly and dramatically. Floatplane access, river knowledge, and self-rescue skills are prerequisites. The reward is primeval rainforest with no other human presence.

adventures.title: Bibbulmun Track
adventures.description:
The Bibbulmun Track runs roughly 1,000 km from Kalamunda in the Perth Hills to Albany on the Southern Ocean, waymarked the whole way by yellow triangles bearing the Waugal, the rainbow serpent of Noongar tradition. The walking is never technical but the landscape keeps changing: jarrah and marri woodland in the north, the giant karri forests around Pemberton, the red tingle groves of the Valley of the Giants near Walpole — some of the tallest flowering trees on earth — and finally a coastline of granite headlands and empty white beaches where sea eagles patrol.

Purpose-built three-sided shelters with rainwater tanks and sleeping platforms sit a day's walk apart, free and unbookable, so a thru-hike needs a tent only as insurance. The variables that matter are water and heat: tanks can run low by late spring, and summer (December–February) is genuinely dangerous walking weather with bushfire risk — go August to November for wildflowers or April to May for cool stability.

An end-to-end takes six to eight weeks with resupply in trail towns like Dwellingup, Balingup, Pemberton, Walpole and Denmark. Budget about £5,500 including town nights; snake gaiters earn their place from October.
highlights: Valley of the Giants tingle trees

adventures.title: Antarctica Expedition Cruise
adventures.description: An expedition cruise to the Antarctic Peninsula is the most extreme mainstream adventure travel destination on earth — 11 days aboard an ice-strengthened vessel from Ushuaia to the peninsula, landing by Zodiac on beaches with 10,000 chinstrap and gentoo penguins, approaching humpback whales from open inflatable boats, and crossing the Drake Passage twice. Nothing in travel prepares you for the scale and silence of Antarctica. Camping on the ice is the optional upgrade.

adventures.title: Sahara Ahaggar Plateau Trek
adventures.description:
The Ahaggar (Hoggar) massif rises out of the central Sahara above Tamanrasset: a shattered volcanic landscape of basalt plugs, organ-pipe pinnacles and black plateaux, with Mount Tahat (2,908 m), Algeria's highest point, at its heart. The essential pilgrimage is Assekrem, the 2,780 m plateau where Charles de Foucauld built his hermitage in 1911 — sunrise from its rim, with hundreds of volcanic towers igniting one by one across the Atakor, is among the great desert spectacles anywhere. Trekking here is done Tuareg-style: on foot with camel support, guides from Tamanrasset, nights under astonishing skies.

The logistics are the gatekeeper. Independent travel is not permitted — foreigners must travel with a licensed Algerian agency and registered guide, and the visa process itself takes planning (Algeria has been trialling visa-on-arrival for Saharan tourism; check current rules early). Winter, November to March, is the season: warm days, near-freezing nights.

Water discipline is absolute — plan for many litres per person per day between wells. Ten days with agency support, 4WD transfers and full board runs around £3,500 excluding flights to Tamanrasset via Algiers.
highlights: Assekrem sunrise from de Foucauld's hermitage
Mount Tahat 2,908 m, Algeria's highest point

adventures.title: Manaslu Circuit Trek
adventures.description: Circle Manaslu (8,163 m) — the eighth highest peak in the world — on a restricted area trek that follows the Budhi Gandaki gorge through Gurung and Tibetan communities before crossing the Larkya La (5,106 m), one of the most spectacular high passes in Nepal. The circuit takes 14-18 days; the crossing of the Larkya La is the physical and visual climax. The Manaslu Conservation Area protects snow leopard habitat; sightings are rare but tracks are found regularly in winter. Less crowded than the Annapurna and Everest circuits but rapidly growing in popularity.

adventures.title: Upper Dolpo Trek
adventures.description: Trek the Upper Dolpo restricted area — the setting for Peter Matthiessen's The Snow Leopard — a high Trans-Himalayan plateau of turquoise lakes, rock art, ancient Bon-po monasteries, and yak caravans that crosses three passes above 5,000 m in a 25-day circuit. The permit is expensive and number-limited; the region's isolation is its primary quality. The Crystal Mountain's Shey Gompa is the circuit's centrepiece. The route follows the historic trade route between Tibet and Nepal that predates Hinduism and Buddhism in the Himalayas. One of the most remote trekking experiences in Nepal.

adventures.title: Rolwaling Valley Trek
adventures.description: The Rolwaling Valley is one of Nepal's most remote trekking destinations, a sacred valley beneath Gauri Shankar at 7134m that the Sherpas consider the mythical home of the Yeti. The Tashi Lapcha pass at 5755m connects Rolwaling to the Khumbu Valley and is one of Nepal's most technically demanding trekking passes, requiring fixed ropes and glacier navigation. The valley's complete isolation from motorable roads preserves a Buddhist culture of exceptional authenticity.
highlights: Tashi Lapcha high pass at 5755 metres

adventures.title: Nanga Parbat Rupal Face Trek
adventures.description:
Nothing on earth out-scales the Rupal face: from the meadows at Tarashing you look up 4,600 vertical metres to the summit of Nanga Parbat at 8,125 m — the greatest single mountain wall in the world, close enough that you hear it. Avalanches peel off the face day and night, arriving as a delayed boom that rolls around the valley. The trek itself is surprisingly gentle for the setting: three to five days up the Rupal Valley through summer pastures and willow-lined villages to Herrligkoffer Base Camp and on to the Latobah meadows, with an optional push toward the Mazeno side of the mountain for wilder ground.

Access is the real undertaking. Fly or drive to Gilgit, then jeep via Astore to Tarashing — landslides and road closures are routine, so pad the itinerary by a day at each end. Foreigners should expect police registration checkpoints in the Astore Valley; a local guide smooths everything and costs little.

July and August give the best weather window and full wildflower meadows. This is one of the great value treks anywhere: around £900 for ten days including guide, porters and jeeps — Pakistani hospitality included at no charge.
highlights: The 4,600 m Rupal face, Earth's biggest mountain wall

adventures.title: Spiti Valley Motorcycle Journey
adventures.description:
Spiti is Ladakh's rawer, quieter cousin: a high-altitude cold desert where the turquoise Spiti River cuts through crumbling ochre badlands and thousand-year-old monasteries balance on eroded crags. By motorcycle from Manali, the Atal Tunnel now shortcuts the old Rohtang crossing into Lahaul, but the real filter is the Gramphu–Batal–Kaza road: 60-odd kilometres of rock, dust and snowmelt streams that must be forded before afternoon melt swells them, then over Kunzum La (about 4,550 m) with its wind-torn prayer flags and down to Kaza.

From Kaza the set pieces stack up — Key Monastery photogenic above the river bend, Kibber and Komic villages above 4,200 m, the fossil village of Langza beneath its giant Buddha, Dhankar's cliff-top gompa, and the side trip into Pin Valley's snow-leopard country.

Fuel is the trip's arithmetic: Kaza has the only pump in the valley, so carry spare litres. Acclimatise a night in Manali and consider riding the loop clockwise — up via Shimla and Kinnaur, out over Kunzum — for gentler altitude gain. Season is mid-June to September. Around £700 covers 12 days with bike hire at £12–15 a day, homestays and dal-heavy dinners.
highlights: Kunzum La prayer flags at about 4,550 m
Key Monastery above the Spiti River
Kibber and Komic villages above 4,200 m

adventures.title: Markha Valley Trek
adventures.description:
The Markha Valley is Ladakh's classic trek for good reason: it packs two high passes, a river-carved gorge of purple and ochre rock, whitewashed chortens and village homestays into nine days, all within Hemis National Park — the best snow-leopard habitat in India (you will not see one in summer; you may well see blue sheep and golden eagles). From Chilling the trail crosses the Zanskar and climbs gently through Skiu and Markha village, wading the river repeatedly — strapped sandals are not optional — before the landscape opens at Hankar into the high pasture bowl of Nimaling (4,700 m), where yaks graze beneath the glaciated pyramid of Kang Yatze (6,270 m).

The final day is the test: over Kongmaru La at about 5,260 m, then a long, knee-hammering descent through a slot gorge to Shang Sumdo. Altitude is the variable that ruins trips — spend at least two full days in Leh (3,500 m) first, or take the Ganda La approach from Spituk for gentler gain.

The homestay system makes this the rare Himalayan trek that needs no tent or cook crew: about £15 a night buys a mattress, dinner and butter tea. July to mid-September is the window; around £600 covers the lot from Leh.

adventures.title: Chadar Trek - Frozen Zanskar River
adventures.description:
For a few weeks each January and February the Zanskar River freezes into a chadar — a 'blanket' of ice — and the gorge it has cut through the Ladakh Himalaya becomes a walking route, as it has been for Zanskari traders for centuries. You shuffle along a canyon 300 m deep on ice that creaks, booms and changes colour underfoot, past frozen waterfalls the size of buildings, sleeping in caves and expedition tents while night temperatures sink towards minus 30°C. Where the ice fails at a bend, you climb the bank and traverse — or wait while the guides read the river.

Be clear-eyed about what this now is: climate change has made the ice less reliable, the road being blasted up the gorge shortens the wild section each year, and the trek is heavily regulated — ALTOA-registered guides, insurance, medical checks in Leh and porter welfare rules are all mandatory, and rightly so. Trips are cancelled outright when the chadar fails to form; book flexibly.

Acclimatise three nights in Leh (3,500 m) before starting, and treat glacier glasses, double-layer boots and a minus-40-rated sleeping bag as survival kit, not comfort. Nine days runs around £800 from Leh including permits, guide and camp crew.

adventures.title: Fann Mountains Traverse, Tajikistan
adventures.description:
The Fann Mountains compress the best of Central Asian trekking into a pocket-sized range a couple of hours from Samarkand: 5,000 m peaks, larch-fringed lakes in improbable shades of blue, and a hospitable Tajik valley culture that has barely registered tourism. The classic traverse links the Kulikalon bowl — a half-dozen lakes beneath a mile-high rock wall — with the Alauddin Lakes over the Alauddin Pass (3,860 m), then pushes over the Chimtarga Pass (4,740 m), grazing the foot of Chimtarga (5,489 m), the range's highest point, before dropping to the Haft Kul, the 'Seven Lakes' staircase of the Shing Valley, or to Iskanderkul, the big lake named for Alexander the Great.

There is no rescue service, no signage and little reliable mapping in English — go self-sufficient or hire a guide and donkeys at Artuch Alpine Camp for a few pounds a day. Water is everywhere; food resupply is not, so carry the lot.

The reopened border crossing from Samarkand (Uzbekistan) to Penjikent makes access straightforward. July to September is the season; nights frost even in August. Two weeks runs around £900 including transfers from Dushanbe or Samarkand.
highlights: Iskanderkul lake of Alexander the Great

adventures.title: Wakhan Corridor Trek
adventures.description:
The Wakhan is where the Pamir and the Hindu Kush stare at each other across a river you could throw a stone over. Travelling the Tajik side of the corridor — the practical option — you follow the Panj upstream from Khorog through Ishkoshim to Langar, with Afghanistan a field's width away the entire time: mud-brick villages, donkey trains and 7,000 m Hindu Kush summits stacked behind them. The set pieces en route are Yamchun Fort, an ancient citadel high above the valley, the hot springs of Bibi Fatima just beyond it, and the Buddhist stupa at Vrang — layers of Silk Road history in a day's drive.

Beyond Langar the road climbs onto the high Pamir toward the Khargush Pass (4,344 m) and, with an extra permit, the Zorkul reserve — a lake at over 4,100 m with Marco Polo sheep on the slopes above. Treks from villages like Langar up to the summer pastures give the corridor's best walking.

Everything runs on the GBAO permit (arranged with your Tajik visa), cash and a hired 4WD with driver — shared from Khorog if you are patient. July and August are the window; nights are cold at altitude year-round. Reckon on £2,500 for 18 days including vehicle share and homestays at £10–15 a night.
highlights: Hindu Kush wall across the river
Zorkul Lake and Marco Polo sheep

adventures.title: Tian Shan Kyrgyz Circuit
adventures.description: Trek through the Central Tien Shan Mountains of Kyrgyzstan — a wilderness of glacier-fed turquoise lakes, alpine meadows grazed by herds of yak and sheep, and jagged 5,000+ m summits that appear unexpectedly around valley bends. The Karakol region and Terskey Ala-Too range offer some of the finest trekking in Central Asia with minimal tourist infrastructure. Homestays in yurt camps provide food and accommodation; horses can be hired to carry gear. The region borders China's Xinjiang province at the Khan Tengri massif.

adventures.title: Ausangate Circuit, Peru
adventures.description: The Ausangate Circuit in the Cordillera Vilcanota south of Cusco is one of South America's most spectacular high-altitude treks, circling Ausangate peak at 6,384 metres through a landscape of turquoise glacial lakes, red and yellow mineral springs, and vicuna herds. The route crosses four passes above 5,000 metres and passes through Quechua herding communities where alpaca wool weaving is still practised. The adjacent Rainbow Mountain has become famous, but this circuit remains the authentic experience.
highlights: Mineral hot springs at high camp

adventures.title: Cordillera Real Traverse, Bolivia
adventures.description: The Cordillera Real forms the spectacular eastern backbone of the Bolivian Andes, with seventeen peaks above 5,000 metres accessible from La Paz. The Condoriri Circuit passes beneath hanging glaciers and electric-blue glacial lakes before crossing the high ridge at 5,000 metres with panoramic views toward the Amazon basin. Bolivian mountaineering culture is concentrated here, with numerous 6,000-metre peaks accessible to acclimatised trekkers.
highlights: Condoriri group mirrored in Laguna Chiar Khota

adventures.title: Quilotoa Loop, Ecuador
adventures.description:
The Quilotoa Loop is Andean village trekking at its most accessible: three to five days of self-guided walking between Kichwa farming villages in Ecuador's central sierra, finishing — walk it in this direction, the climax matters — at the rim of Quilotoa itself, a flooded caldera at 3,914 m whose mineral-green lake sits 250 m below the crater lip.
