The standard line runs Sigchos to Isinliví to Chugchilán to Quilotoa, descending and climbing the canyon of the Río Toachi each day on a web of farm paths where wrong turns are traditional — download the offline route and ask everyone you pass.

Each village has family-run hostals (£15–25 with dinner and breakfast, wood stoves, resident llamas), which is why packs stay light and the trek suits first-time altitude walkers — though the days still top out near 4,000 m, so spend a night or two in Latacunga or Quito first. Afternoon cloud swallows the crater with punctuality: aim to reach the rim before 2 pm.

Buses from Latacunga serve both ends cheaply, and luggage can be left at hostels in town. June to September is driest, but the loop is walkable most of the year. The whole thing, beds and dinners included, runs around £250.

adventures.title: Ciudad Perdida Trek, Colombia
adventures.description: The trek to Ciudad Perdida, the Lost City of the Tayrona people, winds through Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta jungle for four to six days to reach a pre-Columbian city that predates Machu Picchu by over 600 years. The route crosses the Rio Buritaca numerous times and climbs over 1,200 stone steps carved by the Tayrona into the jungle hillside. Indigenous Kogi, Arhuaco and Wiwa communities still consider this site sacred.

adventures.title: Pacific Crest Trail - Sierra Nevada Section
adventures.description: The Sierra Nevada section of the Pacific Crest Trail from Kennedy Meadows to Tuolumne Meadows covers the most dramatic 500 kilometres of the entire 4,300-kilometre trail. The route crosses Forester Pass at 4,009 metres (the highest point on the PCT), traverses the John Muir Trail, and passes through Kings Canyon, Sequoia, and Yosemite National Parks. This is the definitive American long-distance hiking experience at its most spectacular.
highlights: Forester Pass at 4009 metres highest PCT point

adventures.title: Wrangell-St. Elias Backpack
adventures.description: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park is the largest national park in the United States, encompassing four major mountain ranges with nine of America's sixteen highest peaks. The Chitistone and Nizina canyon routes follow Native Athabascan travel corridors through a wilderness larger than Switzerland. Grizzly bears, Dall sheep, and wolverines share the tundra above the historic Kennecott copper mines. Fly-in access from McCarthy is half the adventure: bush planes drop you on gravel bars with a pickup date and nothing else — carry everything, tell someone your route, and build in a weather day for the flight out.
highlights: Largest US national park no maintained trails

adventures.title: Gates of the Arctic Traverse
adventures.description: Backpack through the Brooks Range in Gates of the Arctic National Park — the northernmost national park in the United States, with no roads, no trails, no facilities, and no rangers in most of the park. The wilderness is accessed by bush plane from Fairbanks or Bettles to a gravel bar landing strip. Grizzly bears, wolves, caribou, and wolverines are the primary inhabitants; human visitors number in the hundreds per year. Navigation is by map and compass through tundra, river valleys, and unnamed passes. The solitude here is absolute.

adventures.title: Greek Island Hiking - Sporades Arc
adventures.description:
The Sporades are Greece for walkers who want their islands green: Skopelos and Alonnisos are draped in Aleppo pine that runs right down to the water, threaded with kalderimia — old cobbled mule tracks — linking monasteries, olive terraces and coves where the only footprints are yours. Alonnisos is the anchor: its hill-top Old Village, half-abandoned after the 1965 earthquake and now beautifully restored, sits above a freshly waymarked trail network, and the island fronts the National Marine Park of Alonnisos — Europe's largest marine protected area and the stronghold of the Mediterranean monk seal, one of the world's rarest mammals. Boat trips into the park pass islets patrolled by Eleonora's falcons.

Skopelos adds shady forest walking to the rock-cut Sendoukia tombs and a coastline of chapel-topped rocks; Skyros, a ferry-hop away, has its own pony-dotted interior. Distances are short, so this is a trip of mornings on trails and afternoons swimming.

Go in May–June or September–October: spring gives wildflowers, autumn warm seas, and midsummer is too hot for the exposed stretches. Ferries run from Volos and from Skiathos's airport. Ten days of island-hopping with guesthouses runs about £1,200.

adventures.title: Via Dinarica, Bosnia and Herzegovina
adventures.description: The Via Dinarica is a pioneering long-distance route through the Dinaric Alps connecting Slovenia to Albania through some of Europe's most remote mountain communities. The Bosnian section through the Prenj massif and Sutjeska National Park offers genuine wilderness, pristine rivers, and a chance to experience a region still emerging from the shadow of its recent conflict. Primeval Perucica Forest contains trees over 300 years old.

adventures.title: Finland Lakeland Canoe Route
adventures.description:
Lake Saimaa is Europe's fourth-largest lake and its most intricate: a 4,400 km² labyrinth of islands, sounds and open reaches in Finland's south-east, and the finest flat-water canoe touring on the continent. The premium circuits paddle out of Oravi or Savonlinna around Linnansaari National Park and into Kolovesi, where motorboats are banned and the silence is total but for your bow wave. Both parks are the home water of the Saimaa ringed seal — one of the world's rarest seals, around 400 animals — and a whiskered head periscoping beside the canoe is the trip's jackpot moment. Ospreys and black-throated divers are daily company.

Everyman's Right lets you camp on almost any wild shore, and the parks add laavu lean-to shelters with fire rings and stacked wood. June brings near-24-hour light; late August adds warm water and no midges. The variable to respect is open-water wind: crossings that look short on the map build real waves by afternoon, so plan island-hopping lines and paddle early.

Outfitters in Oravi rent canoes, dry barrels and route maps and will shuttle between trailheads. Finish in Savonlinna beneath Olavinlinna castle, sauna included. Three weeks of paddling, hire and food runs about £800; a one-week loop is the popular version.

adventures.title: Laos Gibbon Experience Ziplines
adventures.description:
You reach your bedroom by zipline. The Gibbon Experience strings a network of steel cables, some over 500 metres long, through the forest canopy of the Nam Kan National Park in Bokeo province, north-western Laos, linking treehouses built 30 metres up in emergent trees. Clip in, check your trolley, and commit: the cable sags, the forest floor drops away, and you land on a platform where dinner also arrives by zipline. The moment that stays with you comes at about 5am, when the western black crested gibbons begin to sing, a rising, whooping duet that carries for miles through the mist below your bed.

The catch is the season: in the June to September rains the cables still run, but leeches multiply and the ridge trails turn to grease, so aim for November to March. Book weeks ahead directly with the project (profits fund forest protection and anti-poaching patrols) and reach Huay Xai the night before; it is a short hop from the Chiang Khong border crossing with Thailand. From around £280 for the three-day Classic including guides, food and treehouse nights. Bring nothing you would mind dropping 30 metres.

adventures.title: New Zealand Heaphy Track
adventures.description:
New Zealand's longest Great Walk, 78.4 kilometres across Kahurangi National Park, is really five walks stitched together. You climb from the Aorere valley through beech forest to Perry Saddle, cross the strange golden tussock of the Gouland Downs (limestone arches, giant carnivorous snails, great spotted kiwi calling in the dark), then drop through moss-hung goblin forest to the Heaphy River. The finale is the part nobody forgets: the last day to Kohaihai threads between nikau palms and the Tasman Sea, with surf detonating on limestone reefs a few metres from the track.

Huts must be booked through DOC months ahead for the December to February peak. The track is walkable year-round, but the West Coast end takes serious rain and the sandflies at Heaphy Hut are legendary, so treat repellent as safety kit. The awkward logistics are the real planning problem: the trailheads are a 460-kilometre drive apart, so book a shuttle or the light-plane hop from Karamea back to Takaka. Budget around £400 with hut fees and transport; November to March gives the best weather window, and from May to November the track also opens to mountain bikes.
highlights: Nikau palm forest on the West Coast
Five ecological zones in one walk

adventures.title: New Zealand Paparoa Track
adventures.description:
New Zealand's newest Great Walk, opened in 2019, was built as a living memorial to the 29 men killed in the 2010 Pike River Mine disaster, and it feels different from the classics: a purpose-built 55-kilometre benched trail that climbs from the Blackball side through rainforest to spend a full day riding the crest of the Paparoa Range. From Moonlight Tops and Pororari Hut you look west over rank after rank of limestone escarpments to the Tasman Sea; the descent drops into the Pororari River gorge, all nikau palms and hundred-metre karst walls, to finish at Punakaiki near the Pancake Rocks.

It is also the only Great Walk designed from the outset for shared use: trampers take three days, mountain bikers ride it in two, and the huts (book through DOC well ahead) mix both tribes over the evening brew. The variable that catches people is the weather switch. The tops are utterly exposed, and a westerly front turns the ridgeline day into horizontal rain, so build in a spare day. About £350 covers hut fees, shuttles and a night either side in Greymouth or Punakaiki; November to March is the reliable season.

adventures.title: West Coast Trail, Canada
adventures.description:
Cut in 1907 as a lifesaving trail for shipwrecked sailors on the "Graveyard of the Pacific", the West Coast Trail still behaves like a rescue route: 75 kilometres of ladder towers, hand-cranked cable cars, surge channels and calf-deep mud along Vancouver Island's wildest shore. The rhythm is what hooks people. Forest boardwalk gives way to a tidal-shelf walk beneath sea stacks, then camp on sand at Tsusiat Falls, where a freshwater cascade drops straight onto the beach. Grey whales blow offshore; wolves and black bears patrol the tideline at dawn.

The tide table is the variable that catches hikers out: several beach sections are impassable above half tide, and misjudging them means hours pinned against the cliffs. Parks Canada caps numbers, so book your permit the day reservations open in January; the trail operates May to September only. Budget roughly £700 including the permit and ferries, the famous crab shack at Nitinaht Narrows, and buses to the Pachena Bay or Gordon River trailheads. Allow six to eight days, train with a loaded pack, and respect the route's Nuu-chah-nulth guardians whose territory it crosses - evacuation rates hover around one hiker in a hundred.

adventures.title: Mount Kenya Technical Climb
adventures.description:
Everyone climbs Kilimanjaro; climbers climb Mount Kenya. Point Lenana at 4,985 metres is the trekkers' summit, but the mountain's real prizes are Batian (5,199m) and Nelion (5,188m), jagged plugs of an ancient volcano that demand genuine rock climbing on the equator. Most parties take the classic South-East Face of Nelion, around 18 pitches of sound rock, bivouac in the tiny tin hut on its summit, then abseil into the Gates of Mist to cross to Batian. In a single day you move from giant groundsel and lobelia moorland past the fast-dying Lewis Glacier, which has lost around 90% of its ice since 1900.

Acclimatise properly on the walk-in through the Chogoria or Sirimon valleys; failure high on this mountain is almost always altitude, not difficulty. Season choice matters more than on Kilimanjaro: the south-facing routes come into condition from late December to early March, the north faces from July to September. A guided technical ascent over eight days from Nanyuki, with park fees, porters and a strong local guide, runs £1,200 to £2,500 - a fraction of an 8,000er apprenticeship, for a harder, quieter and more beautiful climb.

adventures.title: Trans-Siberian Cycling Expedition
adventures.description:
Riding from Vladivostok's Golden Horn Bay to Moscow is cycling's ultimate distance problem: more than 10,000 kilometres and seven time zones of taiga, steppe and truck-stop Russia, shadowed the whole way by the world's longest railway. The route's emotional centre is Lake Baikal - after weeks of forest the road crests near Kultuk and the world's deepest lake fills the horizon - followed by the Buryat Buddhist datsans around Ulan-Ude and the long grind over the Urals, where a roadside obelisk marks the Europe-Asia line.

The catch is arithmetic. Ninety days means averaging over 110 kilometres every single day, so most riders take four to five months or leapfrog the emptiest Amur sections by train. Summer, June to August, is the only sensible window; outside it you trade mosquitoes for frost. Camp wild, refuel in stolovaya canteens, and carry spares for the days between bike shops. Budget around £3,000 on the road excluding flights - but research visa and border realities carefully before committing, as independent travel logistics in Russia have tightened considerably in recent years and support options are thin.

adventures.title: Africa Cycling - Cairo to Cape Town
adventures.description:
Pedalling away from the Giza pyramids with Cape Town four months ahead is Africa's defining ride: roughly 12,000 kilometres through ten countries, from the Nile's date-palm villages to the Cape of Good Hope. The route builds like a symphony - desert tailwinds past the Meroe pyramids in Sudan, where roadside hospitality is among the warmest on Earth, then the brutal 3,000-metre climbs of the Ethiopian highlands, Rift Valley lake camps in Kenya and Malawi, and the long open gravel of Botswana's elephant country before the vineyards of the Western Cape roll you into Cape Town.

Most riders copy the organised expeditions and leave Cairo in January, so Sudan comes before the furnace months and southern Africa arrives in autumn. The variable that breaks schedules is not legs but paperwork and politics: visas shift constantly and route security must be re-checked country by country before you commit, with reroutes (occasionally by bus or flight) part of the game. Self-supported riders should budget about £6,000 for four months plus a serious contingency fund. Malaria prophylaxis from Ethiopia southwards is non-negotiable.

adventures.title: Caribbean Diving - Turks and Caicos Wall
adventures.description:
Ten metres down off Providenciales the reef shelf simply stops: the Wall drops vertically into the indigo of the Columbus Passage, a channel more than 2,000 metres deep between the Caicos and Turks banks. You hang at 20 metres with black coral fans below your fins and grey reef sharks cruising the edge; out at the remote West Caicos and French Cay sites, visibility routinely hits 30 metres and silky sharks appear mid-water. From January to April humpback whales migrate through the passage towards the Silver Bank breeding grounds, and their song carries into the water column - hearing it mid-dive is the trip's goosebump moment.

This is easy, warm, boat-based diving, but the best sites are exposed: winter swell can blow out West Caicos for days at a time, so book at least five diving days to be sure of the walls. Avoid the August to October hurricane peak; February to April combines calm seas with whale song. A week with two-tank boat dives, gear and Provo accommodation runs about £2,200 excluding flights, and an Advanced Open Water card earns you the deeper wall starts.
highlights: The Wall's vertical drop from 10m into the Columbus Passage
Humpback whale song underwater, January to April
Silky and reef sharks at French Cay and West Caicos
Night dives over black coral on the wall lip

imageAttribution.artist: the manta ray had a family (Flickr)

adventures.title: Borneo Headhunter's Trail
adventures.description:
The Headhunters' Trail is the adventurous back door out of Gunung Mulu National Park in Sarawak, following the route along which Kayan war parties once hauled their canoes between the Melinau and Terikan rivers. You go in by longboat and on foot to Camp 5, a riverside base beneath the sheer walls of the Melinau Gorge, and most groups spend a punishing extra day climbing to the Pinnacles viewpoint on Gunung Api, where 45-metre blades of silver limestone erupt from the jungle. Then the trail proper: eleven easily-lost kilometres of primary rainforest to Kuala Terikan, and a long, glorious longboat ride down the Medalam and Limbang rivers, with a night in an Iban longhouse before Limbang town.

Leeches, heat and humidity are constant companions; the variable that wrecks plans is river level, because after heavy rain the boats cannot run and after drought they scrape, so build slack into both ends. A Mulu-licensed guide is compulsory. March to September brings the drier months. Around £1,400 for five days including park fees, guides, boats and the longhouse stay - and catch the Deer Cave bat exodus at Mulu before you leave.
highlights: Melinau Gorge and Camp 5 riverside base
The Pinnacles of Gunung Api side ascent
Longboat descent of the Terikan, Medalam and Limbang rivers
Overnight in an Iban longhouse near Nanga Medamit
Deer Cave bat exodus at dusk in Mulu
gear: Cash for park, guide and boat fees

adventures.title: Sri Lanka Coastal Cycle
adventures.description:
Sri Lanka rewards the touring cyclist like nowhere else in Asia: within 18 days you can roll out of Colombo's chaos, spin through coconut country to the Cultural Triangle, and climb into tea country where the air suddenly smells of eucalyptus. The set pieces land hard - dawn at Sigiriya's rock fortress before the coaches arrive, the sacred city of Anuradhapura explored by bicycle among cycling pilgrims, and the long staircase of hairpins up to Ella and Nuwara Eliya, where plantation roads contour at 1,800 metres past Tamil tea pickers. Finish south at Mirissa, where blue whales feed offshore, or ride north to Jaffna for the peninsula's resurgent Tamil culture and utterly different food.

The monsoon geography is the catch: December to March is dry on the west and south coasts and in the hill country, while the east coast flips seasons entirely, so plan your loop direction around it. Traffic thins dramatically off the A-roads; ride at first light and siesta at noon. About £900 covers guesthouses, rice-and-curry lunches and the odd train leg with the bike in the parcel van. Carry a sarong for temple entries.

adventures.title: Himalayan Bike Descent - Mustang
adventures.description:
Upper Mustang is the closest thing left to old Tibet: a rain-shadow desert kingdom of ochre canyons, cave cities and whitewashed gompas, opened to outsiders only in 1992 and still gated by a US$500 restricted-area permit. Riding it by mountain bike beats walking it. You cover the wind-scoured plateau between Kagbeni and the medieval walled capital of Lo Manthang at a natural pace, then earn the trip's great prize: the long descent following the Kali Gandaki, by some measures the world's deepest gorge, with the 8,000-metre walls of Annapurna and Dhaulagiri framing the valley ahead.

Expect rough jeep track, technical single-track options and altitudes between 2,800 and 4,000 metres that punish the unacclimatised. The valley wind is the daily variable: it builds like clockwork by late morning and blows upvalley all afternoon, so ride at dawn. Because Mustang sits in the rain shadow it rides well even during the June to September monsoon, though spring and autumn are ideal. Ten days from Jomsom with permit, compulsory guide, lodges and bike hire runs about £1,500; fly in via Pokhara and pad the schedule, because Jomsom flights cancel on wind more mornings than not.
highlights: Tibetan cave city ruins 3000 years old

adventures.title: Dogsledding - Svalbard Wilderness
adventures.description:
Nothing about Svalbard is tame: polar bears outnumber people, rifles are legally required outside the settlements, and in March the archipelago is still locked in white - which is exactly when the dogsledding is at its best. You learn to drive your own team of Greenland dogs within an hour, then settle into the rhythm of runners hissing over wind-carved snow as you cross Adventdalen and the glaciated valleys beyond Longyearbyen, covering up to 30 kilometres a day. The silence when the teams stop, broken only by panting dogs and wind, is the thing people try and fail to describe afterwards. Nights are spent in heated wilderness tents or trapper cabins, with a real chance of aurora overhead into early April.

Cold management decides your trip: minus 20 Celsius with wind is normal, so use every layer the operator issues and nurse your camera batteries somewhere warm. No experience is needed, but expect to work - feeding, harnessing and anchoring dogs is half the fun. Six-day expeditions from Longyearbyen run about £2,800 including expedition clothing; fly via Oslo or Tromso, and carry your passport, because Svalbard sits outside the Schengen area.
highlights: Polar night and aurora winter option
gear: Arctic outer clothing provided by the operator
Down sleeping bag rated to minus 30

adventures.title: Cook Islands Sea Kayaking
adventures.description:
Aitutaki's lagoon is a 50-square-kilometre pool of impossible blues, rimmed by motu - uninhabited coral islets - that only shallow-draught boats and paddlers can reach. By sea kayak you set your own itinerary: glide over giant clams and eagle rays in water with 30-metre visibility, beach on Honeymoon Island's sandbar, and picnic at One Foot Island (Tapuaetai), where the famous passport-stamp hut is the only building in sight. Some operators arrange overnight motu camping, and falling asleep with the reef roaring on the outer edge and nothing but hermit crabs for company is as close to a private tropical island as most of us will ever get. Base yourself on Rarotonga first for reef paddles and the cross-island track.

The trade winds are the planning variable: the May to October dry season brings steady 15 to 20 knot south-easterlies, so make crossings in the morning calm and keep to the lagoon's sheltered side after lunch. Cyclone risk runs November to April. Ten days split between Rarotonga and Aitutaki, with inter-island flights, guided lagoon days and kayak hire, comes to about £2,000 excluding long-haul flights. Take reef shoes - the coral rubble is merciless.

adventures.title: Scottish Highland High Route
adventures.description:
This is not a waymarked trail, and that is the point. The Highland High Route is a self-devised 160-kilometre traverse from Aviemore to Torridon that stays high wherever Scotland allows: across the sub-arctic gravel of the Cairngorm plateau, over Creag Meagaidh's cliff-rimmed tableland, through the ancient pines of Glen Affric, along the Five Sisters of Kintail, and finally onto the 750-metre quartzite and sandstone ramparts of Liathach and Beinn Eighe above Torridon. For a fortnight you navigate ridge to ridge by map and compass, sleeping in a mix of wild camps and bothies, and when the cloud is down - it often is - every summit is an act of faith in your bearing.

June to September is the window, but the true adversaries are Scottish: midges that make June to August evenings unbearable without a head net, spate rivers after rain, and multi-day blows that force valley detours, so build in two spare days. Resupply at Fort Augustus or Shiel Bridge; otherwise you carry everything. The whole traverse costs perhaps £600 including trains and food, which may be British adventure's best value - but the navigation and commitment are a full grade beyond any waymarked national trail.
highlights: Cairngorm plateau, Britain's highest arctic ground
Five Sisters of Kintail ridge traverse
Liathach and Beinn Eighe quartzite finish above Torridon
Bothy nights and full off-trail navigation
gear: Midge head net for June to August

adventures.title: Peru Amazon Headwaters Expedition
adventures.description:
The journey into Manu is a descent through every layer of life on Earth. You leave Cusco across 3,500-metre puna, drop into cloud forest where Andean cocks-of-the-rock display at dawn leks, and keep descending until the road ends and the Madre de Dios drainage takes over. From Atalaya, motorised canoes carry you downriver into the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, a forest that records more bird species than the whole of North America. Days settle into river rhythm: macaw clay licks at first light, giant otter families hunting the oxbow lakes, tapir at mineral springs after dark, and always the outside chance of a jaguar stretched along a beached log.

This is expedition travel rather than a lodge holiday: entry to the reserved zone is by licensed operator only, and you sleep in simple platform camps. The dry season, May to September, is the variable that matters - wet-season river levels drown the beaches and clay licks, and the road from Cusco slips. Twelve days runs about £2,000 with permits, boats, guides and full board. Yellow fever vaccination and malaria prophylaxis are essential, binoculars non-negotiable, and there is no phone signal for a week, which turns out to be the best part.
highlights: Oxbow lake caiman and giant otters

adventures.title: Iran Alborz Mountain Ski Touring
adventures.description:
Iran is Asia's most unexpected ski destination: an hour above Tehran's traffic the Alborz wall rises into genuinely big mountains, and the dormant volcano Damavand - at 5,610 metres the highest peak in the Middle East - makes a superb ski-mountaineering objective. Warm up at Dizin and Shemshak, resorts with vintage lifts, empty midweek pistes and a young, welcoming local ski scene, and use the Tochal gondola out of Tehran itself, which rises to about 3,740 metres with a hut for acclimatisation nights. Then Damavand: skinning above 5,000 metres with sulphur drifting from the crater rim and the whole Alborz range below is a summit day to measure all others against.

The season has a subtlety: the resorts run December to April, but Damavand carries dangerous wind-slab in deep winter, and most ski ascents go in April and May once the snowpack consolidates. Altitude, not technique, is what turns parties around, so respect the acclimatisation schedule. A local mountain guide is effectively mandatory on the volcano, and visas need arranging well in advance - check current entry advice for your nationality. Eight days with guide, transport and huts runs about £1,500, remarkable value for 5,000-metre skiing.
highlights: Dizin ski resort Asia best conditions

adventures.title: Trans-Himalayan Winter Ski Tour
adventures.description:
In February the Zanskar and Lahaul ranges are cut off, silent and loaded with cold, dry Himalayan snow - and almost nobody skis them. Expeditions staged from Manali or flown into Leh work peaks and couloirs above 4,000 metres where the line you ski may well be a first descent; the celebrated prize is the Drang-Drung glacier below the Pensi La, a 23-kilometre river of ice beneath Doda Peak offering enormous, remote ski terrain. Days are short, the cold is absolute (minus 25 Celsius nights are routine), and the skiing swings between perfect recycled powder and wind-hammered crust, often on the same run.

This is expedition-grade in the honest sense: avalanche self-sufficiency, crevasse rescue skills and a strong guide team are prerequisites, outside rescue is days away, and the winter road closures mean approaches lean on porters, ponies and pre-placed camps. January to March is the season. Two weeks with an IFMGA-led team and full India logistics runs about £3,000 excluding flights - modest by heli-skiing standards for terrain this wild. The variable that breaks trips is warm storm cycles pushing up from the south, so hold a week of weather margin against any summit ambitions.

adventures.title: Tanzania Zanzibar Spice Tour Cycling
adventures.description:
A bicycle is the perfect speed for Zanzibar. You thread out of Stone Town's coral-stone labyrinth - past carved Omani doors, the old dhow harbour and the night food market at Forodhani Gardens - and within half an hour you are on red-earth lanes under mango and jackfruit, waving back at schoolchildren. The spice farms around Kizimbani explain the island's history better than any museum: crush cloves, cardamom and vanilla between your fingers on the island that once supplied most of the world's cloves. The north road ends at Nungwi, where dhow-builders still shape hulls with hand adzes and the swimming is ludicrously turquoise.

Riding is flat to gently rolling and distances are short, with 30 to 50 kilometre days leaving time to snorkel the Mnemba atoll reefs or walk Jozani forest among endemic red colobus monkeys. Heat and humidity are the real opponents: ride at dawn, rest at noon, and skip the March to May long rains - June to October is dry-season perfection, with December to February a good second window. Dress modestly through villages and carry small notes for fruit stalls. A week with a local guide, guesthouses and bike hire is about £800 excluding flights.
highlights: Clove and vanilla spice farm visits

adventures.title: Yakushima Forest Trek, Japan
adventures.description:
Yakushima receives up to 10,000 millimetres of rain a year in its mountains, and the payoff for staying soaked is the most enchanted forest in Japan: moss a hand-span deep, sika deer stepping through the mist, and yakusugi cedars that were already ancient when Kyoto was founded. The pilgrimage walk follows an old logging tramway up the Anbo valley to Jomon Sugi, a cedar variously dated between 2,000 and 7,200 years old. Go also to the Shiratani Unsuikyo gorge, whose "Mononoke forest" directly inspired Studio Ghibli's Princess Mononoke, and push on up Miyanoura-dake - at 1,936 metres the highest point in the Kyushu region - where the granite summit breaks out of cloud forest into wind-flattened bamboo.

Here rain is not a risk, it is the weather: full waterproofs, spare warm layers and dry bags for everything are the kit list, and the mountain huts are unstaffed shelters, so carry a sleeping bag and food. The trap is timing - the June rainy season and late-summer typhoons can shut trails for days, so aim for March to May or October and November. Four days with ferries from Kagoshima, guesthouse nights and buses runs about £600.

adventures.title: Madagascar Lemur Trek
adventures.description:
Madagascar has been on its own evolutionary path for 88 million years, and you hear it before you see it: at dawn in Andasibe-Mantadia the indri, the largest living lemur, begins a territorial song that swells through the rainforest like whale-song crossed with a siren. Over two weeks you can stack up the island's greatest hits - night walks for mouse lemurs and chameleons, sifakas bounding across open ground, the razor-limestone labyrinth of the Tsingy de Bemaraha in the west (crossed on ladders, cables and swaying bridges), and sunset at the Avenue of the Baobabs near Morondava. More than a hundred lemur species live nowhere else, and neither do most of the reptiles, frogs and even trees you will meet.

Distances are the catch. Roads are slow and internal flights unreliable, so a fortnight honestly covers three or four regions at most, and a driver-guide is the standard, sanity-preserving choice. The dry season from May to October is best, with September and October adding baby lemurs; the Tsingy is only accessible roughly April to November. Around £2,500 for 14 days with driver, park fees and the compulsory local guides, excluding international flights.
highlights: Avenue of the Baobabs iconic trees

adventures.title: Mozambique Island Diving
adventures.description:
Northern Mozambique is the Indian Ocean as it was decades ago. The Quirimbas Archipelago strings thirty-odd islands and sandbanks down a barely dived coast where coral walls drop off the continental shelf and dhows under lateen sails remain the working transport. Base at Pemba or on Ibo Island, a hauntingly faded Portuguese-Swahili trading town, and dive channels swept clean by big tides: turtles, reef sharks, huge groupers and, in season, humpback whales passing offshore. Sailing between islands by dhow and sleeping at sandbank camps is the mode of travel that makes the trip; further south, Ilha de Mocambique's 16th-century Fort Sao Sebastiao anchors a UNESCO-listed island town that deserves two full days.

Logistics demand patience - flights via Pemba or Nampula, boat transfers on tide time, a cash economy - and Cabo Delgado's security situation must be checked against current advice, with itineraries booked through operators holding genuinely current local knowledge. June to October brings dry weather and clear water, with humpbacks roughly July to October; cyclone season runs December to March. Ten days of diving, dhow passages and island lodges is about £2,000 excluding flights, and malaria precautions are essential.
highlights: Quirimbas channel drift dives on untouched reefs
Humpback whales offshore, July to October
Dhow sailing and sandbank camps between atolls
Fort Sao Sebastiao on UNESCO-listed Ilha de Mocambique

adventures.title: Venezuelan Tepui Climbing
adventures.description:
Mount Roraima inspired Conan Doyle's Lost World, and the trek to its 2,810-metre summit plateau still feels like crossing into another geological era. From the Pemon village of Paraitepui you walk for two days across the Gran Sabana's golden grassland, the tepui's 400-metre prow growing until it fills the sky, then climb La Rampa, the single natural ledge that breaches the cliffs. On top lies a black labyrinth of wind-carved rock: valleys floored with quartz crystals, carnivorous sundews and heliamporas, tiny endemic black frogs, and camps in sandy overhangs the guides call hotels. When the mist tears open you look down sheer walls to Kukenan's plume-like waterfall and the savanna a mile below.

A Pemon guide is compulsory (arranged in Santa Elena de Uairen), and the December to March dry season is the sensible window - in the rains the plateau lives inside cloud and the Tek and Kukenan river crossings become dangerous. The summit is cold and permanently wet, so a genuinely waterproof tent and warm layers matter more than the trekking difficulty, which is moderate with one long summit day. Six to eight days from Santa Elena runs about £1,200 all-in, but weigh Venezuela's wider travel situation and current government advice before you book.

adventures.title: Tibetan Kailash Kora
adventures.description:
Mount Kailash has never been climbed: no permit has ever been granted, and for the Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon practitioners who hold the mountain sacred, the summit is not the point. The point is the kora - 52 kilometres around the mountain, walked clockwise from Darchen between 4,600 and 5,630 metres. Day two is both crux and wonder: the slow climb into the prayer-flag storm of the Dolma La at 5,630 metres, moving in a river of pilgrims, some of whom are prostrating the entire circuit body-length by body-length over weeks. The north face, a 1,500-metre pyramid of banded rock and ice, reveals itself above Dirapuk and justifies the journey alone; the turquoise mirror of Lake Manasarovar below completes it.

Access is the hard part. Tibet requires an organised tour with permits arranged weeks ahead, plus a long 4WD approach from Lhasa that usefully forces acclimatisation - even so, the Dolma La flattens the underprepared, and the guesthouses en route are basic. May, June and September are ideal; the Saga Dawa festival is unforgettable but busy. Budget about £3,500 for the full Lhasa to Kailash circuit including permits, guide and transport.

adventures.title: Alaska Range Ski Mountaineering
adventures.description:
The trip begins with the best commute in skiing: a ski-plane out of Talkeetna that threads the granite gates of the Alaska Range and sets you down on the Kahiltna Glacier with three weeks of food and fuel. Base camp life at 2,200 metres runs on the near-24-hour daylight of April and May - you can ski corn at midnight if the freeze is right - and the terrain is effectively endless, from warm-up classics around Control Tower and Kahiltna Dome to serious lines on Mount Frances and the flanks of Hunter and Foraker for teams with the skills. Denali's West Buttress traffic passes through, but ski parties mostly have the side glaciers entirely to themselves.

Two disciplines keep you alive here: crevasse protocol (roped, always, even on tracked glacier) and patience, because flat light and storms can pin camp for days and the plane only returns when Talkeetna Air can see the strip. Everything is expedition logistics - National Park Service registration, waste kits, sleep systems rated to minus 40. Eighteen days with glacier flights, food and shared guiding runs about £5,000 excluding travel to Alaska; the memory of an untracked first descent under midnight alpenglow is permanent.
highlights: Mount Hunter and Foraker ski lines

adventures.title: Iceland Winter Ice Climbing
adventures.description:
Between January and March, Iceland's waterfalls and glacier snouts freeze into one of Europe's most atmospheric ice-climbing venues - and one of the most accessible, with roadside ice barely two hours from Reykjavik. Beginners learn tool placement and crampon footwork on the blue seracs of Solheimajokull on the south coast; the connoisseur's venue is Kaldakinn in the north, where farmland crags stack multi-pitch WI4 and WI5 pillars with the sea glinting at your back. Between routes there are ice caves beneath Vatnajokull's outlet glaciers, black-sand storm beaches, and, on clear nights, the aurora directly above your guesthouse.

The Icelandic winter is the wildcard: freeze-thaw cycles and Atlantic storms build and wreck routes week by week, so climb with local guides who follow conditions and keep the itinerary flexible - chasing the ice is half the sport here. Daylight is short in deep winter, four to seven hours, so early starts are standard and a headtorch is not optional. A week with guiding, technical kit hire, a 4WD and guesthouses runs about £1,400 excluding flights; bring full mountaineering layers and expect wind that redefines the phrase sheltered belay.
highlights: Solheimajokull's blue glacier ice for first swings
Kaldakinn multi-pitch pillars, WI4 to WI5
Ice caves under Vatnajokull's outlet glaciers
Aurora over the ice on clear nights

adventures.title: Gobi Desert Camel Trek
adventures.description:
The Gobi confounds expectations: it is mostly a vast gravel steppe of saxaul scrub and dinosaur bones, which makes its set pieces land even harder. At Khongoryn Els a hundred-kilometre river of sand rises to nearly 300 metres against the Gobi Altai foothills - climb the crest at dusk and, when the wind moves, the whole dune groans like a distant aircraft, the famous singing sands. At Bayanzag's Flaming Cliffs you walk the orange badlands where Roy Chapman Andrews found the first recognised dinosaur eggs in the 1920s, and in the shaded gorge of Yolyn Am, sheets of ice persist into midsummer. Between the set pieces, Bactrian camels carry you at a rocking pace between ger camps where herder families pour salty milk tea.

Riding a camel for days is harder on the body than it looks: pad the saddle and alternate riding with walking. Season is the key decision - May-June and September-October dodge both the 40-degree summer surface heat and spring's brutal winds, and nights are near freezing even then, so pack a proper sleeping bag. Eight days from Dalanzadgad with driver, guide, camels and ger stays runs about £900. Cash only once you leave town, and no phone signal - which is rather the point.

adventures.title: Tonga Humpback Whale Swimming
adventures.description:
Tonga is one of a tiny handful of countries where you may legally swim with humpback whales, and Vava'u's sheltered waters are the heart of it: every July to October, mothers raise newborn calves in water so clear you watch a 15-metre whale materialise out of the blue beneath you. Encounters run at the whales' pace - four swimmers and a licensed guide slip in quietly, and if the mother is settled, a curious calf may spiral up for a look you will replay for the rest of your life. Between swims come the limestone sea caves of the archipelago: Swallows Cave shafted with afternoon light, Mariner's Cave entered by a short free-dive, plus kava evenings and empty island anchorages.

Book a licensed operator months ahead (permits cap boat numbers) and plan at least four whale days, because weather and whale mood vary daily and a single-day punt often misses. You need to be a relaxed snorkeller: scuba on the whales is not permitted, and comfort duck-diving transforms the experience. A week based in Neiafu with five boat days runs about £2,000 excluding flights via Fiji or Auckland. Motion-sickness tablets are the unsung essential.

adventures.title: Costa Rica Jungle to Coast Traverse
adventures.description:
Corcovado protects the largest remaining sweep of Pacific lowland rainforest in Central America, and its wildlife density is frankly unfair: on the traverse from Los Patos ranger station to Sirena you can reasonably hope for all four Costa Rican monkey species, tapir tracks that turn into actual tapirs, scarlet macaws shrieking overhead in pairs and, for the lucky, a puma crossing the trail at dawn. Sirena station itself - reachable only on foot, by boat or by airstrip - sits between river mouths where bull sharks and crocodiles share the estuary, and the final day out to Carate alternates steaming forest with long, empty Pacific beach where you time the headland passes to the tide.

Independent walking is no longer permitted: a licensed guide and station reservations are compulsory, and Sirena's bunks sell out months ahead for the December to April dry season, which is firmly the time to go - wet-season trails are leech-rich mud and some rivers become uncrossable. Carry three to four litres of water, start each leg at first light for wildlife and heat, and lock food away from the raccoons and coatis that raid camp. A week from Puerto Jimenez with guide, permits, meals and station nights runs about £800.
highlights: Jaguar tapir and four monkey species
Pacific beach camp to jungle return
gear: Sealed food storage against raccoons and coatis

adventures.title: Altai Republic Horse Trek, Russia
adventures.description:
The Altai Republic is where Siberia stops being flat forest and becomes a mountain crossroads, its ranges running out towards the glaciated Tavan Bogd massif on the Russia-Mongolia-China tripoint. Horse trekking is how the Altai is meant to be travelled: sure-footed Altaian horses carry you over passes and flowered meadows into the Chulyshman valley, whose kilometre-deep canyon is breached by the Katu-Yaryk pass - a dirt shelf road plunging 800 vertical metres in hairpins that you will be glad to descend on four legs rather than four wheels. The valley floor leads past waterfalls and the ancient burial kurgans of the Pazyryk culture towards Lake Teletskoye, after Baikal the deepest lake in Siberia and sacred to the Altai people.

July and August are the season, and even then mountain nights drop towards freezing and rain fronts sweep through fast, so pack for four seasons. Riding experience helps, but local guides pair novices with patient horses; camps are wild or at summer herders' stations. Twelve days from Gorno-Altaysk with horses, guide and food runs about £1,400 - though check current visa and travel practicalities for Russia carefully before planning.
highlights: Pazyryk burial kurgans of the Ulagan plateau
Altai sacred sites with local guides

adventures.title: Namib Desert Dune Trek
adventures.description:
Set out in the dark from Sesriem gate and you can be climbing Big Daddy's knife-edge crest as the sun hits it: 325 metres of glowing orange dune with the Atlantic fog bank silvering the horizon far to the west. Below lies Deadvlei, a cracked white clay pan studded with camel-thorn trees that died around 900 years ago and never rotted in the desiccated air - you reach it by running down the dune's slip-face in one glorious, thigh-burning minute. The Namib is the world's oldest desert, and guided multi-day treks through the Namib-Naukluft dunes and canyons turn the postcard into a real walking journey: dune crests at first light, camps among oryx and barking geckos, yesterday's tracks read before the wind erases them, and the cool narrows of Sesriem Canyon as a finale.

Heat is the discipline. All serious walking happens before ten and after four, and treks are vehicle-supported because you cannot carry enough water otherwise - drink five litres a day regardless. May to September brings cold, brilliant nights, so pack for near-freezing camps and the southern Milky Way at its most outrageous. A week with a guiding outfit, park fees and camps runs about £1,800 excluding flights to Windhoek.
highlights: Big Daddy dune's 325m crest at dawn
Deadvlei's white pan and 900-year-old dead camel-thorns
Oryx and springbok among the dunes
Southern Milky Way over desert camps

adventures.title: Ladakh Zanskar Valley Trek
adventures.description:
Zanskar is the Indian Himalaya with the volume turned down: a high-desert kingdom of barley fields and cliff-hung monasteries, cut off by snow for more than half the year. The classic traverse walks out of the valley from Padum towards Lamayuru and Leh, roughly 170 kilometres through gorges of folded purple and ochre rock, over a ladder of passes that culminates in the Singi La at around 5,050 metres. Karsha Gompa's whitewashed tiers above Padum and the improbable monastery villages of Lingshed and Photoksar punctuate the days; nights alternate village homestays with meadow camps, and the silence in between is total.

Go from July to September, when the passes are clear while Zanskar's rain-shadow position keeps the monsoon at bay, and acclimatise in Leh first - the altitude and the long 800-to-1,000-metre pass days are what make this trek hard rather than technical ground. Be aware that new roads are eating the old trail stage by stage, so routings adjust every year; a local guide and horseman team keeps you on the walking line and safe at river crossings. Sixteen days from Leh with guide, ponies and homestays runs about £900.
highlights: Remote valley cut off by snow

adventures.title: Silk Road Cycling Uzbekistan
adventures.description:
Cycling the Uzbek Silk Road means earning cities travellers have dreamt about for two millennia. Out of Tashkent you ride steppe and cotton country, cross the Syr Darya, and climb gently towards Samarkand, where the Registan's three madrasas stand in a single square of turquoise tile and gold that no photograph survives contact with - linger for the Shah-i-Zinda necropolis at dusk after the coaches leave. The riding then turns properly remote: the Kyzylkum desert stages towards Bukhara are long, shadeless and punctuated by chaikhanas where you will be fed plov, poured green tea and asked about your entire family. Bukhara's old town, still a functioning medieval city around the Kalyan minaret, is the reward.

Heat rules the calendar: ride in March-April or September-October, never high summer, and carry five litres of water on desert legs. Roads are mostly decent and drivers courteous if curious; modest dress at religious sites and hotel registration slips are the small admin to respect. Uzbekistan is now visa-free or e-visa for most nationalities, and the fast train can cover any stage you need to skip. Two weeks self-supported runs about £700 - Central Asia's best-value grand tour.
highlights: Bukhara old town and the Kalyan minaret
Kyzylkum desert stages between oasis cities
gear: Five litres of water for desert stages
Modest dress for mosques and madrasas
E-visa or visa-free entry for most nationalities

adventures.title: Halong Bay Kayaking, Vietnam
adventures.description:
Ha Long Bay hosts millions of visitors a year, and a sea kayak is the instrument that makes them all disappear. Paddling at dawn from a liveaboard anchored among the bay's 1,969 limestone karsts, you slip through tide-gated tunnels into hidden lagoons - collapsed sinkholes walled by hundred-metre cliffs where the only sounds are dripping rock and the occasional crash of a langur through the greenery. The dark passage of Hang Toi, floating villages where families still farm pearls and fish from stilted platforms, and night squid-fishing off the boat's stern round out a three-day trip that beats any cruise-deck view of the World Heritage seascape.

Timing matters on two axes. First, book a smaller boat with genuine paddling time - many "kayaking" cruises mean forty minutes in a roped-off bay - or base in quieter Lan Ha Bay next door. Second, aim for October to December or March to April: summer brings heat, storms and the odd typhoon, while deep winter can be cold and grey. Tides gate the best tunnels, so a good guide plans the day around them. Three-day liveaboard trips with kayaks run about £350 including transfers from Hanoi.

adventures.title: Flores Island Trek, Indonesia
adventures.description:
Most travellers treat Flores as the springboard for Komodo; stay and walk it instead. From the highland town of Bajawa, trails thread between perfect volcanic cones through Ngada villages such as Bena, where megalithic altars and high-gabled ancestor houses stand as they have for centuries and hot springs steam in the river below. Eastwards, the dawn ritual at Kelimutu repays every alarm-clock complaint: three crater lakes in one summit caldera, each a different colour - turquoise, rust, ink - and each liable to change shade from one year to the next as the volcano's chemistry shifts. Descend through rice terraces to the coast, then finish west at Labuan Bajo for Komodo dragons on Rinca and manta rays over the reefs.

The Trans-Flores Highway is slow, winding and spectacular, so budget full days for what look like short hops or hire a car and driver between trekking stages. April to September is the dry season and the time to come; the rains wash out village paths and drown Kelimutu's dawn in cloud. Eight days with local guides, homestays and a Komodo boat day runs about £700 excluding flights into Ende or Labuan Bajo. Carry small notes for village donations and dress modestly in Ngada country.

adventures.title: Scottish Islands Sailing Voyage
adventures.description:
Sailing out of Oban drops you into a cruising ground that stands comparison with anywhere on Earth when the weather plays along: the Sound of Mull opens into a maze of islands, sea lochs and tide gates where you plan each day around the tidal atlas rather than a road map. A ten-day loop might pass Duart Castle to Tobermory's painted seafront, round the wild Ardnamurchan lighthouse - the most westerly point of the British mainland - and anchor off the Small Isles of Rum, Eigg, Muck and Canna beneath the jagged skyline of the Skye Cuillin, with minke whales, porpoises and white-tailed eagles as regular escorts. Runs ashore mean hill walks straight from the anchorage and single-malt pilgrimages, from Tobermory's distillery to a southward detour for Islay.

This is proper pilotage water: the races off Ardnamurchan and through the sounds demand real seamanship, so charter bareboat only with solid RYA miles, or take a skippered berth and learn as you go. May and June bring the driest, brightest sailing and endless daylight; midges own the anchorages ashore from July. A skippered shared-boat week-plus works out around £2,000 per person with food and moorings. Pack full offshore waterproofs whatever the forecast promises.
highlights: Rum Eigg Muck Coll remote islands
Isle of Skye Cuillin ridge backdrop
gear: Anchor and chain for remote bays

adventures.title: Orinoco Delta Dugout Canoe
adventures.description:
The Orinoco spends itself into the Atlantic through a 22,000-square-kilometre maze of channels, and the Warao - "the boat people" - have lived above its water for thousands of years in palafito stilt villages laced together by dugout canoes. Travelling out of Tucupita with Warao boatmen, you move at the delta's pace: paddles dipping through flooded igapo forest, scarlet ibis flighting to roost in their hundreds at dusk, pink river dolphins rolling in the main channels, and nights in hammocks under thatch with the frog chorus at full volume. Fishing for piranha, tasting moriche palm starch and watching the delta's celebrated basket-weavers at work opens a genuine, unstaged window onto a pre-industrial river culture.

The dry season, roughly January to April, concentrates wildlife along the channels and keeps the mosquitoes merely persistent rather than biblical. Either way, permethrin-treated clothing, a hammock net and serious repellent are the kit that matters, with malaria prophylaxis on medical advice. Trips run three to five days from Tucupita with boat, guide and full board at about £500 all-in - but conditions in Venezuela change, so book through operators with current local knowledge and check travel advice first.
highlights: Sunset egret and scarlet ibis flocks

adventures.title: Austrian Alps Hochkonig Circuit
adventures.description:
The Hochkönig circuit is Alpine trekking with the difficulty dialled to pleasure: four days looping Salzburg's great limestone massif from Maria Alm and the Arthurhaus, across karst plateaus and pastures where cattle still summer, with the Dachstein glacier and the Berchtesgaden peaks stacked across the valley. The crux and the highlight is the ascent to the Matrashaus, the hut perched improbably on the 2,941-metre summit itself - the last hours cross the bare stone sea of the Ubergossene Alm plateau, and sunset from the hut door, with pink light on limestone in every direction, is the image you take home. Descent days deliver the Austrian hut trinity: Kaspressknodel, Kaiserschmarrn and a terrace beer.

Paths are well marked, but the summit day is long, exposed to weather and holds snowfields into July, so an early start and a stable forecast matter. Book bunks well ahead for July and August, the Matrashaus especially; late June and September are quieter. Four days including hut half-board and travel from Salzburg runs about £400 to £700, some of the best value-for-scenery trekking in the Eastern Alps. Bring cash - the huts do not take cards - and a sheet sleeping-bag liner.

adventures.title: Papua New Guinea Sepik River Journey
adventures.description:
The Sepik is one of the world's great art rivers. Along its middle reaches, Iatmul and neighbouring villages raise haus tambaran - spirit houses - whose carved posts, orator's stools and masks stand in the ancestry of half the tribal art in Western museums. Travelling by motorised canoe out of Pagwi or Wewak, you sleep in villages such as Tambunum and Kanganaman, meet crocodile-clan men whose backs carry the raised scars of crocodile-spirit initiation, and buy carvings directly from the artists in the shade of the houses where they were made. The river sets the rhythm: glassy dawn water, children paddling to school, sago processing on the banks, fireflies after dark.

There is no infrastructure here in any conventional sense - no roads, no power, kina cash only - and everything runs through your boatman-guide, so travel with an operator holding genuine village relationships; it is the difference between welcome and intrusion. May to October's drier months keep the river navigable and the mosquitoes survivable, and malaria prophylaxis, strong repellent and a treated net are non-negotiable. Ten days including Wewak flights, boat, fuel and village stays runs about £2,000. Carvings are heavy: arrange freight before you fall for a two-metre crocodile prow.
highlights: Iatmul spirit houses at Tambunum and Kanganaman
Crocodile-scar initiation culture of the middle Sepik
Buying masks directly from the carvers

adventures.title: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta Ascent
adventures.description:
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is the world's most dramatic coastal range: from Caribbean beaches its forested ridges rise to the twin summits of Pico Cristobal Colon and Pico Simon Bolivar, around 5,700 metres, in barely 45 kilometres - the greatest sea-to-summit relief on Earth. It is also sacred ground. The Arhuaco, Kogi, Wiwa and Kankuamo peoples regard the massif as the heart of the world, and access to the high peaks is theirs to grant; since the mid-2010s summit permission has in practice been closed, and any legitimate expedition depends entirely on consent arranged months ahead through community authorities. Parties that climbed in earlier years passed from jungle through cloud forest into frailejon paramo and glacier remnants with the sea glittering below - one of mountaineering's most singular panoramas.

Treat this as an aspiration that opens rarely, if at all, and never attempt an unofficial ascent - it does real harm and gets future doors closed. The accessible alternative is superb: the four-to-five-day Ciudad Perdida trek crosses the massif's northern foothills to a 1,200-year-old Tairona city, best in the drier December to February window. A full expedition, were permission granted, would run about £2,500; the Lost City trek costs nearer £400 from Santa Marta.
highlights: Fastest sea to summit elevation gain Earth

adventures.title: Baja California Whale Watching Kayak
adventures.description:
Every winter, grey whales complete one of the longest mammal migrations on Earth - Arctic feeding grounds to Baja California's Pacific lagoons - to calve in the warm, protected water of San Ignacio and Magdalena Bay. What happens next has no parallel anywhere: "friendly" whales approach the small pangas by choice, mothers pushing month-old calves up to the gunwales to be touched. No feeding, no baiting; the behaviour began with a single curious whale in the 1970s and her descendants continue it. Days alternate panga sessions inside the strictly regulated whale zones with sea kayaking the mangrove shorelines for pelicans, dolphins and coyotes patrolling the tideline; nights are desert camps where whale blows carry across the water in the dark.

January to March is the season, with mid-February to mid-March the peak for mothers and calves. The lagoon camps are remote - fly to Loreto or drive the long desert road via Guerrero Negro - and visitor numbers inside the El Vizcaino Biosphere Reserve are capped, so book licensed operators months out. Mornings on the water are surprisingly cold, so take windproof layers. A week with camps, pangas, kayaks and meals runs about £900 before flights.
gear: Warm layers for cool lagoon mornings

adventures.title: South Georgia Island Expedition
adventures.description:
Nothing prepares you for St Andrews Bay: a two-kilometre sweep of black sand and glacier outwash occupied by a king penguin colony well over a hundred thousand pairs strong - a sound, a smell and a sheer mass of life that silences even seasoned wildlife hands. South Georgia stacks such scenes shore after shore: beachmaster elephant seals warring at Gold Harbour, fur seal nurseries at Salisbury Plain, wandering albatrosses - the largest flying birds on Earth - brooding on Prion Island, and at Grytviken the rusting whaling station and Shackleton's grave, where tradition pours a toast to "the Boss". The island is reached only by sea, on expedition ships usually pairing it with the Falklands and Antarctic Peninsula, across 800 miles of Southern Ocean.

Weather is the governing variable: katabatic gusts can cancel a landing in minutes, so itineraries are written in pencil and the expedition team calls each bay on the day. November and December bring peak elephant-seal drama and courting albatross; January and February add armies of brown, woolly king chicks. Biosecurity is drilled seriously - every velcro strap vacuumed before you land. Fifteen-to-twenty-day voyages start around £10,000 per person: brutal on the wallet, unmatched on Earth.
highlights: 300000 king penguin colony St Andrews Bay

adventures.title: Ethiopian Omo Valley Tribal Journey
adventures.description:
The lower Omo Valley concentrates more distinct living cultures than almost anywhere on Earth: Mursi, Hamar, Karo, Dassanech, Arbore and more, each with its own language, dress and ceremony along a river that has sustained them for millennia. Travel is by 4WD out of Arba Minch or Jinka with local guides, and the encounters are the journey - a Hamar bull-jumping initiation with its whipcracks, bells and a young man running the backs of cattle into adulthood; the Karo painting themselves in chalk above a great bend of the Omo; the Key Afer weekly market where the valley's peoples trade goats, honey and gossip. Done well, with community guides and unhurried village time, it is among the most powerful cultural journeys travel can offer.

Done badly it becomes a zoo of camera fees thrust through car windows, so choose operators committed to long stays and fair, agreed payment - and always ask before photographing, carrying small birr notes for the per-photo fees that are the local norm. The dry months, roughly September to February, keep the dirt roads passable. Ten days with 4WD, driver, local guides and simple lodges or camps runs about £1,500 excluding flights to Addis Ababa; check current regional travel advice when planning.

adventures.title: Pamir Highway Cycling
adventures.description:
The M41 Pamir Highway is the cyclists' rite of passage. From Osh's Silk Road bazaar you climb onto a 4,000-metre plateau where yaks graze against snow peaks, cresting the route's high point at the Ak-Baital pass (4,655m) before the strange deep blue of Karakul lake. Then comes the stretch riders talk about for the rest of their lives: days along the Panj river gorge with Afghanistan a stone's throw across the water, villages and donkey paths mirroring your road on the far bank. The Wakhan Valley detour beneath the white wall of the Hindu Kush adds hot springs, ruined forts and homestays where dinner is whatever the garden grew.

Altitude and washboard do the damage: acclimatise in Osh or Murghab, gear low, and expect 60 to 80 kilometre days to feel heroic. June to September is the window - outside it the plateau is genuinely arctic - and you need the GBAO permit alongside your Tajik e-visa, plus enough cash for the whole route, because working ATMs between Osh and Khorog are near-mythical. Homestays at a few pounds a night keep 18 days to roughly £1,200 with food and permits. A water filter, four-season sleeping bag and spare spokes are the kit that earns its weight.

adventures.title: Yukon River Canoe Expedition
adventures.description:
Paddling the Yukon from Whitehorse to Dawson City is 715 kilometres of moving meditation through the landscape of the Klondike Gold Rush - the same water thirty thousand stampeders floated in 1898. The river does much of the work, sliding along at eight to ten kilometres an hour, which leaves your attention free for what matters: moose hock-deep in the sloughs, black bears on gravel bars, bald eagles in every third cottonwood. Lake Laberge's fifty windbound kilometres open the trip; Fort Selkirk, a Northern Tutchone settlement and trading post abandoned in the 1950s and beautifully preserved, is its historical heart; Five Finger Rapids provides the one genuine pulse-raiser - take the right-hand channel, as the sternwheelers did.

June and July give near-24-hour daylight and the fiercest mosquitoes (bring a head net and mean it); August brings dark enough nights for aurora and the first autumn gold. The river is remote but forgiving for competent canoe campers, with wind on Laberge, bear-camp discipline and cold water the real risks. Canoe hire from Whitehorse outfitters, the shuttle back from Dawson, food and camp kit for 16 to 18 days runs about £1,200.

adventures.title: Jordan Desert to Dead Sea Cycling
adventures.description:
The King's Highway is three thousand years of history laid onto tarmac, and by bicycle you feel every metre of its geography. From Madaba's Byzantine mosaic map the road rolls south across a sequence of colossal wadis, none more dramatic than Wadi Mujib - Jordan's Grand Canyon - where you lose and regain a vertical kilometre in one sweltering afternoon. Crusader castles at Kerak and Shobak break up the climbing; then comes Petra, where you walk the bike-free Siq at dawn as the Treasury ignites in reflected pink light. The route's coda drops through Wadi Rum's red sandstone desert for a night at a Bedouin camp under a preposterous sky, before the final surreal freewheel to the Dead Sea at 430 metres below sea level - the lowest road finish on Earth.

Spring (March-April) and autumn (October-November) dodge both the heat and the winter squalls; even then carry four-plus litres and start the big climbs at first light. Traffic is light on the King's Highway itself, though Jordanian drivers are enthusiastic - a mirror helps. Buy the Jordan Pass before arrival to bundle the visa with Petra entry. Ten days with guesthouses, the Wadi Rum camp and food runs about £900 excluding flights to Amman.
highlights: Dead Sea minus 430m sea level finish

adventures.title: Papua Indonesia Bird of Paradise Quest
adventures.description:
New Guinea's western half holds the greatest concentration of birds-of-paradise on Earth, and seeing them means joining a tradition that runs straight back to Alfred Russel Wallace. The itinerary splits between two worlds. On Waigeo in Raja Ampat you sit in a palm-frond hide before first light for Wilson's bird-of-paradise - a bird so improbably coloured, scarlet back, turquoise skullcap, spiralled tail wires, that it looks designed by committee - and for red birds-of-paradise dancing in the canopy. Then the Arfak Mountains above Manokwari, where homestay lodges run by Hatam families put you beside the bower of the Vogelkop bowerbird, architect of the most elaborate structure any animal builds, and the dawn display courts of parotias and magnificent birds-of-paradise. Cenderawasih Bay adds the world's most reliable whale shark snorkelling at the fishing platforms near Nabire.

This is patient, pre-dawn, guide-dependent travel: hides are booked through village landowners and every fee helps keep forest standing. March to May and September to November are driest, and internal flights via Sorong and Manokwari need slack for delays. Twelve days with local guides, homestays, permits and boats runs about £2,500 excluding international flights. Bring a long lens and leech socks.
highlights: Wilson's bird-of-paradise at a dawn hide on Waigeo
Vogelkop bowerbird's decorated bower in the Arfaks
Whale shark snorkelling in Cenderawasih Bay
Alfred Russel Wallace's historic collecting grounds

adventures.title: Kamchatka Volcano Trek
adventures.description:
Kamchatka is what the planet looks like while still under construction: a peninsula of some 300 volcanoes, 29 of them active, where you trek across lava fields that steamed into existence within living memory. Treks from Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky circle the accessible giants - Avachinsky's cone, Gorely's chain of craters, Mutnovsky's ice-choked fumarole gorge - while helicopter days reach the Valley of Geysers and the Uzon caldera, and the ambitious eye Klyuchevskaya Sopka, Eurasia's highest active volcano at around 4,750 metres and in eruption more often than not. The nightly ritual is a soak in a thermal river while an ash plume catches the sunset. Brown bears are everywhere - Kamchatka holds one of the densest populations on Earth - hence the armed escort that accompanies every group.

July and August are the only reliable trekking months, and even then you get four seasons daily, with itineraries rewritten around eruptions and fog: the helicopters fly perhaps two days in three. Costs are dominated by those helicopters - a 14-day trek-based expedition runs about £4,000, more with multiple Valley of Geysers flights. Russia's visa and access logistics have grown far more complicated in recent years, so verify the current situation with a specialist operator before paying deposits.

adventures.title: Seychelles Island Kayaking
adventures.description:
The granite inner Seychelles are made for paddling: short crossings, sheltered leeward coasts, and shorelines where 750-million-year-old boulders slump into water the colour of bottled light. Basing on Praslin and La Digue, you kayak beneath the sculpted granite of Anse Source d'Argent - arguably the world's most photographed beach, and best seen from the seaward side at sunrise before the day-trippers arrive - circle the islet of St Pierre over coral gardens, and land on Curieuse to walk among free-roaming giant Aldabra tortoises. Praslin's Vallee de Mai adds a UNESCO-listed palm forest where the coco de mer grows its infamous double nut, and a boat day to Cousin Island delivers the once-nearly-extinct Seychelles warbler and nesting seabirds at arm's length.

Paddle the calm windows between the trade-wind seasons - April-May and October-November - when the sea glasses off and visibility peaks; the June to September south-easterlies demand more respect on crossings. Guided kayak days, inter-island ferries and self-catering guesthouses (the affordable Seychelles most visitors never find) bring ten days to about £3,000 excluding international flights. Reef-safe sunscreen and a bow line for granite beach landings are the two bits of kit everyone forgets.
highlights: Anse Source d'Argent's granite boulders from the water
Giant Aldabra tortoises on Curieuse Island
Vallee de Mai coco de mer palm forest, Praslin
Seychelles warbler and seabirds on Cousin Island

adventures.title: Snowdonia Mountain Running
adventures.description:
Eryri (Snowdonia) packs Britain's most exhilarating mountain-running terrain into a startlingly small compass. The centrepiece is the Snowdon Horseshoe: roughly 12 kilometres taking in Crib Goch's genuinely exposed knife-edge - hands-on rock with 300-metre drops on both sides - over Garnedd Ugain to the summit of Yr Wyddfa and back along the quieter cliffs of Y Lliwedd. Running it early on a still morning, with cloud pouring off the arete and Glaslyn's cirque below, is as close to alpinism as a pair of trainers gets. Build a three-day hit list around it: the Glyderau's shattered rockscape via Cwm Idwal one day, and for the strong, the Welsh 3000s - all fifteen summits over 3,000 feet in roughly 48 kilometres and 4,000 metres of climbing in a single push.

Welsh weather is the examiner. Rock that is joyful when dry becomes treacherous in wind and rain, and Crib Goch in a gale is a mountaineering problem rather than a run, so check forecasts obsessively and keep valley alternatives ready. May to September gives the best odds. Base in Llanberis, carry map, compass, windproof and an emergency bivvy even on short rounds, and budget about £300 for three days of bunkhouse, food and trains - world-class mountains at youth-hostel prices.

adventures.title: Atacama Desert Stargazing Trek
adventures.description:
The Atacama is a high-desert double bill: by day you trek some of the most otherworldly terrain on the planet, and by night you stand under what astronomers measure as the clearest sky on Earth. From San Pedro de Atacama the classics stack up - ridge walks above the salt-crusted amphitheatres of the Valle de la Luna at sunset, the 4,320-metre dawn pilgrimage to El Tatio, where dozens of geysers steam hardest in the freezing first hour of light, flamingo lagoons on the Salar de Atacama, and altiplano lakes ringed by 6,000-metre volcanoes. Then the night shift: dedicated astro-tours with serious telescopes are superb, and at weekends the ALMA observatory, the world's great millimetre-wave array, opens its base facility to pre-booked visitors.

Altitude is the quiet hazard. San Pedro sits at 2,400 metres but day trips repeatedly punch above 4,000, so sequence the itinerary low-to-high and drink relentlessly. June to September brings the crispest skies with brutally cold dawns - minus ten at El Tatio - while the January-February altiplanic winter can bring storms; and check the moon calendar, because a full moon erases the Milky Way you came for. Seven days with tours, park fees and guesthouses runs about £800 excluding flights to Calama.
highlights: The clearest night skies on Earth
El Tatio geysers at 4,320m at dawn
Valle de la Luna ridge walk at sunset
Flamingo lagoons on the Salar de Atacama

adventures.title: Chilkoot Pass Historic Trail
adventures.description:
Thirty thousand stampeders hauled a tonne of supplies apiece over this pass in the winter of 1897-98, and walking the Chilkoot today still feels like moving through their story. From the Dyea trailhead near Skagway you climb through coastal rainforest to Sheep Camp, then tackle the Golden Staircase -- a lung-busting boulder field where the gold-rush chains of climbers once inched upward -- to cross into Canada at the 1,067-metre summit. Rusting boilers, sled runners and boot leather from 1898 lie exactly where exhausted miners dropped them; the whole trail is a protected archaeological site, so touch nothing.

The pass is the crux and the weather gamble: fog, rain and snow can shut it even in July, and the scramble is brutal with a full pack. Parks Canada caps crossings at 50 hikers a day, so book permits months ahead for peak season. Most parties take three days to Bennett Lake, then ride the White Pass & Yukon Route railway out -- book that too. Bear canisters are mandatory, and carry your passport: you clear customs on a mountaintop.
highlights: USA Canada border crossing on foot
Lake Bennett historic railway end point

adventures.title: Komodo Island Dragon Trek
adventures.description: Komodo Island in the Indonesian archipelago is home to the world's largest lizard, the Komodo dragon, which reaches 3 metres in length and hunts deer, pigs, and occasionally humans using venom-laced saliva. Trekking the island's three routes with a park ranger allows close encounters with these prehistoric predators in their natural habitat. The surrounding Komodo National Park waters contain some of the most biodiverse coral reefs in the world, with manta ray cleaning stations at Manta Point.

adventures.title: Patagonia Dientes Circuit, Chile
adventures.description: The Dientes de Navarino circuit on Navarino Island in Chilean Patagonia is the southernmost trekking circuit in the world, circling the jagged black peaks of the Dientes range with views over the Beagle Channel to Tierra del Fuego. The five-day route has no maintained infrastructure and requires cross-country navigation through peat bogs, lenga beech forest, and granite boulder fields. Wind speeds of 100 kilometres per hour are routine and the weather changes in minutes.
highlights: Beagle Channel views to Tierra del Fuego

adventures.title: Socotra Island Walk, Yemen
adventures.description:
Socotra has been adrift in the Arabian Sea for six million years, and roughly a third of its plants exist nowhere else. Trekking the Diksam Plateau you camp beneath dragon's blood trees -- umbrella-crowned, crimson-sapped, found only here -- then drop into the sheer Wadi Dirhur canyon and finish on the blinding dunes at Detwah Lagoon near Qalansiyah. Bedouin drivers and goat-track guides run the logistics; nights are wild camps under some of the darkest skies you will ever see.

Access is the crux: effectively one weekly charter flight from Abu Dhabi, booked through a licensed Socotri operator who also arranges the Yemeni visa -- count on 1,400-2,500 pounds for ten days excluding the flight. Go between October and April; the June-September monsoon brings winds that historically cut the island off entirely. Mainland Yemen's war has largely spared Socotra, but check FCDO advice, carry cash (there are no ATMs) and expect basic everything -- that is the price of the most alien landscape on Earth.
highlights: Dragon Blood Tree endemic alien landscape

adventures.title: Romania Transylvanian Alps Trek
adventures.description:
The Fagaras ridge is the roof of Romania: a 70-kilometre crystalline crest that rarely drops below 2,000 metres, crossing Moldoveanu at 2,544 metres -- the country's highest point -- and a chain of glacial cirques cradling lakes like Balea and Capra. You walk for days with the Transylvanian plain far below on one side and the Southern Carpathians rolling away on the other, sharing the range with Europe's largest brown bear population outside Russia, plus chamois on the crags and the occasional lynx track in late snow.

The catch is the weather: afternoon thunderstorms build fast in July and August and the ridge offers few escape routes between passes, so start each stage at dawn. Shelter is a mix of basic refuges and wild camping -- carry a tent and treat old map markings with suspicion. Access is easy by Romanian standards: bus from Sibiu, or the spectacular Transfagarasan road to Balea Lake. Around 500 pounds covers the week including transfers and huts; finish with the Brukenthal museum in Sibiu.

adventures.title: Colombia Coffee Region Cycling
adventures.description:
Colombia's Eje Cafetero -- the UNESCO-listed Coffee Cultural Landscape across Quindio, Risaralda and Caldas -- is cycling country of a very particular kind: every road either climbs or plunges through a patchwork of coffee, plantain and bamboo on the flanks of the Cordillera Central. Riding finca to finca on rough byroads, you sleep in working farmhouses, learn cupping from growers whose families have farmed the same slopes for generations, and freewheel into Salento or Filandia for trout and colour-drenched colonial balconies. The detour into the Valle de Cocora, where 60-metre wax palms stand in drifting cloud, is unmissable.

Do not underestimate the gradients: this is eight days of 10-15 per cent ramps between 1,200 and 2,400 metres, and afternoon downpours arrive most days around three -- ride mornings. A gravel or mountain bike is the right tool. October-November brings the main harvest if you want to pick; December-February and July are the drier riding windows. Around 600 pounds covers finca stays and food, and Willys jeep transfers rescue tired legs.
highlights: Valle de Cocora wax palms 60m tall

adventures.title: Tierra del Fuego Ski Touring
adventures.description:
Ushuaia calls itself the End of the World, and ski touring here feels like it: from the summits of the Martial range you look straight down onto the Beagle Channel, with the islands toward Cape Horn scattered beyond. The touring is short-approach and serious -- couloirs and treeless faces dropping toward salt water, lenga forest glades lower down, and almost nobody on any of it. Cerro Castor, the world's southernmost ski resort, makes a civilised warm-up and a bad-weather fallback with reliably cold, dry snow.

June to August is midwinter: at 55 degrees south the days shrink to about seven hours around the solstice, so tours are planned tight and headtorches carried always. The maritime snowpack changes by the hour, avalanche information is thin and rescue is a long way off -- hire a local UIAGM guide.
