Kigali is under three hours away by road, so a week is unhurried. Expect £3,000–4,000 all-in with one gorilla trek, good lodges and transfers. Gardening gloves and waterproof gaiters are the two items everyone wishes they had packed.

adventures.title: Lofoten Islands Cycling
adventures.description:
The Lofoten archipelago throws granite walls straight out of the Norwegian Sea, and the E10 threads them by bridge and causeway for 130 kilometres from Fiskebøl to the road's end at Å. On a bike you get the full drama: the cliff gate of Trollfjord by side-trip boat, the cod-drying racks of Henningsvær, and the postcard climax where Reine and Hamnøy's red rorbuer huddle beneath the spire of Olstind. Distances are short but never flat for long, and the Atlantic wind is the real gradient — a headwind day on the exposed causeways can halve your speed.

Ride between June and August and the midnight sun removes all time pressure: locals cycle at 11pm in golden light, and Unstad's surf beach or the white sand at Ramberg fill the small hours. Wild camping is legal under Norway's allemannsretten, which rescues the budget — Lofoten hotels are brutal. Waterproof panniers are essential; squalls arrive off the sea with ten minutes' notice.

Reach the islands via Svolvær by air or the ferry from Bodø. A week costs around £1,400 with campsites and one or two rorbu nights; the Borg Viking longhouse museum and stockfish soup in Å are compulsory culture stops.
highlights: Hamnoy red fishing village iconic view

adventures.title: Egypt Sinai Desert Camel Trek
adventures.description:
The high Sinai around St Catherine is Bedouin country, and a week's camel-supported trek with Jebeleya guides moves at the desert's own pace: walking the cool hours, brewing sweet tea in wadi shade at noon, and sleeping in the open under a starfield with zero light pollution. The route weaves between granite massifs to climax on Mount Sinai at 2,285 metres, climbed in darkness to reach the summit chapel for sunrise — the 3,750 Steps of Repentance are steeper but far quieter than the camel path.

At the mountain's foot, St Catherine's Monastery has been continuously inhabited since the sixth century; its icon collection and the Burning Bush enclosure justify a full afternoon. The catch is the temperature swing: days stay warm even in winter, but high-desert nights drop towards freezing and almost everyone under-packs insulation. October–November and February–April are ideal; midsummer is punishing.

Access is via Sharm el Sheikh with a road transfer to St Catherine village. Trekking here is remarkably good value — Bedouin cooperatives run all-inclusive camel treks for £70–100 a day, so £800 covers the week. Check current government travel advice for South Sinai before booking; the St Catherine area sits well away from the northern no-go zones, but it deserves a look.

adventures.title: Xinjiang Tian Shan Mountain Cycling
adventures.description:
The Tian Shan — the Mountains of Heaven — wall the northern edge of the Taklamakan for 2,500 kilometres, and Xinjiang's roads across them are among the great high-mountain rides in Asia. The centrepiece is the Duku Highway from Dushanzi to Kuqa: 560 kilometres over four passes above 3,000 metres, dropping from spruce forest and Kazakh yurt pastures near Nalati through red-rock gorges to the desert's oasis rim. Sayram Lake, an alpine sea at 2,070 metres ringed by snow peaks, makes the classic warm-up loop.

Logistics, not gradients, are the crux. The Duku Highway opens roughly June to September and closes on snow without notice; police checkpoints are frequent, passports must be carried at all times, and some sections need permits arranged through a local agency. Accommodation between towns is yurts or camping, so carry a stove and cold-weather kit even in July — the passes can see August snow.

Bookend the ride with culture: Turpan's Flaming Mountains and karez irrigation channels at one end, Kashgar's Sunday livestock market at the other, linked by train. A supported week on the Duku with agency permits and transfers runs around £2,400 land cost.
highlights: Turpan Flaming Mountains and karez wells

adventures.title: Svalbard Polar Expedition Hiking
adventures.description:
At 78 degrees north, Svalbard is the most accessible piece of the High Arctic on Earth — three flights from London and you are in Longyearbyen with glaciers pouring off every skyline. It is also one of the few places where you are legally required to be prepared for polar bears: outside the settlement, every group must carry a rifle and flare gun, which is why almost everyone travels with guided expeditions. A summer week combines glacier travel on Longyearbreen and Larsbreen, the ridge summit of Trollsteinen, and boat-supported days to walrus haul-outs and the calving front of Nordenskiöldbreen in Billefjorden.

Under the midnight sun from late April to late August there is no schedule but weather; hiking at 2am in gold light is normal. The terrain is raw moraine, scree and braided rivers — nothing is waymarked, crevasse work is managed by the guides, and the cold maritime wind never quite stops.

Expect £4,000–5,000 for a guided week including Longyearbyen accommodation; independent trekking is possible only with rifle hire, insurance and route notification to the Governor's office. June and July bring flowers, bird cliffs at full volume and open water; late August adds enough darkness for a first aurora.
highlights: Armed-guide trekking in polar bear country

adventures.title: Sikkim Kangchenjunga Circuit
adventures.description:
Kangchenjunga, the world's third-highest mountain, straddles the Sikkim–Nepal border, and the Goecha La trek is India's closest legal approach: eight to ten walking days from the roadhead at Yuksom through the Khangchendzonga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The trail climbs through orchid and rhododendron forest — in full crimson bloom through April — to the yak pastures of Dzongri, where a pre-dawn scramble to Dzongri Top delivers the first full sweep of the massif: Kabru, Pandim and Kangchenjunga's summit pyramid burning orange.

The push to Goecha La itself, at about 4,940 metres, starts at 3am from Lamuney, passing the glacial mirror of Samiti Lake to the viewpoint over the Talung face. Altitude is the catch — the itinerary gains height quickly after Dzongri, and the acclimatisation day there is not optional.

Sikkim wraps the walk in bureaucracy done properly: foreigners need an Inner Line Permit plus trekking permits arranged through a registered agency in Gangtok, walking with a guide while yaks and dzos carry loads. An 18-day trip including Pelling's Pemayangtse monastery or Darjeeling either side runs about £2,600 land cost. March–May and October–November are the windows; the monsoon drowns the trail in cloud and leeches.
highlights: Dzongri Top dawn panorama of Kabru and Pandim
Rhododendron forest in full April bloom
Inner Line Permit trek from Yuksom
gear: Down jacket prayer flags col crossings

adventures.title: New Zealand Te Araroa Thru-Hike
adventures.description:
Te Araroa runs 3,000 kilometres from Cape Reinga's lighthouse to Bluff — the full length of New Zealand and one of the world's youngest great thru-hikes. The North Island alternates beach (90 Mile Beach on day one), farmland, Auckland suburbia and the volcanic heart of the Tongariro Alpine Crossing; it also does something no other major trail does — the route becomes the Whanganui River for 87 kilometres, paddled by canoe. The South Island is the payoff: the Richmond Ranges, Waiau Pass and Southland's tussock tops, with unbridged river crossings that are the trail's genuine hazard. People wait out rain for days, and should.

Most hikers walk southbound, starting October to December and finishing around March; 100 to 130 days is typical, resupplying every four to eight days. Backcountry huts on a hut pass mix with camping, and the sandflies south of Nelson become a psychological event of their own.

Budget realistically: NZ$8,000–10,000 (£3,500–5,000) covers the walk with hut passes, the canoe section and town zeroes. You do not need to be an athlete to start — but you need river judgement, and the humility to sit still in a country where the weather changes four times a day.
highlights: Bluff to Cape Reinga full island spine
gear: Sand fly repellent South Island essential
Dry bags for Whanganui canoe stage

adventures.title: South Africa Cape Point Cycling
adventures.description: Cycle the Cape Peninsula from Cape Town to Cape Point — 65 km of rolling coastal road past the Cape of Good Hope, Boulders Beach penguin colony, Hout Bay fishing harbour, and Constantia wine farms on the reverse route. The Cape Point climb to the lighthouse on a dirt track is a classic; the descent on the west coast back toward Cape Town is fast and exposed to Atlantic headwinds. The Cape Argus Cycle Tour in March is one of the world's largest individually timed cycle races; the route is available for recreational riders throughout the year.
highlights: Chapman's Peak cliff drive Atlantic views
Cape of Good Hope Africa southernmost feel
Boulders Beach penguin colony cycling past
gear: Water Cape Peninsula no shade stretches
Lock security Cape Town urban sections

adventures.title: Borneo Mulu Caves Expedition
adventures.description:
Gunung Mulu National Park wears its superlatives lightly: beneath the rainforest lies the Sarawak Chamber, the world's largest known cave chamber, the vast corridor of Deer Cave, and hundreds of kilometres of surveyed passage still growing every expedition season. The accessible show is extraordinary enough — at dusk, two to three million wrinkle-lipped bats spiral out of Deer Cave in smoke-like ribbons, one of Borneo's great wildlife spectacles — while guided adventure-caving routes through Racer and Clearwater caves run from beginner wades to full expedition trips.

Above ground, the Pinnacles are the test: a three-day return climb to a viewpoint amid 45-metre blades of silver karst on Gunung Api's flank. The final morning gains 1,200 metres in 2.4 kilometres, the last stretch on ladders and fixed ropes — brutally humid, with park-enforced turnaround times. The five-day Headhunters' Trail continues out of the park by longboat as an alternative exit.

Mulu is fly-in only, thirty minutes from Miri, which keeps it quiet; book park accommodation and guides ahead. A week including Miri flights, guides and the Pinnacles permit runs around £1,400. It is hot, wet and leech-rich year round — February to April is marginally drier.
highlights: Sarawak Chamber worlds largest cave room
Deer Cave 3 million bat exodus dusk

imageAttribution.artist: Eric Lanning from Grand Rapids, MI, USA

adventures.title: Scottish Highlands Winter Mountaineering
adventures.description:
Scottish winter mountaineering is the sport at its most honest: modest altitudes, ferocious conditions. A week split between Fort William and Aviemore covers the two great arenas — Ben Nevis's North Face, with snowed-up classics like Tower Ridge and Ledge Route alongside the gullies that invented winter grading, and the Cairngorms' Northern Corries, where Coire an t-Sneachda's mixed buttresses sit forty minutes from the ski-road car park. Buachaille Etive Mòr's Curved Ridge in Glen Coe makes the classic first winter route.

The weather is the whole game. Freeze-thaw cycles build the ice; storms strip it overnight. Each day is planned off the Scottish Avalanche Information Service forecast and the summit winds — 70mph over the Cairngorm plateau is unremarkable — and whiteout navigation by pacing and bearing is a core skill, not an emergency one. December to March is the season; February is usually most reliable.

Courses are the sensible entry: Glenmore Lodge and independent guides run winter skills and climbing weeks at around £700 for five days plus bunkhouse beds. Expect to be spat off by weather two days in five; the days that come good repay the lot.
highlights: Ben Nevis Tower Ridge Grade III classic
Creag Meaghaidh Grade IV ice lines
Whiteout navigation on the Cairngorm plateau
gear: Layer system Scottish wind chill extreme

adventures.title: Bolivia Salt Flat Cycling
adventures.description:
Cycling the Salar de Uyuni is as close as the planet gets to riding across a blank page: 100 kilometres of hexagon-tiled salt at 3,656 metres, with nothing to steer by but Incahuasi Island's cactus silhouette on the horizon. Most riders cross the salar in a day or two, camping on the salt for a horizon-to-horizon sunset, then continue south on the Lagunas route through the volcanic southwest: Laguna Colorada's brick-red water crowded with James's flamingos, the Sol de Mañana geyser field steaming at 4,850 metres, and Laguna Verde beneath the cone of Licancabur.

Season is the variable that undoes people. The famous mirror photographs come from the December–March wet season — when the salar is flooded, corrosive and effectively unrideable. For cycling you want the dry months, roughly April to October, trading reflections for a bone-dry white plain and Altiplano nights that fall to −15°C. Wash the bike ruthlessly afterwards; salt eats drivetrains.

The Lagunas section is deep sand and washboard — 2.4-inch tyres minimum, fat bike ideal, and carry two days of water. Uyuni town has the last real supplies. Seven to ten days Uyuni to San Pedro de Atacama, about £800 self-supported including park fees.
highlights: Sol de Manana geysers steaming at 4850m
gear: Sun protection salt flat UV amplified
Water salt flat zero shade sections

adventures.title: Croatia Dalmatian Coast Sailing
adventures.description:
A week on a chartered yacht out of Split turns the Dalmatian coast into a chain of decisions you cannot get wrong: over a thousand islands, ten-mile hops, and a reliable rhythm of morning calm with the afternoon maestral filling in at 15–20 knots for the passage to the next anchorage. The classic loop runs Split–Šolta–Vis–Hvar–Brač: swim stops in the Pakleni islands, the Blue Cave on Biševo lit electric at midday, and Vis's Stiniva cove approached under sail. With more ambition, head north-west to the Kornati archipelago — 89 bare limestone islands whose moonscape ridges drop straight into national-park water.

Book moorings ahead in July and August (Hvar town quay is a contact sport); June and September give the same wind with half the raft-ups. Keep one eye on the forecast for the bora — the cold north-easterly that arrives with little warning and closes down the northern channels.

A bareboat 40-footer runs £2,000–3,500 for the week split between crew, plus fuel, moorings and park permits; add a skipper for about £1,200 if nobody aboard holds an ICC. Split's Diocletian's Palace and the konoba seafood of the outer islands supply the culture between passages.
highlights: Hvar old town lavender fields arrival
Anchor overnight secluded cove wild swim
gear: Light layers Bora wind evening cool

adventures.title: Australia Larapinta Trail Hike
adventures.description: Walk the Larapinta Trail — 223 km through the West MacDonnell Ranges in the Northern Territory — on one of Australia's finest long-distance desert walks. The trail follows the spine of an ancient mountain range above the red desert floor, with the highest point at Mount Sonder (1,380 m). The night sky in the Central Australian desert is among the darkest in the world; the Milky Way is visible as a dense band of light. Aboriginal Arrernte cultural heritage is woven throughout the landscape; traditional owners maintain custodianship of the land traversed.
highlights: Aboriginal cave art ochre ancient gallery

adventures.title: Silk Road Cycling Central Asia
adventures.description:
The Pamir Highway is a ride measured in weeks, not days: the M41 from Dushanbe to Osh crosses the roof of Central Asia, topping out on the Ak-Baital Pass at 4,655 metres of thin air and broken tarmac. Most cyclists take about a month — climbing out of the Panj gorge with Afghanistan a stone's throw across the river, detouring through the Wakhan Valley beneath the Hindu Kush, then rolling the high desert plateau past Karakul lake to the Kyrgyz border at Kyzyl-Art.

Daily life is the adventure: homestays with bottomless tea in Wakhi and Kyrgyz villages, hundred-kilometre gaps between water sources, and a week straight above 3,500 metres. Acclimatise deliberately — strong riders regularly get turned around on Ak-Baital by going up too fast. The GBAO permit for Gorno-Badakhshan comes with the Tajik e-visa; check it is currently being issued before you commit, as closures happen.

June to September is the window, and even then snow can dust the passes. Finish or start with the Silk Road cities — Samarkand and Bukhara connect by train from the Fergana Valley. A month self-supported runs about £3,000 including homestays at a few pounds a night and a mountain of plov.
highlights: Pamir Highway M41 worlds great adventure road
Wakhan Corridor Hindu Kush river valley
Samarkand Registan square silk road gold
gear: Mountain bike tough frame Pamir roads
Spare parts remote no bike shops

adventures.title: Namibia Sossusvlei Dune Trekking
adventures.description:
Sossusvlei is the Namib at its most theatrical: a corridor of apricot dunes — some of the highest on Earth — funnelling the dry Tsauchab river to a dead end among white clay pans. The ritual is fixed and worth obeying: through the Sesriem gate at dawn, up the tar as the light comes good, then Dune 45 or the long crest-line grind up Big Daddy (325 metres) while the sand is cool and firm. From the top, drop straight down the slip-face into Deadvlei — the white pan studded with 900-year-old camel thorn skeletons, black against orange dune walls; the most photographed scene in Africa, and still better in person.

By 10am the sand is oven-hot and the light flat; retreat to the shaded pools of Sesriem Canyon and return for the evening show. A week gives slack for a night at the NWR campsite or Sossus Dune Lodge inside the gate — the only way to reach Deadvlei at true first light — plus the drive out through the Naukluft mountains via Solitaire's apple pie.

April to September brings crisp air and cold nights; summer hits 45°C. Namibia is a self-drive country: a 2WD does everything except the final five kilometres of sand (shuttle available), and about £1,600 per person covers a week of car hire, park fees and mixed camping and lodges.
highlights: Dune 45 sunrise climb iconic orange crest
Dead Vlei white pan ancient black acacia
Big Daddy dune 325m climb run descent
Sossusvlei pan oryx herds at golden hour
Sesriem Canyon shaded pools at midday

adventures.title: Alaska Denali Base Camp Trek
adventures.description:
Denali National Park has almost no trails — that is the point. Rangers issue backcountry permits by unit quota, you step off the single park road, and everything from there is your own navigation: braided river bars, tussock tundra, caribou paths that dissolve, and glacial creeks best crossed early while snowmelt is low. The reward is walking country where a grizzly on a ridgeline two kilometres away is your only company, with the 6,190-metre bulk of Denali filling the southern sky whenever the cloud allows — it hides two days in three.

A classic week works the units around Wonder Lake and the Muldrow Glacier moraines, the mountain doubling itself in the lake on still mornings. This is not a trek to a climbers' base camp — expeditions fly to the Kahiltna Glacier — but a self-directed wilderness loop in the mountain's shadow, and the quota system means you may meet nobody between bus stops.

Logistics are pleasingly analogue: permits in person at the Backcountry Information Center, bear-resistant food containers compulsory and lent free, and the camper bus drops you anywhere along the road. June to August is the season; rivers and mosquitoes both peak in July. Around £1,800 covers the week from Anchorage — the wilderness itself is nearly free.
highlights: Wonder Lake perfect reflection still morning
Denali National Park one road access
gear: River crossing technique trekking poles pair

adventures.title: Philippines Tubbataha Reef Diving
adventures.description:
Tubbataha is the Philippines' remote crown jewel: two coral atolls rising from the open Sulu Sea, 150 kilometres from the nearest port, diveable only by liveaboard and only from mid-March to mid-June when the sea lies down. The isolation is the product. Reef walls drop past 100 metres with near-guaranteed grey reef and whitetip sharks on every dive, tornado schools of jacks and barracuda, regular manta and hawksbill traffic, and a genuine chance of a whale shark cruising out of the blue. Rangers living on a sandbar station guard the park year-round, and the no-take rules in force since 1988 show in fish biomass few reefs on Earth still match.

Conditions are advanced-diver territory: walls, current, blue-water safety stops and up to four dives a day. Most boats want 50-plus logged dives, and nitrox earns its upgrade fee. Departures run from Puerto Princesa on Palawan on roughly six-day itineraries; the open-sea crossing takes a night each way and can be lumpy.

Book a year out — the season is barely twelve weeks. Expect £2,800–3,800 for the liveaboard including park fees, plus flights to Puerto Princesa. There is no plan B if weather steals a crossing day; that is the price of a reef this untouched.
highlights: Grey reef shark density highest Philippines
Manta ray cleaning station Tubbataha Pass
Sea turtle nesting beach restricted area

adventures.title: Iceland Highlands Laugavegur Extension
adventures.description:
The Laugavegur between Landmannalaugar and Þórsmörk is Iceland's most famous trail for good reason — but the crowds thin the moment you extend beyond it into the wider Fjallabak highlands. The classic days deliver the postcard: steaming rhyolite hills above Landmannalaugar in mustard, rust and green; obsidian fields and fumaroles at Hrafntinnusker; the black-sand desert of Emstrur with the Markarfljót canyon cut through it; then the birch woods of Þórsmörk between two ice caps. The extension strikes east towards Eldgjá — the largest volcanic fissure on Earth, a 40-kilometre gash whose 939 AD eruption dimmed skies across Europe, with the Ófærufoss falls tucked inside the canyon.

River crossings are the honest hazard: several fords run thigh-deep with glacial melt, coldest truth first — cross early in the day, unclip your hip belt, use poles. Weather is the other: July and August are the only reliable window, and even then gales and whiteouts sweep through with an hour's notice.

Huts on the classic section book out by winter; the extensions need a tent and full self-sufficiency, supported by the highland 4x4 buses from Reykjavík. About £1,300 covers a week including buses, huts and food carried from home — Icelandic resupply prices are their own hazard.
highlights: Eldgja volcanic fissure largest Europe eruption
Emstrur black sand lava desert crossing
River crossings waist deep glacial melt
gear: River crossing poles mandatory glacier melt

adventures.title: China Yangtze River Kayak
adventures.description:
Tiger Leaping Gorge is one of the deepest river canyons on Earth: the Jinsha — the upper Yangtze — squeezes between Jade Dragon Snow Mountain (5,596 m) and Haba Snow Mountain (5,396 m), with nearly 3,800 metres of relief from river to summit. The rapids thundering through its core were first fully run only in 1986, at the cost of lives, and the biggest drops remain expedition-grade whitewater that most teams portage. Modern trips paddle sections of the Jinsha and its tributaries at Class III–V, scouting everything — in a gorge this steep, rescue and escape are serious undertakings in themselves.

This is a guided-expedition river, not a turn-up-and-paddle destination: access permits, dam releases and roadworks change the runnable sections year to year, and outfitters in Lijiang or Shangri-La hold the current picture. The water is cold and silt-laden — drysuits even in autumn — and April–May and October–November dodge both the monsoon flood and winter's rocky low flows.

Pair the paddling with the high trail through the gorge: a two-day trek past Naxi guesthouses with the river a vertical kilometre below, plus the First Bend at Shigu where the Yangtze swings north instead of following Asia's other great rivers south. Around £1,900 for a week with a professional outfitter, including permits and Lijiang transfers.
highlights: Upper Yangtze Class V rapid succession
Jade Dragon Snow Mountain glacier backdrop
gear: Advanced whitewater kayak skill class V

adventures.title: Turkey Lycian Way Coastal Trek
adventures.description: Walk Turkey's first long-distance trail — 540 km along the ancient Lycian coastline from Fethiye to Antalya — through ruined Lycian cities, Byzantine churches, and Ottoman hamlets perched on clifftops above turquoise bays. The trail is waymarked but requires navigational attention on faded sections. Accommodation ranges from pensions in villages to wild camping on secluded headlands. Spring brings wildflowers and mild temperatures; summer is hot and sections near sea level are brutal in July and August.
highlights: Oludeniz blue lagoon aerial paraglide view
Kekova sunken Lycian city snorkel swim
Lycian rock tombs carved cliff faces
gear: Sun hat Turkish coastal summer heat
Waymark red white trail easy navigate

adventures.title: Zambia Kafue River Canoe Safari
adventures.description:
Kafue National Park is Zambia's biggest and emptiest park — the size of Wales, with a fraction of the vehicles that work the Luangwa — and the Kafue River is its spine. A canoe safari drifts you silently down broad, fig-lined water where the engine noise that normally announces humans simply never comes: elephants keep drinking as you slide past, malachite kingfishers work the reeds an arm's length away, and fish eagles call from the dead trees. What matters is hippo etiquette — your guide reads the pods, hugs the shallow inside lines, raps the hull to announce you, and gives crossing channels an unhesitating wide berth.

Days end at simple fly-camps on the bank: bucket showers, firelight, and a soundtrack of hyena and Pel's fishing owl. Add game drives on the Busanga Plains in the park's north — floodplain lion country with Zambia's best cheetah odds — to round out the week.

The dry season, May to October, concentrates game on the river and keeps channels navigable; October is hottest and best for density. Packages run out of Lusaka (a five-hour transfer or short charter flight) at roughly £2,200–2,800 for a week all-in. Malaria prophylaxis and a soft bag under 15kg for the charter are the practical notes people miss.
highlights: Hippo pod canoe proximity heart-rate moment
Elephant herd river crossing before camp
Fish eagle call iconic Africa morning
Bush camp star trail Africa dark sky
gear: Quick dry clothes humidity river spray

adventures.title: Costa Rica Multi-Sport Adventure
adventures.description:
Costa Rica compresses more adventure per square kilometre than anywhere else in the Americas, and a well-built week strings it together without feeling rushed. Start at Arenal: the volcano's near-perfect cone (quiet since 2010) rises over hot-spring rivers, the hanging bridges of the Místico park and the 1968 lava-flow trails. Raft the Río Sarapiquí or the bigger Pacuare — Class III–IV through primary forest — then climb into the cloud at Monteverde for canopy walkways, zip lines and night walks that turn up sloths, side-striped vipers and, with luck, a resplendent quetzal.

The wild finale is Corcovado on the Osa Peninsula — by National Geographic's famous reckoning the most biologically intense place on Earth. Day hikes from Drake Bay with the compulsory guide reliably produce scarlet macaws, tapir tracks and spider monkeys, and the boat ride in doubles as a dolphin watch.

December to April is dry season and high season both — book Corcovado permits and Monteverde lodges ahead. Distances look short but roads are slow; allow five hours between regions by shuttle. Around £1,600 per person covers mid-range lodges, guides, rafting and shuttles, padded by £5 casado lunches that keep it honest.
highlights: Arenal 1968 lava-flow trails and hot springs
Monteverde canopy zip line cloud forest
Rio Sarapiqui white water rafting class IV

adventures.title: Corsica South-North Traverse
adventures.description:
Corsica's full south-to-north traverse is the connoisseur's alternative to the GR20 conveyor: around three weeks linking the Mare a Mare and Mare e Monti paths with sections of the high route, from Bonifacio's white cliff-top town to the maquis ridges of Cap Corse. The south opens gently — Alta Rocca's granite villages, then the needle spires of Bavella, where the exposed Alpine variant threads the towers — before the interior hardens into proper mountain days over Monte Incudine and, if you join the GR20 spine, the 2,000-metre passes above the Asco valley.

The north pays it back: Castagniccia's chestnut forests and half-abandoned hamlets, balcony paths above Genoese watchtowers, and sea swims at day's end. June and September are the months; July and August bring heat, crowds and full refuges, and snow holds the high cols into early June.

Refuges and village gîtes let you walk with a light pack, but the GR20 sections book out months ahead — bivouacking beside the refuges is the flexible fallback. Sail into Bonifacio via Sardinia or fly to Figari. Around £800–1,000 for three weeks of gîtes, refuge half-board and Corsican charcuterie; the island is not expensive once you are walking.
highlights: Bonifacio limestone cliff village coastal start

adventures.title: Swiss Haute Route Ski Tour
adventures.description:
The Haute Route from Chamonix to Zermatt is ski touring's most famous line: a week linking high cols and a rosary of glaciers between Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn, sleeping in mountain huts where boot-room diplomacy is a skill in itself. The classic Verbier variant runs the Argentière glacier basin, Rosablanche, and the wind-scoured Prafleuri and Dix stages, then climbs past the Pigne d'Arolla to the Cabane des Vignettes, wedged on its rock prow at 3,157 metres. The final day is the epic: three cols including the Col de Valpelline at 3,568 metres, then more than 2,000 vertical metres of descent beneath the Matterhorn's north face into Zermatt's streets.

Fitness matters less than efficiency: 1,000-metre-plus climbing days at altitude with a pack, kick-turn competence on refrozen 35-degree slopes, and crevasse-rescue drills that are current rather than theoretical. Almost everyone goes guided — the daily route-finding through glaciated terrain in flat light is the real difficulty.

Mid-March to late April balances daylight, snowpack and hut openings; book huts and guides by autumn. Around £3,500 covers a guided week in a group of four to six with half-board huts and lift access. Weather rules everything: build two spare days into your flights, and accept that roughly one party in three gets rerouted by storm.
highlights: Cabane des Vignettes clifftop hut night
Matterhorn north face descent into Zermatt
gear: High mountain hut booking advance essential

adventures.title: Indonesia Flores Ring of Fire Trek
adventures.description:
Flores rewards the overlander: a single road — the Trans-Flores Highway — switchbacks along the island's volcanic spine for 670 kilometres, and a trekking-centred week along it collects experiences that would headline anywhere else. The anchor is Kelimutu: three crater lakes on one summit holding different colours — turquoise, rust, ink-black — and changing them independently as volcanic gases shift the chemistry. Be on the rim for dawn from the village of Moni; the mist burns off in bands and the lakes appear one by one.

Westward, the highland village of Wae Rebo sits in a forest amphitheatre reached only by a three-hour climb — its cone-roofed mbaru niang houses take overnight guests, and morning coffee in the smoke-filled main house is the island's cultural high point. The Ngadha villages around Bajawa, Bena above all, add megalithic ancestor shrines beneath Inerie volcano, itself a steep but non-technical pre-dawn climb.

Finish at Labuan Bajo for the Komodo boats — dragons on Rinca, manta cleaning stations, pink-sand snorkelling. April to September is the dry season. Buses are slow and the hairpins blind, so a car with driver (about £40 a day) is the sane option; a comfortable week runs £900 including guides and homestays.
highlights: Kelimutu three crater lakes colour shifting
Bena Ngadha village megalithic ancestor shrine
Komodo dragon Rinca Island prehistoric encounter
Wae Rebo traditional highland village homestay
Labuan Bajo sunset sailing departure point
gear: Dawn alarm Kelimutu colour optimal viewing

adventures.title: Scandinavia Trans-Nordic Ski Tour
adventures.description:
Crossing Arctic Scandinavia on skis is one of Europe's last true winter journeys: a two-week traverse hauling pulks through the border mountains where Norway, Sweden and Finland meet, typically linking Abisko and the northern Kungsleden with the open fell country towards Kilpisjärvi and the Finnmark plateau. February to April gives deep, stable snow and fast-lengthening light; nights are spent in mountain huts where you cut lake ice for water, or in tents pitched behind sawn snow-block walls when the huts run out.

The days find a hypnotic rhythm — kick, glide, navigate — across frozen lakes and reindeer pastures inside Sápmi, the Sámi cultural region, where the herds and the odd snowmobile track are the only company, and the aurora is a near-nightly companion. The catch is wind: above the treeline a ground blizzard can erase visibility in minutes, so camp craft — mitts-on stove work, storm pitching — matters more than skiing technique.

Go guided unless you have genuine winter-expedition experience: operators run supported crossings at £3,500–4,500 for two weeks including pulks, group kit and hut fees. Fly to Kiruna or Tromsø, or take the night train from Stockholm to Abisko. The fitness bar is towing 30 kilograms for 20-kilometre days, day after day.
highlights: Northern Lights aurora borealis nightly camp
Reindeer herd encounter Sami traditional land
Kebnekaise summit Sweden highest ski descent

adventures.title: Ecuador Volcano Avenue Trek
adventures.description:
Ecuador's Avenue of the Volcanoes packs a mountaineering apprenticeship into a single week: a chain of glaciated cones along the Pan-American Highway, each a night's climb from a road-head refuge, with Quito's 2,850 metres doing your base acclimatisation for you. The classic progression runs the training peaks first — Pasochoa, then Illiniza Norte's 5,126-metre scramble ridge — before the main event: Cotopaxi, 5,897 metres of near-perfect cone, climbed from the José Rivas refuge with a 1am start, cramponing glacier ramps between seracs to a crater rim breathing sulphur at dawn. Strong parties add Chimborazo, whose 6,263-metre summit is the point on the planet's surface furthest from its centre — the equatorial bulge puts you closer to space than anyone on Everest.

None of it is technical by Alpine standards, but altitude is undefeated: the difference between summiting and turning around below the Yanasacha wall is almost always acclimatisation days, not fitness. Local ASEGUIM/IFMGA guides are mandatory on the glaciated peaks and excellent value.

June to September and December to January give the driest, calmest windows. About £1,400 covers the week including guides, refuges and Quito transfers — one of the best value-for-altitude ratios in mountaineering. Check volcanic status before booking; Cotopaxi closes when activity rises, as in 2015 and 2022–23.
highlights: Chimborazo furthest point from Earth's centre

adventures.title: Guyana Wilderness Expedition
adventures.description:
Mount Roraima's 2,810m summit plateau anchors the triple border of Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil, and the Guyanese approach is the wild way in. From Georgetown you charter a light aircraft to the Akawaio village of Phillipai, then spend days with local guides cutting through mossy forest and river crossings to the base of the Great Prow — the 450m overhanging quartzite wall first climbed by Joe Brown and Hamish MacInnes's 1973 expedition. Waterfalls pour off the rim into cloud below.

Be clear about what you are buying: there is no walking route to the top from Guyana. The plateau's only non-technical line is the La Rampa ledge from Paraitepui in Venezuela's Gran Sabana, so treat the Guyana side as a jungle expedition to the mountain's foot, or a big-wall objective for climbers. It rains most days even in the December-April dry season; waterproof everything twice.

Budget around £1,800 for the week including the Phillipai charter, village fees and guides. Permissions come through the Akawaio community, and a satellite communicator is non-negotiable.
highlights: The Great Prow — 450m overhanging quartzite wall, first climbed by the 1973 Joe Brown expedition
Triple Point on the summit plateau where Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil meet
Crystal Valley quartz fields and endemic pitcher plants on the plateau
Charter flight to Phillipai airstrip and trekking with Akawaio guides
Waterfalls pouring off the tepui rim into the cloud forest below
gear: Rain gear permanent cloud summit moisture

adventures.title: Himalaya Zanskar River Ice Trek
adventures.description:
Chadar means blanket — the sheet of ice that forms on the Zanskar River each deep winter and becomes, for a few weeks, the only road through a gorge 600m deep. From Chilling you walk the frozen river itself for five days towards Nyerak, reading the ice as your Zanskari guides do: white and squeaky is good, black and wet means climb the bank. At night you sleep in smoke-blackened caves such as Tibb while the temperature falls past minus 25.

The variable that catches people out is the ice itself. A warm spell can break the chadar mid-trek, forcing waist-deep wades or long waits, and the January-February window is narrowing as winters warm. Acclimatise properly in Leh at 3,500m first — medical checks and ALTOA registration are enforced — and know that gumboots from Leh market outperform expensive trekking boots on wet ice.

Expect £900-1,400 for a guided package out of Leh including permits, camp staff and cave-camp equipment; flights to Leh are extra, and build in two spare days for weather.
highlights: Chadar frozen river walk ice gorge
Zanskar gorge ice overhang ceiling walk

adventures.title: Tanzania Ngorongoro Crater Safari Walk
adventures.description:
The Ngorongoro Crater is a 260 sq km caldera holding the densest concentration of large mammals on earth — some 25,000 animals, including East Africa's most reliable black rhino sightings. Game drives on the crater floor start in cold dawn mist at 2,300m on the rim, dropping 600m through fig forest to grasslands where lion prides ignore vehicles entirely and flamingos rim the soda shallows of Lake Magadi.

Know the rules before you book: walking is not permitted on the crater floor. The walking element of this trip happens on the rim and in the wider conservation area — Maasai-guided routes past Olmoti and Empakaai craters, where you descend with an armed ranger to a flamingo lake inside a forested caldera. Rim camps sit above the cloud inversion, and nights are genuinely cold: pack a warm layer you would trust in Scotland.

Fees are the shock. Crater vehicle fees plus conservation and camping charges mean £2,500 per person for a week is realistic, not padded. June-September and December-February give dry tracks and short grass for spotting.
highlights: Black rhino sighting rarest Africa encounter
Lion pride crater floor 40 resident prides
Crater rim camp cloud inversion sunrise

adventures.title: Canadian Rockies Backcountry Skiing
adventures.description:
The Canadian Rockies reward skiers who earn their turns. The classic week is the Wapta Traverse: four days hut-to-hut across the Wapta and Waputik icefields from Bow Lake to Sherbrooke Lake, staying at the Bow, Balfour and Scott Duncan huts beneath St Nicholas Peak, with glacier travel and whiteout navigation between them. Add day tours at Bow Summit and around Lake Louise, where cold continental snow keeps powder dry for weeks after a storm.

The catch is the snowpack. The Rockies run shallow and faceted — a weaker, more avalanche-prone pack than coastal ranges — so transceiver, probe, shovel and the training to use them are entry requirements, not suggestions, and many parties hire an ACMG guide. Check Avalanche Canada's forecast daily and book Alpine Club of Canada huts months ahead.

February to April gives the best mix of daylight and stability. Budget about £3,000 for a guided week including huts; heli-skiing add-ons in the Columbia ranges to the west cost that again by themselves.
highlights: Columbia Icefield ski tour glaciated plateau
Grizzly track fresh powder morning reveal
Lake Louise backcountry larch meadow autumn

adventures.title: Greece Mount Olympus Ascent
adventures.description:
Mount Olympus earns its mythology. From Litochoro, almost at sea level, the trail climbs through the Enipeas gorge to Prionia, then up through beech and black pine to the Spilios Agapitos refuge at 2,100m, where most parties sleep before the summit day. The final push to Mytikas at 2,917m goes via the Kaki Skala — an exposed Grade 3 scramble where the holds are good but a slip would not be — with the rock towers of Stefani, the Throne of Zeus, alongside.

Afternoon thunderstorms are the trap: they build fast off the Aegean in summer, and you do not want to be on the Kaki Skala when the rock is wet. Start the summit leg at dawn and carry a helmet — parties above knock stones down the couloirs. The season runs mid-June to September; May still holds snow that turns the scramble into mountaineering.

This is one of Europe's cheapest big days out: refuge half-board around €50, no permits, and Litochoro is two hours by train from Thessaloniki. £500 covers a comfortable week including a spare weather day.
highlights: Stefani Throne of Zeus dramatic secondary summit
Litochoro approach sea view coastal start
Byzantine chapel ridge line historical site
gear: Sturdy boots summit zone loose rock

adventures.title: Cuba Cycling Revolution Route
adventures.description:
Cycling Cuba works because the traffic never came back. The classic line runs west from Havana's crumbling Malecón to Viñales, where limestone mogotes rise out of red-earth tobacco farms, then east through the Zapata wetlands and the Bay of Pigs to Trinidad's cobbled UNESCO core, finishing among the son and trova bars of the southeast. Casa particular hosts feed you lobster dinners and strong coffee, and conversations at every stop reach places tour buses never do.

The thing that catches cyclists out is scarcity. There are no bike shops worth the name outside Havana, so bring every spare — tyres, tubes, spokes, chain links — plus cash, because cards fail and rural ATMs barely exist. Ride at dawn to beat the Caribbean heat, and treat pothole shadows with suspicion.

November to March is the dry-season sweet spot. Around £900 covers a week of casas, meals and transfers once you have landed; a support vehicle roughly doubles it but rescues the headwind days.
highlights: Havana Malecon colonial architecture cycling start
Bay of Pigs historical cycling detour
Santiago son cubano live music finale
gear: Spare tyres inner tubes Cuban scarcity
Cash Cuban dollars no card access rural

adventures.title: Alaska Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
adventures.description:
The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is nineteen million acres with no trails, no ranger stations and no mobile signal — the biggest stretch of true wilderness left in the United States. A bush plane out of Fairbanks or Arctic Village drops you on a gravel bar under the Brooks Range, and for a week the country is yours: braided rivers to ford, tussock tundra to curse, and in late June the chance of the Porcupine caribou herd — nearly 200,000 animals — flowing across the coastal plain around you.

Self-sufficiency is absolute. Grizzlies patrol the river corridors, so camps run on electric fences and clean protocols; weather can ground your pick-up flight for days, so carry spare food, a satellite communicator and slack at the far end of your plans. Twenty-four-hour daylight in June-August is disorienting and glorious in equal measure.

Costs are dominated by the flying: expect £5,000 upwards for a guided week including charters. Unguided parties need genuine Alaska river-crossing and bear experience, not enthusiasm.
highlights: Grizzly bear salmon river fishing close encounter
Arctic fall tundra colour blueberry crimson
Float plane wilderness access dramatic landing
Brooks Range peaks 2500m above Arctic tundra
gear: Float plane charter remote access required
Leave No Trace strict wilderness ethics

adventures.title: Antarctica South Georgia Expedition
adventures.description:
South Georgia is the densest wildlife spectacle on the planet. St Andrews Bay holds over 150,000 breeding pairs of king penguins in one roaring amphitheatre beneath glaciated peaks; elephant seal bulls the size of vans hold their beaches; wandering albatross ride the wind on 3m wings. Expedition ships sail from Ushuaia or the Falklands, and the mountaineering pilgrimage — the Shackleton crossing from King Haakon Bay over the glaciated spine to Stromness — retraces the most famous survival march in polar history on rope teams with crampons.

Everything here is weather-permitting. Landings depend on swell and katabatic wind, the crossing succeeds perhaps one attempt in two, and biosecurity checks — vacuumed pockets, scrubbed boots — are rigorous and enforced. Grytviken's whalers' church and Shackleton's grave, toasted with whisky, close the circle.

November to February is the season. Berths start around £10,000 for the voyage before flights to South America; the crossing itself is a guided add-on for experienced parties only.
highlights: King penguin 500000 breeding St Andrews Bay
Elephant seal bull beach harem bellowing
Grytviken Shackleton grave whisky tribute toast
gear: Zodiac landing rubber boots ship issue

adventures.title: Italian Alps Via Ferrata Summer
adventures.description:
The Dolomites invented the via ferrata during the First World War, and the iron ways above Cortina are still the best in the Alps. Warm up on the Cinque Torri circuit among restored WWI trenches, then commit to the Ferrata Ivano Dibona across Monte Cristallo's ridgeline — suspension bridge, tunnels and hours of exposure near 3,000m with the whole pale massif spread below. Rifugio nights, with alpenglow turning the towers pink over dinner, are half the point.

Two things catch people out. Afternoon storms make iron cables the worst place in the mountains — start early and be descending by two — and access to the Dibona is longer than older guidebooks suggest since the Cristallo lifts closed, adding serious height gain on foot. A certified lanyard set, harness, helmet and gloves are mandatory kit; clip discipline matters more than strength.

June to September is the season. £1,200 for a hut-to-hut week with cable car passes is typical; a guide for the bigger routes costs from about €400 a day split between the rope.
highlights: Cinque Torri WWI trench restoration historic
Tre Cime circuit via ferrata approach
gear: Via ferrata set lanyard harness helmet
Sturdy mountain boots grip Dolomite rock
Dry bag camera altitude weather change

adventures.title: Newfoundland Viking Coastal Trek
adventures.description:
Gros Morne packs the strangest geology in eastern Canada into one park. On the Tablelands you walk on the earth's mantle — rust-orange peridotite where almost nothing grows — while across Bonne Bay the Long Range Traverse crosses a different massif entirely: a trailless plateau of tuckamore, bog and caribou, reached by boat to the head of the Western Brook Pond fjord, where you climb a steep gully out of 600m cliffs and navigate by compass for four days towards Gros Morne mountain.

Parks Canada treats the Traverse seriously: reservations and a compulsory route-finding briefing are required, and mist that erases every landmark is what actually catches parties out — GPS confidence and bog-proof gaiters earn their weight. Moose and black bears are common; caribou make the plateau feel Pleistocene.

July to September is the window. Budget about £1,200 including the boat drop, permits and nights in Rocky Harbour either side; add a day's drive north for the Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows.
highlights: Long Range Traverse off-trail compass navigation
L'Anse aux Meadows Viking site 1000 CE
Western Brook Pond fjord boat wilderness
Moose herd Gros Morne backcountry abundant
gear: Weather jacket coastal Newfoundland reliable rain

adventures.title: East Africa Cycling Safari
adventures.description:
Cycling between Nairobi and Arusha turns safari country into something you feel in your legs: the long descent off the Rift Valley escarpment, Maasai herders waving you through cattle crossings, and Kilimanjaro floating above the Amboseli plains as you grind across the dust. Wildlife comes to you — elephants crossing the road at dawn, zebra grazing the verges, giraffe necks above the acacias.

Be realistic about the format: you cannot cycle inside most national parks, so good operators ride the Maasai group ranches and conservancy land on the park fringes with a support vehicle, swapping to game drives for Amboseli itself. That mix is the trip's strength — village nights and boma visits happen precisely because you arrive by bike. Heat, corrugated dirt and punctures are the daily tax; ride a mountain bike with serious tyres.

June-September and January-February dodge the rains. Around £1,800 for a supported week including park fees is fair; add malaria prophylaxis and comprehensive travel cover, because rural medical care is thin.
highlights: Maasai Mara cycling savanna wildebeest crossing
Elephant herd road crossing close encounter
Great Rift Valley escarpment descent dramatic
gear: Tent wild camping savanna night sounds
First aid kit remote medical care limited

adventures.title: Galapagos Islands Diving Week
adventures.description:
The Galápagos underwater is the shark capital of the world. Liveaboards run overnight to Wolf and Darwin, where the Equatorial Undercurrent hits seamounts and scalloped hammerheads school in their hundreds; between June and November, 12m whale sharks cruise the same walls. Sea lions dive-bomb your safety stops, marine iguanas graze algae in the shallows, and Galápagos penguins — improbably, on the equator — flash past at Bartolomé.

This is advanced diving: washing-machine currents, surge against the rock, negative entries from pangas and blue-water safety stops. Operators want Advanced Open Water plus 50-100 logged dives, and they mean it. The water runs colder than the latitude suggests — 5mm suits and hoods in upwelling season — and Wolf and Darwin are reachable only by liveaboard, so land-based trips see a different, gentler Galápagos.

Budget £4,500 upwards for a seven-night boat before flights to Ecuador and roughly £150 in park entry and transit fees. Book a year out for the good boats.
highlights: Sea lion torpedo play diving partner

adventures.title: France Pyrenees High Route
adventures.description:
The Haute Route Pyrénéenne shadows the Franco-Spanish frontier for roughly 800km from the Atlantic at Hendaye to the Mediterranean at Banyuls-sur-Mer, taking the high line wherever one exists. Six weeks of walking crosses the Cirque de Gavarnie's headwall country, skirts Vignemale — at 3,298m the highest summit of the French Pyrenees — and threads the remote granite of Ariège and Andorra that even Pyrenean regulars rarely see, before the surreal final descent to a Mediterranean swim.

Unlike the waymarked GR10 and GR11, the HRP is a concept, not a path: sections are trackless, cols hold snow into July, and you move between staffed refuges, unmanned cabanes and wild camps, so navigation and self-sufficiency are the real prerequisites. The Ariège stages are the loneliest and the loveliest.

July to September is the season; carry light crampons for early-summer cols. Six weeks costs surprisingly little — £1,500-2,500 mixing a tent with hut meals — and the route sections cleanly if you only have a fortnight.
highlights: Ordesa Canyon Spanish national park contrast
gear: Crampon option late snow June cols

adventures.title: Japan Nakasendo Historic Trail
adventures.description:
The Nakasendo was the inland samurai road from Edo to Kyoto, and in the Kiso Valley it survives almost intact. The classic walk links Magome to Tsumago over the Magome-toge pass at 801m — eight kilometres of stone paving, cedar forest and bear bells you ring as you pass — arriving in post towns where wooden lattice facades, kosatsu notice boards and lantern-lit inns have barely changed since the Edo period. Sleep in a family ryokan, eat river fish and mountain vegetables, and walk quieter stages around Nagiso and Narai.

The logistical trick worth knowing: the morning baggage-forwarding service between Magome and Tsumago (roughly March to November) lets you walk with a day pack, and local trains on the Chuo line shuttle you between trailheads. Book inns ahead for early-April cherry blossom and November momiji — the two windows when the valley is at its best and busiest.

Five days costs about £700 with ryokan dinners; carry yen in cash, as the older inns do not take cards.
highlights: Tsumago juku-machi Edo period architecture preserved
Magome to Tsumago classic section cedar forest
Cherry blossom April sakura timing perfection
Autumn momiji maple red gold November
gear: Rain jacket Japanese mountain valley climate

adventures.title: Norway Romsdalseggen Ridge Walk
adventures.description:
The Romsdalseggen is the ridge walk Norway puts on its posters. A morning bus from Åndalsnes drops you at Venjedalssetra, and the trail climbs onto a crest that narrows until Romsdalsfjord glitters below one boot and the Romsdal valley the other. Across the void stand Romsdalshorn and the Troll Wall — Europe's tallest vertical rock face — while the finish descends over Nesaksla on the Romsdalstrappa stone staircase straight into town.

The exposure is real but optional: the standard route bypasses the sharpest section, while confident scramblers take the airy crest direct. What actually catches people out is weather — the ridge is no place in wind or rain, and cloud kills the entire point — so build flexibility into your week and hold the traverse for the clear day. The Romsdalen gondola gives a bail-out and a knee-saving descent.

June to September is the season once the snow clears. Norway is expensive, but the hike itself costs only the £25 shuttle bus; £600 covers several days based in Åndalsnes, with the Rauma Railway as your scenic approach.
highlights: Trollveggen — Europe's tallest vertical rock face — in full view across the valley
Romsdalshorn's 1,550m needle rising over the crest
Knife-edge ridge sections with Romsdalsfjord glittering below
Descent over Nesaksla via the Romsdalstrappa stone staircase
Arriving by the Rauma Railway into Åndalsnes under the peaks
gear: Trekking poles descent Romsdal valley steep
Early start avoid afternoon cloud buildup

adventures.title: Ethiopia Omo Valley Cultural Trek
adventures.description:
The lower Omo Valley holds one of Africa's most extraordinary concentrations of living cultures — Hamar, Karo, Mursi, Dassanech — and the difference between a fly-past and a real visit is how you travel. Walking between villages with guides from Jinka or Turmi, sleeping near settlements and timing your days around the markets (Turmi on Mondays, Key Afer on Thursdays) earns slower, warmer encounters: a Hamar bull-jumping initiation if you are fortunate, Karo body-painting on the bluffs above a bend of the Omo River.

Go with your ethics switched on. Photography here runs on negotiated payment, and a good local guide who handles it respectfully is the most important booking you will make. The region is remote — 4WD transfers between walking stages, cash only, malaria prophylaxis essential — and conditions and permissions change, so check current advice for South Omo before committing.

The dry windows, roughly December-February and June-September, make travel workable. £1,500 for a guided week from Arba Minch or Jinka is a sensible floor.
highlights: Karo village body art chalk ochre design
gear: Cash birr only no card remote

adventures.title: California Pacific Crest Trail Section
adventures.description:
The John Muir Trail runs 340km through the High Sierra from Happy Isles in Yosemite Valley to the 4,421m summit of Mount Whitney, the highest point in the contiguous United States. Three weeks of granite: Thousand Island Lake under Banner Peak, the chain of alpine lakes through Evolution Basin, and a final week that barely drops below 3,000m, crossing the stone hut on Muir Pass and topping out on Forester Pass at 4,009m before the Whitney finish.

The permit is the crux — Yosemite's lottery is massively oversubscribed, so apply exactly 24 weeks out, or reverse the route from Whitney Portal or Horseshoe Meadows. Bear canisters are legally required, resupply takes planning (Muir Trail Ranch is the last easy pick-up for the southern half), and early-season snowmelt turns creek crossings into the genuinely dangerous bit. July to September is the window; mosquitoes own July.

Done self-supported it is remarkably cheap — roughly £800 including permits, food and resupply buckets — plus getting yourself to California.
highlights: Mount Whitney 4421m continental US highest summit
Muir Pass 3632m stone shelter historical hut
Yosemite Valley Happy Isles iconic start
gear: Bear canister mandatory Sierra Nevada regulations
Creek crossing poles Sierra snowmelt floods
Mosquito head net June July abundance

adventures.title: Arctic Norway Ski-Sail Expedition
adventures.description:
Ski-and-sail is Svalbard at its purest: an expedition yacht out of Longyearbyen noses along Isfjorden and the west coast, and each morning you skin from the shoreline up glaciated summits nobody has touched all season, then ski a single clean line back to the water. Days end with the anchor down in a silent fjord, drift ice knocking against the hull and the light refusing to fade.

Polar bears set the rules here. Every landing needs a trained rifle carrier and every camp a watch; your guides' bear and glacier judgement is what you are actually paying for. You will want solid off-piste and touring competence — crevassed terrain, snow from wind crust to corn — but the sailing asks nothing beyond a stomach for open-water passages. April and May bring 24-hour light and the most reliable snow; March is colder, darker and quieter.

Berths run £4,000-8,000 for the week depending on the boat, plus flights to Longyearbyen. Book a year ahead — the good yachts carry eight skiers and sell out.
highlights: Pack ice navigation sailboat bow watch
Glacier ski descent Arctic fjord shoreline
Polar bear encounter sea ice safari
Northern Lights aurora bow watch midnight

adventures.title: Brazil Amazon River Expedition
adventures.description:
The Mamirauá Reserve, upstream of Tefé where the Solimões meets the Japurá, is the Amazon at high concentration: the largest protected flooded forest on earth, home to the white uakari monkey found nowhere else, pink river dolphins that surface beside your canoe, and caimans whose eyes stitch the night water with torchlight. From the floating Uakari Lodge, community guides paddle you into drowned várzea forest where you drift at canopy height among squirrel monkeys and hoatzins.

Seasons transform the place. High water (roughly April-June) means silent paddling through the treetops; low water (September-November) exposes beaches, concentrates wildlife along the channels and brings jaguars to the margins — Mamirauá has quietly become one of the better places on earth to glimpse one. Either is superb; pick the experience you want.

Access is a one-hour flight from Manaus to Tefé, then a boat transfer. The lodge model funnels income to local communities; around £2,200 for a week all-in from Tefé is typical, plus yellow fever vaccination and malaria precautions.
highlights: Pink river dolphin boto encounter rare
Giant river otter family group hunting
Jaguar river bank dawn sighting chance
Anaconda swim river edge night encounter

adventures.title: Georgia Caucasus Mountain Trek
adventures.description:
The Georgian Caucasus compresses more drama per day of walking than almost anywhere in Europe. From Stepantsminda, under Mount Kazbek's 5,047m glaciated cone, the hike to the Gergeti Trinity Church puts the iconic cliff-top silhouette an easy morning away; stronger days continue to the Gergeti Glacier moraine, or over to the Chaukhi massif via Juta — the 'Georgian Dolomites' — and into the flower-filled Truso Valley with its towers and mineral springs. A marshrutka along the Georgian Military Highway from Tbilisi reaches the trailheads for a few lari.

Kazbek itself is a serious glaciated climb staged from the Betlemi Hut area at 3,650m — achievable for fit trekkers with a guide and proper acclimatisation, but it is mountaineering, not hiking. What catches people out lower down is Caucasus weather: fierce afternoon build-ups and snow lingering on the passes into July.

June to September is the season. Georgia remains superb value — guesthouses with dinner for £25-30 — so £600 funds a generous week including a local guide for the bigger days.
highlights: Gergeti Trinity Church cliff 2170m iconic view
Mestia Svan tower village mediaeval fortification
gear: Warm layers high altitude Caucasus cold

adventures.title: Greenland Kayak West Coast
adventures.description:
Paddling Disko Bay is kayaking inside a cathedral. The Sermeq Kujalleq glacier — the most productive in the northern hemisphere, source of roughly a tenth of Greenland's icebergs — fills the Ilulissat Icefjord with white towers that drift past your bow, creaking and splitting in the midnight sun, while humpbacks surface close enough to hear their breath. This is also the homeland of the kayak itself: qajaq technique was perfected here over centuries.

Respect the distances your guides insist on. Bergs roll without warning and calving waves travel far — you admire the icefjord mouth from a wide berth, never inside it — and water at 2-4°C makes drysuits and rescue drills the foundation of the trip. June to August brings open water, 24-hour light and the whales; tundra-shore camps mean carrying everything, polar-bear awareness included.

Guided weeks out of Ilulissat run about £3,500 before flights via Copenhagen or Reykjavík, which are the other big line on the budget. Cold-water paddling experience is expected, not optional.
highlights: Sermeq Kujalleq calving glacier active front
Disko Bay pack ice navigation spring
gear: Sea kayak cold Arctic water technique
Spray skirt rough water calving wave
Bear spray polar bear coastal territory

adventures.title: Japan Northern Alps Traverse
adventures.description:
The Northern Alps traverse from Shin-Hotaka to Kamikochi crosses the roofline of Japan with a mountain hut every few hours — futons, hot dinners and beer vending machines at 3,000m — so you climb hard days carrying almost nothing. The centrepiece is Yarigatake, 3,180m, the 'Matterhorn of Japan', whose final spear of rock goes on chains and ladders to a summit shrine; hardened scramblers continue south over the Daikiretto, a notorious knife-edge gap towards the Hotaka peaks, before descending the Yarisawa valley to Kamikochi's clear river and reflection ponds.

Hut logistics are the real skill: reserve ahead (essential around Obon in mid-August and autumn weekends), carry cash, and start every day at dawn because afternoon cloud and thunder are the pattern. The Daikiretto is no-fall terrain — skip it via the valley if the rock is wet — and typhoon season can rearrange any itinerary in late summer.

July to September is the window. Around £1,200 covers a five-day traverse with huts at roughly ¥13,000 half-board, plus the alpine bus into Kamikochi and an onsen soak at the end.
highlights: Okuhida Onsen valley thermal recovery spa
Kamikochi valley floor sunrise reflection pond
Hotaka Daikiretto knife-edge traverse Grade II
Mountain hut futon dinner culture unique Japan
gear: Rain gear Japan monsoon afternoon clouds
Gaiters loose scree mountain hut approach

adventures.title: Namibia Desert Ultramarathon Self-Supported
adventures.description:
Racing 250km across the Namib self-supported means carrying every calorie for a week while the world's oldest desert runs the thermostat: near-freezing dawn starts under the Southern Cross, 40°C by noon on the gravel plains, and dune stages where each step gives half of itself back. The NamibRand's apricot dunes, fairy circles and mountain-ringed valleys make it a strange privilege — oryx watch you suffer past ancient welwitschias, and the night sky over camp belongs to one of the darkest reserves on earth.

The discipline that finishes the race is unglamorous: pack weight under 10kg including seven days of food, electrolytes managed hourly, feet taped before blisters exist, and sand gaiters glued to shoes that drain. Checkpoints ration water; everything else is on your back.

Events run in the cooler April-June and August-September windows. Entry, kit and Windhoek logistics push £3,000 before flights — and train for months with the loaded pack, because the pack, not the distance, is what breaks people.
highlights: NamibRand red dune field dawn crossing
Southern Cross night sky no light pollution
Welwitschia plant 2000 years old desert survival
Oryx herd desert adapted crossing route
Canyon camp overnight dramatic desert geology

adventures.title: Tasmania Southwest Wilderness
adventures.description:
Tasmania's Southwest is the empty quarter of Australia — a World Heritage wilderness of quartzite ranges, button-grass plains and rainforest hiding Huon pines two thousand years old, with no roads at all. A light plane from Hobart to the gravel strip at Melaleuca is the way in, landing beside Bathurst Harbour's tea-dark water where orange-bellied parrots breed. From there parties walk the South Coast Track's 85km of beaches and mud to Cockle Creek, or mount serious expeditions towards Federation Peak — the quartzite fang whose summit scramble above a 600m drop is often called Australia's hardest walk.

The Southwest's weather is the examiner: fronts arrive off the Southern Ocean with horizontal rain in any month, the mud is permanent, and the Ironbound Range has pinned parties for days. Full self-sufficiency, tide timing for the creek mouths and genuine navigation skills are entry requirements.

December to March is the season. Around £3,500 covers the flights in, park passes and two weeks of food; the Melaleuca air service books out, so plan months ahead.
highlights: Southwest Cape southern ocean wilderness end
Port Davey inlet remote float plane access
Undiscovered valleys no human footprint months
gear: Light-plane charter to Melaleuca airstrip booked months ahead
Full storm gear for permanent southwest rain

adventures.title: Nepal Kanchenjunga North Base Camp
adventures.description:
Kangchenjunga's north side is Nepal before the crowds found it. From Taplejung in the far east, the restricted-area trek climbs for a week through cardamom fields, Limbu and Sherpa villages and rhododendron forest — a riot of bloom in April — to Ghunsa's timber gompas, then up the moraine past Jannu's staggering 7,710m profile to Pangpema at 5,140m, where the third-highest mountain on earth fills the sky with its 3,000m north face. You might share the viewpoint with a handful of trekkers; blue sheep will outnumber them.

The logistics do the gatekeeping: the restricted zone requires a registered guide and a minimum of two trekkers, road access via Bhadrapur and Taplejung is long and rough, and beyond Ghunsa you sleep in basic teahouses where the menu is dal bhat and the nights fall well below freezing. Acclimatisation days at Ghunsa and Kambachen are built in for good reason.

March-May and October-November are the seasons. Eighteen days runs about £2,800 with permits, guide and internal flights — remote Nepal at its most rewarding.
gear: Restricted zone permit far east Nepal
Yak hire remote cargo remote sections

adventures.title: Iceland Kerlingarfjoll Highland Hike
adventures.description:
Kerlingarfjöll is the Highlands' best-kept secret hiding in plain sight off the Kjölur route: a rhyolite massif in ochre, rust and rose, steaming from every fold. From the Ásgarður base the boardwalk-and-ridge circuit into Hveradalir — the 'valley of hot springs' — drops you among fumaroles roaring like kettles, boiling mud pots and snowfields that survive all summer beside near-boiling streams, with the Hofsjökull and Langjökull ice caps closing the horizon. Longer days loop the massif or climb Snækollur, the 1,477m high point, for a view across the entire interior.

Access is the filter: the F35 and the final F347 spur demand a genuine 4WD and open only from roughly late June to early September, and Highland weather can serve sleet in August — the wind is permanent, so pack like it is Scotland at altitude. Book the Ásgarður huts or campsite ahead; there is nothing else for 50km.

Five days based there costs about £900 with a shared hire vehicle, hut nights and fuel — a fraction of the crowded south coast, for emptier and stranger country.
highlights: Rhyolite mountain colour orange red spectrum
Hot spring natural pool highland remote
Langjokull ice cap backdrop highland camp

adventures.title: Suriname Amazon Jungle Expedition
adventures.description:
Suriname is more than nine-tenths forest, and the Upper Suriname River is the way into it: hours in a motorised dugout (korjaal) threading rapids from the roadhead at Atjoni, between walls of primary rainforest, to Saamaka Maroon villages founded by people who escaped slavery and rebuilt West African life deep in Amazonia. Village stays and river lodges run by Saamaka families set the rhythm — cassava gardens, drumming, swimming from river beaches while howler monkeys argue at dawn.

The cultural protocol matters as much as the jungle craft: villages are private homes, so you travel with a Saamaka guide, ask before photographing, and accept that the river sets the timetable — low water means pushing the korjaal over rocks. Malaria precautions and yellow fever vaccination are required kit, and a hammock with a good mosquito net beats any tent.

The long dry season (August-November) and the short one (February-March) give the easiest travel. A week from Paramaribo costs around £1,800 including the road-and-river transfer, guides and village fees.

Howler monkey dawn chorus jungle wake up

adventures.title: Oman Hajar Mountains Trek
adventures.description:
The Hajar Mountains put 3,000m of rock between the Gulf of Oman and the desert, and Jebel Shams — the Mountain of the Sun, 3,009m — presides over the lot. The signature walk is the W6 Balcony Walk: a ledge path along the wall of Wadi Ghul, the 'Grand Canyon of Arabia', with a kilometre of air below your feet, ending at the abandoned cliff village of As Sab, whose stone houses and falaj channels cling under the rim. Around it, days link Nizwa's Friday livestock market, the terraced falaj village of Misfat al Abriyeen, and summit-plateau camps where the stars are ferocious.

Winter is the season — November to March brings perfect walking temperatures, while summer is dangerous heat. Carry more water than feels reasonable regardless, because springs are few, dress modestly in the villages, and hire a 4WD: the final climb to the plateau is steep gravel.

Oman is safe, courteous and easy to travel. A week self-driving with guesthouse and wild-camp nights runs about £700 plus flights to Muscat.

adventures.title: South Korea Baekdu-Daegan Ridge Trek
adventures.description:
The Baekdu-daegan is Korea's sacred mountain spine, and its southern anchor Jirisan makes the perfect week: a ridge traverse across the mainland's highest ground, sleeping in the national park shelters strung below the crest, rising in the dark to watch sunrise from Cheonwangbong at 1,915m with cloud seas filling every valley. Buddhist temples such as Hwaeomsa guard the approaches — add a temple-stay night for the 3am moktak drumming — and Korean hiking culture is half the joy: immaculate trails, and shared soju at the shelters.

Book before you fly: shelter berths on Jirisan release online weeks ahead and vanish for weekends and autumn foliage, and you carry your own food between them. Summer monsoon (July-August) soaks the range, so aim for May-June green or the October colour spectacular. Some connecting sections of the full Baekdu-daegan are officially closed for restoration — respect the barriers and route around by bus.

Korea makes this cheap and easy: £600 covers a week including intercity buses, shelter nights at a few pounds each and post-hike barbecue.

Buddhist temple mountain overnight stay experience
Korean autumn foliage ridge colour display

adventures.title: Algeria Sahara Hoggar Trek
adventures.description:
The Hoggar is the Sahara with its bones showing: a volcanic highland rising from Tamanrasset to the Assekrem plateau, where basalt plugs and spires crowd the horizon like a petrified storm. Charles de Foucauld's 1911 hermitage still stands on the plateau rim, and watching dawn ignite the peaks from it is one of the desert's great set pieces. Trekking here means moving camp with Tuareg guides and their camels between wind-carved gorges, gueltas — hidden rock pools — and sand valleys, with tea brewed three times over the coals each evening.

This is expedition Africa in logistics if not in gradient: an Algerian visa arranged well in advance, a licensed local agency and guide (mandatory for the deep south), 4WD support, and six litres of water a day. Winter nights at 2,700m drop below freezing, so pack a proper sleeping bag alongside the sun kit.

October to March is the season; summer heat makes trekking impossible. A guided week from Tamanrasset costs around £2,500 including the domestic flight from Algiers.
highlights: Assekrem plateau dawn over a horizon of volcanic plugs
Charles de Foucauld's 1911 hermitage on the plateau rim
Gueltas — hidden rock pools deep in the basalt gorges
Tuareg camel camp and the three-glass tea ceremony
Atakor massif's lunar skyline above the sand valleys

adventures.title: Spain Sierra Nevada Winter Ski
adventures.description:
Sierra Nevada above Granada is Europe's most southerly ski area and its strangest brag: carve above 3,000m in the morning with the Mediterranean glittering 40km away — on the clearest days the Rif mountains of Morocco line the horizon — and eat free tapas in Granada by night. The resort skiing off Veleta (3,398m) is high, sunny and reliable for its latitude, and when spring firms the snowpack, ski tourers skin from the Hoya de la Mora roadhead towards Mulhacén, at 3,479m the highest summit in mainland Spain, for long corn-snow descents.

The sun is the variable to respect: south-facing slopes cycle from ice to slush fast, so time descents like a spring alpinist and carry serious sunscreen — the UV at this latitude and altitude is brutal. Weekends bring Granada's crowds; midweek the pistes empty.

December to April is the season, with March-April best for touring. A week runs about £1,200 with passes and apartments far below Alpine prices — and the Alhambra is your rest day.

Granada Alhambra palace cultural evening après
Sierra Nevada spring corn snow April

adventures.title: Laos Mekong River Slow Boat
adventures.description:
The slow boat from Huay Xai to Luang Prabang is two days of the Mekong doing the driving: limestone karst walls, water buffalo on the sandbars, villages where the boat noses in to trade sacks of rice, and the brown river turning gold as the light drops. You cross from Chiang Khong in Thailand, overnight in Pak Beng's hillside guesthouses, then rejoin the current for the second day, finishing beneath the temple spires of Luang Prabang with a stop at the Buddha-crammed Pak Ou caves where the Nam Ou meets the Mekong.

Seat strategy is the local knowledge that matters: board early at Huay Xai for the repurposed car seats near the bow — the stern belongs to the engine's roar — and bring cushions, snacks and a book, because each day runs eight hours or more. In Pak Beng, agree your room price before you follow anyone uphill.

November to March is dry, cool and clear. The boat itself costs about £25; a week including Luang Prabang's night market, alms ceremony and Kuang Si falls runs £300 in guesthouses.

adventures.title: China Guilin to Yangshuo Cycle
adventures.description:
The karst country between Guilin and Yangshuo is the landscape on the back of the 20-yuan note, and a bicycle is the right speed for it. Ride out of Yangshuo along the Yulong River, where limestone towers repeat to the horizon over rice paddies and bamboo rafts drift the shallows; climb to Moon Hill's natural arch viewpoint; and take the ferry crossing at Xingping to stand on the exact 20-yuan view as cormorant fishermen pose in the dusk. Quiet concrete farm lanes make the riding easy and endlessly rearrangeable.

The Longji 'Dragon's Backbone' rice terraces are worth adding, but know they are a separate excursion two-plus hours north of Guilin, not on the riverside route — plan them as a day trip rather than expecting one continuous ride. Summer is hot, hazy and wet; April-May and September-November give the clear light everyone comes for.

Bike hire in Yangshuo costs a few pounds a day and guesthouses are excellent value: £400 covers a comfortable week including the Li River boat or raft trip.

Li River limestone karst 20 yuan note view

adventures.title: Zambia Lower Zambezi Canoe
adventures.description:
Paddle the Lower Zambezi in open canoes, camping on white sandbanks while hippos and elephants drink metres away in the golden late-afternoon light. Zambia's Lower Zambezi National Park lines the northern bank; across the river lies Zimbabwe's Mana Pools, so the whole valley works as one vast wildlife corridor with barely any boat traffic. On guided 4-6 day canoe safaris you will watch elephants swimming the channels, crocodiles basking on every bar, and fish eagles calling from dead trees that overhang the current.

The hippo protocol is the trip: your guide reads the pods and taps the hull to announce you, threading the quiet water behind sandbars while you keep your strokes calm — this is one wildlife environment where obedience is everything. Nights are wild-camped under mosquito nets with lions audible across the water; malaria prophylaxis is essential.

May to October is the dry-season window, with September-October thickest with game. Guided safaris run about £2,500 for the week before flights to Lusaka and the road or air transfer to Chirundu or the valley airstrips.

Elephant herd river bank feeding metre
