adventures.title: Austria Grossglockner High Alpine
adventures.description:
The Grossglockner, 3,798m, is Austria's highest mountain and its most coveted summit day. The normal route from Lucknerhaus above Kals climbs past the Stüdlhütte onto the Ködnitzkees glacier, reaching the Adlersruhe — the Erzherzog-Johann-Hütte, at 3,454m Austria's highest refuge — for a short night before the dawn push: cramponed snow to the Kleinglockner, then the famous squeeze across the Glocknerscharte notch, a metre wide with 600m of air on either side, to the summit cross.

It is a genuine mountaineering route — glacier travel, fixed-rope scrambling, absolute no-slip ridge — and summer weekends produce queues at the scharte that can turn a two-hour summit round into five. Go midweek, go early, and book the hut months ahead. Most parties hire a guide in Kals, which is money well spent for the descent alone.

July and August offer the most settled conditions. Around £900 covers a five-day acclimatisation-and-summit programme with hut half-board; a 1:1 guide adds roughly €500.

adventures.title: Bhutan Lungchutse Monastery Trek
adventures.description:
Bhutan's best-value mountain day starts at the Dochula pass, where 108 memorial chortens line the Thimphu-Punakha road at 3,100m. The trail climbs through hemlock draped in old man's beard and spring rhododendron to Lungchutse Goemba at about 3,600m, whose prayer-flag ridge unfurls a 180-degree sweep of the Bhutan Himalaya — on a clear morning you can trace the chain to Gangkhar Puensum, at 7,570m the highest unclimbed mountain on earth. Loop down via Trashigang Goemba for a quiet, monk-tended descent, and bank the Tiger's Nest cliff monastery from Paro in the same week.

Timing is the trick: haze swallows the big views by mid-morning outside the October-November window, so start at dawn and hold your cloudless days for the ridge. March-May trades some clarity for rhododendron colour.

Bhutan's Sustainable Development Fee (US$100 per night) plus guided-travel rules mean a five-day itinerary lands around £2,500 before flights to Paro — the price of a country that measures tourism in thousands, not millions.

adventures.title: Peru Huascarán National Park Trek
adventures.description:
The Cordillera Blanca crams the highest tropical mountains on earth into a range you can see end-to-end from Huaraz's rooftop cafés. The Santa Cruz trek is the classic four-day line, from Cashapampa's canyon up to Punta Union at 4,750m, where Taulliraju's fluted face fills the pass and turquoise lakes stair-step the valley below; acclimatisation hikes to Laguna Churup and Laguna 69 are stunning enough to be goals in themselves. Climbers graduate to Pisco or Chopicalqui, with Alpamayo — often called the most beautiful mountain in the world — as the range's poster summit and Huascarán, Peru's 6,768m apex, looming over everything.

Altitude is the whole game: Huaraz sits at 3,050m and the treks live above 4,000m, so build in three acclimatisation days before Santa Cruz or pay for it in misery. Colectivos make trailhead logistics absurdly cheap; the park entrance fee and a registered guide for the high routes are the paperwork.

May to September is the dry season. £1,500 covers a fortnight of trekking with guides, mules and Huaraz recovery days.
highlights: Santa Cruz Trek Punta Union 4750m pass
Alpamayo perfect pyramid world's most beautiful
Churup turquoise lake hanging glacier backdrop
Llanganuco twin glacial lake sapphire blue

adventures.title: Finland Fell Country Ski Tour
adventures.description:
Finnish Lapland skis differently: no lifts, no drama, just rolling treeless fells, frozen mires and pine forest silvered with rime, crossed on light Nordic touring skis at a pace that lets the silence in. Urho Kekkonen National Park's 2,550 square kilometres hold a network of open wilderness huts — free, stove-warmed, first-come — and marked winter routes from Saariselkä and Kiilopää, so you can plan days hut-to-hut past reindeer herds with the aurora as evening entertainment.

The cold is dry, beautiful and serious: minus 20 is routine in February and minus 30 possible, so this is a trip about systems — layered wool, spare mitts, a stove you can light with numb fingers — rather than technical skill, which makes it a perfect first polar journey for competent cross-country skiers. Sámi reindeer-herding culture is present and living here; visit it on its own terms.

February to April balances light and snowpack, with aurora odds best away from the full moon. A week mixing sauna-equipped base nights and hut tours runs about £1,800 including Ivalo flights from Helsinki.

adventures.title: Argentina Patagonia Overland
adventures.description:
Ruta 40 down Argentine Patagonia is the loneliest great drive on earth: three weeks of steppe, guanacos and horizons that never quite arrive, punctuated by scenery that resets your standards. The southern anchors are unmissable — the 9,000-year-old stencilled hands of Cueva de las Manos in the Pinturas canyon, El Chaltén's granite skyline of Fitz Roy and Cerro Torre, Perito Moreno glacier calving thunder into Lago Argentino — before the road runs out of continent towards Tierra del Fuego.

Fuel discipline is the survival skill: stations at Bajo Caracoles and Tres Lagos can be 200km apart and occasionally dry, so fill at every opportunity, carry a jerry can, and treat the remaining ripio (gravel) stretches with respect for your windscreen and rims. The wind is a permanent passenger; open the car doors with both hands.

November to March gives long days and open passes. Around £3,000 per person covers three weeks of hire car, fuel and cabañas — book the El Chaltén and El Calafate stops ahead in high summer.

adventures.title: Pantanal Jaguar Safari
adventures.description:
The northern Pantanal in the dry season is the best place on earth to watch wild jaguars. From Porto Jofre, at the end of the Transpantaneira's dust and 120-odd wooden bridges, boat safaris work the Cuiabá, Piquiri and Three Brothers rivers where the cats patrol the banks in daylight — hunting caimans in full view, swimming the channels, sprawled on the beaches. Sighting rates in August-October approach certainty, and the supporting cast is absurd: giant river otters hunting in family packs, hyacinth macaws, capybaras everywhere, giant anteaters on the drive in.

Heat and glare are the working conditions — long boat days under tropical sun — and the lodges and flotels near Porto Jofre are remote and price accordingly, so operator choice is most of the decision. A 500mm lens, hired if necessary, earns its baggage fee daily.

July to October is the season; the Transpantaneira needs care but not 4WD heroics when dry. Budget about £2,800 for a week from Cuiabá with three full jaguar-boat days.

adventures.title: Atlas Mountains Mountain Bike
adventures.description:
Mountain biking the High Atlas strings Berber villages together on mule tracks, singletrack and old colonial pistes, with mint tea appearing whenever you stop. The classic traverse crosses the range over Tizi n'Tichka at 2,260m, then swaps tarmac for the Ounila valley's magnificent descent past Telouet's crumbling kasbah to the film-set fortress of Aït Benhaddou; further east the red walls of the Dades and Todgha gorges give canyon riding beneath 300m cliffs before the land tips towards the Draa's palm oases and the desert fringe.

Remoteness is the planning factor: there are no bike shops in the mountains, so carry spares for everything and know your own mechanics, or ride with an operator whose support vehicle does. Nights in village gîtes and kasbah guesthouses are the trip's soul — basic, warm and cash-only, so carry small dirham notes.

March-May and September-October dodge both snow on the passes and killing summer heat. A supported week from Marrakech runs about £900 including guide, vehicle and half-board.

adventures.title: Senegal Casamance River Kayak
adventures.description:
The Casamance is Senegal with the volume turned down: a slow green river system of bolongs — tidal mangrove creeks — where a kayak is the perfect tool. From Ziguinchor or the fishing village of Elinkine you paddle glassy channels between oyster-crusted mangrove roots to Jola villages reachable only by water, to Karabane island's ruined Breton mission church at the river mouth, and past the huge impluvium roundhouses of Enampore. Atlantic humpback dolphins work the estuary, ospreys and bee-eaters own the air, and West African manatees survive in the quieter creeks.

Tides are the timetable — plan each leg with the flow, not against it, because the bolongs empty to mud — while the paddling itself is flat and beginner-friendly, making this one of Africa's gentlest water journeys. Casamance's old troubles have largely faded, but check current advice; on the ground the welcome is famously warm.

November to March is dry, breezy and mosquito-light (prophylaxis still essential). A guided week with village campements costs around £500 plus flights to Dakar and the ferry or short flight south.

adventures.title: Caucasus Georgia Wild Camping
adventures.description:
Racha is the Georgia that even Georgians describe with a sigh: a high, green province of beech forest, alpine meadows and stone villages beneath the wall of the central Caucasus, where wild camping is legal everywhere and shepherds will fix your dinner plans by insisting on them. Walk from Shovi or Ghebi into the headwater valleys — the trail towards Udziro Lake at 2,800m is the signature route, with Caucasian tur on the screes — then descend to Ambrolauri for the 11th-century dome of Nikortsminda Cathedral and a glass of Khvanchkara, the semi-sweet red that made the valley famous.

Self-sufficiency is the deal: waymarking is thin, weather turns fast above 2,500m, and villages sell bread and cheese but not gas canisters, so arrive provisioned from Kutaisi or Tbilisi. A chacha toast with strangers is a when, not an if.

June to September is the window; late September adds autumn gold. £400 funds a generous week of marshrutkas, guesthouse nights either side and total freedom in between.

adventures.title: South Africa Wild Coast Hike
adventures.description:
The Wild Coast is South Africa's Eastern Cape at its rawest: green hills dropping into the Indian Ocean, Xhosa villages of turquoise rondavels, empty beaches walked mostly by cattle. The classic hiking stage runs south from Coffee Bay along cliff paths and river mouths to Hole in the Wall — the wave-cut arch the Xhosa call esiKhaleni, 'the place of sound', for the boom of swell through the gap. Multi-day versions continue village-to-village with nights in community-run huts and family homestays, or take the hotel-to-hotel comfort of the Wild Coast Meander further south.

River mouths set the itinerary: several crossings are wade-or-swim jobs, so time them for low tide, keep valuables in a dry bag, and hire a local guide — it puts money in the right hands and the unmarked paths make far more sense. Winter (May-August) brings dry days, whales, and in June-July the sardine run offshore.

It is superb value: guided village-stay hikes run about £600 for a week including meals; getting to Mthatha or Coffee Bay is the long part.

adventures.title: Myanmar Golden Triangle Trek
adventures.description:
Kengtung is the capital of Myanmar's Golden Triangle — the far-eastern Shan hills near the Thai and Lao borders — and its treks reach villages of the Akha, Lahu, Ann and Loi peoples through terraced rice, tea gardens and forest ridges. Walks start from the lakeside market town, climbing to stilted bamboo settlements where the Ann women's lacquered black teeth and the Akha silver headdresses belong to living tradition, not costume; overnights in village homes come with rice wine, wood-fire cooking and conversation through your guide.

Go carefully and with current information: Myanmar's civil conflict has closed regions and border crossings on and off since 2021, and most Western governments advise against travel to much of Shan State — research thoroughly, book through operators with genuine local standing, and be ready to wait for the moment when going is responsible again. A licensed guide is mandatory for village access regardless.

The cool dry months of November-February are the season. On the ground it is inexpensive — guide, homestays and meals around £500 a week — with kyat cash the only money that works.

adventures.title: Ecuador Amazon Rainforest Stay
adventures.description:
Yasuní may be the most biodiverse forest on earth — more tree species in a single hectare than in all of North America — and the lodges off the lower Napo put you inside it. From Coca a motorised canoe runs down the river, then a paddled dugout glides you up a blackwater creek to lodges like the community-owned Napo Wildlife Center in Añangu Kichwa territory. Days build around the parrot clay licks, where hundreds of parrots and parakeets swirl down to eat mineral clay, and the 36m canopy towers where a kapok crown becomes your birding balcony; nights are for caiman eyes in torchlight and an insect orchestra you will never forget.

Manage expectations honestly: this is rich rainforest, not a zoo — monkeys, macaws and hoatzins are daily, jaguars and tapirs are luck — and the humidity is total, so waterproof the camera kit. Community-owned lodges send tourism money where it belongs; book them first.

It rains year-round, with somewhat drier spells around December-March. A four-night lodge stay plus Coca flights lands near £1,800; yellow fever vaccination is required kit.

adventures.title: Scottish Islands Sea Kayak Circuit
adventures.description:
The Outer Hebrides serve Britain's finest sea kayaking: white shell-sand beaches that would pass for the Caribbean until you taste the water, machair meadows loud with corncrakes, and tidal channels threading Harris, the Uists and Barra where seals follow your stern like dogs. The crux is the Sound of Harris — a maze of drying banks and racing tide that demands real passage planning — and the reward is camps on empty strands like Luskentyre's fringe under enormous Atlantic skies, with minke whales and white-tailed eagles as regular company.

The Atlantic makes the rules: swell wraps everything, weather windows open and slam shut, and a drysuit is year-round kit in 12°C water, so this is a trip for competent paddlers or a guided group with flexible plans and ferry-hopping alternatives for storm days. Scotland's access laws make wild camping legal and glorious.

May to August gives the most light and the kindest sea. A guided week runs about £1,200; self-organised trips cost little beyond the CalMac ferries and food.

Sound of Harris tidal race navigation challenge
Minke whale surface bubble net feeding

adventures.title: Canary Islands Interisland Cycle
adventures.description:
Island-hopping the Canaries by bike and ferry is a volcanic grand tour in shirtsleeve weather while northern Europe shivers. Tenerife brings the queen stage: the grind from sea level to 2,300m in the Teide caldera — among the longest continuous road climbs in Europe, finishing in a lava moonscape beneath Spain's highest peak — plus the hairpin madness of the Masca gorge road. Gran Canaria's interior coils around Roque Nublo like a velodrome designed by geology; Lanzarote adds wind-scoured laps through Timanfaya's lava fields; little El Hierro offers the emptiest circuits of all.

The trade winds are the tactical layer — plan loops so the wind blows you home, not out — and altitude turns Teide's heights cold even when the coast reads 24°C, so carry a shell for every big descent. Fred Olsen and Armas ferries take bikes free or nearly so, which makes the logistics genuinely easy.

November to April is the sweet spot, which is exactly why the pro peloton winters here. A week with apartments, ferries and bike hire runs about £1,400.

adventures.title: Nepal Mera Peak Climb
adventures.description:
Mera Peak, 6,476m, is the highest of Nepal's trekking peaks and the most summit for the least technicality in the Himalaya: the standard route up the northern glacier is a walk on crampons — roped for crevasses, with a fixed line on the final dome — yet the top serves a panorama of five 8,000ers at once: Everest, Lhotse, Makalu, Cho Oyu and Kangchenjunga. The approach is half the prize, crossing the Zatrwa La from Lukla into the roadless Hinku valley, where rhododendron forest gives way to yak pasture at Khare, base for glacier-school days and the high camp at about 5,800m.

Altitude is the whole examination. The summit stands far above the trekking Nepal most people know, and rushed itineraries fail routinely — take an 18-day programme with built-in rest days, and treat a guide, the climbing permit and proper double boots as the entry fee. Summit morning starts around 2am in serious cold.

April-May and October-November are the seasons. Around £2,200 covers a guided expedition from Kathmandu including the Lukla flights and permit.

Hinku Valley rhododendron forest April bloom
Mera Central 6476m Nepal highest trekking peak

adventures.title: Iceland Snaefellsjokull Crater Trek
adventures.description:
Snæfellsjökull is the glacier-capped volcano Jules Verne chose as the door to the centre of the earth, and it presides over the whole Snæfellsnes peninsula — visible from Reykjavík across Faxaflói on clear days. The guided ascent, on crampons and rope or by ski-touring in spring, climbs from the Jökulháls track to the 1,446m summit craters, where the view runs from the island-flecked sweep of Breiðafjörður to the lava coast at your feet. Build the week around the peninsula's greatest hits: the basalt arches and bird cliffs at Arnarstapi, black-pebble Djúpalónssandur with its shipwreck iron, and Kirkjufell's absurdly photogenic cone near Grundarfjörður.

The glacier is crevassed and only sensible with a guide — book from Arnarstapi — and the season is short: firm spring snow beats late summer, when bare ice and opening slots can close the route. Weather cancels more attempts than fitness; hold two possible summit days.

Around £800 covers a five-day self-drive with one guided glacier day; two hours from Reykjavík, no permits needed.
highlights: Jules Verne Journey Centre Earth real entrance
Arnarstapi sea arch coastal lava platform

adventures.title: Vietnam Central Highlands Trek
adventures.description:
Kon Tum province is the Vietnam that lowland tourism never reaches. You walk village to village through the Bahnar, Jarai and Sedang heartland, sleeping beneath the soaring thatched prows of rong communal houses that tower above the treeline like upturned axe blades. The moment that stays with you is a Jarai communal cemetery: carved wooden figures crouched in mourning around the tombs, a funerary tradition found nowhere else in Southeast Asia. Between villages the trail crosses coffee and pepper plantations and the cool pine hills around Mang Den, and if your visit coincides with a ceremony you will hear the gong music UNESCO lists as a masterpiece of intangible heritage.

The catch is paperwork, not terrain: several minority villages require a licensed guide and local registration, so book through a Kontum-based operator rather than turning up solo. Go in the November to March dry season - from May the afternoon storms turn the red-clay paths to grease. Around £400 covers a week of guiding, homestays and food; carry small-denomination dong, as there are no ATMs beyond Kontum city.
highlights: Bahnar village rong communal house traditional
Jarai cemetery statue carved wooden mortuary
Mang Den highland lake pine forest
gear: Cash dong only remote highland villages
Rain poncho Central Highland afternoon storms

adventures.title: Kenya Mathews Range Trek
adventures.description:
North of Samburu the tarmac ends and the Mathews Range rises out of the acacia scrub like a forested island - ridges of cedar and ancient cycad that trap enough rain to stay green while the plains below crack in the heat. You trek with Samburu guides and camels carrying camp, following elephant paths through forest that shelters buffalo, colobus monkeys and the elephants themselves, climbing high to escape the furnace of the flats. The moment that sells it: cresting a ridge at dawn to watch Grevy's zebra grazing a kilometre below, with no vehicle, fence or lodge in any direction.

Walking here recalibrates you fast - you learn wind direction, fresh dung and silence, because everything is met on foot. Nothing about the trip is casual: it is guided camping only, water comes from forest springs through a filter, and the nearest hospital is a day away, so evacuation cover and a proper first-aid kit are non-negotiable. Time it for the dry windows - January to February or July to September. Around £1,200 buys a week with guides, camels and camp crew, arranged from Wamba or through one of the Namunyak conservancy operators.
highlights: Elephant forest shelter cool mountain haven
Samburu guide cultural navigation north Kenya
Grevy's zebra rare stripe plains below
Colobus monkey forest canopy endemic mountain
Ngeng Valley waterfall remote gorge discovery
gear: Malaria prophylaxis north Kenya high risk
First aid kit remote medical zero

adventures.title: Australia Kimberley Wilderness Drive
adventures.description:
The Gibb River Road runs 660 kilometres of corrugated dirt from Derby to the Pentecost crossing near Wyndham, straight through the heart of the Kimberley - 420,000 square kilometres of sandstone ranges, boab trees and cattle stations the size of small nations. Your days find a rhythm: drive the corrugations early, then walk into a gorge - Bell, Manning, Galvans - and swim beneath a waterfall in water the colour of dark tea. Wandjina and Gwion Gwion rock art galleries wait in the escarpments, and Horizontal Falls, where 10-metre tides force the sea sideways through twin cliff gaps, is reached by seaplane from Derby.

The season is the variable that catches people out: the road opens around May as the wet-season floodways drop and shuts again by November, and even in the dry a single storm can close crossings for days. Two spare tyres are standard Kimberley practice, fuel stops run up to 300km apart, and there is no mobile signal - carry a satellite communicator. Around £3,500 per person covers a week of 4WD hire from Broome, fuel, station camps and park fees; the Horizontal Falls flight is a worthwhile splurge on top.

Mitchell Falls four-tier cascade on the remote plateau
Horizontal Falls tidal sluice by seaplane from Derby
Wandjina and Gwion Gwion rock art galleries

adventures.title: Swiss Alps Eiger North Face Trek
adventures.description: The Eiger Trail beneath the north face of the Eiger follows the base of one of mountaineering's most legendary walls from Eigergletscher to Alpiglen, close enough to watch the live drama of active rock fall and to spot climbers on the face above. The Bernese Oberland landscape of Grindelwald valley, Jungfrau massif, and wildflower meadows frames Switzerland's most charged mountain encounter. Alpiglen restaurant serves Rosti with the best view on earth.
highlights: Eiger north face Mordwand close base trail
Alpiglen Rosti lunch best mountain view Swiss

adventures.title: Mexico Copper Canyon Railway Trek
adventures.description:
The Barrancas del Cobre are six linked canyons in the Sierra Madre Occidental, together deeper and four times more extensive than the Grand Canyon. You arrive the only sensible way: aboard El Chepe, one of the world's great railway journeys, climbing from sea level at Los Mochis through 86 tunnels and across 37 bridges to the rim at Divisadero, where the land simply stops and drops 1,300 metres at your feet.

Then you walk. Trails descend from the rim villages through Raramuri (Tarahumara) country to the subtropical canyon floor at Batopilas or Urique, passing three climate zones in a single day. The descent is the trap: 1,500 metres of downhill hammers the knees, and the floor can run 20C hotter than the rim - start at first light and carry more water than feels reasonable. The Raramuri, the famed ultrarunners, live in dispersed ranchos throughout the canyons; a local guide smooths both navigation and etiquette, and your fee stays in the community. October to March gives crisp rim air and a bearable floor. Around £800 covers a week of trains, guesthouses and guides - book El Chepe's first-class carriages a few weeks ahead in high season.
highlights: Copper Canyon 4x Grand Canyon depth scale
El Chepe train spectacular railway descent
Barrancas del Cobre canyon floor tropical
gear: Train ticket El Chepe advance booking
Descent layers tropical floor to rim cold

adventures.title: Central Asian Steppe Cycling
adventures.description:
From Almaty, with the snowline of the Tian Shan still filling your mirrors, the road tips north into the largest dry steppe on earth - and for the next fortnight the horizon simply never closes. Almaty to Astana is roughly 1,400 kilometres of grassland, salt-pan depressions and wind: as much a psychological challenge as a physical one, because the land barely changes for days and a headwind can halve your speed without warning or shelter. Detour east early for Charyn Canyon's red hoodoos, then settle into steppe rhythm - 100-kilometre days, six litres of water aboard, camp pitched behind the only bush since lunch.

The reward arrives unscripted: shepherds waving you into yurts for tea, fresh bread and kurt, the hospitality of people who measure their neighbours in days of travel. Villages with shops can be 150 kilometres apart, so carry five days of food, and there is no bike shop between the two cities - pack spare spokes, tyres and tools. May, June and September are kindest; July cooks. Around £1,500 covers a self-supported crossing, with a night or two in Astana's surreal glass capital to finish.

Yurt camp shepherd tea bread hospitality
Charyn Canyon Kazakhstan mini Grand Canyon
Almaty Tian Shan mountain backdrop start
Bayterek tower Astana futuristic capital end

adventures.title: Canada Yukon Dog Sled Winter
adventures.description:
Within an hour of the briefing at a mushing kennel outside Whitehorse you are standing on the runners of your own sled behind a team of shrieking huskies - and the instant the snow hook lifts, the noise stops dead and there is only the hiss of runners and dog breath smoking in air at minus 30. Multi-day expeditions run the frozen rivers and black-spruce forest on the old trails of the Yukon Quest, overnighting in wall tents heated by wood stoves or in trappers' cabins, with the aurora as a regular bonus overhead.

The dogs come first, always: you learn to harness, feed and check paws at every stop, and feeding your team at minus 40 before you eat is part of the contract - it is also, unexpectedly, the part people remember most fondly. Cold management is the variable that catches novices: operators lend expedition parkas and boots, but bring your own base layers, a balaclava for wind chill on the runners, and hand warmers taped to camera batteries, which die fast. January to March gives reliable trails and lengthening daylight; late February is prime. A guided five-day expedition costs around £3,500 from Whitehorse, tuition included - no experience needed beyond the fitness to jog uphill beside the sled.

Northern Lights aurora drive camp night
Yukon River frozen highway winter travel
Musher overnight camp wall tent wood stove

adventures.title: Mozambique Bazaruto Dive Safari
adventures.description:
The Bazaruto Archipelago shelters the last viable dugong population in the western Indian Ocean - a few hundred animals grazing the seagrass flats between five dune islands off southern Mozambique. Diving centres on Two Mile Reef between Bazaruto and Benguerra: hard-coral gardens at snorkel depth, walls patrolled by potato bass and green turtles, and manta cleaning stations on the outer edge. Whale sharks cruise the channel in the warm months and humpbacks pass between June and October; the dugong itself is the lottery ticket, most often seen from the boat crossing the flats at high tide, so keep a camera to hand between dives.

Tide is the variable that runs this place: spring tides rip through the island channels and visibility swings from ten metres to thirty, so good operators plan the day around the tide table rather than your wish list. Water sits at 24-27C - a 3mm suit is plenty. Base yourself in Vilankulo and dive by speedboat for around £2,800 a week including marine park fees, or double it for the island lodges. April-May and September to November bring the calmest seas.
highlights: Dugong last viable East Africa population
Manta ray cleaning station outer reef
Two Mile Reef pristine coral diversity

adventures.title: Norway Preikestolen Hike
adventures.description: Pulpit Rock is a flat-topped cliff rising 604 metres above the Lysefjord in Norway, one of the most dramatic natural viewpoints in Europe. The 8-kilometre round trip hike gains 330m through birch forest and rocky plateau to a summit overlooking the fjord in both directions. The Kjeragbolten rock wedged in a crevasse above a 1000-metre drop is accessible on a more challenging trail nearby for those seeking the ultimate vertiginous photograph.
highlights: Pulpit Rock 604m vertical Lysefjord cliff drop
Stavanger Viking heritage city fjord base

Wind jacket fjord wind exposed plateau

adventures.title: China Sichuan Panda Trekking
adventures.description:
Wolong is the giant panda's official capital: a reserve of bamboo-cloaked mountains west of Chengdu where China's breeding programme raises the cubs you have seen in every documentary. You split the week between volunteering at the Shenshuping base - mucking out enclosures, weighing bamboo, mixing the steamed 'panda cakes' fed to animals in the rewilding programme - and trekking the Qionglai valleys above, where a genuinely wild population lives in the cloud forest between 2,000 and 3,500 metres.

Be clear-eyed about the odds: a wild giant panda sighting is a lottery win. What you will realistically find is the evidence - bitten bamboo stems, droppings, day beds - plus red pandas, golden pheasants, tufted deer and, in early summer, hillsides of blue poppies. The mist is the variable: Sichuan's mountain weather soaks everything it touches, so waterproof boots and a dry bag for optics are not optional. Volunteer places must be booked weeks ahead with passport details, and a guide is mandatory on reserve trails. Around £1,200 covers the week with programme fees, permits, guiding and simple guesthouse lodging; go in March-May or September-October between snow and monsoon.
highlights: Giant panda encounter wild bamboo chance
Red panda sighting more common forest
gear: Waterproof boots Sichuan mist rain bamboo
Quiet movement no noise wildlife encounter

adventures.title: Himalayas Annapurna Base Camp
adventures.description:
The trail into the Annapurna Sanctuary threads the Modi Khola gorge so tightly that the mountains stay hidden - then at Machhapuchhre Base Camp the walls fall back and you are standing inside a ring of giants. Base Camp proper, at 4,130m, sits beneath the South Face of Annapurna I: three vertical kilometres of rock and hanging serac on the deadliest of all the 8,000ers. At dawn the amphitheatre ignites peak by peak - Annapurna South, Fang, Machhapuchhre's fishtail - and you understand why the Gurungs held this basin sacred.

It is teahouse trekking all the way, through Chhomrong's stone staircases and bamboo forest alive with langurs, with dal bhat and a warm blanket every night. The avalanche corridor between Deurali and MBC is the serious variable: it loads after any heavy snowfall and has killed trekkers, so cross it early in the day and heed lodge advice without ego. Seven days works from the Siwai jeep road with sensible acclimatisation; carry the ACAP and TIMS permits from Pokhara. Around £900 covers permits, lodges, meals and a porter shared between two. October-November gives glassy air; March-April trades a little haze for rhododendron forest in full scarlet bloom.
highlights: Annapurna I 8091m south face dramatic view

adventures.title: Reunion Island Piton Traverse
adventures.description:
Reunion crams an improbable amount of vertical into one Indian Ocean island: three collapsed cirques - Cilaos, Salazie and roadless Mafate - walled by kilometre-high cliffs, crowned by Piton des Neiges at 3,071m, the Indian Ocean's highest point, with Piton de la Fournaise, one of the world's most active volcanoes, smoking away to the south-east. The traverse links them on the GR R1 and GR R2: down into Mafate, where supplies arrive by helicopter and the ilet hamlets feel a century away, then the pre-dawn scramble up Piton des Neiges to watch sunrise over a sea of cloud, and finally the lunar Plaine des Sables to la Fournaise's lava fields.

Only la Fournaise is active - des Neiges has slept for millennia - and eruption closures are managed by the prefecture, so check bulletins before committing to the crater walk. Cloud is the daily variable: summits are clear at dawn and drowned by mid-morning, so alpine starts are the rule. Mountain gites must be booked ahead (Mafate especially) and the May to October dry season is the window. Around £1,500 covers a week of gites, meals and transfers; it is France, so your EHIC/GHIC works and the wine in Cilaos is properly good.

Mafate cirque helicopter access only gorge

adventures.title: Lake District Wainwright Fells
adventures.description: Alfred Wainwright's 214 Lakeland fells form the ultimate bagging challenge in English hill walking, and completing all 214 is a rite of passage for British hillgoers. Scafell Pike at 978m is England's highest point, while Helvellyn's Striding Edge offers the most thrilling scramble approach in England. The combination of lakes, literary history from Wordsworth, and the particular quality of light in the English fells creates an intimate mountain world.

Catbells family fell Derwent Water view
Sharp Edge Blencathra dramatic Grade I

adventures.title: Kenya Loita Hills Wild Trek
adventures.description: The Loita Hills are sacred Maasai highlands in southern Kenya where no roads penetrate the ancient cedar forest and Maasai ceremonial groves. Walking with Maasai guides through wildlife-rich open grassland and forest habitat encounters buffalo, elephant, and on fortunate days, African wild dogs. The Loita Hills are rarely visited and represent the Kenya of pre-mass-tourism, where the relationship between human and wild is still negotiated daily.

Maasai sacred cedar forest ceremonial grove
Elephant herd forest highland Loita Hills
No roads no infrastructure complete wilderness

adventures.title: Greece Islands Sailing Circuit
adventures.description:
A sailing week through the Cyclades strips the Aegean back to its elements: white villages stacked on volcanic cliffs, water so clear the anchor chain seems suspended in air, and islands of radically different character an easy day-sail apart. Out of Athens the classic line runs south - Kythnos's double-sided sand spit at Kolona, Milos's pirate coves at Kleftiko and the lunar white rock of Sarakiniko, Folegandros's clifftop Chora - before the finale, if weather allows: a mooring under Santorini's caldera wall as the villages along the rim light up at dusk.

The Meltemi is the variable that makes or breaks the plan. From July it can blow 25-30 knots for days, funnelling between islands and closing harbours; skippered and flotilla boats plan around it, but if your own qualification or heavy-weather mileage is thin, hire a local skipper and learn from them. May-June and September bring gentler wind, warm water and empty anchorages. Expect from about £2,500 per person for a shared bareboat week including berthing, fuel and food - more with a skipper - and book Cyclades charters months ahead for high summer.

Milos Sarakiniko lunar beach volcanic white
Folegandros cliff village Chora remote escape
Naxos Apollo Temple Portara sea approach
Meltemi wind reliable afternoon sail system

adventures.title: Italy Via degli Dei Trek
adventures.description:
The Via degli Dei - the Way of the Gods - walks out of Bologna beneath the Portico di San Luca and over the Apennine watershed to arrive, 130 kilometres later, in front of Florence's Duomo. The gods are the mountains it crosses: Monte Adone's sandstone tower above the Setta valley, Monzuno, Monte Venere, Monte Luario. For long stretches you walk the Flaminia Militare, a Roman military road of 187 BC whose original paving still surfaces through the chestnut woods, and at Monte Sole you pass the memorial to the 1944 Marzabotto massacre - the route's sobering, necessary pause.

This is civilised long-distance walking: red-and-white waymarks throughout, village B&Bs and agriturismi each night, tagliatelle and Sangiovese as recovery strategy. The climbs are honest - repeated 400-600 metre pulls, around 4,000m of total ascent - but trail shoes beat boots and luggage transfer is easy to arrange. Book accommodation ahead for the May-June and September-October sweet spots, and avoid the airless heat of late July and August. Around £500 covers six nights, meals and transfers; both ends are an easy train ride apart, which makes the logistics the simplest of any Italian trek.

Monte Sole partisan WWII memorial poignant
Florence Duomo cathedral arrival via hike

adventures.title: South Africa Drakensberg Traverse
adventures.description: Trek the Drakensberg escarpment — the basalt barrier between KwaZulu-Natal and Lesotho, with summits above 3,400 m and vertical rock walls 1,000 m high — on a 5-day traverse linking Cathedral Peak, the Monks Cowl, and Giants Castle. San Bushmen rock art galleries containing thousands of paintings are accessible on day walks from the base camps. The Giant's Cup Hiking Trail in the southern Berg is a well-maintained 5-day route with overnight huts. The combination of subtropical lowveld and alpine summit experience within a single day is unique to the Drakensberg.

Amphitheatre Tugela Falls 948m world top five
Sentinel Peak plateau hike chain ascent

adventures.title: India Zanskar High Mountain Trek
adventures.description:
Zanskar spends more than half the year sealed off by snow, and the summer trekking window is your only walking door into it. From Darcha the trail climbs to the Shingo La at 5,091m - prayer flags snapping over a moonscape of scree and glacier - then drops into the Lungnak valley, where barley fields glow implausibly green against 6,000-metre walls. The route's great moment is Phugtal Gompa: a honeycomb of whitewashed cells built into a cliff cave above the turquoise Tsarap river, still reachable only on foot, where the monks will pour you butter tea. Beyond lie Padum, Zanskar's tiny capital, and Karsha Gompa stacked up its hillside.

Altitude is the variable that ends trips here: the route lives above 3,800m for days, so acclimatise properly first - three nights around Leh or Lahaul minimum - and know the symptoms that mean descent. July to September only; the passes hold snow either side. A guide or agency crew with mules is the sensible format (around £1,400 for nine days including permits and food), and go soon with clear eyes: the new Shingo La road is punching through year by year, and the walking route will not outlive it in this form.
highlights: Phuktal Monastery river canyon cave position
Zanskar River gorge cliff balcony path

adventures.title: Nepal Mardi Himal Trek
adventures.description:
Mardi Himal is the Annapurna region's quiet ridge: a trail that climbs out of the Pokhara foothills through oak and rhododendron forest, breaks the treeline at High Camp (3,580m), and walks a grassy crest with the entire Annapurna wall unrolling to the north. The prize is Machhapuchhre. The sacred Fishtail - closed to climbers for ever - fills the eastern sky closer here than on any other permitted trail, near enough at dawn to watch the light slide down both summits of the fork.

The classic move is a pre-dawn push from High Camp to the Base Camp viewpoint at roughly 4,500m, sunrise on Annapurna South and Hiunchuli, and back down for a late breakfast. Exposure is the variable: the ridge catches full weather, and afternoon cloud swallows the views by mid-morning, so walk early and treat the altitude gain seriously - it is quick for Nepal. Teahouses run the whole route but are small; book ahead in high season. March-April wraps the lower trail in pink and scarlet rhododendron bloom, October-November gives the glassiest air. Around £700 covers ACAP and TIMS permits, lodges and meals for the week - one of the best value-to-view ratios in the Himalaya.

High Camp 3,580m sunrise above a sea of cloud
Base Camp viewpoint at 4,500m beneath Mardi Himal 5,587m
Rhododendron forest in full bloom, late March to April
Low Camp's mossy oak and bamboo cloud forest

adventures.title: Congo Gorilla Tracking Expedition
adventures.description:
An hour with a habituated gorilla family in Virunga is the same electric privilege as in Rwanda next door, at a fraction of the permit price - and with a rawness Rwanda polished away long ago. Rangers walk you into the Mikeno sector's forest until, suddenly, a silverback is browsing an arm's length away, infants tumbling through the vegetation around him. The park's other headline, Nyiragongo, lost its famous lava lake in the 2021 eruption; the lake has been slowly rebuilding since, and the brutal, spectacular crater-rim climb reopens only as conditions allow.

Be honest with yourself about risk before you book. Eastern DRC's security situation shifts month to month, and Virunga has suspended tourism repeatedly in recent years - sometimes for long stretches. Book only through the park's official channels, follow FCDO advice, treat any itinerary as provisional until the week you travel, and carry comprehensive medical and evacuation cover. Logistics run via Goma, usually crossed on foot from Gisenyi in Rwanda. Around £2,800 covers a week with a gorilla permit (about US$400), park lodges and transfers - money that funds the bravest conservation project in Africa.
highlights: Mountain gorilla silverback DRC Virunga forest
Nyiragongo lava lake crater overnight camp
Goma volcanic city active slopes base

adventures.title: Himalayan Kingdom Bhutan Bike
adventures.description:
Cycling Bhutan is a staircase ridden in the sky. From the Indian border at Phuentsholing the national highway climbs out of banana-palm lowlands and never really stops: to Thimphu, over the Dochula with its 108 chortens and a horizon of Himalayan snow, down through rice terraces to Punakha's great riverside dzong, and finally up the pedalling crux - the Chele La at 3,988m, Bhutan's highest road pass, a 35-kilometre climb through blue pine and rhododendron between the Paro and Haa valleys, with Jomolhari's snow pyramid rising behind.

The rules are the variable, not the roads: Bhutan's Sustainable Development Fee (US$100 per day) plus mandatory tour arrangements mean you ride with an agency support vehicle - which, on 1,500-metre climb days at altitude, you will not resent. Traffic is sparse and courteous, and the descents are enormous; check your brake pads daily. Build in a rest-day hike to Taktsang, the Tiger's Nest monastery on its cliff. March-May brings rhododendron bloom, October-November the clearest air. Around £3,500 all-in for the week, fees included - expensive, and worth it for roads this empty through a landscape this intact.
highlights: Chelela Pass 3988m Bhutan highest road cycling
Tiger's Nest monastery cliff switchback approach
Bhutan Gross National Happiness policy cycling
gear: Bhutan daily fee minimum per person
Warm layers high pass cold descent

adventures.title: Iceland Westfjords Kayaking
adventures.description:
Paddle north out of Isafjordur and you are quickly beyond Iceland's last road, tracing cliffs into Hornstrandir Nature Reserve - abandoned by its farmers in the 1950s and now the country's wildest corner. From the cockpit of a sea kayak the scale sinks in: 500-metre bird cliffs streaming with puffins and guillemots, beaches without a footprint, and Arctic foxes - fully protected here and boldly curious - trotting into camp to inspect your tent pegs. Across the fjords, Dynjandi spreads its 100-metre bridal-veil cascade down the mountainside.

The sea is the variable that sets the rules. Water at 5-8C makes a drysuit non-negotiable, katabatic gusts spill off the plateaus without warning, and fog can erase the coastline in minutes - so this is a trip for a guided expedition (around £2,000 for five days from Isafjordur, boats and camps included) unless you hold serious cold-water qualifications. June to August brings the midnight sun, which changes the game: with 24-hour light you paddle when the sea allows rather than when the clock says, and some of the finest crossings happen at two in the morning on water like mercury.
highlights: Dynjandi waterfall tiered cascade approach kayak
gear: Expedition sea kayak with full cold-water outfitting
VHF radio for tide and fog calls on crossings
Pogies or neoprene mitts for paddling warmth
Dry-bagged camping kit for Hornstrandir landings

adventures.title: Vietnam North Mountain Cycling
adventures.description:
The mountain roads of Vietnam's northwest stack more scenery per kilometre than almost anywhere you can legally ride a bicycle. The loop from Hanoi swings through Yen Bai and the Khau Pha pass, where the rice terraces of Mu Cang Chai cascade down entire mountainsides - pure gold at the late-September harvest - then on through Sapa beneath Fansipan, Indochina's 3,143m high point, to the battlefield basin of Dien Bien Phu and the long river valleys of Son La. Between the passes you freewheel through Hmong, Thai and Dao villages where the Sunday markets, Bac Ha above all, are a blaze of traditional dress.

The gradients are the variable: passes here climb 1,000 metres and more, often steeply, and the reward is earned. Road surfaces swing from fresh tarmac to potholed gravel within a kilometre, so ride a tourer or hardtail with proper spares - rural mechanics can fix anything but stock nothing for modern groupsets. Time it for September-November (harvest colours) or March-April; the summer monsoon brings landslides. It is gloriously cheap: around £500 for the week in guesthouses, eating pho at plastic tables, with cash dong essential once you leave the towns.

Sapa Muong Hum valley deep rice terraces
Dien Bien Phu historical French defeat battleground
Hmong market Bac Ha Sunday traditional dress

Repair kit puncture tool kit basic

adventures.title: Mongolia Trans-Altai Motorcycle
adventures.description:
Riding west from Ulaanbaatar to Khovd is the distilled Mongolian problem: around 1,400 kilometres, most of it without pavement, navigating braided tyre tracks across open steppe by GPS bearing and the pointing arm of the last herder you passed. The Khangai leg delivers Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur's volcanic crater lake; then the land dries and rises into the Altai, where river fords - walk them first, every time - and 3,000-metre passes guard Kazakh eagle-hunter country in Bayan-Olgii. Time a September ride and you can finish at the Golden Eagle Festival, burkitshi in embroidered coats launching eagles from horseback.

Bogs are the variable nobody expects: after rain, innocent green valley floors swallow motorcycles to the axle, and the recovery is yours to perform. Fuel range of 300+ kilometres is essential, as is a toolkit you actually know how to use - there is no mechanic between sums. Carry spare levers, tubes, filters and a satellite communicator. June to September is the window; outside it the steppe is brutal. Around £2,500 covers bike hire in UB, fuel, food and ger-camp or wild camping - plus the eagle festival entry if your timing lands.
highlights: Mongolian steppe trackless riding GPS navigation
Altai river ford water crossing technique
Terkhiin Tsagaan Nuur volcanic crater lake
gear: Recovery kit bog steppe melt spring

adventures.title: Brazil Chapada Diamantina Hike
adventures.description: The Chapada Diamantina is a highland plateau of table mountains, waterfalls, and caves in the Bahia interior that served as the setting for the Brazilian diamond rush. Fumaca Falls drops 340 metres into an abyss and is one of Brazil's highest, while Poco Encantado enchanted well glows turquoise in morning light when the sun enters the cave. The highland trails through cerrado vegetation connect a series of natural wonders in compact sequence.
highlights: Fumaca Falls 340m free-fall into a sheer abyss
Poco Encantado's turquoise shaft of morning light
Morro do Pai Inacio table-mountain panorama
Gruta da Lapa Doce cave galleries and dusk bat exodus
gear: Sturdy boots rock slabs waterfall approach
Rain jacket Bahia highland afternoon showers
Swimwear natural pool cave well compulsory

adventures.title: Namibia Brandberg Rock Art Trek
adventures.description:
The Brandberg is a granite blister on the Namib gravel plains - Namibia's highest mountain at 2,573m, rising sheer and alone, its rock glowing furnace-red at sunset (the name means 'fire mountain'). The classic walk climbs the Tsisab Ravine with a compulsory local guide to the White Lady: a delicate figure painted by San artists some 2,000 years ago, centrepiece of one of the richest rock-art mountains on earth, with thousands of paintings hidden through its ravines. Reaching the Konigstein summit itself is a serious two-to-three-day undertaking - waterless, trackless granite that demands a permit, a specialist guide and heavy water carries.

Pair it with Spitzkoppe, the 'Matterhorn of Africa', a day south: granite domes and arches made for scrambling and some of the darkest night skies anywhere. Heat is the variable that dictates everything - hike at first light, carry more water than seems rational, and come between April and September; summer on the rock is dangerous. Watch for desert-adapted elephant along the Ugab riverbed on the drive in. Around £800 covers a week with guides, permits, camping and a hire 4x4 from Swakopmund.
highlights: White Lady rock painting, some 2,000 years old
San rock-art galleries hidden through the ravines
Desert-adapted elephant along the Ugab River
gear: Guide mandatory rock art site protection
Sun protection Namib UV granite reflection

imageAttribution.artist: Greg Willis from Denver, CO, usa

adventures.title: Arctic Ski to North Pole
adventures.description:
The Last Degree is polar travel distilled: 111 kilometres from 89 degrees North to the top of the world, hauling a pulk across sea ice that is itself adrift beneath you. Days are a rhythm of hauling over pressure ridges - blue slabs stacked like ruined masonry - and negotiating leads of open black water that you ski around, bridge, or wait out. Some nights the drift gives your hard-won kilometres back to the sea. Then the GPS finally reads 90 degrees and you stand at the one point on earth where every direction is south, an anticlimax and a lightning strike at once.

The honest logistics matter more than the romance. The Russian-operated Barneo ice camp, the traditional April launch pad, has not run reliably for years; recent seasons have been cancelled or restaged via Svalbard, so treat every booking as conditional, expect date shifts, and use an operator with a track record of handling them. You need the fitness to haul eight hours a day at minus 30, cold-management discipline, and around £25,000 or more when the season actually happens - plus the equanimity to accept that some years the top of the world is simply closed.
highlights: Standing at 90 degrees North, where every direction is south
Pressure-ridge hauling with a loaded pulk
Leads of open water skied round or bridged
24-hour April daylight over the drifting pack
Helicopter insertion onto the sea ice at 89 degrees North
gear: Custom polar pulk and hauling harness
Cold-rated ski bindings checked against brittle failure
Iridium satellite phone and tracker mandatory
Frostbite-prevention kit and daily skin checks

adventures.title: Chile Easter Island Trek
adventures.description: Explore Rapa Nui (Easter Island) — the most remote inhabited island in the world, 3,700 km from the Chilean mainland in the Pacific — on foot and by bicycle, visiting the moai platforms (ahu) that ring the coast and the quarry at Rano Raraku where 397 unfinished statues remain frozen in the hillside. The island is 24 km long; the entire circuit by bicycle takes a day. Hiking to the rim of Rano Kau, the extinct volcano in the southwest corner, rewards with a view of a rare freshwater crater lake in the ocean. The Rapa Nui people maintain strict cultural protocols around the moai.

Rano Raraku moai quarry 400 statues unfinished
Rano Kau volcano crater lake trekking
Birdman ceremony site Orongo cliff edge

adventures.title: Thailand Doi Inthanon Summit Trek
adventures.description:
Doi Inthanon is Thailand's rooftop: 2,565m of mountain rising from the Chiang Mai plain, its summit wrapped in a mossy cloud forest that feels borrowed from the Himalaya. Birders come from across the world for the dawn shift on the Ang Ka boardwalk, where green-tailed sunbirds of the endemic summit race flare iridescent through the rhododendrons and ashy-throated warblers work the moss - two of the four-hundred-plus species recorded in the park. Below the summit, the twin royal chedis stand in flower gardens with a view across the whole range, and the Kew Mae Pan trail (open November to May, local guide required) walks the escarpment rim above a sea of cloud.

Cold is the surprise: summit dawns in December and January hover near freezing - Thailand's only regular frost - so bring a real fleece for the pre-dawn birding and shed layers by mid-morning. Wachirathan and Sirithan waterfalls punctuate the road up, and Karen and Hmong villages inside the park sell some of Thailand's best coffee. November to March is the dry, clear window. Around £400 covers four days from Chiang Mai with a birding guide, park fees and simple lodging near the summit road.
highlights: Royal Project twin pagodas garden view
Summit cloud forest orchid moss drape
gear: Warm layers summit cold early morning 2565m

adventures.title: Mediterranean Sea Sail Race
adventures.description:
Crewing a Mediterranean offshore classic gets you racing pedigree without owning so much as a winch handle. The autumn pairing is the one to chase: the Maxi Yacht Rolex Cup out of Porto Cervo in September, superyachts hardening up along the Costa Smeralda, then the Rolex Middle Sea Race from Malta in late October - a 606-mile anticlockwise lap of Sicily that squeezes the fleet through the tidal gates of the Strait of Messina and past Stromboli, whose crater glows above your night watch as you ghost by under spinnaker.

Berths are winnable, not bought: race programmes recruit through crew lists, sailing CVs and deliveries, and an offshore personal survival course plus genuine miles open doors fastest. Say yes to the delivery trips - that is where you earn the race seat. The Mediterranean's gentle reputation dies offshore in autumn: Middle Sea fleets have been hammered by 40-knot mistral one year and becalmed the next, so bring full offshore kit and a stomach for watch systems. Budget around £2,000 for a campaign of flights, kit and shore costs; the racing itself, for crew, is usually free - paid for in sweat, sail changes and rail time.
highlights: Porto Cervo Sardinia superyacht race start
Strait of Messina tidal race navigation
Stromboli volcano night sailing glow active
Aeolian Islands volcanic chain approach race
Finish line champagne classic race ceremony

adventures.title: Nepal Helambu Valley Circuit
adventures.description: The Helambu Valley north of Kathmandu is the most accessible Himalayan trekking destination in Nepal, a circuit through Sherpa villages, apple orchards, and rhododendron forests without the crowds of the Annapurna or Everest regions. Gosaikunda Sacred Lake at 4380m is the spiritual centrepiece, a Hindu pilgrimage site where Lord Shiva is believed to have formed the lake with his trident. The Laurebina Pass connects the lake with the Helambu valley below.
highlights: Sherpa village apple orchard autumn harvest
Rhododendron Langtang Valley pink April bloom
Day trip Kathmandu Valley accessible short

adventures.title: Kenya Samburu Walking Safari
adventures.description:
Samburu is Kenya's northern frontier distilled: red earth, doum palms along the Ewaso Ng'iro river, and the 'Special Five' found in few other places - Grevy's zebra with their pinstripe flanks, reticulated giraffe, Beisa oryx, the blue-necked Somali ostrich and the absurd, elegant gerenuk standing on hind legs to browse. Leopards den along the river at the highest density in Kenya, and the elephants here are studied by name.

The walking is what changes you. Game walks run in the neighbouring community conservancies - Westgate, Kalama - since the reserve itself is vehicle-only, and on foot behind an armed Samburu guide the bush recalibrates your senses within an hour: wind direction suddenly matters, and elephants at sixty metres feel very different without a bonnet in front of you. Your guides' tracking knowledge, read from bent grass and dung beetles, is the deepest wildlife education on offer in East Africa. The dry months - June to September, January to February - concentrate game on the river. Around £2,500 covers a week mixing a conservancy walking camp with reserve game drives, conservancy fees included; those fees are what keep this land wild.
highlights: Grevy's zebra endangered species Samburu endemic
Leopard highest density Kenya Ewaso River
Somali ostrich blue neck northern endemic
Samburu warrior guide cultural knowledge deep

adventures.title: Morocco Toubkal Winter Climb
adventures.description: Jebel Toubkal in winter transforms from a summer trekking peak into a genuine mountaineering challenge requiring crampons, ice axe, and winter navigation skills. The Normal Route from Imlil gains 2500 metres through snowfield and ice to the North Africa summit at 4167m. December to February delivers the most dramatic conditions with ice couloirs, wind crust, and the extraordinary experience of standing on a summit above the snow line while the Sahara shimmers below.
highlights: Toubkal winter summit 4,167m via ice-crusted slopes
The Sahara shimmering on the southern horizon from the top
Imlil walnut terraces and Berber hospitality
Tizi n'Toubkal col under wind-packed snow

Down jacket summit cold night hut

adventures.title: Russia Trans-Siberian Cycle
adventures.description:
Moscow to Vladivostok by bicycle is about 9,000 kilometres and roughly three months of your life: the Urals, then taiga that runs unbroken for days, the endless birch of the West Siberian plain, and finally the green hills of the Far East rolling down to the Pacific. Lake Baikal arrives mid-ride like a promise kept - the deepest lake on earth, cold and impossibly clear, with the Trans-Siberian railway threading its shore as your constant companion east. Beyond Chita, the Amur highway's vast empty stages begin, and in the Far East forests you are cycling through genuine Amur tiger country - an idea that sharpens evening camp routines wonderfully.

This is a summer-window expedition: leave Moscow in May and ride the season east, because the sums do not work outside it. Truck traffic on two-lane sections, 200-kilometre resupply gaps and mosquito plagues are the real daily adversaries. The paperwork is the variable now: long-stay Russian visas and current entry rules need checking honestly against your nationality before you plan anything at all. Budget around £5,000 self-supported - wild camps, cafes, guesthouses - and pack the patience of a freight train.
highlights: Lake Baikal deepest lake deepest blue overnight
Amur tiger territory Russian Far East cycling
gear: All season gear Siberian weather extreme
Spare parts Moscow departure full toolkit

adventures.title: Australia Ningaloo Reef Dive
adventures.description:
Ningaloo does what the Great Barrier Reef cannot: it starts at the beach. Australia's longest fringing reef runs 260 kilometres down the North West Cape, close enough at Turquoise Bay that you drift-snorkel over coral gardens straight off the sand. The headline act is reliable to the point of near-guarantee: whale sharks aggregate here every year from March to July after the coral spawn, and licensed operators use spotter planes to place you in the water metres from a cruising eight-metre fish - one of wildlife tourism's genuinely great moments, and open to snorkellers, no dive card required.

Divers get the Navy Pier (routinely ranked among the world's best shore-accessible dives) and manta cleaning stations off Coral Bay year-round; humpbacks stream past from July to October and turtles nest on Jurabi's beaches in summer. The variable is simply remoteness: Exmouth is 1,200 kilometres from Perth, so fly to Learmonth and book whale shark boats and accommodation well ahead in season. Water runs 24-28C - a 3mm suit does it. Around £1,800 covers a week with a whale shark trip (about £250), two-tank dives and a self-catering base in Exmouth.

Manta ray coral garden year round glide
Fringing reef walking beach access unique
Turtle nesting Jurabi Point beach rookery

adventures.title: Ecuador Galapagos Land Tour
adventures.description:
You do not need a cruise for the Galapagos. Basing yourself in the islands and hopping the public ferries between Santa Cruz, Isabela and San Cristobal delivers evolution's laboratory at half the cost - and the animals' total indifference to your presence is exactly the same. On Santa Cruz, giant tortoises graze wild through the El Chato highlands like slow boulders; marine iguanas pile up on the white sand of Tortuga Bay; sea lions commandeer the benches of Puerto Baquerizo Moreno. Day boats fill the gaps a land tour cannot: North Seymour's blue-footed booby colonies, the snorkel walls of Kicker Rock with hammerheads below, Isabela's lava fields and flightless cormorants.

The rules are the framework: a US$200 national park fee on arrival, licensed naturalist guides mandatory at protected sites, and strict biosecurity - clean your boots between islands. Ferry crossings are two hours of open-ocean bouncing, so take the seasickness tablets seriously. December to May is warm and calm with the clearest water; June to November brings the cool, nutrient-rich Humboldt flow and peak seabird activity. Around £3,500 covers a week of guesthouses, ferries, day trips and fees, flights from mainland Ecuador aside.

Blue-footed boobies on North Seymour day trips
Marine iguanas piled on Tortuga Bay's white sand
Kicker Rock snorkel with hammerheads below
Sea lions owning the waterfront benches of San Cristobal

adventures.title: Albania Albanian Alps Trek
adventures.description: The Albanian Alps, known as the Accursed Mountains or Bjeshket e Namuna, are one of Europe's last genuine wild frontiers, where Kanun customary law, sworn virgins, and blood feuds echo in remote villages largely bypassed by modernity until 1991. The Peaks of the Balkans trail circuit connects Albanian, Montenegrin, and Kosovar mountain territory through landscapes of extraordinary beauty rarely visited by outsiders. The isolation is profound.

Theth village traditional kulla tower house
Peaks of the Balkans tri-border mountain circuit
Komani Lake ferry approach stunning fjord
Accursed Mountains Kanun culture ancient law

adventures.title: Japan Traverse the Kii Peninsula
adventures.description: The Kumano Kodo pilgrimage network on the Kii Peninsula is UNESCO-listed alongside the Camino de Santiago as one of only two pilgrim routes with World Heritage status. The Nakahechi route from Tanabe to Kumano Hongu Grand Shrine passes through ancient cedar forest, riverside shrines, and oji subsidiary shrine stations over five days. The contrast between sacred natural landscape and dramatic Nachi Falls creates a journey of aesthetic and spiritual power.
highlights: Kumano Hongu Taisha Grand Shrine UNESCO arrival
Nachi Falls 133m Japan highest sacred waterfall
Oji shrine network pilgrim stamp collection
Yunomine Onsen world's oldest hot spring

adventures.title: Norway Svalbard Snowmobile Arctic
adventures.description:
March and April are Svalbard's sweet spot: the sun is back, the island is still frozen solid, and a snowmobile will take you in a day to places a ski expedition needs a week to reach. Guided trips run out of Longyearbyen up Adventdalen and over glaciated passes to Tempelfjorden or clear across Spitsbergen to the east coast, where the sea ice stretches away towards Barentsoya and the polar bear becomes a genuine prospect - watched from a respectful distance, engines idling, beside a guide whose rifle is not a prop but a legal requirement here.

The riding itself is a joy - throttle, balance and 60 kilometres of untracked white valley - but the cold is the variable that separates good trips from miserable ones: wind chill at speed hits minus 30 even on mild days, so use every layer the operator issues and tape hand warmers to your camera batteries. Early season may still deliver aurora above the headlights; by late April the light never leaves. No licence beyond a driving licence is needed, and operators brief novices thoroughly. Around £2,500 covers five days from Longyearbyen with machines, suits, guiding and hut or camp nights.
highlights: Polar bear watched from snowmobiles with an armed guide
Tempelfjorden sea ice beneath Templet's rock walls
The east-coast crossing of Spitsbergen in a day
Spring Arctic light for round-the-clock photography
Barentsburg, the Russian mining settlement time forgot
gear: Polar bear rifle guide mandatory safety
Balaclava face protection wind chill speed

adventures.title: Colombia Cocora Valley Trek
adventures.description:
The wax palms of the Cocora valley are a botanical joke played at altitude: the world's tallest palms, sixty metres of bare silver trunk topped with a pom-pom of fronds, growing not on a beach but in Andean cloud forest at 2,400m. The classic circuit runs clockwise from the trailhead: up the Quindio river on a muddy track that crosses and recrosses the water on wobbling suspension bridges, a steep pull to the hummingbird house at Acaime - where dozens of species mob the feeders while you drink hot agua de panela with cheese - then over the ridge at Finca La Montana and down into the open valley where the palms stand against drifting mist like green candles.

Mud is the constant: this is cloud forest, so waterproof boots or hired wellingtons beat trainers every time, and an early start beats both the afternoon rain and the crowds. You reach the trailhead by shared Willys jeep from Salento's plaza - an experience in itself - and the coffee fincas around town turn the trip into a proper week: tours, tastings and some of Colombia's prettiest streets. December to February and July to August are driest. Around £400 covers a week of guesthouses, jeeps, coffee and unreasonable quantities of arepas.
highlights: Wax palm 60m national tree cloud forest
Salento colonial coffee town base camp
Zona Cafetera coffee farm tour harvest
Spectacled bear cloud forest chance sighting
gear: Rain jacket cloud forest permanent mist
Waterproof boots muddy trail after rain

adventures.title: Sweden Kungsleden Summer Hike
adventures.description:
The Kungsleden runs 440 kilometres through Swedish Lapland, but the northern week from Abisko to Nikkaluokta is the distilled version: above the birch line almost throughout, over the Tjaktja pass at 1,150m, and down the great glacial trench of the Tjaktjavagge with mountains stacked grey and green to the horizon. STF huts every 10-20 kilometres set the rhythm - wood-fired saunas, lake swims, hut wardens selling chocolate in the middle of genuine wilderness - and in July the midnight sun means you walk whenever you like. The classic detour climbs Kebnekaise, Sweden's highest peak, whose melting summit glacier has now dropped it just below the 2,100-metre mark.

Sami reindeer herding is the living culture of the whole route - respect closures during calving and marking. The bogs and river braids are bridged and plank-walked, but mosquitoes rule July: a head net weighs nothing and preserves sanity. Sarek National Park, visible to the south, is the pathless graduate option; the Kungsleden itself needs no navigation beyond attention. Huts take no advance bookings for beds but rarely turn walkers away; STF membership pays for itself in three nights. Around £1,200 covers the week with huts, hut meals and the mountain station splurge at Kebnekaise.
highlights: Kebnekaise summit detour to Sweden's highest peak
Tjaktja pass 1,150m, the trail's highest point
Alesjaure's lake-strewn valley under the midnight sun
Rapa valley overlook into pathless Sarek
STF hut saunas and icy lake plunges

adventures.title: US Alaska Denali Climb
adventures.description:
Denali is the cold test. At 6,190m it is North America's highest peak, but the latitude is what makes it bite: barometric pressure this far north makes the summit breathe like 7,000m, and the weather comes straight off the Bering Sea with nothing to slow it down. The West Buttress is the classic line - a ski plane drops you on the Kahiltna Glacier at 2,200m, and for the next three weeks you move like an ox: double-carrying loads by sled and pack through the crevasse fields to the 4,330m basin camp, up the fixed lines of the headwall, and onto the exposed ridge to high camp at 5,240m, where storms routinely pin teams in reinforced snow walls for days.

Summit day crosses Denali Pass - the route's frostbite factory - before the final ridge to the top of the continent. Nothing here is technical by alpine standards; everything is serious. The variables are weather patience (build a 21-day window and mean it) and cold discipline: minus 40 at high camp is normal in May. Register with the National Park Service at least 60 days ahead. Unguided teams can do it for around £6,000 including flights to Talkeetna and the glacier plane; guided expeditions cost roughly double. May to early July is the season.
highlights: West Buttress Route standard mountaineering line
Kahiltna Glacier ski plane landing base camp
gear: Down suit expedition minus 40 sleeping bag
Sled haul doubles glacier load system

adventures.title: India Spiti Frozen River Walk
adventures.description:
Winter empties Spiti. The passes from Manali close, the tourists vanish, and the high desert valley settles into minus-25 nights, wood smoke and silence - which is exactly when to come. You travel the ploughed river-road corridor from the Shimla side, walking sections along the frozen Spiti river beneath 5,000-metre walls, between villages that winter transforms: Key Monastery's thousand-year tiers rimed white above the valley, Kibber at 4,270m sitting in snow, prayer flags cracking in wind that arrives straight off Tibet.

The honest reason most people come is the snow leopard. Winter drives blue sheep down to the valley rims, and the cliffs around Kibber and Chicham have become the most reliable place on earth to see the cat - local spotters work the ridgelines at dawn with scopes, and multi-day patience is usually rewarded. Cold management is everything: layered systems for minus 25, microspikes for icy paths, and a vehicle-supported itinerary, because self-rescue margins are thin. Acclimatise properly - Kaza sits at 3,800m and winter air feels thinner. Around £700 covers a week with homestays (heated by yak-dung stoves), guides, spotters and permits. January to March is the season.
highlights: Frozen Spiti river walking beneath 5,000m walls
Key Monastery's thousand-year tiers rimed in snow
Kibber and Chicham cliffs, earth's best snow leopard odds
Dawn scope sessions with local spotters
Homestay winters around a yak-dung stove

adventures.title: Western Australia Ningaloo Coast Drive
adventures.description: The Northwest Cape and Ningaloo Coast road from Exmouth through Shark Bay to Kalbarri is one of Australia's great remote coastal drives. Stromatolites at Shark Bay are living descendants of the first life forms on earth, Monkey Mia dolphins receive hand-fed fish from rangers daily, and Hamelin Pool's ancient rock formations predate complex life by billions of years. This drive through geological time ends at Kalbarri's red sandstone gorge country.

adventures.title: Turkey Cappadocia Hot Air Balloon
adventures.description:
You launch in the half-dark, the burner roaring above your head, and as the light comes up the whole absurd landscape of Cappadocia assembles itself below: fairy-chimney valleys, cave-riddled cliffs, and a hundred other balloons hanging in the pink air around you. The dawn flight over the Goreme valleys is rightly one of travel's great set pieces - and the essential tactic is to book it for your first morning, because wind cancels flights roughly one day in three and you want spare mornings in hand.

Between flights, Cappadocia works hard: walk the Rose and Red valleys between rock-cut Byzantine churches, descend eight storeys underground at Derinkuyu, where thousands once sheltered from raiders, tour Goreme's Open Air Museum frescoes, and ride horses - the 'land of beautiful horses' earns its name - through Sword valley at sunset. Spring and autumn (April-May, September-November) give the most reliable flying weather and comfortable hiking; winter flights over snow are magical but cancel often. Around £800 covers a week with a cave-hotel base in Goreme, a standard balloon basket (£150-200 - pay more for fewer people), museum fees and a rental scooter for the valley trailheads.

Rose Valley fairy chimney morning walk
Goreme Open Air Museum cave church frescoes

adventures.title: Iran Alborz Mountains Trek
adventures.description: The Alborz Mountains north of Tehran hide a trekking culture largely unknown outside Iran, with hundreds of kilometres of marked trails through the forests and high meadows above the Caspian coast. Tochal peak accessible by gondola from Tehran provides a day hike to 3964m above one of the world's largest cities, while the remote Alam Kuh north face is a major mountaineering objective. Persian mountain hospitality in trail huts offers genuine cultural exchange.

Alam-Kuh's 4,850m north wall, Iran's big-wall classic
Caspian cloud forest spilling over the northern slopes
Darband trailhead tea houses, Tehran's open-air hiking club
Damavand 5,610m volcano on the eastern skyline

adventures.title: Uganda White Nile Rafting
adventures.description:
The White Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja with the entire outflow of Africa's largest lake behind it, and the rafting is correspondingly enormous: warm, deep, big-volume water where flips end in friendly pools rather than rock gardens. Honesty first - two hydropower dams (Bujagali in 2012, Isimba in 2019) drowned many of the famous rapids. What survives is still world class, centred on Itanda: a Grade V staircase where crews walk the biggest hole and rejoin for the wave trains, and where your guide's 'run or portage' call is the day's defining moment. Safety kayakers shadow every raft, and swimming a rapid here - most people do, once - is a rite of passage rather than a crisis.

The water is 25C, crocodiles keep to the quiet margins away from the rapids, and the dam-regulated flow means the river runs all year; June to August and December to February bring the most settled weather. Jinja itself has grown into East Africa's adventure hub - kayak schools, riverside camps under fig trees, horse trails and the obligatory sunset boat to the source of the Nile. Around £700 covers a week of day runs, a river camp overnight and lodging, with malaria precautions non-negotiable year-round.

Nile Special standing wave surf session
