adventures.title: France Ecrins High Mountain Tour
adventures.description:
The Tour of the Ecrins (GR54) circles the highest massif entirely within France - around 176 kilometres and more than 12,000 metres of ascent looping the Barre des Ecrins, 4,102m, through country that makes the Tour du Mont Blanc feel like a promenade. Ten days link deep, dead-end valleys over a ladder of high cols - Col d'Arsine, Col de la Muzelle, the scree haul of Col de l'Aup Martin at 2,761m - with nights in refuges where the gardien's soup arrives by mule or helicopter. The detour that lifts the trek: the walk up to Glacier Blanc's snout, the massif's great ice stream pouring off the north face of the Barre.

It is a walker's route throughout - no glacier travel required - but the cols hold snow into July and the descents are long and rough, so poles and genuine fitness matter more than technical skill. La Berarde, the historic climbing hamlet at the massif's heart, was devastated by the 2024 floods and is rebuilding slowly; check current route variants through the Veneon valley before you commit. Refuges must be booked ahead for July-August, the only reliably snow-free window. Around £1,200 covers ten nights half-board in the huts - and far fewer people than any comparable Alpine circuit.
highlights: Barre des Ecrins 4,102m crowning the massif
Glacier Blanc snout walk beneath the north face
Col de l'Aup Martin 2,761m, the tour's high point
La Berarde and the wild upper Veneon valley
Refuge nights a valley away from any road
gear: Ice axe optional Barre des Ecrins summit
Hut reservation advance July August essential

adventures.title: Botswana Okavango Delta Canoe
adventures.description:
The mokoro is the Okavango's perfect vehicle: a poled canoe that draws a hand's width of water and makes no sound at all. From the pole seat behind you, your guide pushes through papyrus channels and lily lagoons while you travel at water level - frogs on reeds at eye height, elephants crossing ahead with only their backs above the flood, the delta soundtrack of bell frogs and fish eagles completely unbroken by engines. Days alternate poling with guided island walks among elephant, giraffe and lechwe; nights are fly camps on palm islands with lions audible somewhere across the water.

Hippos are the serious variable, and this is precisely why the poler-guide system exists: they read the channels, know each pool's residents and give them the room they demand - your job is to sit still and trust the local knowledge. The delta's paradox sets the timing: peak flood arrives in the dry season, June to October, months after the Angolan rains, concentrating wildlife onto shrinking islands just as the water spreads. Budget mokoro trails run out of Maun from about £150 a day; the classic week mixing a trails camp with a fly-in lodge runs around £2,800. Malaria precautions and a dry bag for everything are non-negotiable.
highlights: Mokoro dugout canoe pole guide elephant island
Sitatunga antelope reed bed water specialist
African fish eagle call iconic delta sound
Chief's Island lion leopard density reserve
gear: Dry bag all electronics essential mokoro splash

adventures.title: Nepal Nar Phu Valley Trek
adventures.description:
The door to Nar Phu is a slot gorge off the Annapurna Circuit at Koto: a day of cliff-hung trail through dripping rock, and you emerge into a high desert valley that was closed to outsiders until 2002 and still requires a restricted-area permit and registered guide. Phu is the far prize - a fortress village stacked on a defensive ridge at 4,080m, where life runs on yaks, barley and the prayer wheel, and Tashi Lhakhang gompa keeps centuries of unbroken practice. Nar, a day south across ammonite-strewn hillsides, is greener and busier: medieval alleys, chortens banded in ochre, and blue sheep on the slopes above - which means snow leopards are up there too.

The exit is the trek's crescendo: the Kang La at 5,320m, a hard pre-dawn climb rewarded by the entire Annapurna II-IV wall filling the horizon, then a long scree descent to Ngawal on the Annapurna Circuit. Acclimatisation drives the itinerary - you live above 4,000m for days - and accommodation is simple homestay and basic lodge, so carry a proper sleeping bag. October-November and March-April are the windows. Around £3,000 covers the full permit stack, guide, and two weeks door to door from Kathmandu.
highlights: Phu's fortress ridge and Tashi Lhakhang gompa
Nar's medieval alleys and ochre-banded chortens
Kang La 5,320m crossing to Ngawal on the Annapurna Circuit
Blue sheep and snow leopard country above 4,000m
Restricted-area permit: a valley closed until 2002
gear: Yak hire village cargo transport option

adventures.title: South Africa Pilanesberg Game Drive
adventures.description:
Pilanesberg fills the ring of a 1.2-billion-year-old volcanic crater two hours' drive from Johannesburg, and the circular geography does the work for you: game concentrates around Mankwe Dam at its centre. Get to the Mankwe hide before dawn and watch the day assemble — white rhino easing down to drink, elephant bulls shouldering through the thornveld, brown hyena loping home along the shoreline. All of the Big Five are here, and the network of tarred and good gravel loops is fine in a standard hire car, which is what makes this the best-value self-drive safari in South Africa.

Come in the May-September dry winter, when the grass is low and sightings stack up at the water. The catch is the temperature swing: mornings start near freezing in an open vehicle, then climb to shirtsleeve warmth by ten, so pack proper layers, not just khaki. Book Manyane or Bakgatla camps well ahead for school-holiday weekends.

Around £400 per person covers a week of shared car hire, park entry and self-catering chalets — a fraction of private-reserve rates for much of the same wildlife.
highlights: Big Five in ancient volcanic crater setting
Mankwe Hide waterhole dawn wildlife theatre
Elephant bachelor herd daily lake visit
Night drive lion hyena darkness encounter
gear: Self-drive car hire standard saloon fine

adventures.title: Slovenia Soča Valley Trek
adventures.description:
The Soča is the river that makes you doubt your own eyes — a glacial emerald-turquoise, clear to the riverbed, running beneath the limestone walls of the Julian Alps. Walk the Soča Trail from the karst spring at its source in the Trenta valley down to Bovec, then continue on Alpe-Adria Trail stages through the gorges to Kobarid and the Tolmin Gorges, the lowest corner of Triglav National Park. The First World War is everywhere underfoot: this was the Isonzo Front, and the Kolovrat open-air trenches and the Kobarid museum turn a valley walk into a history lesson.

The swim is the moment you will remember — snowmelt holds the river at eight to ten degrees even in August, and the gasp is involuntary. If you extend to Triglav itself (2,864 m, Slovenia's highest), the summit ridge is a protected scramble and the Kredarica and Planika huts need booking weeks ahead in summer.

June to September; Bovec makes the natural base, with rafting and canyoning for rest days. Around £700 covers five days of guesthouses, huts and enormous portions.
highlights: Soca River emerald green impossible kayak swim
Tolmin Gorge turquoise slot canyon swim
Bovec adventure base whitewater kayak centre
gear: Wetsuit Soca River swim cold emerald water
Via Alpina red white marking navigation

adventures.title: Tibet Kailash Parikrama Circuit
adventures.description:
The 52 km kora around Mount Kailash (6,638 m) is the one walk sacred to four religions at once — Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bonpos all circle it, the last of them anticlockwise. Day two is the crux: a pre-dawn start from Dirapuk monastery, under the striated north face, for the long pull to the Dolma La at 5,630 m, a saddle buried in prayer flags, then a knee-hammering descent past the emerald Gauri Kund lake. You share the trail with Tibetan pilgrims doing the whole circuit in a day, and with some prostrating its entire length over weeks.

Altitude is the variable that catches people: Darchen, the trailhead, already sits at 4,575 m and there is no easy bail-out once you are committed. Build in Lake Manasarovar (4,588 m) beforehand and acclimatise properly in Lhasa or Kathmandu first.

Independent travel is impossible — Tibet Travel Permit, Alien's Travel Permit and a booked guide and vehicle are mandatory — so budget around £3,500 for a typical 15-day overland tour from Lhasa or Kathmandu, May to September.
highlights: Kailash kora 5630m Dolma La sacred pass
Tirthapuri hot spring pilgrimage circuit add
gear: Tibet permit China group travel required
Down jacket Tibetan plateau wind cold

adventures.title: Baja California Whale Watching
adventures.description:
San Ignacio Lagoon is the only place on earth where wild whales routinely seek out human contact. Every winter the eastern Pacific gray whale population funnels into three Baja lagoons to breed and calve, and at San Ignacio the friendlies — often mothers pushing their calves forward — come to the pangas to be touched. A 14-metre animal choosing to rest its head under your hand rewires something permanently; the guides never chase, and the whales decide everything.

The season runs late January to mid-April, with February and March the sweet spot for mothers and calves. Wind is the daily variable: pangas go out only when the captains judge the chop safe, so give yourself three or four lagoon days rather than one. The lagoon sits inside the El Vizcaíno Biosphere Reserve, and shore camps such as Kuyimá run comfortable eco-tent operations with daily boat sessions included.

Fly to Loreto or La Paz and drive Highway 1 across the desert, or take a light aircraft to the lagoon strip. Around £1,500 covers a week with camp, meals and whale sessions.
highlights: Gray whale mother calf approach touch experience
San Ignacio Lagoon UNESCO World Heritage
gear: Waterproof bag panga splash open boat
Warm jacket Baja January cool ocean
Camp permit San Ignacio lagoon edge

imageAttribution.artist: Joe McKenna from San Diego, California

adventures.title: Himalaya Kora Around Amnye Machen
adventures.description:
Amnye Machen (6,282 m) is the great mountain god of Amdo, and its kora is what Tibetan pilgrimage looks like away from the crowds: roughly 180 km of high grassland, glacier snouts and mani walls at 4,000-4,600 m, walked in eight to ten days alongside nomad families driving yaks between summer pastures. You will be offered butter tea in black yak-hair tents, pass prayer walls of carved stones centuries old, and quite possibly meet no other foreigners at all.

Logistics are the real difficulty here rather than technical ground. Access runs from Xining across the Qinghai plateau by hired 4WD — two long days — a local Tibetan guide is essential for navigation and courtesy, and you carry or horse-pack everything; resupply amounts to a handful of monastery villages. The weather can throw snow across the trail even in July.

Go July to September when the grasslands are green and the passes clear. Around £2,000 per person covers transport from Xining, guide, horses and permits for the ten-day circuit.
highlights: Amnye Machen pilgrimage kora nomadic Amdo
Tibetan nomad camp yak butter tea ceremony
Glacier face 6282m Amnye Machen summit backdrop
Mani wall prayer stone ancient inscription
Wild yak herd Qinghai plateau encounter
gear: Horse hire Amnye Machen option trek pace

adventures.title: Jordan Dead Sea to Red Sea
adventures.description:
The Jordan Trail runs 675 km from Umm Qais in the olive-green north to the Red Sea at Aqaba, and thru-hiking it takes about 40 days through every landscape the country owns. The section everyone remembers is Dana to Petra: four days descending the Great Rift escarpment through the Dana Biosphere Reserve's gorges, then arriving at Petra the back way — cresting a ridge to find the Monastery (ad-Deir) below you, no ticket queue in sight. South of Petra the trail crosses Wadi Rum's sandstone towers before the final dry ranges drop to the sea.

Water is the variable that organises everything: southern desert stages need caches or vehicle support arranged through the Jordan Trail Association, and four litres a day is a minimum in the warm months. Villages en route offer genuinely warm homestay hospitality — learn a few Arabic courtesies and accept the tea.

Walk it in March-April or October-November; summer is dangerous, and spring desert nights still drop near freezing. Budget around £4,500 for the full traverse with homestays, Bedouin camps and supported desert stages.
highlights: Petra rose-red city treasury approach on foot
Dead Sea minus 430m lowest point earth
Wadi Rum desert towers Lawrence of Arabia
Aqaba Red Sea finish warm water dip

Sun protection Jordan April heat intense
Warm layers desert nights cold contrast

adventures.title: Norway Jotunheimen National Park
adventures.description:
Besseggen is the ridge Ibsen sent Peer Gynt across, and it earns the drama: on one side Lake Gjende glows glacial green 400 m below, on the other the deep-blue Bessvatnet lies almost level with the path, and for an hour you walk the narrowing rock between two colours. Do it the classic way — morning boat from Gjendesheim up the lake to Memurubu, then walk back east over the ridge; the scrambly step below Veslfjellet is far easier going up than down.

Use the rest of the week for the Home of the Giants proper: Galdhøpiggen (2,469 m), Norway's highest, is a guided rope-team glacier walk from Juvasshytta or a longer glacier-free route from Spiterstulen, and the DNT hut network links high routes beneath Glittertind. Weather is the catch — Jotunheimen manufactures rain and summit cloud in any month, so build in slack days and book huts ahead for July and August.

The season runs late June to September, once the Gjende boat starts. Around £900 covers a week of DNT huts with meals, the boat and bus transfers from Otta.
highlights: Besseggen Ridge Ibsen Norway most dramatic
Lake Gjende Bessvatnet blue contrast ridge
Peer Gynt folklore landscape literary tradition
Juvass glacier ski June late season
gear: Hut booking DNT hut network advance
Rain jacket Norway reliable summer precipitation

adventures.title: Greenland Disko Island Arctic
adventures.description:
Disko Island sits across the bay from Ilulissat, and the ferry to Qeqertarsuaq is an event in itself — the Diskoline boat threads an armada of icebergs calved from Sermeq Kujalleq, the most productive glacier in the northern hemisphere. From the brightly painted town you walk out to Kuannit, where columnar basalt cliffs drop to a shore of arctic angelica, and up the Blæsedalen valley between flat-topped volcanic fells. Above town, sled dogs are staked across the slopes: Qeqertarsuaq keeps a living dog-sledding culture that long predates European contact, and summer sled trips have traditionally run up on the Lyngmark Glacier — check locally what is operating.

Midnight sun lasts from late May to late July and turns the bergs gold at two in the morning; humpbacks feed offshore all summer. The ferry is the variable — weather-dependent and not daily — so build a buffer day each way or risk missing every onward connection.

June to August. Around £2,500 for five days including ferries, a Qeqertarsuaq guesthouse and a glacier dog-sled trip. Greenland is never cheap, but this is its most affordable slice of the high Arctic.
highlights: Disko Bay iceberg armada largest in world
Greenlandic sled dog culture Inuit heritage
Basalt cliff seabird colony guillemot auk
gear: Arctic fox patience still approach technique

adventures.title: Kenya Great Rift Valley Walk
adventures.description:
The East African Rift announces itself the moment the escarpment road drops you onto the valley floor, and this walk strings its Kenyan greatest hits southwards from Lake Naivasha. Climb Mount Longonot first — a steep two hours to the rim, then a circuit of the perfect 2,776 m crater with its own sealed-in forest. Continue through Hell's Gate's sandstone gorges, where you walk and cycle among zebra and giraffe, then follow Maasai cattle tracks across the acacia plains to Lake Magadi, a blinding pink-and-white soda pan where flamingos shimmer in the heat haze.

This is walking with an escort, not a waymarked trail: arrange Maasai guides through the community conservancies — it is their land, their route-craft and their snake-lore, and the exchange is half the trip. Heat and water dictate the day's shape; start at dawn and rest out the furnace hours.

Go in the January-February or June-September dry windows. Around £500 covers a week with community guides, camping fees and Nairobi transfers — remarkable value for a geology lesson on foot through the cradle of humankind.
highlights: Rift Valley escarpment dramatic geological drop
Lake Magadi soda ash flamingo pink extreme
Longonot crater volcano climb interior circuit
Maasai cattle herder escort cultural service
gear: Maasai guide Rift Valley pastoral land respect
First aid snake encounter protocol aware

adventures.title: Arizona Grand Canyon Rim to River
adventures.description:
Go down the South Kaibab, up the Bright Angel, and give the Canyon three nights rather than the day-dash the Park Service rightly discourages. The South Kaibab drops 1,450 m in 11 km along an exposed ridgeline — Ooh Aah Point, Cedar Ridge, Skeleton Point — with two billion years of strata scrolling past and no water or shade anywhere on it. Cross the Black Bridge and the Colorado is suddenly loud and cold beneath cliffs of black Vishnu schist. Camp at Bright Angel Campground (or enter the lottery far ahead for Phantom Ranch bunks), day-hike to Ribbon Falls, then climb out past the cottonwoods of Havasupai Gardens.

Heat is the variable that kills here, literally: the inner gorge runs 10-15°C hotter than the rim, and warm-season days demand pre-dawn starts, a litre of water an hour and electrolytes. Spring and autumn are the sane windows.

Backcountry permits go by lottery on recreation.gov about four months out — that, not fitness, is the real bottleneck. Around £400 covers permits, camp fees and Flagstaff or Tusayan logistics for the week.
highlights: South Kaibab sunrise ridgeline past Ooh Aah Point and Cedar Ridge
Black Bridge crossing of the Colorado, 1,450 m below the rim
Bright Angel Campground and Phantom Ranch beside Bright Angel Creek
Ribbon Falls side trip up the North Kaibab trail
Two billion years of strata from Kaibab limestone to Vishnu schist
gear: Water 1L per hour heat mandatory summer
Permit Phantom Ranch advance lottery required
Night hiking headlamp summer heat avoidance
Shelter camp 3 days Phantom Ranch essential

adventures.title: Nepal Gosaikunda Sacred Lakes
adventures.description:
This is two treks joined at the hip, and worth ten days. Go up the Langtang Valley first — rebuilt teahouse by teahouse since the 2015 earthquake buried Langtang village — to Kyanjin Gompa at 3,870 m, with a dawn push up Tserko Ri (4,984 m) for the full Langtang Lirung panorama. Then double back down-valley and climb south via Thulo Syabru and the yak-cheese monastery at Sing Gompa to the Gosaikunda lakes at 4,380 m, a chain of dark glacial tarns where Shiva is said to have driven his trident into the mountain to drink.

At the Janai Purnima full moon in August thousands of Hindu pilgrims climb barefoot to bathe in the freezing lake — an extraordinary thing to witness, and the one week the trail is genuinely crowded. Otherwise you will have the Lauribina ridge largely to yourself.

Go March-May for rhododendrons or October-November for the sharpest skies. Langtang National Park permit and TIMS card required; teahouses run the whole route. Around £700 for ten days from Kathmandu — the closest big-mountain trek to the capital, seven rough road hours away.
highlights: Gosaikunda's sacred lakes at 4,380 m, Shiva's trident-struck waters
Tserko Ri (4,984 m) dawn panorama of Langtang Lirung
Langtang village rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake
Kyanjin Gompa monastery and its yak cheese factory
Janai Purnima full-moon pilgrimage bathing in August
gear: Trekking poles descent steep from Tserko Ri
Tea house route lodging standard available

adventures.title: Chile Atacama Cycling Desert
adventures.description:
Cycling the Atacama is riding across a planet with the atmosphere turned off: zero cloud, ferocious UV, and silence so complete you hear your own tyres on the salt crust. Base at San Pedro de Atacama (2,400 m) and ride out in loops — the Valle de la Luna's salt ridges at sunset, Laguna Chaxa's flamingos out on the Salar de Atacama, the mineral-striped Valle del Arcoíris, and the big one: the pre-dawn climb to El Tatio at 4,320 m, where a hundred geysers steam hardest in the freezing first hour of light.

Altitude plus aridity is the combination that catches people. Acclimatise in San Pedro for two days before anything high, carry five litres minimum on remote roads, and respect the swing — 30°C afternoons fall below freezing by night. A support vehicle for the Tatio day is money well spent.

March-May and September-November dodge both the January altiplano storms and the coldest mid-winter nights. Around £900 for a week with bike hire, a guesthouse base and one supported high-altitude day.
highlights: El Tatio geysers at 4,320 m steaming hardest at dawn
Valle de la Luna salt ridges under a full Milky Way
Laguna Chaxa flamingos on the Salar de Atacama
Valle del Arcoíris mineral-striped rock bands
Absolute desert silence on the altiplano roads
gear: Sun protection extreme Atacama UV zero cloud
Water capacity desert 5L minimum per day
Warm jacket Atacama night temperature drop

adventures.title: India Hampi Historical Trek
adventures.description:
Hampi is what remains when a city of half a million — capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, described by Persian envoys as without equal in the world — is sacked and left for 450 years among granite boulders. The ruins scatter across 40 square kilometres of surreal rockscape along the Tungabhadra River: the Vittala Temple with its stone chariot and musical pillars, the royal enclosure's stepped tank and elephant stables, and the still-living Virupaksha temple, in worship since the 7th century, where the resident elephant blesses pilgrims each morning.

Do it slowly, on wheels and feet together: hire a bicycle for the temple circuit, cross the river by coracle, and climb Matanga Hill for sunrise before the heat — 5 am, headtorch, and the whole boulder city turning gold beneath you is the trip's defining moment.

November to February is the season; by April the granite bakes past 40°C. Guesthouses in Hampi Bazaar and across the river in Virupapur Gaddi are simple and cheap — £200 covers a very comfortable week including bikes and a local guide.
highlights: Virupaksha Temple, in worship since its 7th-century origins
Vittala Temple stone chariot and musical pillars
Matanga Hill sunrise over the boulder city
Elephant stables and royal enclosure of Vijayanagara
Coracle crossing of the Tungabhadra River
gear: Camera wide angle temple scale grandeur
Sunrise alarm Matanga Hill 5am crowd avoid

adventures.title: Japan Daisetsuzan Traverse
adventures.description:
Daisetsuzan is Japan with the volume down and the scale up — the country's largest national park, where the Grand Traverse runs above treeline for days at a stretch. Ride the ropeway from Asahidake Onsen, climb Asahidake (2,291 m, Hokkaido's highest and visibly steaming), then head south across a tundra plateau of crater rims and pumice to Tokachidake's raw volcanic bowl, finishing in the onsen village below it.

This is brown bear country — higuma prints on the trail are routine — so carry a bell and know the protocol. Shelter is spartan: bare-bones refuges such as Hakuun-dake and Kamihoro — some warden-staffed in high summer — and campsites, so you carry food, stove and a proper sleeping bag, and September nights freeze. That timing is the reward, though — Japan's earliest autumn colours torch the plateau in mid-September, ptarmigan turning white beneath crimson leaves.

July to September only; snow lingers into early summer and returns by October. Around £800 including Asahikawa access, the ropeway and huts. Finish in Tokachidake Onsen's iron-red pools, watching steam rise off the range you just crossed.
highlights: September foliage Hokkaido Japan earliest autumn
Brown bear territory Japan wild encounter
Kurodake hut mountain refuge wilderness view
gear: Bear spray Japan Hokkaido brown bear
Rain jacket Hokkaido climate mountain change

adventures.title: Chile Aysén Kayak Expedition
adventures.description:
The Aysén fjords are Patagonia with the crowds subtracted and the consequences multiplied: a labyrinth of drowned valleys, hanging glaciers and Valdivian rainforest where the nearest road can be three days' paddle away. The classic line works the channels around Puyuhuapi and the Queulat fjord, where the Ventisquero Colgante hangs its ice over a 200-metre rock lip and meltwater falls free into the sea beside your kayak. Chilean dolphins ride bows, huemul tracks stitch the beaches, and the silence between rain squalls is total.

Be honest about the grade: 4,000 mm of rain a year, williwaw gusts that arrive without warning off the icefields, and water cold enough to make a swim a genuine emergency. Drysuits, bombproof self-rescue, satellite comms and ten days of food are the entry ticket, and most parties rightly go guided out of Puyuhuapi or Puerto Cisnes.

November to March gives the longest weather windows. Around £4,000 for a supported week — expensive, and worth it for fjords Norway would envy, with nobody else in them.
highlights: Queulat hanging glacier fjord descent spray
Puma tracks beach remote coastal sighting
gear: Expedition sea kayak for exposed Pacific fjord water
Drysuit — Chilean fjord water is a hypothermia risk
10-day food supply for the remote fjord section

adventures.title: Nepal Dhaulagiri Circuit Trek
adventures.description:
The Dhaulagiri Circuit is the connoisseur's answer to the teahouse crowds next door on the Annapurna: a full camping expedition around the world's seventh-highest mountain, with no safety net through its high week. From Darbang the route climbs the Myagdi Khola through terraced villages into an increasingly feral gorge — Italian Base Camp, then the moraine labyrinth to Dhaulagiri Base Camp at 4,750 m beneath the avalanche-raked north face. French Pass (5,360 m) follows, a night or two in the snow-bowl of Hidden Valley, then Dhampus Pass and the enormous descent to Marpha's apple orchards in the Kali Gandaki.

The catch is the compressed altitude profile: you gain height faster than the textbooks allow, and the two 5,000 m passes come back to back — weather days are not extras but part of the plan. Crampons, ice axe and glacier-travel competence are required kit, and porters here earn every rupee.

April-May and October are the windows. Around £3,500 for 18 days with guide, cook crew, tents and permits. Marpha's apple brandy at the end tastes like a medal.
highlights: French Pass at 5,360 m over glacier and technical snow
Dhaulagiri Base Camp (4,750 m) under the seventh-highest mountain
Hidden Valley's remote 5,100 m glacier plateau
Dhampus Pass and the huge descent to the Kali Gandaki
Marpha village apple orchards and brandy to finish
gear: Crampons ice axe French Pass glacier
High altitude camping sleeping bag minus 25
Rope team glacier Hidden Valley crossing

adventures.title: India Valley of Flowers Trek
adventures.description:
The Valley of Flowers does its whole year in three months. From Govindghat on the Badrinath road, a shared jeep and a day's walk up the Pushpawati gorge bring you to Ghangaria at 3,050 m; the national park gate lies an hour above, and beyond it the glacial valley runs eight kilometres deep in July-August bloom — Himalayan blue poppies against wet black rock, drifts of cobra lilies, some 500 species flowering between the avalanche fans. Entry is day-only, no camping inside: you walk in with a packed lunch and out by evening, and that discipline is why it stays pristine.

Give the same trip Hemkund Sahib too — the 4,329 m glacial lake and gurdwara above Ghangaria, where Sikh pilgrims climb singing and the tea at the top tastes of altitude and woodsmoke.

Monsoon is not the catch, it is the point: the flowers need the rain, so waterproof everything and embrace walking in cloud. Landslides can close the Rishikesh-Joshimath road, so pad the itinerary by a day. Around £500 from Rishikesh including jeeps, permits and Ghangaria lodges.
highlights: Peak bloom of some 500 species in July and August
Himalayan blue poppy, the valley's rarest signature flower
Hemkund Sahib gurdwara and lake at 4,329 m
Pushpawati River gorge walk up from Govindghat
Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve's UNESCO-listed core zone
gear: Monsoon rain gear July August constant
National park permit daily limit entry

adventures.title: Myanmar Inle Lake Kayak Trek
adventures.description:
Inle Lake works on stilts: whole villages, monasteries and tomato farms stand in two metres of water, tended by Intha farmers who row standing up with one leg wrapped around the oar. A kayak gets you off the tourist longtail circuit and into the quiet capillaries — floating gardens creaking on their reed anchors, the lotus-silk weavers of In Paw Khon spinning thread from snapped stems, and the creek up to Indein, where mossy stupas crowd a hillside like a stone forest.

Dawn is the lake's hour — mist to the waterline, fishermen posing their conical nets against a white sun — so sleep in Nyaungshwe or a lakeside guesthouse and be paddling by six. November to February is the cool dry season; bring a fleece, because mornings on the water are genuinely cold at 900 m.

Dress modestly for monastery stops and carry cash — nothing takes cards. A local boatman shadowing your kayak solves navigation and lunch at once. Around £300 for the week. Check current FCDO guidance before committing: Myanmar's political situation has kept much of the country off-limits.
highlights: Floating tomato gardens tended from one-oar canoes
Intha leg-rowing fishermen in the dawn mist
In Paw Khon lotus-silk weaving villages
Indein's overgrown stupa forest up a paddleable creek
Nga Phe Kyaung teak monastery on the open lake
gear: Kayak hire Nyaungshwe local boat town
Sun protection Shan plateau heat exposure

adventures.title: Antarctica Weddell Sea Expedition
adventures.description:
The Weddell Sea is the Antarctica that crushed Shackleton's ship, and it still only admits icebreaker-class vessels. Helicopter-equipped expeditions push south along the pack edge for the emperor penguin colony at Snow Hill Island — go in November, while the chicks are still grey and woolly and the fast ice holds — and cruise a coastline of tabular icebergs the size of boroughs, calved from the Larsen shelves. Adélie cities crowd Paulet Island, Weddell and crabeater seals haul out on the floes, and somewhere below, at 3,008 m, lies Endurance herself, found upright and eerily preserved in 2022.

Understand what you are buying: pack ice writes the itinerary in pencil. Helicopter reconnaissance decides daily whether the emperors are reachable, and some sailings never get there — book with operators who say so plainly rather than promise.

Departures run from Ushuaia, November to February, roughly two weeks door to door. From about £18,000 per person in the cheapest cabins — the most expensive trip in this catalogue, and for a wildlife photographer arguably the one.
highlights: Snow Hill Island emperor penguin colony reached by helicopter
Endurance wreck site — found 3,008 m down in 2022
Tabular icebergs calved from the Larsen ice shelves
Weddell and crabeater seals hauled out on the pack
Adélie penguin colonies at Paulet Island
gear: Zodiac launch pack ice navigation safety

adventures.title: Bolivia Yungas Road Cycling
adventures.description: Ride the North Yungas Road from La Cumbre pass (4,650 m) to Coroico (1,200 m) — once the world's most dangerous road, now the world's most famous mountain bike descent. The 64 km route drops 3,400 m in vertical elevation through fog-shrouded cloud forest on a narrow unpaved track carved into cliffs above 600 m drops. Commercial operators provide quality mountain bikes, full-face helmets, and support vehicles following each group. The road surface is loose gravel and clay in places; the speed of descent is rider-controlled. An extraordinary natural environment compressed into half a day's riding.
highlights: Death Road 3600m descent cloud forest drama
Waterfall section wet slippery cliff edge
Coroico valley subtropical arrival warm arrival
La Cumbre pass 4650m road start highest

adventures.title: Scotland Cairngorm Plateau Ski
adventures.description:
Nothing in Britain feels more Arctic than the Cairngorm plateau in February: a granite tableland above 1,100 m where storms arrive at 100 mph and a good winter looks like Svalbard. Based out of Aviemore, mix days on the Cairngorm Mountain lifts with the real prize — ski-touring across the plateau to Ben Macdui (1,309 m), backcountry turns off the Fiacaill ridges and Coire an t-Sneachda, and, in a strong snow year, the classic Nordic through-route of the Lairig Ghru.

Be under no illusion about the skills bill. Whiteout navigation by compass bearing and pacing is the core competence, avalanche awareness is non-negotiable — read the SAIS Cairngorms forecast every morning — and ice axe and crampons live on your pack. The snow itself is the gamble: some winters deliver weeks of Alpine cover, others rain it away, so book flexibly and late.

December to March. Around £700 for a week with bunkhouse lodging, lift days and a guided plateau day. The Ptarmigan at 1,097 m is Britain's highest café — earn your flapjack.
highlights: Lairig Ghru winter ski traverse classic
Ptarmigan restaurant highest in Britain view
gear: Ice axe crampons winter plateau crossing
Nordic ski touring binding Lairig Ghru

adventures.title: Colombia Sierra Nevada Surfing
adventures.description:
Set your expectations honestly and Colombia's Caribbean coast over-delivers: Palomino and Costeño Beach are mellow, sand-bottomed beach breaks, warm as bathwater — but they are the only waves on earth you can ride while the snowfields of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta hang 5,700 m above the palms behind you. Surf camps between Tayrona and Palomino run cheap boards, hammock dorms and bonfires; mornings glass off before the trade winds fill in.

December to March is the season, when the trades push consistent chest-high swell. The rivermouth currents that make Palomino's paddle-out easy demand respect after rain — that is the local catch. Flat days solve themselves: Tayrona's jungle coves at Cabo San Juan, tubing the Palomino river, or four days walking to the Lost City with the Kogi and Wiwa communities whose sierra this is.

Getting there is a beach-road bus from Santa Marta. Around £700 for a week of camps, boards and park fees — one of the cheapest surf weeks in the Americas, with the strangest backdrop.
highlights: Punta Gallinas northernmost South America point
Tayrona National Park pristine beach jungle
Sierra Nevada backdrop snow cap beach unique
gear: Reef shoes coral protection shallow reef
Light wetsuit rash guard sun protection

adventures.title: Himalaya Kanchenjunga South Trek
adventures.description:
Kangchenjunga's south side is what Nepal trekking felt like decades ago: a restricted-area permit, a mandatory guide, and days of cardamom fields, leech-happy forest and Limbu villages before the mountains even show themselves. From Taplejung the trail works east through Yamphudin, then up the Simbua Khola past Tortong to Ramche, where an easy morning brings you to the Oktang viewpoint (about 4,780 m) — and the entire south face of the world's third-highest mountain stands up in front of you, an 8,586 m wall filling half the sky.

Accommodation is basic teahouses with the odd camping night; food turns simple and dal-repetitive high up, and evacuation from this corner of Nepal is slow — treat it as a serious, self-reliant undertaking rather than an Everest-style teahouse highway. Strong parties cross the Sele La to the north base camp for the full three-week circuit.

April-May sets the rhododendrons burning on every hillside; October-November gives the sharpest skies. Around £2,800 for 14 days with permits, guide and porters, via the flight to Bhadrapur.
highlights: Yamphudin village remote far east Nepal
Oktang south base camp 4780m full view
Combine north south complete circuit option
gear: Restricted area permit far east Nepal
Yak hire remote south approach cargo

adventures.title: Portugal Alentejo Wine Walk
adventures.description:
Alentejo is slow walking under Portugal's biggest sky: cork oaks stripped glowing terracotta to the waist, sheep bells, whitewashed villages, and wine estates that treat a dusty walker like a returning cousin. String a week between quintas around Évora and the Alqueva — the walled hill village of Monsaraz floating above Europe's largest reservoir, tastings at estates such as Esporão, and a megalithic detour to the Almendres cromlech, millennia older than Stonehenge. Nights under the Alqueva Dark Sky Reserve end with the Milky Way at full brightness.

If you want drama to bookend the pastoral, finish on the Rota Vicentina's Fishermen's Trail between Porto Covo and Odeceixe, where storks nest on Atlantic sea stacks above empty surf beaches.

Go in March-May for wildflowers or September-October for the grape and cork harvests — high summer regularly passes 40°C and the shadeless plains do not forgive it. Around £700 for a week of guesthouses, estate dinners and luggage transfers. The most civilised trek in this catalogue, and unapologetic about it.
highlights: Cork oak harvest, bark stripped to glowing terracotta
Estate dinners and tastings at Alentejo wine quintas
Monsaraz walled village above the Alqueva reservoir
Rota Vicentina Fishermen's Trail finale on Atlantic cliffs
gear: Comfortable walking shoes cork forest soft
Wine tasting notes estate visits essential

adventures.title: Russia Altai Republic Trek
adventures.description:
Belukha (4,506 m) is Siberia's highest mountain and the Altai's holy centre — twin-peaked, heavily glaciated, and guarded by three days of walking from the last village. From Tyungur the trail climbs the Ak-Kem valley (or crosses the 3,060 m Kara-Tyurek pass for the grandstand view) to Lake Ak-Kem, where the 2,000-metre Ak-Kem Wall fills the head of the valley and glacier melt turns the water a milky turquoise. Kyira ribbons flutter at every pass, and Scythian burial mounds dot the steppe on the drive in along the Katun and Chuya valleys.

This is genuine backcountry: carry or horse-pack full supplies, expect river fords and snow on the passes in any month, and arrange the border-zone permit in advance — Belukha stands on the Kazakh frontier. A local guide earns their keep in navigation and culture alike.

June to August only. Around £2,000 including Gorno-Altaysk transfers, guide and pack horses for an eight-day round trip. Check current visa and access practicalities for Russia carefully before planning — they change, and the flights are the hard part.
highlights: Belukha (4,506 m), Siberia's highest, above Lake Ak-Kem
Kara-Tyurek pass (3,060 m) view of the Ak-Kem Wall
Turquoise glacial water of the Katun and Ak-Kem rivers
Scythian kurgan burial mounds on the steppe approach
Kyira prayer ribbons at the Altai passes
gear: Permits sacred sites Ukok plateau required

adventures.title: Zimbabwe Victoria Falls Walk
adventures.description:
Victoria Falls runs two different shows. February to May the Zambezi is in flood and Mosi-oa-Tunya — the smoke that thunders — earns the name, a 1.7 km curtain whose spray soaks you from half a kilometre away. August to December the river drops and the adventure season opens: Devil's Pool on Livingstone Island, where you swim to a natural rock lip on the very edge of the 100 m drop; full-length rafting through the Batoka Gorge's Class V rapids; and the 111 m bungee off the 1905 Victoria Falls Bridge with the gorge boiling below.

Base in Victoria Falls town (Zimbabwe) or Livingstone (Zambia) and get the KAZA UniVisa so you can cross freely — the widest falls viewpoints are Zimbabwean, Devil's Pool is Zambian. At full moon, book the after-hours entry to watch the lunar rainbow arc through the spray. A Chobe day trip into Botswana, 80 km away, adds the world's densest elephant population.

Around £1,500 for a week including two big-ticket activities; USD cash smooths every border kiosk.
highlights: Devil's Pool swim on the falls' edge in low water
Batoka Gorge Class V rafting below the falls
111 m bungee from the Victoria Falls Bridge
Lunar rainbow through the spray at full moon

adventures.title: Nepal Api Base Camp Trek
adventures.description:
Api (7,132 m) rules the far north-western corner of Nepal, in Darchula district where the country wedges between India and Tibet — and almost nobody goes. The trek to its base camp runs up the Chameliya river valley through the Api Nampa Conservation Area: stone villages where a trekking group is still an event, oak and pine forest, then the last settlement at Ghusa and shepherd pastures leading to base-camp meadows around 4,000 m, with Api's huge snow architecture climbing three vertical kilometres above.

This is expedition-style in logistics if not technicality: full camping, supplies carried in from the roadhead bazaars, a crew who know the far west, and route information that ages badly — trails wash out and bridges move. Getting there is half the undertaking: fly to Dhangadhi, then two long jeep days up the Mahakali corridor.

April-May and October-November. Around £3,000 for a 14-day supported trek. If you want proof the Himalaya still has empty valleys, this is it — you may not meet another party all fortnight.
highlights: Api (7,132 m) base-camp meadows, rarely visited
Chameliya valley villages of the Api Nampa Conservation Area
Ghusa, the last village before the shepherd pastures
Mahakali frontier country wedged between India and Tibet
A fortnight without meeting another trekking party

adventures.title: Spain Camino del Norte
adventures.description:
The Camino del Norte is the pilgrim route for people who would choose a cliff over a wheatfield: 830 km along Spain's green northern coast from Irun to Santiago, five weeks of Basque headlands, Cantabrian fishing ports and Asturian cider country, with the sea at your right shoulder most of the way to Galicia. The first week alone earns the trip — over the hills to San Sebastián's La Concha, the tilted flysch cliffs at Zumaia, and into Bilbao past the Guggenheim.

The Norte's catch is spacing: albergues are thinner on the ground than on the Camino Francés, so stages regularly run 25-35 km, and the route climbs and drops relentlessly for a nominally coastal path. Rain is possible any month — green Spain is green for a reason — and the credencial needs its daily stamps for your Compostela in Santiago.

April-June and September-October dodge the crowds and the worst heat. Budget £900-1,200 at pilgrim pace: municipal albergues at €10-15, menú del día lunches, and the occasional pensión when the Atlantic empties on you.

San Sebastian pintxos pilgrimage start reward
Asturias green cliff path coastal drama

adventures.title: Thailand Koh Tao Scuba Course
adventures.description:
Koh Tao certifies more new divers than anywhere on earth, and the reasons hold up: calm, shallow, warm water on the sheltered west side, marine life that shows up on schedule, and Open Water courses — three and a half days, all kit included — for less than a European weekend course. Sairee Beach's dive schools run like friendly factories; choose one for its instructor ratios, not its bar.

Qualified, you graduate to the real sites: Chumphon Pinnacle's granite towers wrapped in trevally and batfish, White Rock's turtles, and day trips to Sail Rock, the Gulf of Thailand's best pinnacle, with its vertical swim-through chimney. Whale sharks cruise through year-round, with the best odds March to May. Visibility is the variable — the Gulf blows out in the November-December monsoon, so aim for March to September.

A week runs about £500 including the course, fun dives and a beach bungalow; ferries connect from Chumphon and Surat Thani. Do the night dive: switch off your torch and the plankton lights up like green static.
highlights: Sail Rock pinnacle whale shark aggregation
Chumphon Pinnacle grey reef shark school
Whale shark seasonal chance all year

adventures.title: Bulgaria E4 Rila-Pirin Traverse
adventures.description:
Bulgaria's leg of the E4 is the Balkans' best-kept alpine secret: from Vitosha's stone-run plateau above Sofia the route runs south through Rila and Pirin — the ranges that hold every summit over 2,900 m between the Alps and the Caucasus — towards the Greek border. Climb Musala (2,925 m), the peninsula's highest point, traverse the glacial staircase of the Rila Seven Lakes cirque, then cross into Pirin's marble country for Vihren (2,914 m) and the Koncheto ridge, a knife-edge with a steel cable where the drop goes both ways.

The hut (hizha) network is cheap, characterful and gloriously unreformed — dormitories, bean soup, no Alpine booking apps; arrive by mid-afternoon and carry lev in cash. Afternoon thunderstorms are the summer metronome: summit early, be off the ridges by two.

June to September; the Seven Lakes draw weekend crowds, the rest stays quiet. Around £500 for a week of huts and mountain dinners. Detour to the UNESCO-listed Rila Monastery on the way out — its frescoes are the cultural summit of the walk.

Rila Seven Lakes glacial cirque staircase
Vihren (2,914 m) and Pirin's marble ridges
Koncheto knife-edge with its steel safety cable

adventures.title: Chile Huilo Huilo Bioreserve
adventures.description:
Huilo Huilo is a 100,000-hectare private reserve of Valdivian temperate rainforest around Neltume in Chile's Los Ríos lake district — an ecosystem so wet and green it reads as jungle, beneath the glacier-capped cone of Mocho-Choshuenco. Trails wind between 40-metre coigüe trunks and tree ferns to the Salto Huilo-Huilo, where the Fuy river detonates into a basalt bowl; guided treks climb towards the volcano's ice cap, and dusk walks go looking for pudú — the world's smallest deer — crossing the paths. The reserve also runs South America's most significant huemul programme, breeding Chile's endangered national deer for rewilding.

Stay in Neltume village guesthouses or, if the budget stretches, the reserve's celebrated fantasy lodges — the waterfall-topped Montaña Mágica is the one from the photographs.

November to March is the driest window, and it still rains — this forest exists because it rains, so pack accordingly. Around £900 for a week with lodging and guided volcano and canopy days. Fly to Valdivia or Temuco, then three hours by road via Panguipulli.

Pudú, the world's smallest deer, on dusk walks
Huemul rewilding programme for Chile's national deer
Mocho-Choshuenco volcano climb to the ice cap
Ancient coigüe and alerce cathedral forest

adventures.title: Canada Baffin Island Arctic Trek
adventures.description:
Auyuittuq — the land that never melts — is where the planet keeps its most extreme rock walls: Thor's 1,250 m overhanging west face, the biggest purely vertical drop on earth, and Asgard's twin flat-topped towers. The Akshayuk Pass traverse runs about 97 km from Overlord, a boat ride up the fjord from the Inuit hamlet of Pangnirtung, through the glaciated heart of Baffin Island to Qikiqtarjuaq — a week and more of moraine, emergency shelters and 24-hour July daylight under granite that makes Yosemite look domestic.

The river crossings are the crux: glacial melt pulses through the afternoon, so big fords happen early in the morning, linked and deliberate. This is polar bear country at both coasts — firearms are not permitted in the national park, so carry deterrents and follow the protocol from the mandatory Parks Canada orientation, and register every camp.

July and August only. Charter logistics — flights to Pangnirtung via Iqaluit, boat drops both ends — dominate the roughly £5,000 budget for eight days. Cold, committing, and the emptiest great landscape most walkers will ever cross.
highlights: Thor Peak 1250m vertical drop world's greatest
Akshayuk Pass Baffin Island through park
Polar bear territory Arctic tundra constant

adventures.title: Southeast Asia Mekong Cycle
adventures.description:
Riding the Mekong from Chiang Rai to Angkor is the great linear tour of mainland Southeast Asia: about 1,800 km over three weeks, with the river as your handrail and the traffic thinning the moment you cross at Chiang Khong into Laos. The Lao weeks are the heart of it — quiet riverside tarmac and red-dirt lanes to Pakbeng and Luang Prabang (take two rest days: the alms procession at dawn, Kuang Si falls by bike), the long climb inland to Phonsavan and the Plain of Jars if your legs vote yes, then south through Vientiane to Si Phan Don, where the river spreads ten kilometres wide around four thousand islands.

Cambodia brings Kratie's Irrawaddy dolphins, the run in to Phnom Penh — visit the Killing Fields memorial; it reframes everything you ride past — and a finale across rice country to Angkor's moat at sunrise.

November to February is the season: dry, and as cool as this region gets, though 30°C afternoons remain standard — roll at first light. Visas on arrival throughout; USD cash smooths Cambodia. Around £1,200 for three weeks of guesthouses and noodle-stall lunches.

Luang Prabang alms ceremony monk procession
Plain of Jars Laos megalithic mystery ride

adventures.title: Sardinia Sea Kayak Circuit
adventures.description: Paddle around the wild coast of Sardinia — sea stacks, sea caves, turquoise coves accessible only by water, and cliffs of pink and orange porphyry rising from water so clear the seabed is visible at 15 m — on a multi-day kayaking circuit of the island's most dramatic sections. The Gulf of Orosei on the eastern coast is the centrepiece: 40 km of vertical limestone cliffs accessible only by boat or on foot, with hidden beaches reachable through sea cave passages. The Archipelago della Maddalena on the northern coast provides sheltered island-hopping in a Marine National Park.

Costa Verde dune beach isolated boat only
Nuraghe Bronze Age tower coastal archaeology

adventures.title: Nepal Tsum Valley Cultural Trek
adventures.description:
Tsum Valley was closed to outsiders until 2008, and it shows in the best way: this Tibetan Buddhist side-valley off the Manaslu circuit still lives by the shagya code, a centuries-old vow that forbids killing any animal within the valley — wildlife barely bothers to move off the trail. From Lokpa the route climbs through gorge forest into an opening upper valley of barley terraces and chortens: Chhokangparo, Milarepa's meditation cave at Piren Phu, the ancient nunnery at Rachen, and finally Mu Gompa at 3,700 m, a monastery facing the walls that seal the valley from Tibet.

Nights are homestays and simple teahouses; bring cash for everything and accept the butter tea — hospitality here is liturgy. Paperwork is the entry fee: Tsum restricted-area and Manaslu conservation permits, a registered guide, and a minimum group of two.

March-May and October-November. Around £2,000 for 16 days from Kathmandu including the long jeep approach to Machha Khola. Come for the culture and let the mountains be the backdrop — that is the right way round here.
highlights: Mu Gompa (3,700 m) at the head of the valley towards Tibet
Shagya non-violence code — wildlife that does not flee
Milarepa's meditation cave at Piren Phu
Rachen nunnery and its ancient frescoes

adventures.title: Corsica Calanques Sea Kayak
adventures.description:
Corsica's west coast drops into the Mediterranean in towers of orange granite, and the only honest way to see it is from the water. Launch at Porto and work south beneath the Calanques de Piana, where 300-metre spires glow like embers in the evening light, or north along the roadless coast to Girolata — a village still reachable only by sea or mule track — and the edge of the UNESCO-listed Scandola reserve. Check the current rules before you plan: approach limits in the protected core have tightened to shield the ospreys nesting on its sea stacks.

The Mediterranean here keeps a strict timetable: glassy at dawn, thermal wind by early afternoon. Paddle at first light, be ashore by two, and treat the open crossings with respect — swell arrives from weather you cannot see. Wild camping is prohibited on Corsica, so plan legs around the campsites at Porto, Ota and Galéria.

May-June and September give warm water without the August boat traffic. Around £1,000 for a week with kayak hire and campsites. Snorkel every lunch stop — the granite carries on underwater in boulder gardens full of bream.

adventures.title: China Three Parallel Rivers Trek
adventures.description:
Yunnan's north-west corner stacks three of Asia's great rivers — Yangtze, Mekong, Salween — side by side within 50 km, and this trek samples both ends of that UNESCO landscape. Start with the two-day high trail through Tiger Leaping Gorge, a path cut into the wall far above the Yangtze with the 5,596 m Jade Dragon massif directly opposite; the Naxi Family and Halfway guesthouses serve the best-earned fried rice in China. Then travel north over 4,000 m road passes to Feilai Si, where dawn lights the full 6,740 m pyramid of Kawagarbo — a mountain so sacred that climbing it is banned, and no one has ever stood on its summit.

Walk in from there to roadless Yubeng village for the Sacred Waterfall pilgrimage circuit, through forest that holds a quarter of China's plant species.

April-May and September-November dodge monsoon cloud and snow on the passes. Around £800 for a week including Lijiang and Shangri-La transport. Respect the altitude arithmetic: Lijiang (2,400 m) to Yubeng (3,200 m) comes quicker than your body wants.
highlights: Tiger Leaping Gorge 3900m relief trek classic
gear: Warm layers Meili Snow Mountain approach

adventures.title: Montenegro Via Dinarica Trek
adventures.description:
Montenegro owns the most dramatic stretch of the Via Dinarica's White Trail, and a week here delivers the 1,200 km route's greatest hits without the thru-hike. Base first in Durmitor National Park: the Black Lake under Međed's cliffs, the summit scramble of Bobotov Kuk (2,523 m) with half the Dinarides at your feet, and the lip of the Tara Canyon — at around 1,300 m the deepest gorge in Europe, with rafting below when your knees want a day off. Then jump south-east for the trail's wild finale in the Prokletije, the Accursed Mountains along the Albanian border, where the karst turns vertical and the villages still measure visitors per week.

Infrastructure is charmingly uneven — mountain huts, katuns (shepherd summer camps) that will feed you cheese and rakija, and village guesthouses — and so is the waymarking: carry the official GPX tracks and expect the trail to think for itself between valleys.

June to September, with July the wildflower peak. Around £600 for the week — the best-value serious mountain walking left in Europe.

Tara Canyon, Europe's deepest gorge at around 1,300 m
Black Lake beneath Međed's limestone cliffs
Prokletije, the Accursed Mountains of the Albanian border
Katun shepherd camps serving cheese and rakija
gear: Mountain hut booking advance peak season

adventures.title: Mongolia Naadam Festival Trek
adventures.description:
Naadam is Mongolia at full volume: every 11-13 July the three games — wrestling, archery and horse racing — take over the country, and Ulaanbaatar's National Stadium hosts the biggest of it, opening with a pageant of cavalry, standard-bearers and throat singers. The wrestling brackets run for two days of eagle-dance entrances and sudden falls; the horse races happen out at Khui Doloon Khudag on the open steppe, where half-wild horses run 20-30 km cross-country under child jockeys and the finish line is a dust cloud full of galloping families.

Pair the festival with two days at Hustai National Park, 100 km west, where takhi — Przewalski's horses, extinct in the wild by the late 1960s — graze free again after one of conservation's great reintroductions. A ger stay with kumis, fermented mare's milk, completes the education.

The catch is capacity: Ulaanbaatar's beds and internal flights sell out months before Naadam, so book by March. Days are hot, nights genuinely cold, and the steppe UV is fierce. Around £1,200 for five days with festival tickets and Hustai transfers.

Przewalski wild horse Khustain Nuruu herd
Ger ceremony kumiss fermented mare milk

adventures.title: Nepal Island Peak Climb
adventures.description:
Island Peak (Imja Tse, 6,189 m) is the classic first Himalayan summit, and the smart itinerary makes the Everest Base Camp trail do your acclimatisation: Namche, Tengboche, Dingboche, then the branch to Chhukung and an ascent of Chhukung Ri before base camp at 5,087 m. Summit day starts around 1 am — moraine and a rock scramble by headtorch, crampons on at the glacier, ladder-bridged crevasses, and then the crux: 250-plus metres of fixed line up the headwall to a startlingly airy summit ridge. From the top, Lhotse's south face fills the northern sky and Ama Dablam looks small.

Be honest about the skills bill: jumar and abseil technique, crampon footwork and cold management need practising before Nepal, not on the headwall. Ropes queue in peak season, so an extra day in the schedule beats summit-day pressure.

April-May and October-November. Around £2,800 including the NMA climbing permit, guide and teahouses along the EBC route. As a package with Everest Base Camp itself, it is the most complete high-altitude fortnight the Khumbu offers.

Everest Base Camp combination ultimate circuit
Lhotse south face dramatic view from summit
Khumbu Glacier moraine Island Peak approach

adventures.title: Brazil Chapada dos Veadeiros
adventures.description:
Chapada dos Veadeiros is the cerrado — Brazil's overlooked savanna, botanically among the richest on earth — carved into quartz canyons on a plateau of enormous skies. Base in Alto Paraíso or the village of São Jorge and work the classics: the twin 120-metre drops of Salto do Rio Preto inside the national park, the Cânion 2 river gorge, and — with a local guide, as the community requires — Cachoeira Santa Bárbara's implausibly turquoise pools in Kalunga territory, land held by descendants of escaped slaves since the 1700s. Overnight the 23 km Travessia das Sete Quedas if you want the park to yourself at dawn.

Crystal-seamed rock glitters underfoot, rheas and giant anteaters cross the red-dirt tracks, and the night sky is among the darkest in South America.

May to September is the dry season: reliable trails, swimmable pools, cold clear nights. The wet season doubles the waterfalls but shuts the canyons on flash-flood risk. Around £400 for a week with guesthouses, guides and park fees; Brasília is the gateway, three hours by road.

Cachoeira Santa Bárbara's turquoise pools in Kalunga territory
Travessia das Sete Quedas overnight crossing
Quartz-crystal ridgelines of the cerrado plateau
Some of South America's darkest night skies
gear: Sun protection cerrado plateau UV exposed

adventures.title: Kyrgyzstan Alay Valley Trek
adventures.description:
The Alay Valley is Central Asia gone widescreen: a 3,000 m grass corridor between the Alay range and the Trans-Alay wall, whose crest — Lenin Peak (7,134 m) among a hundred kilometres of snow summits — stands across the southern horizon like a second sky. From Sary-Mogol, trek south to the yurt camps at Tulpar-Kul lake (3,500 m), climb through edelweiss meadows to Lenin Peak's Achik-Tash base camp, and top out on the Travellers' Pass (4,150 m) viewpoint, where the mountain's north face and its glaciers fill your entire field of view.

This is nomad country in July and August: CBT-organised yurt stays, kumis offered at every camp, and horses available for any stage. Nothing is technical, but everything is high — a night in Osh (963 m) barely counts as acclimatisation, so build the ascent gradually and expect below-freezing nights even in midsummer.

June to August only; snow closes the valley otherwise. Around £800 for five days with Osh transfers, yurt lodging and a horseman. The Pamir Highway junction at Sary-Tash makes an epic add-on towards Tajikistan.

adventures.title: Alaska Kenai Fjords Sea Kayak
adventures.description:
Kenai Fjords is calving-glacier kayaking with the full Alaskan supporting cast. A water-taxi from Seward runs you down Resurrection Bay and drops you on a gravel beach in Aialik Bay; for the next days you paddle the ice line — holding a respectful half-mile off Aialik or Holgate glacier as they drop apartment-sized slabs with a sound like artillery — between camps under the Sitka spruce. Sea otters raft in the kelp with pups on their chests, Steller sea lions bawl from the rookeries, and on the good days a humpback surges through a bait ball or an orca pod threads the channel past your bow.

Cold water is the discipline: a capsize here is a genuine emergency, so drysuits are standard and most parties go guided unless they hold solid rescue skills. Weather can pin you on a beach — carry a spare day's food and a VHF, and use the bear canisters religiously.

June to August. Around £2,500 for a five-day guided expedition with water-taxi drops out of Seward, itself a spectacular two-and-a-half-hour drive from Anchorage.

Steller sea lion colony rookery noise proximity

Sea otter kelp raft maternal wrap
Humpback whale bubble net feeding fjord

adventures.title: Ethiopia Tigray Rock Churches
adventures.description:
The churches of Tigray are carved into the faces of sandstone towers, and reaching the finest of them is a climb of faith in both senses. Abuna Yemata Guh is the one that changes people: a barefoot pitch up handholds polished by centuries of priests, a ledge above a drop of well over 200 m, then a low door in the cliff — and suddenly you stand in a church attributed to the 6th century, its domes swirling with vividly preserved painted saints, dry mountain air having done what no conservator could. Local scouts rope nervous first-timers; the priest turns the pages of a goatskin bible by the light from the door.

Base in the Gheralta towns of Hawzen or Megab for Mariam Korkor and Daniel Korkor, and add Debre Damo — rope ascent, men only — towards Adigrat.

October to February is dry and clear, with cool climbing mornings. Around £800 for a week with a driver-guide and church scouts. Check FCDO guidance carefully before booking: Tigray is emerging from the 2020-22 war, and access and safety must be verified against current conditions, not guidebooks.
highlights: Abuna Yemata Guh cliff scramble no rope access
Debre Damo monastery rope access historic

adventures.title: Canada Haida Gwaii Wilderness Trek
adventures.description:
Gwaii Haanas protects the southern third of Haida Gwaii, and there are no roads and no trails — you travel as the Haida always have, by water. Kayak parties and guided mothership trips thread the east-coast channels; floatplanes from Sandspit collect the time-poor. The great sites are minded by Haida Watchmen, who welcome you ashore with the histories: the hot pools of Gandll K'in Gwaay.yaay (Hotspring Island), the longhouse depressions at T'anuu, and at the far southern tip SGang Gwaay (Ninstints), a UNESCO site where the last standing mortuary poles lean gently back into the rainforest that is reclaiming them.

Wildlife is constant — Steller sea lions, humpbacks, and Haida Gwaii's outsized black bears working the tide line; there are no grizzlies on the islands. Weather is the boss: Hecate Strait manufactures wind, so schedules bend and buffer days are mandatory.

May to August. Bookings, trip registration and the Parks Canada orientation are compulsory, and daily entry numbers are capped. Around £3,500 guided for five days with kayaks and charters included.
highlights: Haida Watchmen welcoming visitors at the village sites
Gandll K'in (Hotspring Island) natural hot pools
Haida Gwaii black bears foraging the intertidal zone
Steller sea lion rookeries and passing humpbacks

Bear cache food safety Gwaii Haanas

adventures.title: Andaman Islands Diving Adventure
adventures.description:
The Andamans are Indian territory 1,200 km east of the mainland, and their reefs collected the isolation dividend: hard-coral gardens, 20-30 m visibility in season, and fish biomass most of Asia lost decades ago. Fly to Port Blair, ferry to Havelock (Swaraj Dweep), and dive the classics — Dixon's Pinnacle boiling with trevally and snapper, Johnny's Gorge with its resident hawksbills and rays, and schools of bumphead parrotfish grazing the coral like bison. The trophy is Barren Island, India's only active volcano, reached by liveaboard or a long fast-boat day when seas allow: mantas cruising past underwater lava fields and black-sand slopes falling away into blue.

November to April is the season, January to March the sweet spot; Barren crossings depend on settled weather, so book flexibility rather than promises. Permits are straightforward on arrival, but tribal-area and island restrictions are real and strictly enforced — the dive operators handle the paperwork.

A 3 mm suit is plenty in 28°C water. Around £1,500 for the week including a liveaboard leg — cheap for diving this good anywhere on earth.

adventures.title: Iceland Reykjanes Volcanic Hike
adventures.description:
Reykjanes has been the most volcanically productive corner of Europe since 2021 — first the Fagradalsfjall eruptions that made Geldingadalir famous, then the Sundhnúkur fissures near Grindavík — and walking here means walking on rock younger than your boots. The honest promise: brand-new lava fields steaming in the rain, cinder cones you can circle, a landscape rebuilding itself in real time. What nobody can promise is an active eruption during your week — that is luck, and access to live sites opens and closes fast. Check SafeTravel.is and the Met Office hazard maps daily and respect the closures; access around Grindavík changes with every event.

Fill the rest of the week with the peninsula's set pieces: the sea cliffs at Reykjanesviti lighthouse, Gunnuhver's roaring mud springs, the Seltún geothermal slopes at Krýsuvík, and the Bridge Between Continents across the plate rift. All of it lies within 45 minutes of Keflavík airport.

May to September for walking weather and light. Around £500 for a week with a hire car and guesthouses — the Blue Lagoon, when open, is the tourist-priced extra.

Sundhnúkur crater row, Iceland's newest volcanic landscape
Gunnuhver mud springs and Seltún's geothermal slopes
Bridge Between Continents across the plate rift

adventures.title: Pakistan Fairy Meadows Trek
adventures.description:
Fairy Meadows is the front-row seat for Nanga Parbat: a grass shelf at 3,300 m looking straight into the Raikot face, four and a half vertical kilometres of ice and seracs rising to the 8,126 m summit of the world's ninth-highest mountain. Getting there is the filter — from Raikot Bridge on the Karakoram Highway, local jeeps grind up a shelf road most people ride once with their eyes shut, then a two-to-three-hour walk through pine forest delivers you to the meadow's wooden huts and campsites.

Stay two nights minimum: the face makes its own weather, and the reward for patience is dawn silence, the mountain pink, and the Raikot Glacier creaking below. The day-walk continues via Beyal Camp to the viewpoint at the Raikot-side base camp, on the line of the 1930s German expeditions.

June brings wildflowers and May-September is the season; the huts are basic, so bring a sleeping bag and buy food up from Gilgit or Chilas. Around £600 including Islamabad-Chilas transport days. Check current security guidance for the KKH corridor as a matter of routine.

Fairy Meadows wildflower carpet in June
Day walk via Beyal Camp to the Raikot base-camp viewpoint

Pine forest walk onto the 3,300 m meadow shelf

adventures.title: West Africa Sahel Desert Crossing
adventures.description:
Say it plainly first: the FCDO currently advises against travel to Mali and most of Niger, and this journey only exists when the security picture allows — through specialist operators, on current advice, or not at all. What waits, when a window opens, is West Africa's deepest cultural landscape. The Bandiagara Escarpment runs 150 km through Dogon country, villages built under the cliff beside the impossibly perched granaries of the vanished Tellem; Djenné's Grand Mosque, the largest mud building on earth, is re-plastered by the whole town in an annual festival. Far to the east, Agadez's mud minaret marks the door to the Aïr Mountains, where Tuareg guides still travel between oasis gardens and Saharan rock-art galleries.

Travel is 4WD-supported with local guides throughout — non-negotiable for navigation and courtesy alike — and November to February is the only sensible season: cool, dry, with harmattan dust as the trade-off.

Budget around £3,000 for two supported weeks, plus flights, visas for both countries and insurance that genuinely covers the region.
highlights: Dogon cliff village Mali escarpment culture
Air Mountains Niger Tuareg nomad encounter
Djenné Grand Mosque largest mud brick world

adventures.title: Pakistan Hushe Valley Trek
adventures.description:
The Hushe Valley is the Karakoram's beautiful back door: the jeep road from Skardu ends at Hushe village (3,050 m) under the colossal tooth of Masherbrum (7,821 m), and the trail heads north through willow thickets and the rose-briar campsites of Saicho towards two of the range's great sights. First Laila Peak, a 6,096 m spear of granite and ice that may be the most photogenic mountain in Pakistan; then, from Khuspang camp, the pre-dawn climb to Gondogoro La (5,585 m). At sunrise from the pass the Baltoro throne room stands in line — K2, Broad Peak and both Gasherbrums, four 8,000ers at once.

The pass is serious: fixed ropes on the steep flank, crampons and ice axe required, and rockfall builds with the sun, so be on top early. Crossing over to Concordia makes it the full circuit and needs the trekking permit and registered guide; an out-and-back from Hushe trims the paperwork.

June to August only. Around £2,500 for eight days with guide, porters and Skardu transfers. Balti hospitality in Hushe — apricots, salt tea, mountain gossip — deserves a rest day of its own.

K2, Broad Peak and the Gasherbrums in a single line

adventures.title: Maldives Island Hopping Sail
adventures.description:
Chartering a traditional dhoni — the lateen-rigged workboat Maldivians have sailed between atolls for centuries — turns the Maldives inside out. Instead of a sealed resort, you anchor off local islands where guesthouses have only been legal since 2009, eat tuna curry with fishing families, and sail on when the wind suits. Out in the channels of Vaavu and Meemu atolls, mantas feed on the current lines and whale sharks cruise the outer reef edges.

The moment that stays with you is night at anchor in mid-ocean: no engine, no light pollution, the Milky Way doubled in a black lagoon. The catch is the culture shift — local islands are dry (no alcohol) and conservative dress is expected ashore, which is precisely why they have stayed themselves. Sail November to April in the dry northeast monsoon; around £2,500 per person for a week covers boat share, crew and meals, and cash rufiyaa is essential as cards rarely work beyond Malé.

Outer atoll manta ray feeding channel drift

adventures.title: UK Orkney Islands Archaeology Hike
adventures.description:
Orkney packs more Neolithic architecture into a morning's walk than anywhere else in Britain — and it is all older than Stonehenge. The Ring of Brodgar's 36 surviving stones stand on a heather isthmus between two lochs, a short walk from the Stones of Stenness and the Ness of Brodgar dig, where archaeologists have been uncovering a ceremonial complex that upended what we thought Neolithic Britain could build. At Skara Brae you look straight into stone dressers and box beds fitted 5,000 years ago, and at Maeshowe a guide leads you down a low passage aligned so the midwinter sun strikes the back wall.

The walking itself is easy coastal and moorland ground; the weather is the variable. Even in June a 40 mph wind off the Pentland Firth can turn a gentle circuit into a battle, so pack a proper shell. Base yourself in Stromness, book Maeshowe tours ahead (they sell out), and budget around £500 for a week of B&Bs, ferries and buses. May to September brings 18-hour daylight and puffins on the cliffs at Yesnaby.

adventures.title: Canada Coast Mountains Ski Tour
adventures.description:
The Waddington Range is what British Columbia looks like with the difficulty turned all the way up: Mount Waddington itself rises 4,019 m straight out of coastal rainforest valleys, and the maritime storms that hammer the range bury its glaciers in some of the deepest snowpack on the continent. Ski touring here means glacier travel from the first hour — you fly in by helicopter or ski plane from Bluff Lake or Bella Coola, establish camp on the ice, and ski descents measured in thousands of metres with no lifts, no huts and no other parties.

The catch is the weather window. The same Pacific systems that deliver the snow can pin a team in camp for days, so build slack into the itinerary and carry full crevasse-rescue and avalanche kit you know how to use. This is expedition skiing for experienced glacier travellers only. Around £4,000 per person covers the air charter, guide and camp logistics for five days; February to April gives the most settled cold-snow conditions.

adventures.title: Peru Cordillera Huayhuash Trek
adventures.description:
The Huayhuash circuit orbits a single compact knot of ice: seven summits over 6,000 m packed into a range just 30 km long, with Yerupajá — at 6,635 m Peru's second-highest mountain — and Siula Grande of Touching the Void fame at its heart. For twelve days you cross pass after pass above 4,500 m, each one revealing a new arrangement of fluted faces, hanging glaciers and turquoise lakes; the camp at Laguna Jahuacocha, with Yerupajá and Jirishanca reflected in the water, is one of the finest in the Andes.

Do not mistake it for a teahouse trek. There is no lodge infrastructure, resupply is limited to villages days apart, and the altitude never relents — Punta Cuyoc tops 5,000 m. Acclimatise in Huaraz (3,052 m) for at least four days first, and carry cash in soles for the community fees each district charges (budget around £60 total). May to September is the dry season; a guided circuit with donkey support runs to roughly £1,200, while self-sufficient teams can do it for less.

adventures.title: Jordan Wadi Dana Trek
adventures.description:
The Dana to Feynan walk drops through four bioclimatic zones in a single day: you leave the Ottoman stone village of Dana perched on the canyon rim at 1,200 m among juniper and cypress, and by late afternoon you are walking through acacia-dotted desert near sea level, watching Nubian ibex pick across the sandstone walls. Jordan's largest nature reserve funnels an astonishing amount of life through this one wadi — sunbirds, foxes and several hundred plant species along the gradient.

The finish is the point: Feynan Ecolodge, candle-lit and solar-powered on the edge of copper country the Romans mined as Phaenon, where Bedouin staff walk you out to 2,000-year-old smelting slag heaps and the stars come up over the rift. Book Feynan well ahead — it is the only place to stay — and carry all your water for the descent, as the wadi is dry most of the year. March-April and October-November dodge both the summer heat and the winter flash-flood risk; around £400 covers a week with guides and the lodge.

adventures.title: Nepal Annapurna Sanctuary Winter
adventures.description:
In winter the Annapurna Sanctuary becomes a different proposition entirely. The Modi Khola gorge — the only way in — threads beneath avalanche paths that load with every snowfall, and above Deurali you move through a white amphitheatre where the 3,000 m south face of Annapurna I and the fluted spire of Machapuchare preside over near-total silence. Reaching Annapurna Base Camp at 4,130 m in January, with a handful of other trekkers at most, is as close as a trekking route gets to a mountaineering experience.

The gorge is the variable that matters: after heavy snow the avalanche corridors between Deurali and Machapuchare Base Camp can close the route for days, and several lodges shut or run skeleton service. Check conditions in Chhomrong daily, move early while the snow is frozen, and be genuinely willing to turn around. Carry microspikes or crampons and a minus-20 bag in case of an unplanned night out. Ten days from Pokhara at around £900 with a guide — hiring one is standard in the Annapurna region anyway, and in winter it is simple good sense.

Modi Khola gorge avalanche risk winter passage
Annapurna I south face winter conditions raw

adventures.title: Kyrgyzstan Celestial Mountains Ski
adventures.description:
Karakol is the anti-Alps: a Soviet-era resort at the eastern end of Issyk-Kul where £30 buys a day's lift pass, the pistes empty into larch glades of untracked powder, and the Terskey Ala-Too rears 5,000 m peaks behind the top station. An hour east, the village of Jyrgalan has reinvented itself as a freeride base — snowcat and horse-supported touring onto ridgelines that drop 1,000 m through consistently cold, dry snow, with guesthouse dinners of laghman and honey tea waiting at the bottom.

The value is extraordinary but the infrastructure is thin: avalanche forecasting barely exists, so travel with a guide who knows the snowpack, carry full rescue kit, and treat every off-piste line as unpatrolled backcountry — because it is. Bring cash in som (cards work almost nowhere beyond Bishkek) and expect minus 20 °C mornings in January. £1,500 covers a five-day guided package including transfers from Bishkek; January to March is the season, with February usually bringing the coldest, driest snow.

Issyk-Kul Lake largest alpine lake backdrop

adventures.title: Australia Blue Mountains Canyoning
adventures.description:
Two hours from Sydney, the Blue Mountains hide hundreds of slot canyons cut into the sandstone plateau — and canyoning here means committing: once you abseil into the Claustral or Empress Falls constrictions, the only way out is through, swimming glassy black pools between walls a few metres apart, ferns and filtered light far overhead. The Grand Canyon near Blackheath makes a perfect first descent, while Empress Falls ends with an abseil straight down a waterfall.

The water is the variable that catches people out. Even in high summer the canyons run cold enough to sap you through a thin wetsuit, and a storm cell over the plateau can flood a slot in minutes — check forecasts obsessively and never enter a constriction with rain about. Go October to March for the warmest water, use a licensed operator for the abseil canyons unless you are rope-competent, and base yourself in Katoomba or Blackheath. Around £300 covers a week of hostel beds and two or three guided canyon days; national park entry is free on foot.
