On the final day there is music, a festival, and your own wobbling crossing 30 metres above the water.

This trip pairs the rebuilding with the living textile culture of the Cusco region: natural-dye demonstrations with the weaving cooperatives of Chinchero, the Sunday market and Quechua-language mass at Pisac, and quiet time in Cusco's San Blas quarter.

The catch is altitude — the bridge sits around 3,700m and Cusco at 3,400m, so build in two gentle days before the festival — and dates, which fall in the second week of June; confirm the year's schedule before booking flights. Seven days from Cusco with a local guide runs about £950–£1,200.
highlights: Three-day communal weaving of the q'oya grass bridge
Offerings to Apu Q'eswachaka before work begins
Crossing the finished bridge above the Apurímac
Pisac Sunday market and Quechua mass
gear: coca tea or sweets for the road
small soles notes for market purchases

adventures.title: Sicily Crossroads: Palermo to Syracuse
adventures.description:
Sicily has been Greek, Roman, Arab, Norman and Spanish, often within the same building. In Palermo's Cappella Palatina, Byzantine gold mosaics sit beneath an Arab honeycomb ceiling built for a Norman king — the whole island's story in one room. This nine-day west-to-east journey eats its way from Palermo's Ballarò market (panelle from the fryer, sfincione from a bicycle cart) to Monreale's vast Christ Pantocrator, then south to the Valley of the Temples at Agrigento — best at dusk when the sandstone glows — the Roman hunting-lodge mosaics of Villa Romana del Casale, and finally Ortigia in Syracuse, where the Duomo's baroque facade wraps a 2,500-year-old Doric temple whose columns still stand in the nave.

You can do it by train and bus with patience, but a hire car unlocks the interior — Sicilian motorway driving is easier than its reputation.

April–June and September–October give warm seas and bearable sightseeing; August is crowded and furnace-hot. Nine days with agriturismo and B&B stays, car hire and a couple of guided visits runs about £1,200–£1,400. Come hungry.
highlights: Ballarò market street food in Palermo
Valley of the Temples at dusk
Ortigia's Duomo built around a Doric temple
gear: international driving permit if hiring a car

adventures.title: Fes el-Bali: Artisans of the Medina
adventures.description:
Fes el-Bali is the largest car-free urban area in the world: 9,000 lanes where everything still moves by donkey and handcart, and the medieval guild economy never stopped. This six-day immersion gets you past the postcard into the workshops. You watch the Chouara tannery's honeycomb of dye pits from a leather-shop terrace (they hand you mint for the smell), then go deeper: a morning cutting zellige tiles with a mallem at a pottery cooperative, the coppersmiths hammering in Place Seffarine, the Nejjarine museum of woodcraft in its restored fondouk, and Al-Qarawiyyin — founded in 859 and arguably the world's oldest university.

A licensed guide on day one is not a luxury, it is the key that unlocks doors; after that, get lost on purpose — the medina funnels downhill to Bab Boujloud eventually. Day-trip options: the Roman mosaics of Volubilis and the whitewashed pilgrimage town of Moulay Idriss.

Stay in a riad inside the walls. March–May and October–November dodge the heat that turns the lanes into ovens. Six days with riad, guide days and a workshop runs about £650–£850. Haggling is theatre — play your part cheerfully.
highlights: Chouara tannery from a leather-shop terrace
Zellige tile-cutting workshop with a mallem
Sunset over the medina from the Marinid Tombs
gear: comfortable closed shoes for uneven lanes
small dirham notes for tips and taxis

adventures.title: Hemis Tsechu and the Indus Valley Monasteries
adventures.description:
In the courtyard of Ladakh's richest monastery, cymbals crash and the masked dancers turn — the two-day Hemis Tsechu honours Guru Rinpoche's birth, and unlike the winter festivals it happens in high summer, when the passes are open and the barley is green. This is the anchor for a nine-day monastery circuit along the Indus: dawn prayers with the monks beneath Thiksey's giant Maitreya, the 11th-century Kashmiri-school murals of Alchi (some of the oldest Buddhist painting anywhere), Lamayuru's gompa above its eroded 'moonland', and slow evenings in Leh's old town below the palace.

The variable that catches people out is altitude: you land at 3,524m straight from sea level, so the first 48 hours are deliberately empty — hydrate, stroll, sleep. Do not schedule the festival for day two.

Festival dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually late June or July — confirm before booking. Nine days with a driver-guide, guesthouses and festival seats runs about £1,000–£1,300 from Leh. Fly Delhi–Leh; the road alternatives take days.
adventures.location: Leh and the Indus Valley, Ladakh
highlights: Two days of cham dances at Hemis Tsechu
Dawn prayers beneath Thiksey's Maitreya statue
Lamayuru monastery above the moonland badlands
Sunset from Shanti Stupa over Leh
gear: altitude plan and medication (consult your GP)
warm layers for cold desert nights

adventures.title: Timkat in Gondar: Epiphany at the Emperor's Bath
adventures.description:
On 18 January the tabots — replicas of the Ark of the Covenant — leave Gondar's churches under embroidered umbrellas, carried on priests' heads through streets packed with white-robed pilgrims. All night the chanting continues around Fasilides' Bath, and at dawn the water is blessed and hundreds of young men leap the walls into the pool in a spray of green water and euphoria. Timkat, Ethiopian Epiphany, is one of Africa's great living festivals, and Gondar is its finest stage.

You base three nights in Gondar for the Ketera procession, the vigil and the plunge, with the seventeenth-century castles of Fasil Ghebbi and the angel-painted ceiling of Debre Berhan Selassie between ceremonies. Then drive to Bahir Dar for Lake Tana's island monasteries — Ura Kidane Mehret's painted walls are the pick — and the Blue Nile outflow.

Book flights and rooms four to six months ahead; Gondar sells out completely for Timkat and rates triple. Check FCDO advice for northern Ethiopia before committing. Around £1,300–£1,500 for eight days with guide and internal flights from Addis.
adventures.location: Gondar and Lake Tana, Amhara Region
highlights: Ketera procession of the tabots on Timkat eve
Dawn blessing and the plunge into Fasilides' Bath
Debre Berhan Selassie's ceiling of angels
Ura Kidane Mehret monastery on Lake Tana
gear: small denomination birr for church donations

adventures.title: Göbekli Tepe and Mesopotamian Turkey
adventures.description:
Göbekli Tepe rewrote the human story: hunter-gatherers raised these carved T-shaped pillars 11,500 years ago — more than six millennia before Stonehenge — and the implication that ritual may have preceded agriculture still unsettles archaeology. Standing under the canopy above Enclosure D, foxes and vultures carved crisp on six-tonne stones, is as close to the beginning of 'us' as travel gets.

This eight-day route explores Turkey's deep south-east from Şanlıurfa: the city's superb archaeology museum and the sacred carp pools of Balıklıgöl (legendary birthplace of Abraham), the mud-brick beehive houses of Harran, then east to Mardin, a honey-stone town stacked above the Mesopotamian plain, and the working Syriac Orthodox monastery of Deyrulzafaran, where services are still sung in Aramaic. West of Urfa, Mount Nemrut's colossal toppled heads catch the sunrise on their 2,000-year-old summit terrace.

Fly to Şanlıurfa via Istanbul and hire a driver-guide; check current FCDO advice, which warns against travel within 10km of the Syrian border — this route stays clear. April–May and September–October avoid the 45°C summer. About £850–£1,100 for eight days, sıra gecesi music dinners included.
adventures.location: Şanlıurfa, Harran and Mardin, south-eastern Anatolia
highlights: Sacred carp pools of Balıklıgöl, Şanlıurfa
Sunrise among Mount Nemrut's colossal heads
Sıra gecesi music dinner in Urfa
gear: modest clothing for mosques and monasteries

adventures.title: Monasteries of Armenia: Geghard to Tatev
adventures.description:
Armenia adopted Christianity in 301 AD, before Rome, and its monasteries sit in landscapes that make the point emphatically. At Geghard, chambers hewn straight into the mountain hold acoustics so pure that a single sung note hangs for seconds. At Khor Virap, the chapel where St Gregory was imprisoned stands against the full white bulk of Mount Ararat across the Turkish border. And at Tatev you ride the Wings of Tatev — at 5.7km the world's longest reversible cable car — over the Vorotan gorge to a ninth-century complex on the cliff edge.

This is an eight-day road journey from Yerevan: Geghard and the pagan temple of Garni, Khor Virap at dawn, Noravank glowing red in its canyon at dusk, Areni's 6,100-year-old cave winery, then south to Tatev and back via the UNESCO-listed Haghpat and Sanahin in the green Debed gorge.

Go May–June or September–October; July hazes out Ararat and winter closes the passes. Self-drive is easy on the main axes, or a driver-guide costs little more shared between four. Roughly £850–£1,050 per person with guesthouses, khorovats dinners and the cable car.
adventures.location: Kotayk, Vayots Dzor and Syunik provinces
highlights: Sung notes hanging in Geghard's rock-cut chambers
Khor Virap with Mount Ararat behind
Wings of Tatev cable car over the Vorotan gorge
Haghpat and Sanahin in the Debed gorge

adventures.title: Temple-Stay Korea: Haeinsa and the Southern Mountains
adventures.description:
The moktak wooden clapper starts at 3.30am, and by the time you shuffle into the main hall the monks are already chanting. Korea's official Templestay programme opens working monasteries to visitors, and this six-day route pairs the two best: Haeinsa, deep in Gayasan's forests, home of the Tripitaka Koreana — 81,258 wooden printing blocks of the Buddhist canon, carved in the thirteenth century and stored in a hall so perfectly ventilated it has never needed restoration — and Golgulsa near Gyeongju, where the monks practise sunmudo, a meditative martial art you train in twice daily.

Expect 108 prostrations (harder than any summit day), barugongyang formal meals eaten in silence to the last grain of rice, tea with a monk who will answer anything, and free afternoons hiking the Gayasan ridge above the temple roofs.

Book both stays on the English Templestay site (templestay.com) a few weeks ahead; you sleep on a heated ondol floor in loaned uniform, and meals are vegetarian. Access via Daegu for Haeinsa, Gyeongju for Golgulsa. Six days runs about £600–£750 including trains, temple fees and two Gyeongju guesthouse nights among the Silla royal tombs.
highlights: Tripitaka Koreana printing blocks in the Janggyeong Panjeon
Gayasan ridge hike above the temple

adventures.title: Way of St Francis: La Verna to Assisi
adventures.description:
The Camino crowds have never found the Via di Francesco, and that is precisely its gift. You walk out of the beech forest at La Verna — the cliff-hung sanctuary where Francis received the stigmata — and follow ten days of Apennine ridge and oak wood south through Tuscany into Umbria, sleeping in convents and family-run agriturismi. The moment that stays with you: rounding the shoulder of Monte Subasio and seeing Assisi's pink stone spilling down the hillside below, the Basilica glowing in late light.

Stages run 15–24km with honest climbs; the variable that catches people out is the heat bouncing off the valleys in July and August — go in May–June or September–October instead. Sansepolcro (Piero della Francesca's Resurrection) and medieval Gubbio break the walking beautifully.

Start from Arezzo by bus to La Verna; finish with a night in Assisi and a train out via Perugia. Self-guided with luggage transfer runs about £850–£1,000 for ten days; carry a pilgrim credential for the stamped Testimonium in Assisi.
highlights: La Verna sanctuary at dawn before the coaches arrive
Piero della Francesca's Resurrection in Sansepolcro
Gubbio's Palazzo dei Consoli and medieval lanes
Hermitage of the Carceri on Monte Subasio
Arriving on foot at the Basilica of St Francis, Assisi

adventures.title: Highland Maya Markets: Chichicastenango to Atitlán
adventures.description:
Copal smoke rolls down the steps of Santo Tomás church while flower sellers spread gladioli across the stones — Thursday and Sunday in Chichicastenango are among the great market days of the Americas, K'iche' Maya traders filling every lane with textiles, masks and fruit. This eight-day highland circuit starts there, then drops to Lake Atitlán, ringed by three volcanoes, for slow lancha-hopping between villages: the natural-dye weaving cooperatives of San Juan La Laguna, the shrine of Maximón — the cigar-smoking folk saint — in Santiago Atitlán, and painting workshops in San Pedro. You finish among the coffee farms and baroque ruins of Antigua.

What catches people out is the afternoon chop on the lake — cross early, when the water is glass — and the Xocomil wind that makes late boats a soaking. Dry season, November to April, is market weather at its best.

Shuttle buses link everything; no driving needed. Guesthouses and family-run hotels keep costs friendly: about £850–£1,100 for eight days including a guided market day and weaving workshop fees. Learn ten words of K'iche' or Kaqchikel and watch faces change.
highlights: Copal smoke on the steps of Santo Tomás, Chichicastenango
Visiting Maximón's shrine in Santiago Atitlán
Natural-dye weaving cooperative in San Juan La Laguna
Dawn lancha crossing beneath three volcanoes
gear: quetzales in small notes for markets

adventures.title: Ohrid: Byzantine Frescoes on the Lake of Light
adventures.description:
Ohrid once held 365 churches — one for every day — and what survives makes this small lakeside town the Balkans' richest concentration of Byzantine art. The image everyone comes for is real: the Church of St John at Kaneo on its clifftop, lake three million years old below, mountains of Albania across the water. But the substance is inside — the eleventh-century frescoes of St Sophia, and Plaošnik, where St Clement founded what is often called Europe's first university and taught the Cyrillic-precursor Glagolitic script.

Six days lets the town breathe: morning fresco visits before the day-trippers, afternoons swimming from rocky platforms below Kaneo, a boat day to the springs at Sveti Naum monastery where the lake wells up through white sand, and an hour with the Talev family, who have guarded the secret of Ohrid pearl emulsion — made from a local fish's scales — for four generations.

Fly to Ohrid direct in summer, or via Skopje (three hours by bus). July–August brings festival season and crowds; May, June and September are the sweet spot. Around £500–£650 for six days with a guesthouse and boat trips — the Balkans' best-value great town.
highlights: St John at Kaneo on its clifftop at dusk
Boat to the springs at Sveti Naum
Ohrid pearl workshop with the Talev family

adventures.title: Persia Classic: Esfahan, Yazd and Shiraz
adventures.description:
Stand in Naqsh-e Jahan Square at dusk as the tiled dome of Sheikh Lotfollah turns from cream to rose, and you understand why seventeenth-century travellers called Esfahan 'half the world'. This twelve-day circuit strings together the great set pieces of Persian civilisation: Kashan's merchant houses, Esfahan's bridges and blue mosques, the mud-brick windcatcher skyline of Yazd with its Zoroastrian fire temple and Towers of Silence, the dawn light through Shiraz's pink-glassed Nasir-ol-Molk mosque, and finally Persepolis, where Achaemenid reliefs march across the Apadana staircase.

The warmth of ordinary Iranians towards visitors is the trip's real signature — expect tea invitations daily. The logistics need honesty: UK, US and Canadian passport holders can only visit on a guided itinerary with pre-arranged visa authorisation, the FCDO currently advises against all travel to Iran (check the live position before paying anything), cards don't work so you carry cash, and women must wear hijab in public.

March–May and October–November dodge the heat. Twelve days with guide, hotels and internal transport runs about £1,600–£2,000 land cost.
highlights: Sheikh Lotfollah dome changing colour at dusk
Khaju and Si-o-se-pol bridges by night
Yazd windcatchers and the Zoroastrian fire temple
Dawn light in Nasir-ol-Molk's pink mosque
Tea in a Kashan merchant house
gear: cash in euros or dollars to change
copies of passport and visa authorisation

adventures.title: Djenné Mud Mosque and the Dogon Escarpment
adventures.description:
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud building on earth, replastered by hand every spring in a festival of ladders, baskets and river clay. Stand in the Monday market beneath its towers — turbaned Fulani traders, pyramids of dried fish, the mosque glowing like risen bread — and you are looking at a scene essentially unchanged for five centuries. Pair it with the Bandiagara Escarpment, where Dogon villages cling beneath cliffs honeycombed with ancient Tellem granaries, and you have West Africa's most extraordinary cultural journey.

Be honest with yourself about the security reality: the FCDO and most Western governments currently advise against all travel to central Mali, insurance is effectively void, and the handful of trips that run do so with vetted Malian guides via Bamako. This is an itinerary to hold ready for the region's reopening, or to attempt only with serious, current local advice.

When conditions allow, November to February is the cool season. Nine days from Bamako with guide, 4x4 and simple auberges runs around £1,600–£1,900. The Dogon walking is hot but never technical.
highlights: Monday market beneath the Great Mosque of Djenné
Crossing the Bani river by ferry at dawn
Tellem cliff granaries above Dogon villages
Togu na meeting shelters and mask traditions

adventures.title: Sufi Shrines of the Punjab and Sindh
adventures.description:
On Thursday nights at Lahore's shrines the drums begin after dark, and at Shah Jamal the dhol players drive dancers into whirling dhamal trance until past midnight. Pakistan's Sufi tradition is among the most alive on earth, and this ten-day journey follows it south: the great shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh and the Mughal splendour of the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, the mud-brick and blue-tile dome of Shah Rukn-e-Alam rising over Multan, the crumbling tomb-city of Uch Sharif, Shah Abdul Latif's shrine at Bhit Shah with its all-night raag singing, and finally Sehwan Sharif, where the dhamal for Lal Shahbaz Qalandar is a nightly ecstasy of drums, incense and red-clad devotees.

Run this with a Pakistani operator: they arrange the visa invitation letter, a car with driver, and access timed to the music. Check current FCDO advice, particularly for interior Sindh, and dress conservatively — women will need a headscarf at shrines and everyone removes shoes.

October to February is the season; summer is punishing. Ten days with guide, driver and mid-range hotels runs about £1,300–£1,700. The hospitality will floor you.
highlights: Thursday-night dhamal drumming at Shah Jamal, Lahore
Badshahi Mosque and the Walled City
All-night qawwali and dhamal at Sehwan Sharif
gear: small rupee notes for shrine offerings
photocopy set of passport and visa

adventures.title: Voodoo Heartland: Ouidah Festival and the Slave Route
adventures.description:
On 10 January the beach at Ouidah fills with drums, white-robed initiates and whirling haystack-shaped Zangbeto guardians: Benin's national Vodun festival is the most accessible window into West Africa's most misunderstood religion — here, a living faith practised openly, with a public holiday to prove it. Egungun masquerades — ancestors returned in sequinned cloth — sweep through the crowds, and priests pour libations where the Door of No Return faces the Atlantic.

The week around the festival builds context: the Sacred Forest of Kpassè and Ouidah's python temple, the four-kilometre Route des Esclaves walked slowly, the royal palaces of Abomey with their bas-reliefs of the Dahomey kings, and a pirogue out to Ganvié, the 20,000-person stilt village on Lake Nokoué built by the Tofinu to escape slave raiders.

Practical honesty: hotels in Ouidah are few and rough — most visitors sleep in Cotonou (45 minutes) and drive in; book months ahead for festival week. E-visa online, yellow fever certificate required, French essential or bring a guide. Seven days with driver-guide runs about £1,100–£1,400.
highlights: Zangbeto whirling guardians at the 10 January festival
Route des Esclaves to the Door of No Return
Bas-reliefs of the Abomey royal palaces
gear: small CFA notes for ceremonies and boatmen

adventures.title: Great Divide End to End: Banff to Antelope Wells
adventures.description:
The Great Divide Mountain Bike Route is the one every bikepacker measures themselves against: roughly 4,400km of gravel, doubletrack and forgotten forest road tracing the Continental Divide from Banff, Alberta to the Mexican border post at Antelope Wells, New Mexico. You will cross the Divide more than 30 times, and the moment that stays with you is topping Union Pass in Wyoming's Winds with pronghorn scattering ahead and no engine noise in any direction.

The variable that catches people out is water. The Great Divide Basin is a 200km sagebrush void where sources are alkaline or absent, and New Mexico's mesas are worse — carry six litres and treat everything. Grizzly protocol matters through Montana; hang food and carry spray.

Start from Banff (fly into Calgary), resupply in trail towns every two to four days, and budget around £2,800 for six to seven weeks of campgrounds, motels and diner breakfasts, excluding flights. September starters gamble with snow in Colorado; July starters cook in New Mexico. The Adventure Cycling Association's maps and GPX are the canonical navigation.
highlights: Rolling out of Banff beneath Cascade Mountain
Crossing Union Pass in the Wind River Range
The waterless sagebrush of Wyoming's Great Divide Basin
Pie and bunkhouse hospitality at Brush Mountain Lodge, Colorado
The final desert straight to the Antelope Wells border post
gear: Hardtail or rigid bikepacking rig with 2.2in tubeless tyres
Frame, bar and seat pack system
Bear spray and food hang kit
GPS unit loaded with ACA Great Divide tracks
Lightweight tent and sub-zero sleeping bag
Chain links, spare mech hanger and tyre plugs

adventures.title: Tour Aotearoa: Cape Reinga to Bluff
adventures.description:
Tour Aotearoa is New Zealand's signature bikepacking route: 3,000km from the lighthouse at Cape Reinga to the signpost at Stirling Point, Bluff, stitched together from beaches, forest trails, rail trails, back roads and six water crossings by boat. Designed by the Kennett brothers to show off the country's best riding, it delivers: Ninety Mile Beach's hard sand at low tide, the Timber Trail's 141m Maramataha suspension bridge, the Whanganui River by jetboat, the West Coast's glow-worm wilderness trails.

The format matters: official brevet waves leave each February with a 30-day maximum and photo checkpoints, but you can tour it independently any summer month. The variables that catch people out are tide timing on the opening beach leg and booking the river and harbour boats — the Hokianga ferry, Whanganui jetboat and Cook Strait crossing all need arranging days ahead.

Fly into Auckland, bus to Kaitaia, and allow around 25 days at a touring pace. Resupply is easy by bikepacking standards but carry two days' food for the Timber Trail and West Coast sections. Budget around £1,900 with holiday parks, backpackers and the various boat fares, excluding flights.
adventures.location: Cape Reinga to Bluff, both islands
highlights: Ninety Mile Beach on a falling tide
The Maramataha suspension bridge on the Timber Trail
Jetboat leg up the Whanganui River
West Coast Wilderness Trail's glow-worm dell
The Stirling Point signpost at Bluff
gear: Full frame-bag set with dry bags
Tide tables and boat bookings arranged ahead
Sandfly repellent for the West Coast
Merino riding layers for four-seasons days

adventures.title: Otago Central Rail Trail
adventures.description:
New Zealand's original Great Ride follows 152km of the old Otago Central Railway from Clyde to Middlemarch, through the big-sky sheep country of the Maniototo. The gradients are locomotive-gentle, the surface is smooth gravel, and the infrastructure is superb — which is why this is the ride to bring a partner or parent who 'doesn't really cycle' and watch them fall for touring by day two.

The drama is quiet and golden: schist tors glowing at dusk, the twin tunnels and viaducts of the Poolburn Gorge, and the lonely Wedderburn goods shed that Grahame Sydney painted into national iconography. Pub accommodation anchors each day — Chatto Creek, Oturehua, Waipiata — and a curling rink detour at Naseby is obligatory in winter.

Start in Clyde, 2.5 hours from Queenstown airport; shuttle companies move bags between stops so you ride unladen. Four days at 40km a day is the standard rhythm. The variable that catches people out is weather whiplash — Central Otago swings from 30°C summer days to sub-zero snaps, and the wind across the Maniototo can halve your speed. Book pubs months ahead for February–March. Budget around £500 with bike hire, transfers and pub beds; the trail itself is free.
highlights: The Wedderburn goods shed of Grahame Sydney's paintings
Pub nights at Chatto Creek and Oturehua
Schist tors glowing over the Ida Valley
gear: Sun protection — Central Otago UV is fierce

adventures.title: Camino Francés by Bike
adventures.description:
Cycling the Camino Francés compresses the 780km pilgrimage from St-Jean-Pied-de-Port to Santiago de Compostela into a fortnight, and it is a different trip from the walk: you cross the meseta's wheat-sea in purposeful mornings, climb O Cebreiro in one push, and still have hours each day for the cathedral cities — Pamplona, Burgos, León — that walkers limp through.

The etiquette matters. 'Bicigrinos' give way to walkers everywhere, ring early and pass slow, and at municipal albergues you queue for beds behind pilgrims on foot — often not until 6pm — so most cyclists mix private albergues and small hotels booked a day ahead. You need 200km minimum by bike to claim the Compostela; carry the credencial and collect two stamps a day in Galicia.

A gravel bike handles the mixed surfaces best; pure roadies follow the parallel N-135/N-120 corridors. The variable that catches people out is the first day — the Route Napoléon over the Pyrenees is a push-fest with a loaded bike, and the Valcarlos road variant is the wiser line in any weather. Ride May–June or September; budget around £900 for beds, menús del día and the botafumeiro moment in Santiago. Fly into Biarritz, out of Santiago.
highlights: Crossing the Pyrenees to Roncesvalles on day one
Riding the meseta's wheat ocean at dawn
Leaving a stone at the Cruz de Ferro
The climb to O Cebreiro's thatched pallozas
The botafumeiro swinging at the Pilgrim's Mass
gear: Gravel or touring bike with 40mm tyres
Lightweight panniers — albergues have no secure storage

adventures.title: White Rim Road in Three Days
adventures.description:
The White Rim Road is a 160km loop below the Island in the Sky mesa in Canyonlands National Park, riding a sandstone shelf suspended between the rim 400m above and the Green and Colorado rivers below. You drop in via the Shafer Trail's stacked switchbacks and spend three days circling a landscape that looks borrowed from Mars, camping at designated sites with names like Airport and White Crack — the latter arguably the finest desert campsite in America, staring straight into the Maze.

The catch is bureaucracy, then water. Permits for camps release months ahead on recreation.gov and evaporate for spring and autumn weekends, and there is no water anywhere on the route — most groups run a support vehicle carrying 15 litres per person, which also turns the Murphy Hogback and Hardscrabble climbs into unladen fun rather than misery.

Base yourself in Moab, 45 minutes from the trailhead; outfitters there rent 4x4s and run guided supported trips. Budget around £500 per person for a self-organised supported loop including permits, vehicle share and food. Ride April–May or September–October; summer on the shelf exceeds 40°C.
highlights: Dropping the Shafer Trail switchbacks off Island in the Sky
Musselman Arch — a natural bridge you can walk
Camping at White Crack overlooking the Maze
The Green River exit up Mineral Bottom's switchbacks
gear: Support 4x4 with 15 litres of water per rider

adventures.title: Taiwan Round-Island: Cycling Route No. 1
adventures.description:
Taiwan is the only country that has built a numbered national highway purely for circumnavigating itself by bicycle. Cycling Route No. 1 loops roughly 960km around the island: west-coast plains stacked with temples and night markets, the tropical cape at Kenting, and the east's headline act — the Pacific road beneath the Qingshui Cliffs, where green mountains fall 800m into ultramarine sea. Riding 'huandao' is a rite of passage for Taiwanese; locals will cheer you at traffic lights.

Logistics are absurdly friendly. 7-Elevens every few kilometres function as feed stations; police stations offer water and pump loans; Giant shops in Taipei rent quality touring bikes one-way. The variable that catches people out is the Suhua Highway — its tunnels carry heavy lorries, and most riders sensibly hop the coastal train between Su'ao and Hualien, bikes aboard.

Ten days suits a steady 90–100km rhythm. Ride October–November or March–April, dodging typhoons and the northeast monsoon's drizzle. Budget around £950 with small hotels, beef noodle soup and more 7-Eleven coffee than you planned. Start and finish at Taipei's Songshan station, where the Route 1 marker makes the obligatory photo.
highlights: The Route No. 1 marker at Songshan, Taipei
Qingshui Cliffs plunging into the Pacific
Paddy-field riding down the East Rift Valley
Rounding the tropical cape at Kenting
Night-market dinners in Tainan and Kaohsiung
gear: Rented touring bike from a Taipei Giant store
Train timetable for the Suhua bypass
EasyCard for trains and convenience stores

adventures.title: Baja Divide: Tecate to La Paz
adventures.description:
The Baja Divide is a 2,700km dirt-road bikepacking route down the spine of Mexico's Baja peninsula, from the border town of Tecate to La Paz on the Sea of Cortez. It criss-crosses between Pacific surf camps and gulf-side fishing villages via the Valle de los Cirios, where boojum trees and cardón cacti make the landscape look invented, and the old Jesuit mission road through San Ignacio's date-palm oasis.

The riding is slow: sand, babyhead rock and endless washboard mean 60km is a solid day, and fat 3in tyres are the difference between riding and pushing. Water dictates everything — 150km stretches between ranchos are normal, and you learn to love warm sodas and machaca burritos at remote comedores. The moment that pays for it all is dropping to Bahía Concepción and camping on white sand metres from bioluminescent water.

Ride November to March; summer is lethal. Fly to San Diego, cross at Tecate, and allow four to five weeks to La Paz, resupplying in Guerrero Negro, San Ignacio, Mulegé and Loreto. Spanish basics transform the trip. Budget around £1,600 in camps, casitas and taco stands — Baja is kind to budgets, brutal to drivetrains: bring spare pads, sealant and a chain.
highlights: Boojum forests of the Valle de los Cirios
The date-palm oasis and mission at San Ignacio
Fish tacos and resupply in Mulegé
The Sierra la Giganta's canyon roads to La Paz
gear: Full frame-bag kit with dry bags
Sun hoodie and desert-rated sleep system
Spare chain, brake pads and sealant

adventures.title: Cabot Trail Loop, Cape Breton
adventures.description:
The Cabot Trail is a 298km loop around the top of Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, and by consensus one of the great road rides of North America. Riding it anticlockwise from Baddeck saves the drama for the middle days: the road through Cape Breton Highlands National Park climbs French Mountain, North Mountain and MacKenzie Mountain in quick succession, with grades hitting 13% and the Gulf of St Lawrence glittering a sheer drop to your left.

The moment that makes it is walking the Skyline Trail at dusk — a headland boardwalk where moose graze and pilot whales roll in the sea below. The variable that catches people out is wind: the Cape's infamous suêtes can gust past 100km/h on the western flank, and a forecast check each morning is as important as your brake pads for the 12% descent into Pleasant Bay.

Fly to Halifax and drive four hours, or connect to Sydney. Four days with nights in Chéticamp, Pleasant Bay and Ingonish spreads the climbing sensibly; book accommodation early for July–October as options are thin. Budget around £550 with inns and chowder suppers. June brings quiet roads; early October, the best colour show in eastern Canada.
highlights: Acadian fiddle music and chowder in Chéticamp
Cape Smokey's coastal descent to Ingonish
gear: Road bike with compact gearing (34x32 minimum)
Rim- or rotor-friendly spare brake pads
Layers for 15-degree swings between coast and plateau
Rear light for park tunnels of spruce shade

adventures.title: Torino-Nice Rally Route
adventures.description:
The Torino–Nice Rally route is the connoisseur's Alpine crossing: roughly 700km from Turin to the Mediterranean at Nice, strung along the highest gravel roads in Europe — the Colle delle Finestre's 33 unpaved hairpins, the Strada dell'Assietta ridgeline, the Colle di Sampeyre, and the Via del Sale's vertiginous military road along the French–Italian border. James Olsen designed it as a friendly autumn 'rally' rather than a race, but the GPX is free and the route ridable all summer.

Expect 15,000m+ of climbing on surfaces from smooth strade bianche to shattered wartime cobbles. The variable that catches people out is altitude weather: these cols hold snow into late June and catch storms in September, and the high military roads offer no shelter or water for hours — rifugio stops need planning, and Rifugio Don Barbera on the Via del Sale deserves booking.

A gravel bike with 47mm+ tyres or a drop-bar MTB is the tool. Eight days is a strong pace; ten lets you eat properly in the Occitan valleys. Rail to Turin; return from Nice. Budget around £720 mixing rifugi and campsites. The final descent from the Col de Turini to the Mediterranean is the finest reward in Alpine cycling.
highlights: Occitan villages of the Valle Varaita
The Via del Sale's clifftop military road
Descending Col de Turini to the Mediterranean
gear: Gravel bike with 47mm+ tyres or drop-bar MTB
Four-litre water capacity for waterless ridges
Rifugio bookings for the Via del Sale
Spare tyre plugs and pads for long descents

adventures.title: Kokopelli Trail: Loma to Moab
adventures.description:
The Kokopelli Trail links Loma, Colorado to Moab, Utah — 228km of slickrock, sandy wash and canyon-rim doubletrack named for the humpbacked flute player of the desert Southwest. The opening kilometres on Mary's Loop, riding the bench high above the brown coil of the Colorado River, tell you immediately what the next four days will look like: red rock, big air, no shade.

Water is the whole game. Reliable sources are the river itself (silty — bring a filter you trust) and almost nothing else, so most riders cache water at the road crossings near Cisco and Dewey Bridge or arrange a support shuttle from Grand Junction or Moab outfitters. The final day climbs unreasonably into the La Sal Mountains before the long, brake-cooking descent to Moab via Sand Flats Road.

Access is easy: fly to Grand Junction or drive from Salt Lake City, leave a car in Moab and shuttle back. Camp at fixed BLM sites along the route (book the Westwater-area ones ahead). Budget around £450 self-supported with a shuttle, more if an outfitter hauls your kit. April, May, September and October only — summer is dangerously hot.
highlights: Mary's Loop above the Colorado River on day one
Crossing the river at historic Dewey Bridge
The improbable climb into the La Sal Mountains
Descending Sand Flats Road into Moab
gear: Full-suspension or hardtail MTB with 2.4in tyres
Water filter plus capacity for 6 litres
Pre-arranged water caches or shuttle support
Desert-rated sun layers and lip balm
Tubeless repair plugs and spare sealant
Lightweight camping kit for BLM sites

adventures.title: Munda Biddi End to End
adventures.description:
The Munda Biddi Trail — 'path through the forest' in the Noongar language — is the world's longest purpose-built off-road cycling trail: over 1,000km from Mundaring, in the hills behind Perth, to the harbour town of Albany on Western Australia's south coast. It threads jarrah, marri and finally towering karri forest on singletrack and old railway formations, with sleeping shelters spaced a day apart — free, first-come, with rainwater tanks and platforms that make this one of the most tour-friendly wilderness routes anywhere.

The moment that makes it comes near Pemberton, when the karri trunks turn cathedral-scale and the trail rolls through green light for hours. Trail towns — Dwellingup, Collie, Nannup, Northcliffe, Denmark — arrive every couple of days for bakeries and resupply.

The variable that catches people out is pea gravel: the ball-bearing surface on northern sections punishes skinny tyres and overconfident cornering. Ride 2.2in or wider. Go April–June or September–October; summer brings 40°C heat and total fire bans. Fly to Perth, train to Mundaring, bus back from Albany. Twelve days is brisk; sixteen is pleasant. Budget around £900 mixing free shelters with town pubs.
highlights: First night in a purpose-built trail shelter
Bakery stops in Nannup and Denmark
Tingle giants in the Valley of the Giants country
Rolling into Albany's Princess Royal Harbour
gear: Hardtail or rigid MTB with 2.2in+ tyres for pea gravel
Sleeping bag and mat for trail shelters
Water treatment for shelter rainwater tanks
Official Munda Biddi map set or GPX

adventures.title: The Badger Divide: Inverness to Glasgow
adventures.description:
The Badger Divide is the route that made Scottish gravel a scene: 340km of estate tracks, old military roads and forest doubletrack from Inverness to Glasgow, linking the Great Glen, the Corrieyairack Pass, Loch Laggan, Rannoch and the Trossachs. Pieced together by Stu Allan and shared freely, it distils everything good about riding in Scotland into a long weekend.

The centrepiece is the Corrieyairack: General Wade's 1731 military road climbing to 770m over the Monadhliath, a steady cobbled-and-rubble grind with the Great Glen shrinking behind you and a wild descent to Melgarve on the far side. Later comes the private road along Loch Katrine — silky, car-free, and impossibly pretty in evening light.

Scotland's access laws make wild camping straightforward, and bothies exist for those who look; most riders take three days, sleeping near Laggan and Aberfoyle. The trap is resupply spacing — shops are 60–80km apart and close early. Midges own June–August evenings; May and September are the sweet spots. Trains carry bikes to Inverness and home from Glasgow (book bike spaces). Budget around £260 self-supported.
adventures.location: Great Glen to the Trossachs, Highland Scotland
highlights: Loch Ness from the Great Glen Way high line
General Wade's road over the Corrieyairack Pass
Wild camp on the shore of Loch Laggan
The car-free road along Loch Katrine
gear: Gravel bike with 45mm+ tyres or hardtail
Bivvy or lightweight tent for wild camping
Two days' food buffer between shops

adventures.title: The Old Ghost Road Overnighter
adventures.description:
The Old Ghost Road is New Zealand's longest continuous singletrack: 85km through the empty quartz-and-beech country between the Lyell (Upper Buller Gorge) and Seddonville on the West Coast, resurrecting a miners' road surveyed in the 1870s gold rush and never finished. Ridden over two days with a night at Ghost Lake Hut — perched at 1,200m above a sea of cloud — it is as close as mountain biking gets to the romance of an alpine hut trip.

Day one climbs 26km from the Lyell's mossy graveyard to the tops, where the trail tiptoes along exposed ridgeline and the Skyline Steps force a short carry. Day two plunges through the earthquake-scarred Boneyard into Stern Valley, then follows the Mokihinui gorge on a bench blasted above the river, swingbridge after swingbridge, to Seddonville's pub.

Huts must be booked well ahead — Ghost Lake sells out months out for summer weekends — and there is no resupply, phone signal or bail-out between the ends. Weather is the trap: the tops are genuinely alpine and storms close the exposed section. Base in Westport, arrange the shuttle back, and budget around £300 for hut bunks, shuttle and beers. Grade 4 riding: solid technical skills required.
highlights: Ghost Lake Hut above the cloud sea
Ridgeline riding past the Skyline Steps
The earthquake rubble of the Boneyard
Gold-rush graves at the Lyell trailhead
gear: Trail or enduro MTB with dropper post
Hut booking confirmation and sleeping bag
Tubeless plugs and spare brake pads

adventures.title: Katy Trail Across Missouri
adventures.description:
America's longest rails-to-trails route runs 386km across Missouri on the old Missouri–Kansas–Texas railbed, from Clinton in the west to Machens near St Louis. It is flat, crushed-limestone easy riding, but the scenery undersells itself: for long stretches between Rocheport and Jefferson City you pedal a corridor pinched between towering river bluffs and the wide brown Missouri, following the exact line Lewis and Clark mapped in 1804.

The rhythm is small-town America at 20km/h — Sedalia's restored depot, the 1893 Rocheport tunnel, Cooper's Landing's Thai food shack on the riverbank, and a ferry-free detour across the river to Hermann, a German wine town that takes its Rieslings seriously. B&Bs in trail towns book out during October's colour season and June's Katy Trail Ride, so reserve ahead; camping is patchier than you would expect.

Start from Clinton (90 minutes from Kansas City) and finish in St Charles for the best transport links. Five days is comfortable at 75–80km a day. Budget around £600 for B&Bs, café lunches and a glass of Norton in Hermann. Spring and autumn are ideal; July and August are humid and buggy.
adventures.location: Missouri River Valley, Clinton to St Charles
highlights: Riding beneath the Missouri River bluffs at Rocheport
Thai curry at Cooper's Landing riverbank camp
St Charles' restored frontier main street finish
gear: Gravel or hybrid bike with 35mm+ tyres
Rack and panniers for B&B touring

adventures.title: Coast to Coast Costa Rica: Ruta de los Conquistadores
adventures.description:
La Ruta de los Conquistadores crosses Costa Rica from the Pacific to the Caribbean, tracing (in reverse) the sixteenth-century route of Spanish conquistador Juan de Cavallón. The race version crams roughly 270km and 8,000m of climbing into three days each November; toured over four days with vehicle support, it becomes one of the world's great mountain bike traverses rather than an exercise in suffering — though the two are never far apart here.

From the beach at Jacó you climb into rainforest where the 'road' is a river of volcanic mud that swallows shoes whole, cross shoulder country between the Irazú and Turrialba volcanoes at over 3,000m — cold enough for full winter kit within sight of the tropics — and finish with banana-plantation railbed and beach riding into Limón on the Caribbean.

The variable that catches people out is the mud-to-altitude double: you will be soaked at 35°C and shivering at 5°C in the same 24 hours. Go with a Costa Rican operator (most run supported tours outside race week) from San José. Budget around £1,900 for a guided, supported crossing with hotels and meals. Ride the December–March dry season unless you are racing.
highlights: Dawn wheel-dip in the Pacific at Jacó
Crossing the flank of Irazú volcano above 3,000m
Coffee-farm tracks in the Orosi Valley
Rolling onto the Caribbean sand at Limón
gear: Full waterproofs and thermal layer for volcano passes
Spare mech hanger and quick links

adventures.title: King Alfred's Way Loop
adventures.description:
King Alfred's Way is Cycling UK's 350km circular route through 10,000 years of English history, looping from Winchester — King Alfred's capital — across Salisbury Plain to Stonehenge, through the stone circle at Avebury (you ride between the sarsens), along the ancient chalk highway of the Ridgeway, and back over the Surrey Hills and South Downs. Nowhere else can you link four UNESCO-calibre prehistoric landscapes on legal bridleways in a long weekend.

The riding is deceptively hard work: endless short, steep chalk climbs, rutted byways, and the sandy tank tracks around the military training areas. The variable that catches people out is chalk in the wet — after rain the Ridgeway becomes a skating rink of slime that doubles journey times and coats drivetrains, so watch the forecast and pack patience in spring.

Winchester is an hour from London by train. Four days at 85–90km suits a fit gravel rider; five is kinder. Off-route villages supply pubs and B&Bs — Amesbury, Marlborough, Goring — and Cycling UK's guidebook and GPX are definitive. Budget around £350 with pub beds and cream teas, far less camping.
highlights: Rolling out from Winchester's Great Hall
Stonehenge from the byway across Salisbury Plain
Riding between the standing stones at Avebury
Devil's Punch Bowl on the Surrey leg
gear: Gravel bike with 45mm tyres or short-travel MTB
Mud tyres and clearance if riding spring
Cycling UK guidebook or GPX tracks
Spare mech hanger for rutted byways

adventures.title: Mawson Trail: Adelaide to Blinman
adventures.description:
The Mawson Trail runs 900km from Adelaide's foothills to Blinman, the highest town in South Australia, riding gravel farm roads, station tracks and vineyard lanes named for the Antarctic explorer Douglas Mawson. It is Australia's classic inland gravel journey: you start among Barossa and Clare Valley vines, pass Burra's copper-rush ruins, and watch the country dry and redden until the Flinders Ranges lift out of the saltbush like the exposed keel of a continent.

The finale is the reason to come: threading Bunyeroo Valley's razorback ridges at golden hour, skirting the ramparts of Wilpena Pound, and climbing through the ochre gorges to Blinman's pub. The variable that catches people out is water and heat planning — north of Burra the towns thin dramatically, tank water needs treating, and a warm spell can push 35°C even in October.

Ride April–May or September–October; summer is off the table. Nine days is a strong tourer's pace at around 100km/day. Resupply carefully at Clare, Burra, Melrose and Hawker. Fly to Adelaide; arrange a shuttle back from the Flinders. Budget around £800 with pubs, caravan parks and a celebratory Blinman counter meal.
adventures.location: Adelaide Hills to the Flinders Ranges
highlights: Vineyard gravel through the Clare Valley
Bunyeroo Valley's razorback ridges at dusk
gear: Gravel bike with 45mm+ tyres or hardtail
Six-litre water capacity north of Burra
Sun protection rated for outback UV
GPX tracks — signage is good but sparse

adventures.title: Pittsburgh to Washington: GAP and C&O Towpath
adventures.description:
Two historic corridors join end-to-end into 539km of car-free riding from Pittsburgh's Point State Park to Mile 0 in Georgetown, Washington DC. The Great Allegheny Passage climbs almost imperceptibly on a crushed-limestone railbed through the Laurel Highlands, crests the Eastern Continental Divide inside the Big Savage Tunnel, then hands you to the Chesapeake & Ohio Canal towpath at Cumberland for a gentle fall along the Potomac all the way to the capital.

The moment that makes it is bursting out of Big Savage's southern portal to find Maryland unrolled below you and 32km of freewheeling into Cumberland. The variable that catches people out is the C&O itself: after rain the towpath turns to peanut butter, and the unlit 950m Paw Paw Tunnel — torch essential — has a rough, narrow boardwalk above the old canal.

Ride it eastbound for the net downhill. Trail towns (Ohiopyle, Confluence, Meyersdale, Hancock, Harpers Ferry) space food and beds conveniently, and free hiker-biker campsites line the C&O every 8km or so. Six days at 90km/day is comfortable. Amtrak's Capitol Limited links DC back to Pittsburgh with roll-on bike service. Budget around £700 mixing B&Bs and camping.
highlights: Cresting the Eastern Continental Divide in Big Savage Tunnel
Torch-lit passage of the Paw Paw Tunnel
Harpers Ferry from the Potomac footbridge
Rolling into Georgetown at C&O Mile 0
gear: Gravel or touring bike with 38mm+ tyres
Front and rear lights for long tunnels
Camp kit for C&O hiker-biker sites
Amtrak bike reservation for the return

adventures.title: Sardinia Gravel Traverse: Olbia to Cagliari
adventures.description:
Ride the length of Sardinia on the white gravel roads shepherds have used for centuries: roughly 500km from Olbia in the north to Cagliari on the southern gulf, through the cork-oak hills of Gallura, over the limestone karst of the Supramonte above Oliena, and across the granite shoulders of the Gennargentu, the island's wild heart. Inland Sardinia is startlingly empty — you can ride three hours between villages, sharing the strade bianche with sheep and the occasional bemused shepherd.

The cultural texture makes it: pane carasau and pecorino from village alimentari, the murals of Orgosolo, and nuraghi — Bronze Age stone towers — on hilltops like punctuation. The variable that catches people out is resupply rhythm: shops shut 1pm–5pm sharp, so carry lunch and shop mornings.

May and October are ideal; high summer cooks the interior above 35°C. A gravel bike with 45mm tyres handles everything. Ferries and flights serve Olbia; Cagliari flies home direct. Seven days at 70km/day of chunky climbing suits strong riders — this island is never flat. Budget around £850 with agriturismo dinners, B&Bs and a seafood blowout in Cagliari's Marina district.
highlights: The Supramonte's limestone ramparts above Oliena
Bronze Age nuraghi on empty hilltops
Seafood finish in Cagliari's Marina quarter
gear: Sun kit for exposed karst plateaus

adventures.title: Southern Gulf Islands by Bike and Ferry
adventures.description:
Between Vancouver and Vancouver Island, the Southern Gulf Islands scatter across the Salish Sea like a decommissioned mountain range, and BC Ferries functions as your sag wagon between them. The classic five-day hop links Salt Spring, Pender, Mayne and Galiano: short, punchy island roads (nothing here is flat), farm-gate honesty stands, and ferry decks where you stand with your bike watching for orcas in Active Pass.

Salt Spring is the hub — ride from Fulford Harbour up to Ganges for the Saturday market, and grind the 25% ramps of Mount Maxwell if your gearing allows. On South Pender, the short hike up Mount Norman buys you the whole archipelago in one view. Galiano saves the best evening: Montague Harbour's shell beach at sunset, cider in hand.

Start from Swartz Bay near Victoria via the Fulford crossing. The variable that catches people out is the ferry schedule — inter-island sailings can be three hours apart, so build each day around the timetable. Budget around £650 with B&Bs and all ferry fares; camping at Ruckle Park and Montague Harbour cuts that sharply. May to September is prime.
highlights: Salt Spring Saturday Market in Ganges
Orca watching from the ferry deck in Active Pass
Mount Norman lookout over the archipelago
Georgina Point lighthouse on Mayne Island
Sunset on Montague Harbour's shell beach
gear: Gravel or touring bike with low climbing gears
BC Ferries timetable app and cash for honesty stands
Light rain shell for marine squalls
Camp kit if using Ruckle and Montague sites

adventures.title: Natchez Trace Parkway by Road Bike
adventures.description:
The Natchez Trace Parkway is 715km of commercial-traffic-free tarmac from Natchez, Mississippi to just south of Nashville, Tennessee, shadowing a footpath used for 10,000 years by Choctaw and Natchez people, boatmen walking home from New Orleans, and the highwaymen who preyed on them. No lorries, no billboards, a 50mph limit: the easiest long-distance road tour in America to love.

The moments that stick are quiet ones — wheels humming past the sunken Trace where two centuries of feet wore the path below ground level, dawn mist on the Cypress Swamp boardwalk, and the double-arched bridge at Birdsong Hollow lifting you 47m above the valley on the final day. The catch is services: the Parkway itself has almost none, so you leave it for food and beds in towns like Port Gibson, Kosciusko and Tupelo, and some gaps demand 90km between resupply. Three free bicycle-only campgrounds help the budget.

Fly into Jackson via connections or start from New Orleans with a bus to Natchez. Seven days at around 100km/day suits a fit tourer. Budget roughly £700 in motels and diners. Ride spring for dogwood blossom or October for colour; summer is a steam bath.
adventures.location: Natchez Trace Parkway, Mississippi to Tennessee
highlights: Emerald Mound — one of America's largest pre-Columbian earthworks
Walking the sunken Trace near Port Gibson
Dawn on the Cypress Swamp boardwalk
Crossing the Tennessee River at Colbert Ferry
The double-arch bridge at Birdsong Hollow
gear: Road or light touring bike with 28-32mm tyres
High-vis layers and daytime running lights
Two large bottles plus backup bladder for long gaps
Basic camping kit for the free cyclist campgrounds

adventures.title: Silfra Fissure: Diving Between Continents
adventures.description:
Silfra is the only dive site where you hang in the crack between two continents. The North American and Eurasian plates pull apart a couple of centimetres a year at Þingvellir, and the fissure fills with glacial meltwater that has spent decades filtering through lava. The result is visibility beyond 100 metres and a blue that does not look real. In the narrows you can put one glove on each continental plate; in the Cathedral the walls fall away beneath you in gin-clear silence.

The water is 2-4°C in every month, so this is a drysuit dive: operators require a drysuit certification or about ten logged drysuit dives. Without one, snorkelling the fissure in a provided suit is nearly as good and needs no card at all.

Silfra sits 45 minutes from Reykjavik, so a long weekend covers it, with a second day at Davíðsgjá in Þingvallavatn or a lava-cave walk. A guided double dive runs about £280 and a three-day trip lands comfortably under £600 before flights. Summer gives easy logistics; winter pairs the fissure with the aurora.
highlights: Touching both tectonic plates in the Silfra narrows
Glacial water filtered for decades through lava
Second-day dive at Davíðsgjá in Þingvallavatn
Hot chocolate ritual at the Silfra car park
gear: Drysuit certification or 10+ logged drysuit dives
Thermal base layers and thick socks

adventures.title: Great Blue Hole and Lighthouse Reef Atoll
adventures.description:
From the air it is a perfect navy circle punched into turquoise; from the dive deck it is oddly quiet water. You drop over the rim at Lighthouse Reef Atoll, follow the wall to 40 metres and swim beneath stalactites the size of church organs — formed when this cave was dry land in the last ice age, drowned as the seas rose. Caribbean reef sharks patrol the twilight below. Bottom time is short and the dive is more geology than fish soup, which is exactly why it belongs in your logbook.

The trick is knowing the Blue Hole is one dive of many: Half Moon Caye Wall and The Aquarium on the same day trip are arguably better dives, with eagle rays, garden eels and a red-footed booby colony at the picnic stop.

Base yourself in San Pedro or Caye Caulker; the atoll run is a bumpy two-to-three-hour crossing, so take seasickness tablets seriously. Operators want an advanced certificate and around 24 logged dives for the 40-metre profile. Budget about £1,500 for a week including the Blue Hole day and reef days; December to May brings the calmest crossings.
adventures.location: Lighthouse Reef Atoll, Belize Barrier Reef Reserve
highlights: Descending past ice-age stalactites at 40m inside the Great Blue Hole
Half Moon Caye Wall and its eagle rays
The Aquarium drift at Long Caye
Red-footed booby colony on Half Moon Caye
Sunset crossings back to San Pedro

adventures.title: Sipadan Permit Week from Mabul
adventures.description:
Sipadan is an oceanic pinnacle rising 600 metres from the Celebes Sea floor, and Barracuda Point delivers the sight every diver keeps on their list: a thousand chevron barracuda wheeling into a silver tornado that swallows you whole. Green and hawksbill turtles are so numerous you stop counting by breakfast, grey reef sharks patrol the Drop-Off — a wall that begins one stride from the old jetty — and South Point occasionally coughs up a hammerhead.

Access is the variable that catches people out. Sipadan is a protected island with no accommodation: you stay on Mabul or Kapalai and your resort secures one of the 178 daily permits, which typically means one or two Sipadan days in a week. The rest you spend on Mabul's genuinely excellent muck diving. Book three months ahead and carry your passport for the ranger checkpoint.

Fly to Tawau via Kuala Lumpur, transfer to Semporna and boat out. April to September is prime. Around £1,300 covers a week full board with dives; the currents at the point are honest, so bring a delayed SMB and twenty-plus logged dives.
highlights: The barracuda tornado at Barracuda Point
Turtles on every dive along the Drop-Off
Mabul's world-class muck diving on non-permit days

adventures.title: Socorro Giant Manta Liveaboard, Revillagigedo
adventures.description:
Twenty-four hours of open Pacific separate Cabo San Lucas from the Revillagigedo Archipelago, and the crossing buys the best big-animal diving in the eastern Pacific. At The Boiler, a seamount off San Benedicto, giant oceanic mantas — seven metres wingtip to wingtip — bank in for slow, deliberate passes over your head; they seem to seek out the fizz of bubbles on their bellies, and no encounter anywhere is as prolonged or as close. Roca Partida, a guano-white fang in a violet ocean, stacks whitetip reef sharks on its ledges while silkies and Galapagos sharks circle the blue.

From January to March humpback song is loud enough to feel through your wetsuit, and a lucky safety stop comes with an escort. This is liveaboard-only, advanced diving: surge, current, depth and nothing but ocean on every horizon.

Boats run November to May from Cabo San Lucas; nine-day itineraries start around £3,300 plus the park fee. Bring a 5mm suit, a hooded vest for the thermoclines and a logbook with fifty-plus dives — operators check.
highlights: Chin-to-belly passes from giant oceanic mantas at The Boiler
Roca Partida's whitetip ledges and circling silkies
Humpback song through the hull from January to March
Bottlenose dolphins joining dives at Cabo Pearce
The 24-hour blue-water crossing from Cabo San Lucas

adventures.title: Truk Lagoon Ghost Fleet
adventures.description:
Operation Hailstone, February 1944: two days of American air strikes sank some sixty ships of Japan's Combined Fleet at anchor. Eighty years on, Chuuk Lagoon is the world's greatest wreck gallery and the Fujikawa Maru its masterpiece — Zero fighter fuselages still crated in her holds, her bow gun furred with soft coral. The Shinkoku Maru does her best work at night, when the whole superstructure blooms with feeding coral polyps. On the deep San Francisco Maru, tanks sit on deck at fifty metres with shells still stacked beside them.

Depth is the honest variable: the showpieces run 30 to 60 metres, so nitrox — and ideally decompression training — turns a good week into a great one. Recreational divers still get a dozen superb shallower wrecks, from the Betty bomber to the Heian Maru's periscopes.

Fly via Guam to Weno and choose between the Blue Lagoon Resort's dive operation and a liveaboard. December to April is the dry season. Ten days runs about £3,000 land-based before flights; bring two torches, a wreck reel and respect — these are war graves.
highlights: Zero fighters in the holds of the Fujikawa Maru
Night diving the coral-smothered Shinkoku Maru
Tanks and trucks on the San Francisco Maru at 50m
Operation Hailstone history briefed wreck by wreck

adventures.title: Sardine Run Bait Ball Expedition, Wild Coast
adventures.description:
Each June the inshore water cools along South Africa's Wild Coast and billions of sardines push north, dragging the entire food chain behind them. When it goes off, it is the greatest wildlife event you can witness underwater: common dolphin super-pods herding bait into panicked silver spheres, Cape gannets hitting the water like tracer fire around your head, bronze whaler sharks slicing through the ball and, on the big days, a Bryde's whale removing most of it in one lunge.

Honesty matters here: this is expedition wildlife work, not guaranteed diving. You launch a RIB through the surf at the Umzimvubu River mouth at Port St Johns, run the coast behind the spotter plane, and some days the ocean is simply empty. Snorkel skills matter more than scuba — kit is donned fast for the minutes a ball stalls.

June and July are the season. A week with launches, skipper and spotter flights runs about £2,600, staying in Port St Johns lodges. Bring a 5mm suit, seasickness resolve and patience; then the gannets start raining and you forget every blank day.
adventures.location: Wild Coast, Port St Johns, Eastern Cape
highlights: Common dolphin super-pods herding bait balls
Cape gannets diving around your snorkel
Bryde's whale lunges through the ball
Surf launches at the Umzimvubu River mouth
Spotter-plane radio calls that start the chase

adventures.title: Scapa Flow German Fleet Wreck Week
adventures.description:
On Midsummer's Day 1919 the interned German High Seas Fleet scuttled itself in Scapa Flow, and seven great ships still lie where they settled. Dropping down the shot line onto SMS Markgraf — 25,000 tonnes of König-class battleship in 45 metres of green Orkney water — is British diving's most atmospheric moment. The light cruisers are the crowd-pleasers: Cöln lies near-intact on her starboard side at 35 metres, while Karlsruhe brings guns and capstans within reach of a 25-metre profile. Between the big ships, the blockships at the Churchill Barriers make shallow, story-soaked second dives.

You live aboard a converted trawler out of Stromness with a wheelhouse full of tea and a compressor humming aft; evenings are for Orcadian pubs, the Italian Chapel and the Scapa Flow Museum at Lyness.

Cold, dark and depth are the variables: a drysuit, good torches and solid 30-metre experience are the sensible minimum, and nitrox earns its fee. The season runs April to October; a week's berth with air and food comes in around £950 before travel to Orkney.
highlights: The shot-line descent onto SMS Markgraf
SMS Cöln's intact bridge and bow
Blockship second dives at the Churchill Barriers
The 1919 Grand Scuttle story told over the wrecks
Stromness harbour evenings and the Scapa Flow Museum
gear: Flask and midge repellent for deck

adventures.title: Jardines de la Reina Shark Sanctuary
adventures.description:
Fidel Castro's favourite fishing ground became Cuba's strictest marine park, and half a century of protection shows the Caribbean as it looked before us: elkhorn thickets, goliath grouper, and more sharks per dive than anywhere else in the region. A dozen Caribbean reef sharks escort you down the mooring line as a matter of routine; silkies gather under the swim platform at dusk. In the mangrove shallows you can snorkel eye to eye with American crocodiles under a guide's exacting choreography.

Access is deliberately hard. Fly to Havana, drive five hours to the little port of Júcaro, then cruise three to five more into the archipelago, sleeping aboard a liveaboard or the Tortuga floating lodge. Visitor numbers are capped, so berths book out months ahead.

November to April is the dry, settled season. Eight days runs about £3,000 including transfers from Havana. Bring cash for the marina, spares for your kit and no expectation of Wi-Fi — that is rather the point.
adventures.location: Jardines de la Reina archipelago, Ciego de Ávila
highlights: A dozen Caribbean reef sharks on every dive
Silky sharks under the boat at dusk
Snorkelling with American crocodiles in the mangroves
Goliath grouper on pristine elkhorn reef
The Tortuga floating lodge deep in the archipelago

adventures.title: Bikini Atoll Nuclear Fleet Technical Expedition
adventures.description:
Bikini is the far end of wreck diving: a nuclear ghost fleet in a lagoon that absorbed 23 atomic tests, reached by a handful of liveaboard departures a year via Kwajalein. The USS Saratoga — a 270-metre aircraft carrier — sits upright with her flight deck at 27 metres and Helldivers still in the hangar. Nearby lies HIJMS Nagato, the flagship that transmitted the Pearl Harbor attack order, capsized on her enormous guns; then the Arkansas, the Carlisle, the submarine Apogon. Every dive is a history lesson with a decompression obligation.

This is a technical expedition, plainly stated. Operators require normoxic trimix or equivalent training; most dives sit in the 45-55 metre band with runtimes past ninety minutes. Residual radiation is negligible for divers — the constraint is your certification, not the physics.

The season runs May to October. Twelve days costs roughly £9,500 before the multi-leg flights through Honolulu and Majuro, and island schedules slip, so build slack into your tickets. Sharks own the lagoon again; you will likely have the entire atoll to yourselves.
highlights: Landing on the USS Saratoga's flight deck at 27m
HIJMS Nagato, the Pearl Harbor flagship, capsized at 50m
The submarine USS Apogon intact on the lagoon floor
Operation Crossroads history over the wrecks it created
A shark-filled lagoon with no other boats
gear: Twinset or CCR as agreed with operator
Comprehensive dive insurance with evacuation cover

adventures.title: SS Yongala Wreck Pilgrimage
adventures.description:
The SS Yongala went down in a cyclone in 1911 with all 122 aboard and lay unfound for nearly half a century. Today she is routinely called the best wreck dive in the world, and it is not really about the ship: alone on open sand inside the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, the 109-metre steamer is an oasis mobbed by life grown absurdly large. Marble rays like patio tables shelter under the bow, Queensland grouper the size of sofas hold the stern, trevally storms wrap the midships, olive sea snakes thread the rails and bull sharks cruise the blue above.

She is protected — no penetration, no touching — and the diving is honest: mooring-line descents, 15-28 metre profiles and current that can pump, which is exactly what feeds the spectacle. Advanced certification, or a guide, is the sensible standard.

Day boats launch through the surf at Alva Beach near Ayr, between Townsville and Airlie Beach; liveaboards visit from Townsville. August to December gives the calmest seas. Three days with four wreck dives runs about £450 — extraordinary value for a bucket-list dive.
adventures.location: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, off Ayr, Queensland
highlights: Marble rays and giant Queensland grouper on the hull
Olive sea snakes threading the rails
The 1911 cyclone story of all 122 souls

adventures.title: Bonaire Shore Diving Freedom Week
adventures.description:
Bonaire runs on a promise painted onto yellow roadside stones: each one marks a dive site, and you may dive any of them whenever you like. You collect a pickup truck, load cylinders at the drive-through filling station and build your own week — 1000 Steps at dawn, the Hilma Hooker wreck lying between the double reef at noon, Salt Pier's sponge-wrapped pillars in the afternoon, then an ostracod night dive after supper when the reef flickers with strings of blue light. The island sits below the hurricane belt, so the season barely matters and the leeward water is pool-calm.

The marine park's rules are old and effective — a park fee, an orientation dive, no gloves, no touching — and the reward is the healthiest reef fish density in the southern Caribbean starting a fin-kick from your apartment.

Fly to Kralendijk via Amsterdam. A week with truck, apartment and unlimited air lands near £1,200 before flights, the best-value warm-water diving anywhere. The variable is the entries themselves: sharp ironshore and surge — pack hard-soled booties and watch the locals' lines.
adventures.location: Bonaire National Marine Park, Leeward Antilles
highlights: Sixty-plus shore sites marked by yellow stones
The Hilma Hooker wreck between the double reefs
Truck-and-tank freedom with no boat schedule

imageAttribution.artist: Michal Strzelecki, Wojtek Strzelecki and Jerzy Strzelecki

adventures.title: Fakarava South Pass Wall of Sharks
adventures.description:
Tumakohua Pass at Fakarava's southern tip holds the famous wall of sharks: several hundred grey reef sharks stacked into the incoming current like traffic over a motorway, holding station while you grip the reef edge and try to keep your breathing polite. At the June and July full moons, thousands of camouflage groupers gather here to spawn and the wall switches from parade to feeding frenzy — one of the great spectacles in the ocean. The dive ends drifting the flood tide over coral gardens to Tetamanu village, where the boat picks you up beside a pension jetty over pink sand.

Fakarava is a UNESCO biosphere atoll in the Tuamotus: one road, two villages, no crowds. Stay in Rotoava for the wide north pass and its wall dives, or sleep at Tetamanu itself and dive the south pass at dawn. Currents are strong and non-negotiable — drift experience and good air consumption matter.

Fly to Tahiti and hop to the atoll. May to October is prime. Eight days with pension full board and two dives daily runs about £2,800 before long-haul legs; French Polynesia is never cheap, and this is worth every pound.
highlights: Hundreds of grey reef sharks stacked in Tumakohua Pass
The camouflage grouper spawning at full moon
Flood-tide drifts over pink-sand coral gardens
Dawn dives from Tetamanu village jetty

adventures.title: Arctic Orca Snorkel, Skjervøy
adventures.description:
In the polar night the herring pack into the fjords around Skjervøy, and the orcas follow by the hundred. You slide off a RIB in a drysuit into black 4°C water and hang dead still while a carousel-feeding pod works a bait ball metres away — the clicks arrive in your chest before the whales arrive in view. Humpbacks lunge through the same shoals, close enough that you learn to read the bubble rings and get out of the lane.

This is snorkelling, not scuba — regulations keep encounters surface-only — but Arctic seamanship makes it as serious as any dive trip. Days are three hours of pale blue twilight; the aurora fills most of the other twenty-one. Everything depends on weather windows and where the herring have moved, and some days you find neither: the whales owe you nothing.

Fly to Tromsø and transfer north to Skjervøy, or sleep aboard a liveaboard that follows the shoals. November to January is the season. Five days runs about £2,300 with drysuit hire; pack proper wool base layers and a healthy respect for the cold.
highlights: Carousel-feeding orca pods at snorkel range
Humpbacks lunging through the herring shoals
RIB launches in survival gear from Skjervøy harbour
gear: Windproof outer layers for the RIB

adventures.title: Malpelo Hammerhead Wall Expedition
adventures.description:
Malpelo is a bare rock 500 kilometres off Colombia's Pacific coast, ringed by some of the sharkiest water on the planet. Scalloped hammerheads school three hundred strong off La Nevera; silky sharks mass in the blue; and in the cool thermoclines of early spring divers meet the smalltooth sand tiger — a deep-water shark reliably seen almost nowhere else on Earth. There is no lagoon and no easy dive: you roll from pangas beneath 300-metre cliffs whitewashed by boobies, and everything happens in current.

The UNESCO sanctuary admits one licensed liveaboard at a time, boarding in Buenaventura for a 30-40 hour crossing that sorts the committed from the curious. Sea state, thermoclines and surge are the honest variables; a hundred logged dives and confident negative entries are the entry ticket.

January to May gives the best hammerhead action and the sand tiger window. Ten-day expeditions run about £4,200 plus park fees, and berths sell out around a year ahead — this is a pilgrimage, not a package holiday.
adventures.location: Malpelo Fauna and Flora Sanctuary, Pacific Colombia
highlights: Scalloped hammerhead schools at La Nevera
The rare smalltooth sand tiger below the thermocline
Hundreds of silky sharks in open blue

adventures.title: Neptune Islands Great White Cage Encounter
adventures.description:
The Neptune Islands off South Australia are the only place in the country where you can cage-dive with great white sharks, and home to the only ocean-floor cage anywhere: winched to the seabed around 20 metres down, it puts you at eye level as a four-and-a-half-metre shark banks past in gin-grey Southern Ocean water. Surface cages need no certification at all; the bottom cage requires a scuba ticket and rewards it with the calmest, closest viewing in the sport.

Winter, May to October, brings the biggest females in to hunt the long-nosed fur seal colonies. Sightings are wild-animal odds — day trips can blank — which is why the multi-day liveaboard stacks the deck so heavily: more anchorages, more hours with lines in the water, plus a night anchored under seabird cliffs.

Boats run from Port Lincoln, a tuna town 45 minutes' flight from Adelaide. A three-night liveaboard runs about £1,650; day trips from £280. Bring seasickness tablets and a thick hood — the Southern Ocean means business even inside a cage.
adventures.location: Neptune Islands, Spencer Gulf, South Australia
highlights: Eye-level great whites from the ocean-floor cage
Winter's four-metre-plus females at the seal colonies
Long-nosed fur seals hauled out on the Neptunes
gear: Scuba certification for the bottom cage
Beanie and gloves for the crossing

adventures.title: Tiger Beach Shark Liveaboard, Grand Bahama
adventures.description:
Tiger Beach is a sunlit sandbank northwest of Grand Bahama's West End where six metres of gin-clear water host the Atlantic's most reliable tiger shark encounters. You kneel in a briefed line on white sand while three-to-four-metre tigers glide over your shoulder, lemon sharks grin from the edges and, from December to March, great hammerheads sweep in with dorsal fins like sails. The Bahamas banned commercial shark fishing in 2011 and built the world's most valuable shark-diving economy instead; the animals here are the dividend.

The skills are simple — shallow, still, no current to speak of — but the protocol is not optional: dark gloves, hands tucked, no white fins, eyes on your sector. Listen to the crew and the dives feel remarkably calm; freelance and you will be sat out.

Liveaboards cross from West Palm Beach, Florida, or day boats run from Freeport. October to March is prime, pairing tigers with hammerheads. A week aboard runs about £2,500 before flights; bring a dark 3mm suit and double the memory cards you think you need.
adventures.location: Tiger Beach, Little Bahama Bank, Grand Bahama
highlights: Tiger sharks gliding over white sand at six metres
Great hammerheads from December to March
Lemon shark packs at the dusk dives
The Gulf Stream crossing from Florida

adventures.title: Fuvahmulah Tiger Shark Arena
adventures.description:
Fuvahmulah is a one-island atoll in the far south of the Maldives with no lagoon, no resort sprawl and a harbour mouth that has become the most reliable tiger shark dive on Earth. Fishermen have cleaned their catch here for generations, and the tigers — three to four metres long, unhurried, many known individually to the local guides — patrol the shallows daily. You kneel in a briefed line at eight to twelve metres while they cruise a body-length overhead; the choreography is strict and the adrenaline is not optional.

Beyond the harbour, the island's plateau drops sheer into blue that produces thresher sharks at dawn, oceanic mantas, and in season mola and hammerheads. This is big-animal diving with real protocol: listen to the briefing and keep your hands folded.

Fly to Malé and take the domestic hop south, staying in guesthouses under local island rules — no alcohol, modest dress in the village. December to April brings the calmest seas. A week with daily two-tank diving and three tiger sessions runs about £1,700 before flights.
highlights: Tiger sharks metres away at the harbour mouth
Dawn thresher shark dives on the deep ledges
Oceanic mantas and mola along the plateau
An island with no lagoon and no resorts
Guesthouse life in the southernmost atoll

adventures.title: Gozo Blue Hole and Malta Wreck Circuit
adventures.description:
Malta's diving is built around freedom: big cylinders, a hire car and shore entries engineered like municipal works. On Gozo the Blue Hole at Dwejra is the centrepiece — you descend inside a collapsed limestone chimney and exit through an archway into open sea at ten metres, then work the boulder field left by the fallen Azure Window, now a dive of its own known as Azure Reef. Across on Malta, the Um El Faraud — a 10,000-tonne tanker scuttled off Wied iż-Żurrieq — and the P29 patrol boat at Ċirkewwa give proper wreck profiles at 20 to 35 metres.

By late summer the Mediterranean here reaches 26°C with 30-metre visibility. The variable is wind: sites are chosen each morning by which coast is sheltered, so hire-car flexibility beats any fixed booking, and the ferry between the islands is part of the rhythm.

May to October is the season. Six days with ten dives, an apartment and the car lands near £750 before flights — and non-diving companions get Victoria's citadel and swimming coves while you blow bubbles.
highlights: The Blue Hole chimney and archway at Dwejra
Azure Reef — diving the fallen Azure Window
The Um El Faraud tanker off Wied iż-Żurrieq
Choosing the sheltered coast each morning

adventures.title: Lembeh Strait Muck Diving Masterclass
adventures.description:
Lembeh Strait is a dark-sand channel between Bitung and Lembeh Island where the world's strangest animals live in plain sight: mimic octopus and wunderpus, flamboyant cuttlefish strobing across the rubble, hairy frogfish luring prey with a worm-shaped rod, blue-ringed octopus the size of your thumb. 'Muck diving' undersells it — this is wildlife spotting at its most forensic, one guide to two divers, eyes trained across thousands of dives to find a pygmy seahorse on a single sea fan.

Conditions are gentle: 15-25 metre profiles, mild current, warm water. The real challenges are buoyancy discipline over silt that punishes a lazy fin kick, and the self-control not to fill your camera's memory card on the first frogfish.
