Fly to Manado in North Sulawesi, then it is ninety minutes over the hill to the Bitung resorts. July to October is peak critter season, though the strait produces year-round. Eight days full board with three guided dives a day runs about £1,400 before flights; a macro lens is practically mandatory kit.
highlights: Mimic octopus and wunderpus on black sand
Hairy frogfish luring at Nudi Falls
gear: Camera with macro lens and focus light

adventures.title: Richelieu Rock and Similan Liveaboard
adventures.description:
Richelieu Rock is a horseshoe pinnacle in the Andaman Sea that barely breaks the surface at low tide and falls to 35 metres of the richest reef in Thailand — discovered, the story goes, by Jacques Cousteau. Purple soft corals smother every surface; trevally and barracuda wheel above pygmy seahorses, harlequin shrimp and ghost pipefish; and from February to April this is the country's best whale shark bet, when the plankton lines drift through and the big fish follow.

The rock sits far offshore, so liveaboards from Khao Lak pair it with the Similan Islands' granite boulder mazes — Elephant Head Rock's swim-throughs are a highlight — and the manta cleaning station at Koh Bon.

The national park opens mid-October to mid-May only, and the boats follow. Six-day liveaboards with four dives daily run about £950 including park fees. Currents on the rock reward a delayed SMB and decent air consumption, but any confident diver with a few dozen logged dives will cope happily.
adventures.location: Mu Ko Similan National Park, Andaman Sea
highlights: Whale shark chances from February to April
Manta cleaning station at Koh Bon
Four-dive liveaboard days from Khao Lak

adventures.title: Cabo Pulmo Reef Revival
adventures.description:
Cabo Pulmo is the ocean's best argument for hope: a Sea of Cortez village that banned fishing on its own reef in 1995 and watched fish biomass rebound by more than 400 per cent. The signature dive is El Vencedor, a wreck where thousands of bigeye jacks form a rotating tornado dense enough to dim the sun; bull sharks patrol the sand in the cooler months, mobula rays flurry past in spring, and the hard-coral heads — among the oldest reefs in the eastern Pacific — hum with grouper and snapper.

It stays small because it is awkward to reach: a washboard dirt road from La Ribera, a village that only recently left generator power behind, pangas launched straight off the beach. That is the charm. Book a casita, dive with the family-run operators and eat wherever is open.

August to November gives 28°C water and 25-metre visibility; storms are the wildcard in September. Five days of two-tank mornings runs about £850 from San José del Cabo, hire car included. National park rules cap group sizes, so reserve dives ahead in high season.
adventures.location: Cabo Pulmo National Park, Baja California Sur
highlights: The bigeye jack tornado at El Vencedor
A reef with 400 per cent biomass recovery
Bull sharks over the sand in cooler months
Beach panga launches from an off-grid village

adventures.title: Poor Knights Arches and Rikoriko Cave
adventures.description:
Jacques Cousteau put the Poor Knights in his top ten, and the claim still holds. Two drowned volcanoes 23 kilometres off Tutukaka, wrapped in a no-take marine reserve since 1998, are washed by the East Auckland Current, which delivers subtropical visitors to a temperate kelp coast. Blue maomao pack the arches in shimmering navy walls; short-tail stingrays the size of dining tables stack up in Northern Arch through late summer; nudibranchs, mosaic morays and Lord Howe coralfish fill in every gap in the guidebook.

Rikoriko — the world's largest sea cave by volume — swallows the dive boat whole, and you surface inside to test the echo. The diving suits any qualified diver, though the arches carry surge when a swell runs.

Day boats leave Tutukaka, three hours north of Auckland; base yourself there for four days and dive each morning. January to May gives the warmest water and the rays, but a 7mm suit is still wise. Two-dive days run about £150, so a long weekend lands near £650 with accommodation.
adventures.location: Poor Knights Islands Marine Reserve, Northland
highlights: Short-tail stingray squadrons in Northern Arch
Blue maomao walls at Blue Maomao Arch
Kelp forest and subtropical fish on one dive
Tutukaka marina fish and chips after the boat
gear: Warm jacket for the ride home

adventures.title: Princess Alice Bank Pelagic Dives, Azores
adventures.description:
Princess Alice Bank is a seamount fifty nautical miles southwest of Faial, its summit at 35 metres in two kilometres of Atlantic — and in late summer it belongs to the sicklefin devil rays. They arrive in squadrons of a dozen or more, circling divers who hang on the line in open blue with nothing below but violet water. The three-hour crossing from Horta is half the adventure: sperm whales blowing on the horizon, loggerhead turtles, rafts of Cory's shearwaters.

This is honest blue-water diving: no reef beneath you for comfort, current across the summit, and the boat only goes when the Atlantic allows. Plan flexible days and treat the bank as a weather lottery, with Faial and Pico's coastal dives — and optional baited blue shark trips — as excellent fallbacks.

Fly to Horta via Lisbon. July to September is the window. Six days with two bank runs, harbour accommodation and inshore dives comes in around £1,300; advanced certification and deep-water experience are required. Paint your crew mural on Horta marina's wall before you leave — tradition insists.
adventures.location: Princess Alice Bank and Faial, Azores
highlights: Sicklefin devil ray squadrons over the seamount
Optional baited blue shark dives off Faial
Painting your mural on Horta marina wall

adventures.title: Zenobia Wreck Long Weekend, Larnaca
adventures.description:
The Zenobia was a brand-new Swedish ro-ro ferry when her ballast computers failed in June 1980; she sank outside Larnaca with 104 articulated lorries chained to her decks and became Europe's finest wreck dive. She lies on her port side, 172 metres long, with her top at 16 metres and the seabed at 42, so a single wreck genuinely fills a long weekend: lorries hang in their chains like toys, the canteen still holds crockery, and escorted penetrations through the cargo decks reward training with pure theatre.

She sits ten minutes from Larnaca harbour, so two boat dives a day is effortless, and 27°C summer water makes a 3mm suit enough. Open Water divers get the upper hull and the atmosphere; the deeper lines and interiors want advanced certification and a guide who knows the routes.

May to October is the season. Four days with six boat dives runs about £480 with a harbour-side hotel — the cheapest world-class wreck trip in Europe and an easy add-on to any Cyprus holiday.
highlights: 104 articulated lorries hanging in their chains
The canteen swim-through with crockery in place
A 172-metre hull ten minutes from the harbour
Upper-deck dives from 16 metres for any certification

adventures.title: Gulf of Tadjoura Whale Shark Season
adventures.description:
Between October and February, juvenile whale sharks gather in the Gulf of Tadjoura to gorge on plankton blooms, and Djibouti remains one of the few places on Earth where you can reliably swim beside them with almost nobody else around. Days find a rhythm: spotters locate feeding sharks in the Bay of Ghoubbet, you slip in ahead of a slow-moving bus of a fish, swim hard, then do it again until your legs give out.

The dives in between are their own oddity — the Ghoubbet sits at the tip of the East African Rift, where the continent is tearing open, and you can fin along the fissure at La Faille with desert volcanoes above the surface. Small liveaboards out of Djibouti City run week-long loops; evenings end with sweet tea on deck under improbable numbers of stars.

November to January is peak. Eight days runs about £1,900 before flights via Addis Ababa or Paris. Visibility in plankton-rich water is honest — ten metres on a good day — and that soup is precisely why the sharks come.
adventures.location: Gulf of Tadjoura and Bay of Ghoubbet
highlights: Snorkelling beside feeding juvenile whale sharks
Diving the rift fissure at La Faille
Desert mountains dropping straight into the sea
A liveaboard fleet you can count on one hand
Deck nights under Horn of Africa stars

adventures.title: Ama Dablam Southwest Ridge Expedition
adventures.description:
Every trekker on the Everest trail photographs Ama Dablam; almost none of them touch her. The 'Mother's Necklace' is the most beautiful 6,000er on Earth and, at 6,812 m, a genuinely technical expedition: sustained rock climbing on the granite towers above Camp 1, the airy jumar of the Yellow Tower, and Camp 2 perched on a ledge the size of a dining table with a kilometre of air on three sides.

The Southwest Ridge is climbed on fixed lines in the post-monsoon window, October to November, when the Khumbu sky turns to polished glass. Above Camp 2 the route weaves past the hanging serac — the dablam itself — whose collapses have shaped the route's history; operators fix the Grey Tower and summit snowfields early. The variable that ends most attempts is not the rock but jumaring efficiency at altitude: slow parties get benighted.

Expeditions run 25 to 30 days from Kathmandu with the classic Namche-Pangboche acclimatisation trek to a grassy base camp at 4,570 m that ranks among the loveliest in the Himalaya. Budget £11,000 to £14,000 with Sherpa support and fixed-line fees included. You need prior rock and ice experience at altitude — this is not a first Himalayan peak.
highlights: Jumaring the Yellow Tower at 6,000 m
Camp 2 on its impossible granite perch
The dablam serac glinting above the summit snowfields
Everest, Lhotse and Makalu from the summit
Grass and gentian base camp below the southwest face

adventures.title: Rainier by the Disappointment Cleaver
adventures.description:
Somewhere above Ingraham Flats, headtorches string out along the Cleaver and the whole of Puget Sound glitters 4,000 metres below your crampons. Mount Rainier is the most heavily glaciated peak in the lower 48, and the Disappointment Cleaver route is America's classic apprenticeship in big-mountain climbing: rope teams, crevasse bridges, a 1 a.m. alpine start from Camp Muir and a lung-scouring push to the 4,392 m crater rim.

The rhythm is simple and brutal. Day one climbs from the wildflower meadows of Paradise to Camp Muir at 3,072 m; day two is rest, rigging and an early night; summit day is eight to twelve hours on ice. The variable that catches people is not fitness but weather — Rainier manufactures its own storms, and roughly half of all attempts turn around.

Base yourself in Ashford, at the park's Nisqually entrance. Guided climbs (RMI, IMG, Alpine Ascents) run May to September and book out months ahead; budget around £1,700 for a four-day programme plus the park's climbing fee. Crampon and ice-axe skills are taught, but arrive hill-fit or the Muir snowfield will find you out.
highlights: Alpine start from Camp Muir under a wall of stars
Crossing crevasse ladders on the Ingraham Glacier
Sunrise from the Disappointment Cleaver spine
Standing on the 4,392 m crater rim of a sleeping volcano
Wildflower meadows at Paradise on the walk-out

adventures.title: Elbrus South Route Ascent
adventures.description:
Europe's highest mountain is a twin-headed volcano standing apart from the main Caucasus chain, and from the saddle between its summits at 5,300 m you look down on the entire range at sunrise — a thousand kilometres of peaks catching fire one by one. Elbrus's west summit, 5,642 m, is the prize of the classic south route from the Baksan valley.

The infrastructure is pure Soviet mountaineering: a cable car from Azau to 3,847 m, barrel huts above, and snowcats that can shorten summit day from the Pastukhov Rocks. Acclimatisation hikes to Cheget build red blood cells; summit day is eight to twelve hours of steady cramponing — a rising traverse under the east summit, the saddle, then fixed-rope slopes to the western dome. The catch is deceptive scale: in cloud the featureless snowfields have taken more lives than the Matterhorn, nearly all whiteout navigation errors. Go with a guide who carries GPS tracks and turns around without sentiment.

The season is June to September, based in Terskol village via Mineralnye Vody. A guided eight-day programme with huts, lifts and permits costs about £1,700. Technically, crampon basics suffice — respect for the weather is the real prerequisite.
highlights: Sunrise over the whole Caucasus from the saddle
Fixed-rope slopes to the 5,642 m west summit
Acclimatisation days above the Baksan valley

adventures.title: Mount Vinson Expedition
adventures.description:
Antarctica's highest mountain rises from ice that stretches unbroken to the horizon in every direction. Mount Vinson, 4,892 m, sits in the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains, 1,200 km from the South Pole, and climbing it is as much polar expedition as ascent: 24-hour daylight, -35C, and silence so complete you hear your heartbeat.

An Ilyushin flies from Punta Arenas to the blue-ice runway at Union Glacier; a ski aircraft hops on to base camp on the Branscomb Glacier at 2,100 m. The route itself is straightforward mountaineering — sledge-hauling to Low Camp, a 1,200 m fixed-line headwall to High Camp at 3,780 m, then a long, bitterly cold summit day along the ridge with the Ellsworths' shark-fin peaks breaking the ice sheet below. Weather rules everything: storms pin teams in tents for days, so check how much slack your itinerary carries.

The season is December to January. Expect £38,000 to £45,000 through Antarctic Logistics & Expeditions' partners — the flight is most of the cost. Technical demands are modest — fixed lines, glacier travel, polar camping — but cold management must be second nature: frostbite, not difficulty, ends attempts here.
highlights: Landing on the Union Glacier blue-ice runway
Fixed-line headwall to High Camp at 3,780 m
Midnight sunshine on the summit ridge
The Ellsworth Mountains breaking an endless ice sheet
The most remote of the Seven Summits

adventures.title: Grand Teton via the Upper Exum Ridge
adventures.description:
The step across Wall Street is the moment: a narrowing granite ledge that simply runs out, leaving one committing move above a thousand metres of air before the Upper Exum Ridge takes you, pitch after golden pitch, to the 4,199 m summit of the Grand. It is arguably the finest moderate alpine rock climb in North America, first soloed by Glenn Exum in 1931 in borrowed football boots.

Most parties take four days with Exum Mountain Guides or Jackson Hole Mountain Guides: two days of climbing school in Garnet Canyon, a night at the Lower Saddle hut camp at 3,536 m, then a pre-dawn start for the ridge and an abseil descent of the Owen-Spalding. The catch is the Teton thunderstorm machine — afternoon lightning arrives on schedule in July and August, so summit parties move fast and early.

Fly or drive to Jackson, Wyoming; the trailhead at Lupine Meadows is twenty minutes away. Budget about £1,500 for the guided four-day programme, camping included. You need scrambling confidence and a calm head for exposure, not an elite CV — the guides supply the rest.
highlights: The exposed step off Wall Street onto the Exum Ridge
Golden granite pitches with Idaho and Wyoming at your heels
A night at the Lower Saddle beneath the Grand's headwall
Abseiling the Owen-Spalding rappel at 3,900 m
Moose and black bears in Garnet Canyon on the approach
gear: rock shoes or sticky approach shoes

adventures.title: Alpamayo Southwest Face
adventures.description:
In 1966 a panel of alpinists voted Alpamayo the most beautiful mountain in the world, and from col camp at 5,500 m you see why: a perfect trapezoid of fluted ice, corrugated like cathedral organ pipes, glowing pink at dawn. The Southwest Face routes — Ferrari and French Direct — climb those very flutes: 400 m of sustained 50-to-65-degree ice runnels to a summit at 5,947 m barely wide enough to stand on.

This is a real technical climb reached by a genuinely lovely expedition. From Huaraz you trek up the Santa Cruz valley behind burros, establish moraine camp, then climb to the col between Alpamayo and Quitaraju, itself steep enough to need fixed lines. Summit day is six to ten hours of calf-burning ice protected by screws and stakes, with abseil anchors threaded down the flutes for descent. The variable is the runnels' condition — a dry year turns them brittle and raises the grade — and queues into the same flute are the modern hazard; start first.

Climb June to August from Huaraz (3,050 m), capital of Andean mountaineering, after solid acclimatisation. Twelve-day guided expeditions cost £3,000 to £3,800; you need confident front-pointing and multi-pitch ice experience.
highlights: The fluted southwest face at dawn from col camp
Sustained 55-degree ice runnels to the summit
Santa Cruz valley approach with burro trains
Quitaraju and Artesonraju across the col
Huaraz's climber cafés and acclimatisation peaks

adventures.title: Eiger by the Mittellegi Ridge
adventures.description:
The journey to the climb is like nothing else in the Alps: you ride the Jungfrau railway into the mountain, step off at Eismeer station inside the Eiger, and exit through a tunnel window onto the glacier. An afternoon's climbing later you are at the Mittellegi Hut, a wooden eyrie bolted to the ridge at 3,355 m, watching evening light run along the crest you will climb at dawn.

The Mittellegi Ridge is the Eiger's proudest reasonable line — a mile of exposed knife-edge rising to the 3,967 m summit, with fixed ropes up the steepest towers and the North Face dropping 1,800 m beneath your left boot. It is climbing you feel in your stomach: never desperate, never casual. The descent continues down the south ridge and across the Eigerjöcher to the Mönchsjoch hut — a complete crossing of the mountain.

This is guide's terrain: Grindelwald bureaux pair you 1:1 and climb with you beforehand to check pace — the catch is speed, for slow parties meet afternoon storms on a ridge with no exits. You need solid rock skills (alpine III+), crampon competence and a very good head. Two days, roughly £2,000 with guide, huts and trains, late July to September when the ridge is dry. Worth every franc.
highlights: Exiting the railway tunnel window onto the glacier
A night in the Mittellegi Hut on the ridge crest
Knife-edge climbing above the 1,800 m North Face
The complete traverse over the 3,967 m summit
Fixed-rope towers with Grindelwald far below

adventures.title: Orizaba by the Jamapa Glacier
adventures.description:
At 5,636 m, Pico de Orizaba is the third-highest peak in North America, and on a clear December dawn its perfect volcanic shadow stretches all the way to the Gulf of Mexico. You watch it happen from the Jamapa Glacier, a steady 30-degree ice ramp that begins where the scrambling maze of the Labyrinth ends and does not relent until the crater rim.

The trip is really a week in the high villages of Puebla state. Operators in Tlachichuca — the Reyes and Cancholas families have been running climbers up the mountain for generations — truck you by 4x4 to the Piedra Grande hut at 4,260 m. Smart itineraries acclimatise first on Sierra Negra or Malinche; the variable that wrecks summit bids here is almost always altitude, not technicality.

Fly to Mexico City or Puebla, bus to Tlachichuca (2,600 m), and climb between November and March when the air is cold and stable. A guided week with acclimatisation peaks, huts and transfers runs about £950. Crampons and axe are essential; the glacier is dry ice by late season and a slip runs a long way.
adventures.location: Pico de Orizaba National Park, Puebla / Veracruz
highlights: The volcano's dawn shadow cast towards the Gulf of Mexico
Climbing the Jamapa Glacier from the Labyrinth to the rim
Piedra Grande hut nights at 4,260 m
Acclimatisation summit on Sierra Negra or La Malinche

adventures.title: Carstensz Pyramid Expedition
adventures.description:
The strangest of the Seven Summits: a 4,884 m blade of grey limestone rising out of equatorial jungle, streaked with rain, within sight of the giant Grasberg gold mine. Carstensz Pyramid (Puncak Jaya) is the highest point between the Himalaya and the Andes, and the only one of the seven that is a genuine rock climb — fixed lines up the slabby north face, a knife-edge summit ridge, and the famous gap crossed by Tyrolean traverse or a heart-stopping stride.

Modern expeditions helicopter from Timika into base camp in the Yellow Valley at 4,250 m, bypassing the week-long jungle approach that some operators still offer for the committed. Summit day starts at 3 a.m. in guaranteed drizzle: five to seven hours up wet limestone on jumars, an hour of exposed ridge, and the same in reverse. The catch is access itself — permits, security and helicopter weather all wobble, and departures routinely slip by days. Patience is part of the kit list.

Trips run 10 to 14 days door-to-door from Bali or Jakarta and cost £15,000 to £20,000 with helicopter access. You need solid jumar skills and comfort abseiling in the wet. It rains on the equator's glaciers nearly every day; count on climbing anyway.
highlights: Tyrolean traverse across the summit ridge gap
Highest point of the Australasian plate at 4,884 m
Helicopter flight over Papuan jungle to Yellow Valley
One of the Seven Summits almost nobody has met

adventures.title: Damavand: Roof of Persia
adventures.description:
Damavand is the mountain of Persian myth — the 5,610 m volcano where the tyrant Zahhak was chained, presiding over every poem and banknote in Iran — and the highest peak in the Middle East. From the south it is a beautifully simple proposition: a village start at Polour, a 4x4 track to the mosque-hut at Goosfand Sara (3,040 m), a day's climb to the modern Bargah-e-Sevom refuge at 4,220 m, and a long summit morning up scree and snowfields to a crater rim that steams.

The final 300 m brings the signature hazard: sulphur fumaroles pour gas across the route when the wind is wrong — time the last pitch for early morning, cover your face and do not linger. Otherwise the summer climb is non-technical — crampons for the frozen waterfall of Abshar-e-Yakhi at 5,100 m, honest altitude above.

Tehran is two hours away, which makes the logistics strangely easy: local operators arrange the climbing permit, hut bookings, mules and a guide for about £750 for a five-day acclimatised ascent. June to September is the season. The reward for the paperwork of an Iranian visa is a great mountain with almost no Western crowds, tea served at 4,220 m and the Caspian forests glittering to the north.
highlights: The steaming summit crater at 5,610 m
Frozen waterfall of Abshar-e-Yakhi at 5,100 m
Bargah-e-Sevom refuge nights with Iranian climbers
Highest summit in the Middle East
Mount of Persian legend above the Caspian forests

adventures.title: Huayna Potosi: The 6000er Next Door
adventures.description:
Nowhere else on Earth can you leave a capital city after breakfast and be roped up on a glacier by mid-afternoon. Huayna Potosi, 6,088 m, stands a two-hour drive from La Paz, and its normal route has earned the label 'easiest 6,000er' — true only in the sense that the climbing is straightforward. The altitude is anything but, and the final 45-degree slope to the summit ridge at dawn will empty your lungs completely.

The classic itinerary is three days: a night at the Casa Blanca refugio at 4,700 m with glacier school on the Zongo ice above, a short day to the Campo Argentino high camp at 5,130 m, then a 1 a.m. start threading crevasse fields and climbing the ramp to a summit ridge with Lake Titicaca silvering to the west and the whole Cordillera Real saw-toothed to the south. The catch: the price attracts the unacclimatised — spend three or four days in La Paz at 3,650 m first, or the mountain will send you down.

La Paz agencies run the climb for £250 to £400 including refugios, gear hire and a guide — insist on one guide per two climbers. June to September brings the stable Altiplano winter. It is the finest value first big summit in world mountaineering.
highlights: Summit ridge above Lake Titicaca at sunrise
Glacier school on the Zongo ice
High camp at Campo Argentino, 5,130 m
La Paz street food two hours after the glacier

adventures.title: Lenin Peak: The Accessible 7000er
adventures.description:
No other 7,000 m summit on Earth lets you drive to base camp through wildflower meadows. Lenin Peak (7,134 m) rises straight out of the Alay Valley in southern Kyrgyzstan, and its northern flank is the classic first step into true high-altitude mountaineering: technically straightforward, logistically simple, physiologically enormous.

From the yurts and marmots of Achik-Tash at 3,600 m, the route crosses the Puza glacier to Camp 1, climbs the notorious 'frying pan' — a solar-oven snow basin — to Camp 2 at 5,300 m, then gains the crest of Razdelnaya Peak for Camp 3 at 6,100 m. Summit day is a ten-to-twelve-hour ridge walk in thin, bitter air with a long false-flat that breaks more spirits than any crux. The catch is the weather: the Pamir fronts arrive fast, and the summit plateau has a history of trapping parties — turn-around discipline matters more than fitness here.

Fly to Osh, six hours by road from base camp. Full-service expeditions (July and August only) cost a remarkable £3,500 to £4,500 for three weeks, making this the cheapest 7,000er in the world. You need prior glacier experience and the patience for a proper rotation schedule; roughly one climber in three summits.
highlights: Base camp yurts in the Achik-Tash meadows
Crossing the 'frying pan' snow basin to Camp 2
The long summit ridge at 7,000 m over the Pamir
Marmots, eagles and Kyrgyz horsemen below the ice

adventures.title: Lobuche East Summit Climb
adventures.description:
From the summit ridge of Lobuche East, the entire Everest massif arranges itself for you: Nuptse's fluted wall, the black pyramid of Everest behind it, Pumori, Cholatse and a hundred unnamed spires floating above the Khumbu Glacier. At 6,119 m, this is the connoisseur's trekking peak — harder and quieter than Island Peak, with a summit day that is a real alpine climb rather than a queue.

The route leaves the yak pastures above Lobuche village for a rocky high camp at 5,400 m, then climbs slabby ledges by headtorch to the glacier. Fixed ropes protect several steep snow-and-ice steps of 45 degrees or more before the crest narrows to the airy final ridge. Many itineraries stop at the false summit; the true top depends on cornice conditions and whether your operator fixes the last section — ask before you book.

Most trips run 17 to 19 days from Kathmandu, acclimatising along the Everest Base Camp trail before doubling back to climb. That rhythm works beautifully: you arrive at high camp already adapted. Budget £2,300 to £2,800 including the NMA permit, flights to Lukla and full climbing support. Solid crampon footwork and abseil competence are expected on summit day.
highlights: Summit ridge panorama of Everest, Nuptse and Pumori
High camp above the Khumbu Glacier moraine
Acclimatisation trek through Namche and Dingboche

adventures.title: Mount Whitney Mountaineers Route
adventures.description:
While three hundred permit-holders zigzag up the trail on the far side, you are front-pointing up a 300-metre snow couloir with the East Face towering overhead — John Muir's own 1873 line to the highest summit in the contiguous United States, 4,421 m. The Mountaineers Route turns Whitney from a long walk into a proper climb: the scramble through the Ebersbacher Ledges, a camp beneath the vertical mile of granite at Iceberg Lake, then the couloir and a final exposed 120 m to the summit plateau.

Do it in spring, when consolidated snow makes the gully a clean ice-axe-and-crampons romp rather than a loose-scree misery. The catch is the 'final 400' above the notch — icy, steep and the site of most accidents; many guided parties rope up or traverse left onto easier ground.

Base in Lone Pine on Highway 395, all diners and Wild-West film history. Permits are by lottery through recreation.gov in February; guided three- or four-day ascents (Sierra Mountain Guides and others) run about £1,100. Acclimatise — you sleep at 3,800 m the night before the top.
adventures.location: Sierra Nevada, Inyo National Forest, California
highlights: Camping at Iceberg Lake beneath Whitney's East Face
Front-pointing the 300 m snow couloir at dawn
The exposed 'final 400' to the summit plateau
Highest point in the lower 48 at 4,421 m
Alabama Hills and Lone Pine's film-set landscape below

adventures.title: Kazbek from the Gergeti Glacier
adventures.description:
The climb starts, improbably, at a fourteenth-century church. From Gergeti Trinity — the most photographed building in the Caucasus — a trail climbs past the treeline into a wilderness of moraine, crossing the snout of the Gergeti Glacier to reach the old Soviet weather station at 3,653 m, now the bunkhouse-style Betlemi Hut. Two days later, if the mountain allows, you stand on Kazbek's 5,054 m ice dome with Russia at your back and all of Georgia unrolled to the south.

Summit day is a long glacier journey: roped travel through a crevasse field, a rising traverse to the 4,500 m plateau, then steady 30-35 degree slopes to the final col and dome. Nothing is technical in good conditions, but the catch is the mountain's notorious weather — cloud boils up from the Terek valley by mid-morning, and parties that start late navigate home by GPS. Build a spare day into the plan.

Stepantsminda, three hours from Tbilisi up the Georgian Military Highway, is the base: guesthouses, khinkali and gear hire. A guided six-day ascent with acclimatisation nights at Betlemi costs about £800; horses can carry kit to the hut. Easy visas and cheap logistics make it the region's most attainable 5,000er.
highlights: Setting out beneath Gergeti Trinity Church
Nights in the old weather station at 3,653 m
The 5,054 m ice dome above two countries
Khinkali and Georgian wine back in Stepantsminda
gear: GPS or phone with offline tracks

adventures.title: Mount Baker Coleman-Deming Climb
adventures.description:
Mount Baker holds more ice than every other Cascade volcano except Rainier, and the Coleman-Deming route uses the best of it: a broad glacier highway rising from the flower meadows of Heliotrope Ridge to the 3,286 m summit plateau. Halfway up you smell it — sulphur drifting from Sherman Crater, a reminder that the mountain under your crampons is very much alive.

This is the Pacific Northwest's great teaching mountain. Most three-day guided trips bundle a full day of crevasse-rescue and rope-team skills at camp on the moraine at 1,800 m before the 2 a.m. summit push, which saves its sting for the Roman Wall — 300 m of 35-degree snow that feels considerably steeper on descent. From the top, the San Juan Islands float in the haze to the west and the North Cascades saw away eastward.

The access town is Glacier, Washington, ninety minutes from Bellingham. Climb June to August; late season opens crevasses and complicates the route. Guided three-day climbs cost about £850. The catch is whiteout: Baker sits first in line for Pacific weather, and navigation on a featureless glacier is the skill that matters most here.
adventures.location: North Cascades, Mount Baker Wilderness, Washington
highlights: Crevasse-rescue school on the Coleman Glacier
Sulphur steam from Sherman Crater at 3,000 m
The Roman Wall in first light
San Juan Islands and North Cascades from the summit plateau

imageAttribution.artist: U.S. Forest Service - Pacific Northwest Region

adventures.title: Shasta via Avalanche Gulch
adventures.description:
Mount Shasta stands alone — a 4,322 m volcano rising three vertical kilometres straight out of the northern California pines, visible from a hundred miles in every direction. Avalanche Gulch is its time-honoured spring line: a huge, direct snow climb from Bunny Flat through Helen Lake camp at 3,140 m, up through the red volcanic gateway of the Red Banks, over the aptly named Misery Hill to a summit pinnacle streaked with fumarole steam.

Climb it in April to June while the gulch is still a firm white ribbon. The moment that stays with people is cresting the Red Banks at sunrise, when the mountain throws a hundred-mile shadow across the valley below. The variable that catches them is timing: by mid-morning the snow softens, rockfall rattles through the chimneys and the descent becomes a knee-deep wallow — summit early or not at all. Late-season the route turns to loose scree and is best avoided.

Mount Shasta City sits at the mountain's foot with gear shops that rent everything. Summit passes and wilderness permits are self-issued; a guided climb runs about £700. Glissading down the gulch in the afternoon is the fastest 2,000 m of descent in American mountaineering.
highlights: Sunrise over the Red Banks chimneys
Camp at Helen Lake snow basin
The great glissade descent of Avalanche Gulch

adventures.title: Gran Paradiso: First 4000er
adventures.description:
There is a Madonna on the summit of Gran Paradiso, and reaching her is a rite of passage: at 4,061 m, this is the highest mountain entirely within Italy and the alpinist's classic first 4,000er. The final metres tell you why it counts — after four hours of easy glacier plodding, the route suddenly narrows to an exposed rock ridge where you shuffle past the statue with the Aosta valley 3,000 m below your heels and Mont Blanc filling the northern sky.

The climb is a perfect two-day package. From the road-end at Pont in the Valsavarenche, a beautifully built mule path zigzags to the Rifugio Vittorio Emanuele II at 2,732 m (or the quieter Rifugio Chabod), where you eat pasta under blankets of marmot whistle. A 4:30 a.m. start puts you on the glacier at first light, roped against modest crevasses. The catch is the summit block: fine in the dry, tense in rime or queues; most parties want a rope and a confident leader.

Base in Aosta or Cogne; climb late June to September. Guided two-day ascents cost about £650 including the hut half-board; the national park — Italy's oldest, thick with ibex — is worth extra days on its own. Book the refuges weeks ahead for July and August weekends.
adventures.location: Gran Paradiso National Park, Aosta Valley
highlights: The Madonna on the exposed 4,061 m summit ridge
Mont Blanc panorama across the Aosta valley
A night at Rifugio Vittorio Emanuele II
Ibex herds in Italy's oldest national park
The classic first 4000er of the Alps

adventures.title: Iztaccíhuatl Arista del Sol
adventures.description:
The Aztecs saw a sleeping woman in Iztaccíhuatl's skyline — you climb along her body, from the Knees to the Breast, on the Arista del Sol, the 'ridge of the sun'. At 5,230 m she is Mexico's third-highest mountain and the country's finest weekend mountaineering objective, with the smoking cone of Popocatépetl filling the southern view the entire way.

From the La Joya trailhead at 3,950 m you climb to the Grupo de los Cien refuge or a high camp near 4,700 m, then follow the undulating summit ridge over false tops and the remnants of the Ayoloco glacier to the highest snowfield. Nothing is technical in good conditions, but the ridge gives and takes back altitude cruelly, and the final hour is a genuine slog.

Go between November and March, based out of Amecameca an hour from Mexico City. Guided two-day climbs cost around £550 including park fees and 4x4 transfers. The catch is acclimatisation: people fly into Mexico City on Friday and feel 5,000 m on Sunday. Build in a night at altitude, carry water for the whole route — there is none — and start pre-dawn for frozen scree.
highlights: Ridge traverse over the Sleeping Woman's Knees and Breast
Popocatépetl steaming across the Paso de Cortés
Sunrise from the Grupo de los Cien refuge
Standing on Mexico's third-highest summit at 5,230 m

adventures.title: Ojos del Salado: World's Highest Volcano
adventures.description:
Ojos del Salado is the highest volcano on Earth and the second-highest summit in the Americas — 6,893 m of wind-scoured scree and penitentes rising from the driest desert on the planet. There is no real glacier, often no snow: just mineral colours, flamingo lagoons at 4,300 m and a sky so dry the stars barely twinkle.

The climb is an exercise in vehicle-supported patience. From Copiapó you ladder up through the salt lakes — camps at Laguna Santa Rosa and the Laguna Verde hot spring, with acclimatisation walks on Mulas Muertas — before 4x4s grind to the Atacama refuge at 5,260 m and the tin-box Tejos refuge at 5,830 m. Summit day is ten hours in savage wind, finishing with a short roped rock scramble out of the crater to the true summit. The catch is wind — Atacama gales close the upper mountain for days, and itineraries without slack fail.

The season is December to March, high austral summer. Fourteen-day guided expeditions from Copiapó cost £3,500 to £4,500 including 4x4 logistics and refuge bookings. Non-technical apart from the last thirty metres, but the altitude, cold and dehydration make it a serious undertaking — many use it as Aconcagua's quieter, stranger sibling.
highlights: Soaking at Laguna Verde's hot spring at 4,300 m
Flamingos against Atacama salt lakes on the drive in
Roped scramble out of the crater to the 6,893 m summit
The clearest night skies in world mountaineering

adventures.title: Mount Hood via the Hogsback
adventures.description:
You leave Timberline Lodge in the dark, climb the groomed edge of the Palmer snowfield, and by 4 a.m. you are standing in Devil's Kitchen with sulphur in your nostrils and a white spine of snow — the Hogsback — arcing up towards the Pearly Gates. Mount Hood, 3,429 m, is Oregon's mountain and the most-climbed glaciated peak in North America, and this pre-dawn theatre is why.

Do not let the statistics fool you into complacency. The final 300 m through the Pearly Gates is genuine 35-degree climbing between rime-plastered walls, falling ice funnels through it as the sun hits the summit slopes, and the bergschrund below the Hogsback swallows careless glissaders most seasons. The climb is short but the margins are, too: summit at dawn, be off the steep ground by mid-morning.

The logistics are the easiest in this category — Portland is ninety minutes away, and you can drink an espresso at the 1937 WPA-built Timberline Lodge an hour after descending. Climb April to early June; register at the trailhead and buy the modest Mount Hood climbing permit online. Guided one-day ascents run about £550. Crampons that fit and an early alarm are the whole game.
highlights: Threading the rime towers of the Pearly Gates
Sunrise summit with Jefferson and St Helens on the skyline

adventures.title: Muztagh Ata: Father of Ice Mountains
adventures.description:
Muztagh Ata, 7,546 m, is the great white whale of the eastern Pamirs — a mountain so vast and so smoothly angled that expeditions climb it on skis. From Lake Karakul on the Karakoram Highway it looks like a single tilted snowfield propped against the Xinjiang sky, and that is essentially what the west ridge route is: forty degrees at its steepest, crevassed in patches, and utterly relentless for three vertical kilometres.

Camels carry loads from the Subashi grasslands to base camp at 4,400 m, where Kyrgyz herders sell yoghurt to acclimatising climbers. Three camps ladder the ridge — 5,400 m, 6,200 m and 6,900 m — and most teams make two full rotations before a summit push. On skis the descent is the reward of a lifetime: 2,500 m of turns off a 7,500 m peak. On foot the endless summit plateau extracts the price; whiteouts demand GPS discipline.

Expeditions stage through Kashgar, the old Silk Road city, with Chinese permits arranged by the operator — allow months for paperwork. The season is June to August; full-service trips run £5,500 to £7,500 over about four weeks. It may be the technically easiest 7,500er on Earth, but the altitude is real: treat it as a full expedition.
highlights: Camel caravan to base camp from Subashi
Ski or snowshoe ascent of the great west ridge
Camp 3 at 6,900 m above the Pamir plateau
A 2,500 m ski descent from near the summit
Kashgar's Silk Road old town before and after

adventures.title: Mount Athabasca North Glacier Ascent
adventures.description:
Mount Athabasca is where Canadian mountaineering begins — literally, for generations of climbers. The 3,491 m peak rises directly above the Columbia Icefield on the Icefields Parkway, and its North Glacier and AA Col routes pack everything into a single long day: a 3 a.m. start from the climbers' car park, crevassed glacier travel by headtorch, a steepening 40-degree snow ramp over the bergschrund and a final windy ridge to a summit overlooking the largest icefield in the Rockies.

The sunrise is the reason people come back. From half-height, the light floods across the Athabasca Glacier and catches Snow Dome and Andromeda in sequence, while the Parkway's tour buses are still hours from waking. The catch is conditions: the bergschrund opens through the season, the glacier's crevasse bridges rot in warm spells, and ACMG guides frequently reroute or turn parties around — flexibility is part of the deal.

Base in Jasper, one hour north, and climb June to September. A guided one-day ascent costs about £550 with a pre-trip skills evening; many treat it as the graduation climb after a crevasse-rescue course. Fitness for 1,500 m of ascent is the entry requirement.
adventures.location: Columbia Icefield, Jasper National Park, Alberta
highlights: Dawn over the Columbia Icefield from the upper ramp
Crossing the bergschrund below the summit slopes
Snow Dome and Mount Andromeda across the glacier
A classic first 'real' alpine summit in the Rockies

adventures.title: Grand Canyon Oar-Raft Expedition
adventures.description:
Fourteen days, 226 miles, and a vertical mile of rock between you and the rim: a full-length oar-raft expedition through the Grand Canyon is the benchmark against which river trips are measured. From the glassy put-in at Lees Ferry the Colorado drops through more than eighty rapids, the geology rewinding two billion years until you camp beneath black Vishnu schist older than complex life.

The rapids arrive as rites of passage — Hance, Crystal, then Lava Falls, the most famous whitewater in North America, scouted with your stomach somewhere around your knees. Between them come the canyon's soft miracles: the vaulted amphitheatre of Redwall Cavern, the impossible blue of Havasu Creek, waterfalls at Deer Creek and Elves Chasm, mule deer in camp at dusk.

Book absurdly early: commercial seats with licensed outfitters (about £4,900 for a full canyon, meals and guides included) sell out more than a year out, and private permits go by weighted lottery with years-long odds. Trips launch April to October; spring and autumn dodge the worst heat. The variable nobody expects is the water — released from Glen Canyon Dam at 8C, it makes every splash a gasp in desert air that can hit 45C.
adventures.location: Grand Canyon National Park, Colorado River, Arizona
highlights: Running Lava Falls, North America's most famous rapid
The turquoise water of Havasu Creek
Waterfall side hikes at Deer Creek and Elves Chasm
226 miles from Lees Ferry to Diamond Creek
gear: Quick-dry layers plus a paddle jacket for 8C splashes
Small dry bag for day access on the raft

adventures.title: Whanganui River Journey by Canoe
adventures.description:
One of New Zealand's Great Walks is not a walk at all. The Whanganui Journey runs 145 kilometres by open canoe from Taumarunui to Pipiriki, through a roadless gorge of fern-hung papa cliffs — a river so central to Māori identity that in 2017 it became the first in the world granted legal personhood. Every bend has a name, a story and, frequently, a cheeky rapid.

More than a hundred of those rapids, none beyond Class II, make this a perfect first expedition — enough splash to keep the bow paddler honest, never enough to require heroics. The set-piece day is the walk from Mangapurua Landing to the Bridge to Nowhere, a full concrete road bridge marooned in deep bush, relic of a failed soldier-settlement scheme. Nights alternate between DOC huts and campsites; at Tīeke Kāinga the hut shares its terrace with a marae.

Book hut and campsite passes for the October-April season through DOC, then hire canoes and barrels in Taumarunui or Ōhakune — shuttles included, from about £420 for five days all-in. The variable is rain: the river can rise metres overnight, and operators hold parties back until it settles. The 50/50 rapid capsizes more canoes than any other; strap the barrels.
highlights: Paddling a river with legal personhood
The Bridge to Nowhere at Mangapurua
One hundred-plus friendly rapids in a roadless gorge
A night at Tīeke Kāinga beside the marae
Glow-worms in the streamside banks after dark
gear: Open Canadian canoe with lashed barrels (hired locally)
Quick-dry layers and a warm fleece — gorge nights chill

adventures.title: Nahanni River Canoe Expedition
adventures.description:
You hear Náįlįcho — Virginia Falls — an hour before you see it: 96 metres of the South Nahanni folding over a sandstone lip around a central spire, nearly twice the height of Niagara, with no road within a hundred kilometres. Most expeditions begin here, floatplane from Fort Simpson, portaging the falls, then a week of big, readable whitewater through four canyons cut a kilometre deep into the Mackenzie Mountains.

The days build a rhythm: Class II-III wave trains, an eddy-out to soak at Kraus Hotsprings, camps on gravel bars in Deadmen Valley beneath 1,200-metre limestone. At The Gate the river hairpins under Pulpit Rock and the walls close to a corridor that silences every boat. This was among the first World Heritage sites ever inscribed, and it still feels like nobody has told anyone.

Tandem whitewater canoe experience (or hard training on day one) is expected; spraydecked canoes handle the rest. Outfitters run 10-14 day guided descents from about £6,200 including the floatplane; self-guided parties need park registration and a shuttle plan out of Nahanni Butte. The variable is water level — a rainy week upstream turns III into a pushy IV, and guides re-rig accordingly.
adventures.location: Nahanni National Park Reserve, Northwest Territories
highlights: Náįlįcho (Virginia Falls), twice the height of Niagara
Running four kilometre-deep canyons of the South Nahanni
The Gate's hairpin beneath Pulpit Rock
Camping on gravel bars in Deadmen Valley
gear: Drysuit or heavyweight wetsuit with paddle jacket

adventures.title: Bowron Lakes Canoe Circuit
adventures.description:
The Bowron is a geographical fluke that feels designed for canoeists: a 116-kilometre rectangle of lakes, rivers and portages looping through the Cariboo Mountains of British Columbia, finishing a short walk from where you started. No shuttles, no backtracking — just a week of paddling beneath 2,000-metre peaks, with bear caches at numbered campsites and moose feeding in the marshes at either end of the day.

The crux is Isaac Lake, 38 kilometres of cold water walled by mountains, where an afternoon wind can raise a genuine sea — experienced parties paddle it early and sit out the blow. The portages (the longest about 2.4 km) go easier than feared because BC Parks allows canoe carts on the graded trails; pack in barrels and roll, don't carry.

Start at the registration centre near Bowron Lake, an hour's gravel drive from the gold-rush village of Wells. You must book a circuit reservation with BC Parks — summer slots go quickly when they release — and clear an orientation talk before launching. Self-guided, the trip costs about £550 with canoe and cart hire; guided departures run around £1,600. June brings mosquitoes, September brings gold birches and quiet water.
adventures.location: Bowron Lake Provincial Park, British Columbia
highlights: Completing the 116 km natural circuit of lakes back to your start point
Dawn mirror-water on 38 km Isaac Lake
Moose feeding in the Bowron River marshes
Rolling portages with a canoe cart between watersheds
gear: Canoe cart for the portage trails
Bear spray and rope for food caches
Neoprene paddling gloves for cold mornings
Paper map — there is no phone signal anywhere on the circuit

adventures.title: Johnstone Strait Orca Kayak
adventures.description:
You are rafted up with the group, mid-channel, when the first blow goes off like a struck pipe — then six black fins rise in line, and a family of northern resident orcas passes within a hundred metres of your bow. Johnstone Strait, the tide-ripped channel off northeastern Vancouver Island, holds the most predictable concentration of orcas on Earth each summer, drawn by salmon runs and the rubbing beaches of the Robson Bight reserve — which kayaks skirt respectfully while the whales do as they please.

Most trips base at a wilderness camp near Kaikash Creek, paddling out on the tides: humpbacks lunge-feeding in Blackfish Sound, Steller sea lions, porpoises stitching the current lines, black bears turning rocks at low water. Evenings, a hydrophone dropped off the beach pipes the whales' calls into camp.

Depart from Telegraph Cove, a boardwalk hamlet an hour from Port McNeill. Guided basecamps of four to six days run about £1,350; book early for late July and August, the salmon peak. The variables are honest ones: fog can pin the group ashore, and orcas sign no contracts — most weeks deliver daily sightings, some don't. The 100-metre wildlife protocol is strict.
adventures.location: Johnstone Strait, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
highlights: Northern resident orca families passing at paddle level
Listening to orca calls on the camp hydrophone
The boardwalk village of Telegraph Cove
gear: Warm synthetic layers for fog mornings
Rubber boots for rocky beach camps
Dry bags for a week under canvas
Earplugs — sea lions argue all night

adventures.title: Northwest Passage Expedition Voyage
adventures.description:
For four centuries this route killed the people who attempted it. Now, in the brief August window when the ice relents, expedition ships thread the channels of the Canadian High Arctic that Franklin's men died trying to map. The emotional centre of the voyage is Beechey Island: three weathered wooden headboards on a gravel beach, graves of the first men lost from the 1845 expedition, fog rolling over the anchorage where Erebus and Terror wintered.

Between the history, the Arctic performs. Zodiacs idle beneath the seabird cities of Prince Leopold Island, polar bears amble the Somerset Island shoreline, and if the ice allows a transit of narrow Bellot Strait you pass the northernmost tip of mainland America. In Gjoa Haven, where Amundsen overwintered and learned from Inuit the skills that later won him the Pole, community visits put living culture alongside the mythology.

Voyages of 14 to 17 days run between Kangerlussuaq in Greenland and Kugluktuk or Cambridge Bay, bookended by charter flights. Berths start around £11,500 and the itinerary is written in pencil: the daily ice chart decides which channels you actually sail. Some years ships turn back — that uncertainty is the point.
highlights: The Franklin expedition graves on Beechey Island
Zodiac cruising beneath Prince Leopold Island's seabird cliffs
Transiting narrow Bellot Strait, ice permitting
Community visit at Gjoa Haven, Amundsen's winter refuge
Polar bears and belugas along Peel Sound
gear: Binoculars — the wildlife rarely comes to you
Dry bag for camera gear in the Zodiac

adventures.title: Futaleufú Whitewater Week
adventures.description:
Kayakers call the Futaleufú the finest whitewater river on Earth with a straight face. It pours out of the Andes into Chilean Patagonia an improbable glacial blue, and a week here is structured like an apprenticeship: mornings drilling technique on the forgiving Bridge-to-Bridge section, afternoons stepping up through the river's famous named water — Mundaca, Casa de Piedra, and eventually the wave-train of Terminator for those who earn it.

You run it in paddle rafts with safety kayakers shadowing every line, or in your own kayak if you bring a solid roll. Off the water there is camp life Patagonian-style: wood-fired hot tubs, asado under southern stars, and valley hikes when your shoulders demand a rest day.

The river sits a long way from anywhere — part of its magic. Fly to Puerto Montt and ferry-bus via Chaitén, or come overland from Esquel in Argentina; either way budget a full travel day. Camps run December to March, from about £2,600 for a week, all meals and river gear included. The variable is the swim: day one is rescue drills in 12C water, and the guides mean it — the Futaleufú is generous but it is not casual. Book peak weeks months ahead; the camps are small.
highlights: Running Terminator, one of the world's great big-water rapids
Glacial-blue Class IV water at Casa de Piedra and Mundaca
Progression coaching on the Bridge-to-Bridge section
Wood-fired hot tubs at riverside camp
gear: 3/4mm wetsuit plus paddle jacket (camps supply river kit)
Whitewater helmet and rescue PFD (supplied, bring your own if certified)
Quick-dry camp clothes and down jacket for evenings
Sun cream — glare doubles off the water

adventures.title: Scoresby Sund Sea Kayak Expedition
adventures.description:
The world's largest fjord system swallows sound. You slide your kayak between icebergs the size of cathedrals off Sydkap, and the only noise is meltwater ticking off blue ice and the exhale of a distant humpback. Scoresby Sund cuts 350 kilometres into East Greenland, and for ten days you paddle a corner of it — the red sandstone walls of Rødefjord, the iceberg labyrinth of the Bjørneøer, muskox grazing the tundra terraces above your camp.

The moment that stays with you is the stillness: an evening paddle at midnight under low golden light, engine-free, in a fjord bigger than Wales with nobody else in it. The variable that catches people out is the katabatic wind — glacier-cooled air that can turn a mirror calm into a foaming fetch in twenty minutes, so itineraries flex and windbound days are part of the deal.

Trips stage through Constable Point airstrip, reached by charter from Reykjavík or Akureyri, with a visit to Ittoqqortoormiit — 350 people, 70-odd sled dogs, one of the remotest settlements on Earth. Guided expeditions run late July to August only, book out nearly a year ahead, and cost about £4,500 before flights. Drysuits are non-negotiable; the water is barely above zero.
highlights: Paddling the iceberg labyrinth of the Bjørneøer (Bear Islands)
Red sandstone walls of Rødefjord under the midnight sun
Muskox grazing above camp on the Jameson Land tundra
Visiting Ittoqqortoormiit, one of the remotest settlements on Earth
Humpback and narwhal sightings in the outer sound
gear: Neoprene pogies and spare paddling gloves
80L of dry bags in mixed sizes

adventures.title: Ardèche Gorges Wild-Camp Descent
adventures.description:
The Ardèche saves its best trick for the first hour: you round a bend from Vallon-Pont-d'Arc and paddle straight beneath the Pont d'Arc, a 60-metre natural arch spanning the entire river. Beyond it the road disappears and the gorge takes over — 30 kilometres of limestone canyon, green water, and readable rapids a determined beginner in a double canoe can manage with wet pride.

What lifts this above a day-trip is the bivouac system: descents overnight at Gaud and Gournier, the only two camps inside the gorge, sleeping under canvas metres from the river. Dawn belongs to you — beavers on the banks at first light, Bonelli's eagles riding the rim thermals, the day-trip flotilla still hours away. Pair the descent with Grotte Chauvet 2, the replica of the 36,000-year-old painted cave, ten minutes from the put-in.

Base in Vallon-Pont-d'Arc (two hours from Lyon, one from Avignon TGV), hire boats and barrels from any licensed outfitter, and pre-book the bivouacs — pitches are capped and July-August sells out weeks ahead. A two-night descent costs around £240 with hire and camping. The variable is water level: spring runs pushy, late August scrapes gravel, June is the sweet spot.
highlights: Paddling beneath the Pont d'Arc natural arch
Bivouac nights at Gaud and Gournier inside the gorge
Beavers on the banks at first light
Bonelli's eagles over the canyon rim
Grotte Chauvet 2 replica cave beside the put-in
gear: Hired open canoe with waterproof barrels
Sun hat and SPF50 — the gorge is a reflector oven
Sleeping bag and mat for the bivouac
Soft cool bag for barbecue supplies

adventures.title: Churchill River Beluga Kayak
adventures.description:
The first touch comes from below: a gentle bump on your rudder, then a white shape rolling under the hull, one eye swivelled up at you. Every July and August roughly four thousand beluga whales crowd into the Churchill River estuary on Hudson Bay to feed and calve, and they treat kayaks as the most interesting thing in the water. They sing constantly — put a bare hand on the hull and you feel the chirps through the fibreglass.

Five days gives you repeat estuary sessions timed to the tides, plus the rest of subarctic Churchill: the 18th-century star fort of Prince of Wales Fort at the river mouth, tundra hikes among fireweed, and a genuine chance of a summer polar bear loafing on the rocks — which is why guides carry deterrents and nobody wanders the shoreline alone.

Logistics are the catch. No road reaches Churchill: you fly two hours from Winnipeg or take the two-night train, and operators bundle everything — expect around £3,800 for five days before the flight north. The variable is the wind: a stiff northerly puts whitecaps on the estuary and swaps your kayak session for a Zodiac. August adds northern lights to the deal.
adventures.location: Churchill River estuary, Hudson Bay, Manitoba
highlights: Thousands of belugas crowding the Churchill River estuary
Whale song vibrating through the kayak hull
Prince of Wales Fort at the river mouth
Summer polar bears loafing along Hudson Bay
Aurora over the tundra on August nights
gear: Warm synthetic layers — the estuary sits at 10C in July
Waterproof action camera with hull mount

adventures.title: Everglades Wilderness Waterway
adventures.description:
Ninety-nine miles of mangrove maze separate Everglades City from Flamingo, and for eight days your world shrinks to a kayak, a chart and the tide table. The Wilderness Waterway threads the Ten Thousand Islands and the rivers behind them — Broad, Shark, the open sweep of Whitewater Bay — past sunning alligators, dolphins herding mullet, and the occasional American crocodile near Flamingo.

Nights are the signature: you sleep on chickees, roofed wooden platforms standing alone over the water, cooking dinner while tarpon roll in the dark. The variable is not wildlife but navigation and water — every mangrove island looks like the last one, wind against tide turns the big bays lumpy, and there is no fresh water on the route, so you carry four to six litres per person per day.

Go in the dry season, December to March, when mosquitoes relent and the heat is civil. Backcountry permits are limited and released close to departure, so keep dates flexible; outfitters in Everglades City rent boats and shuttle the one-way finish. Self-supported costs a few hundred pounds; guided trips run around £1,100. Study the tides — paddling the Broad against a spring ebb is a lesson nobody repeats.
highlights: Sleeping on chickee platforms above the water
Threading the mangrove maze of the Ten Thousand Islands
Alligators and American crocodiles on one route
Star-filled nights days from the nearest road
gear: 4-6 litres of fresh water per person per day
Tide tables for the river mouths
Portable toilet system (required in the backcountry)

adventures.title: Danube Delta Canoe Safari
adventures.description:
Europe's second-longest river ends not with a city but with a wilderness: 4,000 square kilometres of reedbeds, floating islands and secret channels where the Danube unravels into the Black Sea. By canoe you travel it at heron pace — gliding lily-covered canals off the Sulina arm while squadrons of great white pelicans wheel overhead from the largest colony outside Africa, kingfishers strafing the bow, pygmy cormorants drying their wings on every snag.

The delta is a culture as much as an ecosystem. Nights are spent in the guesthouses of Lipovan fishing villages — Mila 23, Crișan — eating storceag, the local fish soup, with hosts whose families have netted these channels for three centuries. The strangest afternoon comes at Letea: an ancient oak forest draped in lianas, wild horses grazing between sand dunes — inside Europe.

The gateway is Tulcea, four hours from Bucharest, where guided canoe safaris depart with support boats carrying the luggage; six days runs about £720 with all meals. May-June brings peak birdlife, September migration and gold light; high summer serves heat and mosquitoes in industrial quantities. Bring optics before optimism — the birds are the point.
adventures.location: Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve, Tulcea County
highlights: Great white pelican squadrons over the reedbeds
Paddling the backwaters of the Sulina arm
Fish-soup dinners in the Lipovan village of Mila 23
Wild horses in the Letea oak forest
Migration spectacle in the September skies

adventures.title: Finnmarksvidda Husky Sled Crossing
adventures.description:
From the first "OK!" your team of five huskies hits the line like a catapult, and Europe's largest mountain plateau opens in front of you: white to every horizon, birch scrub buried to its tips. This is a proper crossing — six days from the Alta valley across the Finnmarksvidda towards Karasjok, sharing terrain with the Finnmarksløpet, Europe's longest sled-dog race. You drive your own sled the whole way, feed and harness your own dogs, and sleep in wilderness cabins heated by the stove you light yourself.

The moment that makes the trip arrives on the second or third night, standing outside the cabin at -25C while the aurora unrolls green over a silence so complete you can hear the dogs dreaming. The variable that catches people out is wind-chill: on the open vidda a modest breeze at -30C strips heat frighteningly fast, and guides will hold a rest day rather than cross exposed sections in poor visibility.

Fly to Alta via Oslo or Tromsø; kennels sit twenty minutes from town. Expeditions run February to April when daylight returns, from roughly £2,600 including thermal suits and boots. Fitness matters — you run uphill behind the sled more than the brochures admit.
highlights: Driving your own five-dog husky team across the vidda
Aurora borealis over snowbound wilderness cabins
Following terrain used by the Finnmarksløpet race
Sami reindeer herds on the winter plateau
Silence at -25C, days from the nearest road
gear: Wool base layers, two full sets
Hand-warmer pouches for camera and phone

adventures.title: Kekova Sunken City Sea Kayak
adventures.description:
Beneath your hull lies a staircase that has led nowhere for eighteen centuries. Kekova Sound, on Turkey's Lycian coast, holds the ruins of ancient Dolchiste — dropped into the sea by a second-century earthquake — and a sea kayak is the only craft allowed close: you drift over submerged walls and doorways, quays a metre underwater, amphora shards catching the light. Swimming over the protected zone is banned, which keeps the water archaeologically still and glass-clear.

Across the sound, Kaleköy village stacks up to the castle of ancient Simena, Lycian sarcophagi standing hip-deep in the shallows. Five days covers the sound and its islands at siesta pace: morning water like oil, grilled fish at a jetty restaurant, a crossing to the Aperlai ruins, gulets ghosting past under sail.

Base in Üçağız, a fishing village reached by dolmuş from Demre; fly to Antalya or Dalaman. Guided trips with licensed operators run from about £680 including guesthouse nights and permits — the sound is protected, so freelancing is restricted. Sea state is rarely the issue; the variable is heat, which is why spring and autumn are the connoisseur's seasons and July departures launch at first light.
adventures.location: Kekova Sound, Lycian Coast, Antalya Province
highlights: Drifting over the sunken ruins of Dolchiste
Lycian sarcophagi standing in the shallows at Simena
Grilled fish at a jetty restaurant in Üçağız
gear: Wide-brimmed hat and UV paddling top
Polarised sunglasses for reading the seabed
3L of water per day on board
Dry bag for camera and lira

adventures.title: Milos & Polyaigos Sea Kayak
adventures.description:
Milos is a volcano the Aegean got at with ten million years of chisel work, and a kayak is the only craft that fits inside the results. You paddle beneath the white pumice moonscape of Sarakiniko, through rock arches at Kleftiko where pirates once hid their boats, and into sea caves like Sykia, whose collapsed roof turns the water to lit turquoise. Day stages link volcanic bays no road reaches, each in a different palette — sulphur yellow, oxide red, bone white.

The wilder half of the week is Polyaigos, the largest uninhabited island in the Aegean, a short crossing away: no houses, no jetties, just cliffs, wild goats, and coves where Mediterranean monk seals haul out. Lunch is bread, tomatoes and cheese on a beach with no footprints.

Base in Adamas, Milos's ferry port (boats from Piraeus, or a short flight from Athens); local outfits run guided weeks from about £950 with camping or guesthouse nights. The variable is the meltemi — the dry northerly that blows hardest in July and August and can cancel crossings for days — which is why May-June and September-October are the smart windows. Modest experience is fine; the guides read the wind and re-order the coastline to suit.
highlights: The pirate coves and arches of Kleftiko
Paddling beneath Sarakiniko's white pumice moonscape
Sykia sea cave lit through its collapsed roof
Monk seal sightings along empty volcanic coast
gear: Long-sleeved sun top and peaked cap
Mask and snorkel for cave stops
3L water bladder — the islands are dry

adventures.title: Åland Archipelago Sea Kayak
adventures.description:
Between Sweden and Finland the Baltic shatters into the Åland archipelago — six and a half thousand islands of pink rapakivi granite, pine and fishing hamlets, threaded by water so sheltered it often behaves like a lake. For six days you island-hop east from Mariehamn, choosing each night's skerry under everyman's right: land, pitch on sun-warmed rock, swim in brackish water that barely tastes of salt, under a midsummer sun that never properly sets.

The rhythm is the reward — sea eagles overhead, eider flotillas parting round your bow, an evening sauna at a guest harbour, silence everywhere else. Kökar, far out in the southeast, is the classic objective: a bare outer-archipelago parish with an 18th-century church and more sheep than people.

The variable that catches people out is fetch: the inner channels flatter you, then a southwesterly builds over open Baltic gaps and the crossings turn serious, so plan routes with escape options. Reach Mariehamn by ferry from Stockholm, Turku or Helsinki; outfitters there rent proper sea kayaks and run guided weeks from about £850. June and July give endless light; August adds warmer swimming and the first dark nights for stargazing.
highlights: Wild camping on your own granite skerry each night
Sea eagles and eider flotillas at close range
Reaching remote Kökar in the outer archipelago
Wood-fired sauna and Baltic swim at a guest harbour
gear: Lightweight free-standing tent for rock pitches
Marine chart of the Archipelago Sea
Swimwear and travel towel for saunas
Sun cream — the water doubles every ray

adventures.title: Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park Kayak
adventures.description:
The Exumas run for 120 miles like a dropped necklace, and at their heart sits the Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park — founded in 1958, the first marine protected area of its kind, and a no-take zone where reef life behaves as if humans were a rumour. For eight days you kayak cay to cay across water in shades the brochure cannot exaggerate, camping on designated beaches, snorkelling coral heads where nurse sharks, eagle rays and turtles drift past unbothered.

The day that makes the trip is Shroud Cay: you ride a tidal creek through the mangroves clean across the island, climb Camp Driftwood's lookout, and drop onto an ocean-facing beach that resets your idea of blue. At park headquarters on Warderick Wells, a sperm whale skeleton lies articulated along the beach — the obligatory photograph.

Logistics take planning: fly to George Town or Staniel Cay, arrange water-taxi transfers to the park, and carry every drop of fresh water — there is none on the uninhabited cays. Guided expeditions handle boats, permits and shuttles for around £1,900. The variable is the winter trade wind: a 20-knot easterly turns the banks choppy, so itineraries hop the lee sides with weather days in reserve.
adventures.location: Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park, Bahamas
highlights: Riding Shroud Cay's mangrove creek to Camp Driftwood
Snorkelling a no-take reserve protected since 1958
The sperm whale skeleton at Warderick Wells
Nurse sharks and eagle rays over the sand flats
gear: Sit-on-top or touring kayak with deck lines
20L minimum fresh water capacity per person
Mask, snorkel and reef-safe sun cream

adventures.title: Labyrinth Canyon Canoe on the Green River
adventures.description:
There are no rapids in Labyrinth Canyon — that is the whole point. For five days the Green River carries your canoe at walking pace through a sandstone trench of deepening reds and golds, and the hardest thing you do all day is choose a camp among the cottonwoods. This is desert paddling as meditation: herons lifting off sandbars, canyon wrens spiralling song down the walls, side hikes to arches and fur trapper Denis Julien's 1836 inscription.

The centrepiece is Bowknot Bend, seven miles of river looping a mesa to arrive a few hundred metres from where it started; climb the saddle and you see both reaches at once. Powell named the canyon on his 1869 descent, and remarkably little has changed since.

Put in at Ruby Ranch and take out at Mineral Bottom, where a shuttle grinds up to Moab — or continue into Stillwater Canyon for the jet-boat pickup above the Colorado confluence. A free BLM permit, fire pan and pack-out toilet are mandatory; hire and shuttles from Moab bring a self-guided trip in around £520. The variables: no drinking water in the canyon, spring winds that can blow a canoe upstream, and summer heat that makes April-May and September-October the sane seasons.
highlights: Climbing the saddle of Bowknot Bend's seven-mile loop
Side canyons to arches and ancestral ruins
gear: Canoe with dry barrels (hired in Moab)
Fire pan and pack-out toilet system (required)
40L of water capacity for the party
Sun shelter or tarp for midday heat

adventures.title: Arrigetch Peaks & Alatna River Packraft
adventures.description:
The Arrigetch — "fingers of the outstretched hand" in Iñupiaq — are the Brooks Range at its most improbable: granite spires like Shot Tower and Caliban erupting from arctic tundra, six hundred miles from the nearest traffic light. A floatplane out of Bettles drops you at Circle Lake, then two days of hauling packs up the Arrigetch Creek valley bring you to basecamp beneath towers that see a few dozen visitors a year.

Then the trip inverts: back at the Alatna River you inflate packrafts and ride a clear Class I-II current south for days, camping on gravel bars, watching grizzlies mousing on the banks and caribou swimming the channels. Take-out is Takahula Lake, where the floatplane finds you again. Late August stains the tundra crimson and switches the night lights on.

This is Gates of the Arctic National Park: no trails, no signage, no rescue on tap — parties must be genuinely self-sufficient, and most go guided (around £6,800, 10 days, from Fairbanks via Bettles). The variable is rain: the Alatna can rise fast, and the tussock-and-boulder walk to the peaks is slow, wet work that laughs at your mileage plans. Book the bush plane early; August seats go first.
adventures.location: Gates of the Arctic National Park, Brooks Range, Alaska
highlights: Basecamp beneath the granite spires of the Arrigetch
Floatplane drop at Circle Lake from Bettles
Packrafting the clear Class I-II Alatna River
Grizzlies and swimming caribou from the water
Autumn tundra and aurora in late August
gear: Packraft with spraydeck and four-piece paddle

adventures.title: Route 66: Chicago to Santa Monica
adventures.description:
America's Main Street still runs 2,400 miles from a brown sign on Adams Street in Chicago to the pier at Santa Monica, and driving it end to end remains the definitive American road trip. The interstate long ago bypassed the Mother Road, which is exactly the point: you trade speed for neon motels in Tucumcari, the half-buried Cadillacs of Cadillac Ranch outside Amarillo, and the burros that mob your car in Oatman, Arizona.

The moment that stays with you comes west of Seligman, where the longest unbroken stretch of original 66 rolls through empty high desert with the railway for company, and you finally understand the fuss. The variable that catches people out is pacing: two weeks is the honest minimum, and squeezing it into ten days turns the trip into interstate slog. Navigation is the other trap — old alignments go unsigned, so carry the EZ66 guide alongside the sat-nav.

Fly into Chicago, drop the hire car in Los Angeles (one-way fees sting), and budget around £2,200 per person for fourteen nights of motor courts, fuel, diners and pie.
highlights: The longest original stretch through Seligman, Arizona
Painted Desert and Petrified Forest National Park
End-of-the-trail sign on Santa Monica Pier

adventures.title: Great Ocean Road: Torquay to the Twelve Apostles
adventures.description:
Built by returned soldiers as a memorial to their fallen, the Great Ocean Road winds 243 km along Victoria's surf coast from Torquay to the shipwreck cliffs beyond Port Campbell. It is Australia's most famous drive, and the trick is refusing to do it as the day-trip it has become.

Start at Bells Beach, pause under the Memorial Arch, and idle through Lorne to Kennett River, where wild koalas doze in the roadside manna gums. Cut through the cool-temperate rainforest of the Great Otways — tree ferns, waterfalls and the Cape Otway lightstation — before the coast turns violent: the Twelve Apostles' limestone stacks, the story-soaked chasm of Loch Ard Gorge, and the collapsed span of London Bridge. The moment is the Apostles at dawn, sea mist threading the stacks, hours before the first coach and helicopter arrive.

The variables: drive it westbound so you hold the ocean-side lane; Melbourne day-trippers make the viewpoints a conga line from mid-morning, so sleep two nights along the way; and total fire ban days in high summer can close the Otways. Four days from Melbourne runs about £600 per person in motels and seafood.
adventures.location: Victoria surf coast and Shipwreck Coast
gear: Layers — four seasons a day on this coast
Head torch for dawn viewpoint starts

adventures.title: Icefields Parkway: Glaciers of Highway 93
adventures.description:
The 232 km of Highway 93 between Lake Louise and Jasper may be the most concentrated mountain scenery you can see through a windscreen anywhere on earth. Glaciers hang off the Continental Divide on both sides, and the pull-offs come so fast — Herbert Lake at dawn, Bow Lake, Peyto's impossibly blue wolf-head — that a drive timetabled at three hours honestly takes a day.

The set-piece is the Columbia Icefield, where you can walk the moraines to the snout of the Athabasca Glacier or climb the Wilcox Pass trail for the panorama the postcards use. Push on past the roar of Athabasca Falls and finish with a quiet morning canoe on Maligne Lake out of Jasper.

Book Banff or Lake Louise beds months ahead for July and August, or do it by campervan. The variable that catches people out is time: wildlife jams, trailheads and afternoon storms eat the schedule, so spread the parkway over three or more nights rather than one. Around £900 per person covers five days of park passes, mid-range rooms and fuel, hiring from Calgary.
adventures.location: Banff and Jasper National Parks, Alberta
highlights: Peyto Lake viewpoint at Bow Summit
Athabasca Glacier toe walk at the Columbia Icefield
Wilcox Pass trail above the icefield

adventures.title: Transfăgărășan and Transalpina Grand Tour
adventures.description:
Romania built two of Europe's most spectacular high roads across the Carpathians within a hundred kilometres of each other, and the only sensible response is to drive both. Base in Sibiu's pastel old town and make a five-day figure-of-eight through the Făgăraș and Parâng mountains.

The Transfăgărășan (DN7C) is the headline: Ceaușescu's folly climbs through glacial scenery to 2,042 m at Bâlea Lake, and the view down the northern ramp — that impossible grey ribbon stitched into the cirque — is the one you have seen and not quite believed. Beyond the tunnel lie Vidraru dam and the 1,480 steps to Poenari citadel, the real fortress of Vlad the Impaler. The quieter Transalpina (DN67C) actually climbs higher, grazing 2,145 m at Urdele Pass on its bald ridge line.

The variables: both passes open only from about late June until October, and weekend traffic on the Transfăgărășan can crawl — sleep at the Bâlea cabana and drive the ramp at dawn instead. Watch for sheepdogs at laybys and never feed the bears that beg along the lower forest sections. Around £550 per person for five days of guesthouses, fuel and papanași.
highlights: Transfăgărășan northern ramp from Bâlea Lake
gear: Cash for pass-top sheep's cheese stalls

adventures.title: Carretera Austral Self-Drive to Villa O'Higgins
adventures.description:
Chile's Route 7 runs 1,240 km from Puerto Montt to the road-end hamlet of Villa O'Higgins, stitched together by ferries where the fjords interrupt it. Driving its full length is Patagonia at drip-feed pace: temperate rainforest, hanging glaciers, turquoise rivers and pioneer villages that still feel a day beyond the map.

The moments: the Ventisquero Colgante hanging glacier calving over its lagoon in Queulat; kayaking into the marble caves at Puerto Río Tranquilo; Cerro Castillo's basalt spires above the road's finest pass; and the final ferry-and-gravel push to O'Higgins, where the southern ice field blocks all further progress and the visitor book reads like a club.

The variables: the Hornopirén–Caleta Gonzalo ferries must be booked weeks ahead in January and February; long ripio sections eat tyres, so take a 4x4 with two spares; fuel planning matters south of Cochrane. Fly into Puerto Montt, out of Balmaceda, and swallow the one-way hire fee — it buys you twelve days instead of twenty. Around £1,700 per person with cabañas, ferries and asado.
adventures.location: Aysén and Los Lagos, Chilean Patagonia
highlights: Marble caves of Puerto Río Tranquilo
Ferry hop from Hornopirén through Pumalín's fjords
gear: Jerry can for the far south
Chilean fuel card or cash for small stations

adventures.title: Utah's Mighty Five via Scenic Byway 12
adventures.description:
