Ten days linking Zion, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, Canyonlands and Arches in one great red-rock loop, with the connective tissue as good as the destinations — above all Scenic Byway 12, whose Hogback section between Escalante and Boulder rides a knife-edge ridge with slickrock canyons plunging away on both sides.

The moments queue up: wading the Virgin River into Zion's Narrows; Bryce's hoodoo amphitheatre firing orange at sunrise; the silhouette crowd at Delicate Arch as the La Sals go pink; dawn light exploding under Mesa Arch above the Colorado's canyons. Capitol Reef's orchards and pie shop make the quiet mid-trip pause.

The variables: summer pushes 40°C at Arches and flash floods close slot canyons, so April–May and September–October are the honest windows; Arches has run timed entry in peak season, and Zion's key trails work on permits and shuttles — check both before fixing dates. Fly into Las Vegas, loop out and back to it. Around £1,500 per person for ten days of hire car, park passes and mid-range rooms in Springdale, Torrey and Moab.
gear: Cool box for desert driving days

adventures.title: Overseas Highway: Miami to Key West
adventures.description:
US-1 leaves the mainland at Florida City and hops 113 miles down the Keys on forty-two bridges, the ocean turning progressively more improbable shades of turquoise until the road simply runs out at Key West, closer to Havana than to Miami. The moment is the Seven Mile Bridge: open water on both sides, the old railway bridge running parallel, pelicans surfing the guardrail updraught.

Break the drive properly. Snorkel the coral gardens of John Pennekamp state park off Key Largo, eat fish tacos in Islamorada, swim at Bahia Honda's white-sand curve — the prettiest beach in the Keys — then give Key West two nights for the Hemingway house, sunset performers at Mallory Square and key lime pie arguments.

The variables: June to November is hurricane season, and a single evacuation order empties the archipelago; and the highway is one lane each way, so weekend traffic crawls — leave Miami before 7am. Keys lodging is genuinely expensive year-round. Four days runs about £850 per person with a hire car from Miami airport.
highlights: Snorkelling John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park
Sunset at Mallory Square, Key West

adventures.title: Going-to-the-Sun Road, Glacier National Park
adventures.description:
Fifty miles of engineering audacity carved into Montana's Lewis Range, Going-to-the-Sun Road climbs from the cedar shores of Lake McDonald over 2,026 m Logan Pass and drops to St Mary Lake, clinging to cliff faces behind low stone parapets the whole way. The moment is pulling over at Big Bend as morning light rakes the Weeping Wall and mountain goats amble along the tarmac as if they built it.

From Logan Pass, walk a stretch of the Highline Trail along the Garden Wall before descending for huckleberry ice cream in Apgar, and give a day to Many Glacier's grizzly country on the east side.

The variables catch everyone: the alpine section rarely opens fully before late June and closes by mid-October; Glacier's timed-entry vehicle reservations sell out within minutes of release; and the Logan Pass car park fills by 8am, so start at dawn or ride the shuttle. Access towns are Whitefish and Kalispell. Four days gives you both sides of the park for about £700 per person in lodges and hire car — more if you snag a seat in a vintage red Jammer bus.
highlights: Logan Pass and the Highline Trail
Wild Goose Island overlook on St Mary Lake

adventures.title: Wild Atlantic Way South: Kinsale to Moher
adventures.description:
The Wild Atlantic Way runs 2,500 km up Ireland's west coast; trying to drive it all in one go flattens it into windscreen scenery. This is the southern half done properly — Kinsale to the Cliffs of Moher over ten unhurried days of peninsulas, pubs and weather.

Start with harbour chowder in Kinsale and the Old Head, round Mizen Head's signal-station bridge, then give the Iveragh and Dingle peninsulas two days each: the Skellig Ring with Skellig Michael pyramiding out of the Atlantic off St Finian's Bay, and Slea Head, where the tarmac squeezes between drystone walls and the surf. The moment is topping the Conor Pass out of Dingle in clearing rain, the whole peninsula laid out in shafts of light. Finish across the Shannon ferry in Clare, walking the cliff path from Doolin to the Cliffs of Moher rather than fighting the visitor-centre coaches, with a session in Gus O'Connor's afterwards.

The variables: single-track detours halve your average speed — plan 150 km days at most; Dingle and Doolin beds vanish in July and August; and rain is a certainty, not a risk. Around £1,300 per person in B&Bs, hiring from Cork airport.
highlights: Skellig Ring views of Skellig Michael
Slea Head Drive on the Dingle Peninsula
Doolin cliff walk to the Cliffs of Moher
Trad session in a Dingle pub

adventures.title: Blue Ridge Parkway End to End
adventures.description:
The Blue Ridge Parkway unspools for 469 miles along the Appalachian crest from Rockfish Gap in Virginia to the edge of the Great Smokies at Cherokee, North Carolina — no lorries, no billboards, and a 45 mph limit that turns driving back into a pleasure. The ridge-top overlooks stack blue on blue to the horizon, and the moment that sells it is dawn at Craggy Gardens in June when the rhododendron balds are in full purple flower.

Break the miles at Mabry Mill's photogenic waterwheel, the Linn Cove Viaduct curling around Grandfather Mountain, and Mount Mitchell, the highest point east of the Mississippi. Asheville sits just off the parkway at the southern end and makes the natural food-and-breweries stopover.

The variable is weather: the parkway lives in cloud, and fog can shut the views (and occasionally the road) for a day at a time, while October leaf season brings the year's thickest traffic. Sections close in winter with no snow clearance. A week one-way with B&B stops runs about £1,100 per person; pick up a car in Washington DC or Charlotte.
highlights: Linn Cove Viaduct around Grandfather Mountain
gear: Camera with long lens for layered ridges

adventures.title: Trollstigen, Geiranger and the Atlantic Road
adventures.description:
Fjord Norway compresses its three most celebrated stretches of road into one six-day loop from the art-nouveau port of Ålesund: the Trollstigen's eleven hairpins, the eagle's-eye descent into Geirangerfjord, and the wave-lashed bridges of the Atlantic Ocean Road.

Climb the Trollstigen under the mile-high face of the Trollveggen and walk out onto the cantilevered viewpoint hanging over the bends you have just driven. Cross the Gudbrandsjuvet gorge, then drop the Ørnevegen's switchbacks to Geiranger, where the ferry to Hellesylt sails past the Seven Sisters falls — do it as a car ferry leg, it is the cheapest fjord cruise in Norway. Finish north on the Atlanterhavsveien, where the Storseisundet bridge corkscrews over the skerries; in a westerly swell the sea explodes across the road, and that is the photograph.

The variables: the Trollstigen opens around late May and has closed for long spells in recent seasons for rockfall protection work — check Statens vegvesen's status before committing the loop; and Norwegian prices make the £1,200 per person budget for six days of guesthouses, ferries and fuel an honest floor, not a ceiling.
highlights: Geiranger–Hellesylt ferry past the Seven Sisters
Storseisundet bridge on the Atlantic Ocean Road
gear: Toll chip arranged with the hire car

adventures.title: Baja Transpeninsular: Tijuana to Cabo
adventures.description:
Mexican Federal Highway 1 runs the length of the Baja peninsula — a thousand miles of desert, missions and two coastlines between Tijuana and Cabo San Lucas. It is the great free-range road trip of the Americas: whales one day, taco stands and boulder fields the next, and long silent stretches where cirio trees twist out of the rock like something Dr Seuss drew.

The moment is a grey whale calf pushing up against your panga in San Ignacio lagoon between January and March, close enough to touch. Before and after come the Valle de Guadalupe wine country, the boulder dreamscape of Cataviña, the date-palm oasis and mission at San Ignacio, and the string of white coves along Bahía Concepción where you camp feet from the water. Finish among the surf towns of the south — Todos Santos, then the arch at Cabo.

The rules that keep it fun: never drive at night (unfenced cattle), treat the narrow, shoulderless tarmac with respect, expect polite military checkpoints, and fill up at every Pemex south of El Rosario. Two weeks southbound with a drop-off in La Paz or Cabo runs about £1,600 per person including whale trips.
highlights: Grey whale encounters in San Ignacio lagoon
Cataviña boulder fields and cirio forest
Camping the coves of Bahía Concepción
Mission San Ignacio and its date-palm oasis
Todos Santos and the Cabo arch
gear: Snorkel set for the Sea of Cortez
Cash in pesos for small towns

adventures.title: Dalton Highway to the Arctic Ocean
adventures.description:
The James Dalton Highway is 414 miles of haul-road gravel built to service the trans-Alaska pipeline, running from just north of Fairbanks across the Yukon River, over the Arctic Circle, and through the Brooks Range to the oilfield settlement of Deadhorse near Prudhoe Bay. It is the loneliest public road in North America, and driving it is a genuine expedition in a hire vehicle.

The moment is cresting 1,444 m Atigun Pass — the highest road pass in Alaska — as the mountains fall away into the treeless immensity of the North Slope, muskoxen grazing the tundra beside the pipeline's silver thread. Coldfoot, roughly halfway, is the last fuel for 240 miles.

The variables are legion: ordinary rental agreements ban the Dalton, so hire from a Fairbanks specialist that supplies CB radio and two full-size spares; windscreen chips from passing trucks are a when, not an if; and Deadhorse beds are oil-camp dorms that must be booked, as must the shuttle onto the security-controlled shore of the Arctic Ocean. Five days return from Fairbanks, around £1,200 per person, June to August only for reliable conditions.
highlights: Crossing the Arctic Circle sign at mile 115
Atigun Pass through the Brooks Range
Muskoxen on the North Slope tundra
Toe-dip in the Arctic Ocean at Prudhoe Bay
gear: Dalton-approved hire vehicle with CB radio
Jerry can and extra washer fluid
Head net and DEET for tundra mosquitoes
Warm layers and waterproofs even in July
Emergency food and water for delays

adventures.title: Garden Route and Route 62 Loop
adventures.description:
South Africa's classic week: out along the N2 coast from Mossel Bay through Wilderness, Knysna and Plettenberg Bay to Storms River, then home through the Klein Karoo on Route 62, the longest wine road in the world. Two utterly different landscapes for one modest loop from Cape Town's doorstep.

The moment is the suspension bridge at Storms River Mouth in Tsitsikamma, where the dark river meets the Indian Ocean's swells beneath forested cliffs. Walk the Robberg Peninsula circuit with Cape fur seals hauling out below, watch the sun drop through the Knysna Heads, and — between June and November — spot southern right whales off Plettenberg Bay without leaving the roadside. The return leg swaps ocean for ostriches: the Outeniqua Pass down to Oudtshoorn, the Cango Caves' dripstone halls, and Route 62's farm stalls and port-style tastings through Calitzdorp.

The variables: this is easy driving on good tarmac, but December–January school holidays book out a year deep, and the Heads' viewpoints reward a wind-free day. Seven days from George or Cape Town runs about £800 per person in guesthouses.
highlights: Robberg Peninsula circuit at Plettenberg Bay
Route 62 farm stalls and Calitzdorp tastings
gear: Swimwear for lagoon and tidal pools
Light rain shell — Tsitsikamma is temperate rainforest
Sun hat for the Karoo leg

adventures.title: Oman Coast and Canyons: Muscat to Jebel Shams
adventures.description:
Oman is the Arabian road trip done right: superb roads, easy camping, and a government that signposts its wadis. This eight-day loop from Muscat strings the sultanate's greatest hits — coast first, then desert, then the mountains.

Run the coast road past the Bimmah sinkhole to Wadi Shab, where a swim through a slot canyon ends in a cave waterfall, and on to Sur's dhow-building yards. At Ras al Jinz, green turtles haul out to nest by torchlight. Turn inland for a night among the apricot dunes of the Sharqiya Sands, then cross to Nizwa for the Friday goat auction beneath the fort's cannon-studded drum tower. The finale is the climb to Jebel Shams, where the rim road skirts Wadi Ghul — the Grand Canyon of Arabia, a sheer kilometre of drop — and the W6 Balcony Walk traverses into the abandoned village of As Sab.

The variables: the final ascent to the Jebel Shams plateau is steep gravel and the Sharqiya Sands require deflated tyres and ideally a convoy, so hire a 4x4 throughout; mountain nights are properly cold in winter; and the season is October to March — summer is punishing. Around £1,300 per person including desert camp and mountain lodge.
adventures.location: Muscat, Sharqiya and Al Hajar Mountains
highlights: Turtle nesting at Ras al Jinz
Nizwa fort and Friday goat market
gear: Swimwear and dry bag for wadis
Warm sleeping layer for mountain nights
Modest dress for towns and souqs
10L minimum water per person per day

adventures.title: Stelvio Pass and the Great Dolomites Road
adventures.description:
Two legends, one five-day Italian loop. The Stelvio Pass stacks forty-eight numbered hairpins up its Prato ramp to 2,757 m — the second-highest paved pass in the Alps, and the most theatrical piece of road engineering on the continent. From the top, the bends fall away beneath you like a dropped ribbon; walk ten minutes from the pass hotels for the full view, then eat bratwurst at a summit stall because this was Austria once.

From Bormio, swing east through the Val Venosta's orchards and pick up the Great Dolomites Road, the 1909 tourist route from Bolzano to Cortina d'Ampezzo. It laces the Passo Pordoi and Falzarego between the pale towers of the Sella and Marmolada, and late light on those walls — the enrosadira, when the rock burns pink — is the trip's quiet climax.

The variables: the Stelvio opens from roughly late May to October and draws motorbikes in droves at weekends — go midweek, early; occasional Bike Days close it to cars entirely; and Cortina's hotels price like the resort it is. Around £850 per person for five days of rifugio lunches and strudel, from a Milan or Innsbruck start.
adventures.location: Ortler Alps and Dolomites, South Tyrol
highlights: Forty-eight hairpins of the Stelvio's Prato ramp
Passo Pordoi under the Sella towers
Passo Falzarego and its Great War tunnels
gear: Warm layers for the 2,757 m summit

adventures.title: King's Highway: Madaba to Petra
adventures.description:
Traders, pilgrims, Nabataeans and Crusaders have all used the King's Highway, and Jordan's slow road south remains the finest way to reach Petra — a ridge-top route between the desert plateau and the Dead Sea rift, punctuated every hour by something extraordinary.

Start in Madaba with its Byzantine mosaic map of the Holy Land and the view over the Jordan Valley from Mount Nebo. Then comes the drive's great set piece: the kilometre-deep plunge and climb through Wadi Mujib, Jordan's Grand Canyon, the switchbacks pouring you down one wall and up the other. Kerak's crusader halls smell of cold stone; further south, sleep on the rift edge in Dana village, where stone cottages hang above a biosphere reserve running from juniper highlands to sand. Shobak castle and the quiet carvings of Little Petra set up the finale — Petra itself, entered early, before the heat and the crowds.

The variables: hire in Amman and treat the Mujib bends with patience rather than power; winter storms occasionally close the high sections with snow; the Jordan Pass swallows Petra's hefty ticket if bought before arrival; and Dana's guesthouses book out, so reserve. Six days, around £900 per person.
highlights: Mount Nebo's view over the Dead Sea
Night in Dana village on the rift edge
gear: Walking shoes for castles and canyons

adventures.title: Route des Grandes Alpes: Geneva to the Med
adventures.description:
France's Route des Grandes Alpes drops from Thonon-les-Bains on Lake Geneva to the palms of Menton in about 700 km — over sixteen alpine passes, including the highest paved through-pass in the Alps. It is a week of continuous hairpins, col-top coffees and valleys that change character with every descent.

The roll-call does the selling: the turquoise reservoir under the Cormet de Roselend; the 2,764 m Col de l'Iseran, bleak and magnificent above Val d'Isère; the Galibier's Tour de France graffiti; the eerie rock pinnacles of the Casse Déserte below the Col d'Izoard. Detour onto the Bonette loop road above 2,800 m for the highest tarmac in France, then wind down through the Turini forest to the sudden blue shock of the Mediterranean. The moment is topping the Iseran early, cloud sea filling the Maurienne behind you.

The variables: the high cols open from about mid-June to mid-October, and early summer can still hold snow walls; July brings Tour crowds and thousands of cyclists — give them the racing line; and Briançon and Val d'Isère beds want booking ahead. Seven days, around £1,100 per person in cols-side hotels and long lunches.
highlights: Col de l'Iseran, highest paved pass in the Alps
Casse Déserte below the Col d'Izoard
Col de la Bonette loop above 2,800 m
gear: Warm layers for 2,700 m col tops

adventures.title: Westfjords Way: Iceland's Forgotten Corner
adventures.description:
While the Ring Road crowds queue for waterfalls, the Westfjords — the great clawed peninsula in Iceland's north-west — stay almost empty. The Vestfjarðaleiðin circuit threads some 950 km of fjord-edge road, mountain passes and the odd single-lane tunnel through the least-visited quarter of the country.

The moments stack up fast: Dynjandi, a 100 m bridal-veil of a waterfall widening as it falls; the Látrabjarg cliffs, westernmost point of Europe's road network, where puffins pose at arm's length above a 440 m drop; and Rauðisandur's kilometres of red-gold sand looking across Breiðafjörður to the Snæfellsjökull ice cap. Base a night in Ísafjörður for the fish restaurants, and add a boat day into the roadless Hornstrandir reserve if the weather gives.

The variables: gravel still covers stretches of the high passes, fuel stops are far apart, and the season is honestly June to August — shoulder months bring closures. Take the Baldur ferry across Breiðafjörður one way to save a day's driving. Six days from Reykjavík runs about £1,150 per person with guesthouses and the hire car's gravel-protection excess.

adventures.title: Cabot Trail Autumn Loop
adventures.description:
The Cabot Trail loops 298 km around the top of Cape Breton Island, riding the plateau edge of Cape Breton Highlands National Park where the road hairpins down French Mountain and MacKenzie Mountain with the Gulf of St Lawrence glittering below. In early October the hardwood forests turn scarlet and gold, and the drive becomes one of the great autumn journeys anywhere.

The moment is the Skyline Trail at dusk: a boardwalk out along a headland ridge, moose in the scrub, whales — pilots and minkes — breaking the surface far below as the sun drops into the gulf. Pull in at Pleasant Bay for a whale-watching zodiac, swim at Ingonish's beaches, and finish with a ceilidh and chowder in Baddeck.

Locals argue about direction; clockwise puts you in the outside lane for the west-coast descents, which is the view. The variable is timing: the Celtic Colours festival in October fills every room on the island, so book months out or come in September. Fly into Halifax, four hours' drive from the trailhead. Four days runs about £600 per person in inns and lobster suppers.
highlights: French Mountain and MacKenzie Mountain hairpins

adventures.title: Causeway Coastal Route: Belfast to Derry
adventures.description:
The A2 out of Belfast hugs the Antrim coast for 120 miles of castles, glens and basalt, and mile for mile it stands with any coastal drive in Europe. Three days is right: one for the nine Glens of Antrim and the hair-raising single-track shortcut over Torr Head, one for the Causeway heartland, one for the run west to Derry's walls.

The moment is the Giant's Causeway an hour before dusk, after the coaches leave, when you can sit alone on 40,000 interlocking columns as the Atlantic booms in. Bracket it with the swaying rope bridge at Carrick-a-Rede, the gaunt clifftop ruin of Dunluce Castle, and a tasting at Bushmills, the world's oldest licensed distillery. Downhill Strand and the Mussenden Temple perched above it close the show before Derry.

The variables: Carrick-a-Rede works on timed tickets that sell out in summer, so book online; the Causeway itself is free if you walk in and skip the visitor centre; and sea mist can erase Torr Head's views — take the main road in poor weather. Around £380 per person for three days in B&Bs, hiring from Belfast.
gear: Binoculars for Rathlin and Scotland views

adventures.title: Jadranska Magistrala: Rijeka to Dubrovnik
adventures.description:
The Adriatic Highway — the D8, Jadranska Magistrala — was Yugoslavia's showpiece coast road, and it still delivers 650 km of limestone mountains dropping into the clearest sea in Europe. Driven over eight days from Rijeka to Dubrovnik, it strings together Roman palaces, Venetian towns and island ferries like beads.

The corniche below the Biokovo massif above the Makarska riviera is the moment: the road a shelf between a 1,700 m wall of grey karst and water in impossible bands of blue. Before it come Senj's Nehaj fortress, Zadar's sea organ moaning to the sunset Hitchcock called the world's best, and Split, where the old town literally inhabits Diocletian's retirement palace. South, cross the elegant new Pelješac bridge, climb Ston's Great Wall above its oyster beds, and roll into Dubrovnik.

The variables: in July and August the magistrala becomes a slow-motion queue, so drive it in June or September; the Pelješac bridge now bypasses the Neum corridor, meaning no Bosnian border stop; and every island ferry you pass will tempt you — build in slack for at least one. Around £950 per person in konoba dinners and family apartments.
gear: Swimwear — the sea is always twenty metres away
Soft cool bag for market figs and cheese

adventures.title: Georgian Military Highway to Kazbegi
adventures.description:
The 208 km Georgian Military Highway has carried armies, tsars and poets from Tbilisi over the Greater Caucasus since antiquity, and it remains one of the world's great mountain roads — now with excellent khinkali at both ends. Four days lets you drive it as a journey rather than a transfer.

Stop first at Ananuri, the fortress-church complex mirrored in the Zhinvali reservoir, then climb through Gudauri's ski country to the Soviet-era Friendship Monument, its mosaic bowl hanging over a thousand-metre drop. Cross the 2,379 m Jvari Pass among mineral springs, and descend to Stepantsminda under the perfect cone of 5,047 m Mount Kazbek. The moment is Gergeti Trinity Church at first light — the 14th-century silhouette floating on its ridge with Kazbek's glaciers behind. Give the last day to the Truso Valley's travertine terraces and abandoned towers.

The variables: this is the freight artery to Russia, so expect lorry convoys queuing towards the Larsi border and give them room on the hairpins; the pass closes intermittently in winter storms; and the Gergeti road is now paved, but Delica taxis will still race you up it. Around £450 per person with guesthouses and supra feasts.
highlights: Gergeti Trinity Church under Mount Kazbek
gear: Layers for a 2,000 m temperature swing
Walking shoes for Gergeti and Truso
Offline maps — signal dies in the gorges

adventures.title: Sani Pass and the Roof of Lesotho
adventures.description:
From the trout town of Underberg, an infamous gravel track climbs 1,300 vertical metres of hairpins up the Drakensberg escarpment to the 2,876 m Sani Pass summit and the Lesotho border — one of Africa's great 4x4 rites of passage. At the top, a toast at Sani Mountain Lodge, the highest pub in Africa, with the KwaZulu-Natal lowlands smoking far below.

Then the trip most people never take: onward across the roof of Lesotho. The tar road past Black Mountain runs above 3,000 m for hour after hour, Basotho shepherds in blankets and balaclavas watching from horseback, before dropping to Mokhotlong and winding west to the engineering spectacle of Katse Dam. Exit through the northern lowlands and finish among the golden sandstone ramparts of Golden Gate Highlands back in South Africa.

The variables: South African border officials enforce 4x4-only on the pass, and the border posts keep daylight hours, so start early; winter snow closes the pass at short notice; and fuel stations in highland Lesotho are scarce, so brim the tank at every chance. Five days from Durban, about £700 per person in lodges and mountain guesthouses.
highlights: Sani Pass hairpins up the escarpment
Highest pub in Africa at the summit
Katse Dam viewpoint and wall tour
Golden Gate Highlands sandstone at sunset
gear: Warm layers — highland nights freeze year-round

adventures.title: Estrada Nacional 2: Chaves to Faro
adventures.description:
Portugal's N2 is the country's Route 66: 739 km of old national road running unbroken from Chaves on the Spanish border to Faro on the Algarve, kilometre stone by kilometre stone through the interior the motorways forgot. Drivers collect stamps in an official N2 'passport' at cafés and town halls along the way, which tells you everything about the spirit of the thing.

From Chaves' Roman bridge the road crosses the Douro at Peso da Régua between staircases of port vineyards — the moment of the trip at harvest time — then climbs through pine and schist to the Serra da Lousã's slate villages. Vila de Rei marks the geodesic centre of Portugal; further south comes the plane-tree tunnel at Montargil and the endless cork-oak dehesa of the Alentejo, before the final twist over the Serra do Caldeirão drops you into Faro for a seafood rice by the lagoon.

The variables: it is deliberately slow — a week is right, and sat-navs will keep trying to bump you onto the parallel motorways; August cooks the Alentejo above 40°C; and rural fuel stations shut on Sundays. Around £850 per person for seven days of family-run pensões, long lunches and vinho verde.
highlights: Crossing the Douro at Peso da Régua
N2 passport stamps in village cafés
gear: Paper map of the old national road

adventures.title: Gulmarg Gondola Freeride, Kashmir
adventures.description:
The second stage of the Gulmarg Gondola hums you up to 3,980m on Apharwat Peak and the Pir Panjal simply drops away — untracked bowls the size of entire French resorts, the Kashmir Valley 2,000m below and Nanga Parbat sharp on the northern horizon. There are no groomed pistes up here; it is one vast avalanche-controlled freeride mountain, and after a January storm you will make the deepest turns of your life for the price of a bowl of rogan josh.

The catch is rhythm. Storm cycles close the top station for days at a stretch, so ten days is the honest minimum: ski the birch and pine trees towards Drang and Babareshi while it snows, then race for the bowls when the ropes drop. Hire a local guide, carry full avalanche kit and read the Gulmarg Avalanche Centre bulletin over breakfast every single morning.

Fly into Srinagar (about 90 minutes by taxi), stay near the gondola base, and check FCDO advice for Jammu & Kashmir before you commit — it changes. Roughly £1,800 for ten days with guiding and half board; the lift pass itself is astonishingly cheap.
adventures.location: Gulmarg, Pir Panjal Range, Jammu & Kashmir
highlights: Top station of the Gulmarg Gondola at 3,980m on Apharwat Peak
Waist-deep storm-day tree runs to Drang and Babareshi
Nanga Parbat on the horizon from the summit ridge
Kashmiri wazwan dinners under kangri heaters
Morning bulletins from the Gulmarg Avalanche Centre before the ropes drop
gear: Down parka for gondola queues at -15°C

adventures.title: Haines Spine Walls Heli Week, Alaska
adventures.description:
Every ski film segment you have ever rewound — fluted spine walls, sluff management, 45-degree faces holding impossible snow — was probably shot in the mountains behind Haines. The Takhinsha and Chilkat ranges catch maritime storms that glue metres of snow to terrain it has no right to stick to, and a small fleet of A-Stars lifts four skiers at a time onto ridgelines above Glacier Bay.

This is the expert end of the sport, and the honest brief matters: you need genuine steep-skiing ability, avalanche training and the patience of a saint. Heli operations here lose 30–50% of days to weather; good operators sell packages by heli-hours with refunds or credits for what you do not fly, so read the terms before you pay. Down days mean sea-level touring, eagle-watching on the Chilkat River and the Fogcutter bar.

Getting in: fly to Juneau, then take the fast ferry or a bush flight up the Lynn Canal fjord — an arrival to remember. February to April, with March the sweet spot. Budget around £7,500 for a seven-day package with guiding and full board, excluding flights to Alaska.
adventures.location: Takhinsha and Chilkat Mountains, Haines, Southeast Alaska
highlights: First drop onto a Takhinsha spine wall
Bush-flight arrival up the Lynn Canal fjord
Bald eagles massing on the Chilkat River flats
Down-day sea-level skinning from the road
gear: Avalanche transceiver, shovel, probe and airbag
Patience and a good book for weather days

adventures.title: Las Leñas Marte Freeride, Mendoza
adventures.description:
When the Marte chairlift opens, Las Leñas becomes the best lift-served freeride mountain in the southern hemisphere — a single ancient double chair unlocking 800m faces, hanging couloirs and traverses that run for kilometres along the Andes crest. Eduardo's, the Paraíso faces, the endless lines back towards the base: it is Chamonix-calibre terrain with Argentine steak at the bottom.

The brutal honesty: Marte is wind-prone and opens perhaps half the days of a good season. You plan a week, ski the lower mountain and the excellent side-country when it is shut, and drop everything when the queue forms. Snow years swing hard here too — check the season before you fly rather than booking blind in April.

Getting in means flying to Mendoza and driving five to six hours south (or via Malargüe, 90 minutes away, on limited flights). Stay slope-side in the compact base village; hotels are dated but you are there for the mountain. About £1,600 for seven days with lift pass and half board. Hire a local guide for the big lines — rescue here is a long way off.
highlights: First chair on Marte after an Andean storm
Eduardo's couloir and the Paraíso faces
Asado and Malbec nights in the base village
Side-country laps when the top lift is on wind hold
gear: Sun cream for high-altitude spring days
Ski straps and spares — the shop stock is thin

adventures.title: Portillo Yellow Hotel Ski Week
adventures.description:
Portillo is a single canary-yellow hotel at 2,880m beside the ink-blue Laguna del Inca, with no village, no queues and a hard cap of around 450 guests. The Saturday-to-Saturday week is the whole product: you ski the same lifts as the US and Austrian national teams in training, eat four-course dinners in a dining room unchanged since the 1960s, and are back on the slingshot lifts before the corduroy softens.

Those lifts are the signature — the va-et-vient sling cables, Roca Jack chief among them, drag five skiers abreast up avalanche paths too steep for towers, then you drop into wide-open Andean faces. Strong skiers hike the Super C couloir for a 1,000m descent back to the hotel terrace; everyone else laps Plateau and the lake runs in ridiculous scenery.

Fly to Santiago and drive two hours up the switchbacks of the Los Libertadores pass — which closes in storms, so never book a same-day international connection on either end. All-inclusive weeks (room, meals, pass) start around £2,600 land cost; shared 'chalet-style' rooms bring it down.
adventures.location: Portillo, Los Andes Province, Valparaíso Region
highlights: Hiking and skiing the Super C couloir
Laguna del Inca glowing below the pistes
National ski teams training on your warm-up run
Pisco sours in the wood-panelled hotel bar
gear: Avalanche kit for the Super C and Primavera side-country
Smart-casual layer for the dining room
Soft boots or trainers for hotel evenings
Cash dollars or card for spa extras

adventures.title: Craigieburn Clubfields Nutcracker Circuit
adventures.description:
New Zealand's clubfields are skiing stripped to its bones: no groomers, no queues, no marketing — just rope tows screaming up big alpine basins, and you clinging on with a leather 'nutcracker' clamped over the wire. Craigieburn is the deepest and steepest of them; Broken River hides beyond a beech-forest walk-in; Temple Basin hauls your kit up by goods lift; Mt Olympus guards the far end of a genuinely alarming 4WD road.

A week's circuit along the Craigieburn Range delivers terrain that would be roped-off double-blacks anywhere else, plus lodge life you will never forget — bunkrooms, communal dinners, chore rosters and honesty-box beer with the club members who built the tows by hand.

Base logistics: fly to Christchurch, hire a 4WD with chains, and allow 90 minutes on SH73 towards Arthur's Pass. Buy a nutcracker harness before your first tow and expect to be humbled by it — everyone is. Snow is all-natural, so keep dates flexible and watch the nor'west storms. About £900 for seven days of lodge accommodation with meals, tow passes and vehicle share.
highlights: First nutcracker tow ride at Craigieburn — and surviving it
Middle Basin powder laps with nobody else on the hill
Broken River's beech-forest walk-in by head torch
Communal lodge dinners with the ski club
The Mt Olympus access road, an adventure in itself
gear: Snow chains for the access roads

adventures.title: Hakkōda Snow Monsters Powder Week, Tōhoku
adventures.description:
The Hakkōda Ropeway rises out of Aomori's cedar forests into a field of juhyō — 'snow monsters', fir trees entombed in metres of rime until they loom like frozen statuary. You ski between them on some of the deepest, driest snow in Japan: Aomori is statistically one of the snowiest cities on Earth, and Hakkōda takes the brunt of it. Pair it with Zaō further south, where you ride between glowing monsters under floodlight before soaking in sulphur-clouded baths.

Hakkōda is not a resort in any normal sense — one ropeway, a couple of marked courses and a vast backcountry where every frozen tree looks identical. Go with a guide, carry full kit and accept that flat light and wind holds will reshape your week; that is the deal for snow this deep.

Take the Shinkansen from Tokyo to Shin-Aomori (about three hours), then a bus to Sukayu Onsen, whose thousand-person hiba-wood bath has steamed skiers back to life since the 1680s. Roughly £2,000 for eight days with guiding, transport and onsen-ryokan lodging.
highlights: Skiing between the juhyō snow monsters off the Hakkōda Ropeway
Storm-day powder laps in the Moya Hills
Aomori fish-market breakfasts before the first bus
gear: Onsen towel and coins for lockers

adventures.title: Tröllaskagi Ski and Sail, North Iceland
adventures.description:
The Troll Peninsula is the closest thing Europe has to Alaska with a harbour: 1,200m corn-snow faces falling straight into grey Arctic fjords, and a sailboat as your mobile base camp. You wake at anchor, skin from the tide line, and by afternoon you are linking turns back to the beach while your skipper motors round to collect you — sometimes with humpbacks surfacing between you and the boat.

April and May are the season: endless northern daylight, a settling snowpack and summit-to-sea descents off peaks such as Kaldbakur across Eyjafjörður. The weather is the variable that owns the trip — the skipper reads the forecast each evening and chooses tomorrow's leeward fjord, so surrender the itinerary and you will ski every day the mountains allow.

Boats sail from Dalvík or from Siglufjörður, the herring town crammed into the peninsula's northern tip; both are about an hour from Akureyri's airport, itself a 45-minute hop from Reykjavík. Six-day berths with guide, skipper and full board run about £3,300 — book a full year out, as each boat takes only six to eight skiers.
highlights: Nights at anchor beneath the peaks you skied
Whale sightings from the transition zone

adventures.title: Wasatch Powder Touring, Little Cottonwood
adventures.description:
Utah's licence plates say 'Greatest Snow on Earth' and Little Cottonwood Canyon is the evidence: 500-inch seasons of cold, low-density powder falling on a compact range where world-class tours start from laybys. Skin up Cardiff Pass or Grizzly Gulch from Alta before the resort wakes, drop into Days Fork's endless aprons, and be back at the trailhead before the road traffic — the infamous 'red snake' — has cleared.

A six-day camp based in the canyon teaches the Wasatch way: dawn starts, avalanche-savvy line choice in a snowpack that rewards respect, and the peculiar local institution of 'interlodge' — mornings when avalanche control locks everyone indoors while howitzers thump the slide paths. It is the best value expert powder skiing in North America once you tour for it rather than queue for it.

Fly to Salt Lake City; the trailheads are 40 minutes from the terminal, so you can land at nine and be skinning by eleven. December to March is prime. Around £1,700 for six days with guiding and shared canyon lodging — book accommodation early, as beds in the canyon are scarce and dear.
adventures.location: Little Cottonwood Canyon, Wasatch Range, Utah
highlights: Dawn skin track up Cardiff Pass from Alta
Cold-smoke laps in Days Fork and Silver Fork
Grizzly Gulch sunrise over Devil's Castle
Riding out an interlodge morning as the guns thump
Landing-to-skinning inside two hours from SLC
gear: Whippet or light axe for firm mornings

adventures.title: Hjørundfjord Summit-to-Sea Ski Touring
adventures.description:
The Sunnmøre Alps do not ease you in: Slogen's granite pyramid rears 1,564m straight from the black water of the Hjørundfjord, and the touring peaks around it — Saudehornet, Kolåstinden, Skårasalen — all end their descents at the tide line. This is Norway's classic summit-to-sea skiing without the Arctic price tag or the crowds that found the Lofoten islands.

Base yourself in Sæbø, a fjord-side village where the ferry doubles as your morning ski lift, or splash out on the wonderfully time-warped Hotel Union Øye, hosting mountaineers since 1891. Days run 1,000–1,400m up and down: skins on at the boathouse, summit views across a hundred white peaks to the sea, then a single unbroken descent to the water. The maritime snowpack is the variable — rain to 800m one day, boot-top powder the next — so a local guide earns their fee choosing aspects.

Fly to Ålesund via Oslo, then it is 90 minutes of road and ferry. March to May gives long days and settled corn. About £1,900 for six days with guiding, half board and ferries. Pack for weather, not for cold.
adventures.location: Sunnmøre Alps, Hjørundfjord, Møre og Romsdal
highlights: Skinning from the Sæbø boathouses at first light
The 1891 time capsule of Hotel Union Øye
Ferry rides that double as ski shuttles
gear: Light ice axe for steep summit ridges
Change of base layers — you will sweat

adventures.title: Riksgränsen Midnight Sun Ski Week
adventures.description:
Riksgränsen sits 200km north of the Arctic Circle on the Norwegian border, and it does skiing backwards: the season barely starts before late February, peaks around May Day, and on selected nights in late May the lifts spin close to midnight so you can ski corn snow under the midnight sun. The light alone is worth the journey — low gold across the Lapporten massif while everyone else in Europe is on a beach.

The terrain is friendly-freeride: short lifts, endless natural lines off the back towards Norway, and a heli option for the fells beyond. This is entirely natural snow in real Arctic weather, so build in flexibility — a May storm can deliver mid-winter powder or shut the hill for a day.

The romance is in the approach: board the night train in Stockholm and step off, eighteen hours later, at a platform a snowball's throw from the lifts. Book the classic Hotell Riksgränsen, ski four days, and budget about £850 for lodging, pass and one heli drop; British Airways and SAS reach Kiruna via Stockholm if the train is full.
highlights: Skiing under the midnight sun on late-May lift nights
Stepping off the Arctic sleeper train straight onto the snow
Freeride lines across the Norwegian border towards Bjørnfjell
Heli-drop day on the fells above Katterjåkk
Aurora over Lapporten if you come in the February opening weeks
gear: Avalanche transceiver, shovel and probe for off-piste
Sunglasses and high-SPF cream for 24-hour light
Sleep mask for the sleeper train and bright nights

adventures.title: Monashee Snowcat Powder Lodge, British Columbia
adventures.description:
Cat-skiing is heli-skiing's calmer, deeper sibling, and the Monashees are its spiritual home. From a timber lodge high above Sugar Lake near Cherryville, a snowcat shuttles twelve of you into old-growth glades that catch the wettest storms in interior BC and dry them into cold smoke. Ten to fourteen runs a day, 1,000m descents, and nobody else's tracks all week — the cat simply moves to the next drainage.

The rhythm is the luxury: ski until your legs give out, then hot tub, enormous dinners, and the guides' evening briefing on where tomorrow's snow is hiding. Interior BC's snowpack carries persistent weak layers most winters; terrain choice is exactly what you are paying the guides for, and they are conservative in the right ways.

Fly to Kelowna, take the operator's transfer to the Cherryville staging area, then ride the cat up to the lodge. Book twelve months ahead — January and February weeks sell out first, often to returning groups. Around £3,800 for a five-day all-inclusive package with guiding, avalanche kit and lodge meals, excluding flights.
adventures.location: Monashee Mountains, near Cherryville, British Columbia
highlights: Cold-smoke glade runs of 1,000m off the snowcat
Old-growth cedar pillows on storm days
Wood-fired hot tub overlooking Sugar Lake
gear: Avalanche transceiver, shovel and probe (checked daily)

adventures.title: Rishiri Island Sea-to-Summit Skiing
adventures.description:
Rishiri is a 1,721m volcano rising straight out of the Sea of Japan — an island Fuji loaded by Siberian storms. You clip in beside the fishing harbour, skin past frozen kelp-drying racks, and by early afternoon you are carving 1,500 vertical metres back towards the water with Rebun Island floating in the strait beyond your ski tips.

This is weather-play as much as skiing. February brings the deepest snow; March and April trade a little depth for the stable windows you need on the upper mountain. Plenty of groups touch the summit ridge only once in a week, spending the other days on the north-west shoulders and the ridgelines above Oshidomari — a guide who knows the island's wind is worth every yen.

Getting there is half the trip: fly Sapporo to Wakkanai at Hokkaidō's northern tip, then take the Heartland Ferry across. Stay in a family minshuku, soak in Rishiri Fuji Onsen each evening and eat uni landed that morning. Budget about £2,200 for six days guided, excluding flights to Japan.
highlights: Summit push on Rishiri-zan, 1,721m straight from sea level
Ferry approach from Wakkanai with the volcano filling the horizon
Rebun Island views from the north-west ridge
Evening soaks in Rishiri Fuji Onsen
gear: Touring skis or splitboard with skins
Ice axe for the summit ridge
GPS or phone mapping for whiteouts

adventures.title: Svaneti Ski Touring from Mestia
adventures.description:
Svaneti is the Caucasus at its most cinematic: medieval stone towers rising out of Mestia's snowbanks, and above them 4,000m walls — Ushba's double horn chief among them — that make the Alps look domesticated. You use the Tetnuldi and Hatsvali lifts as springboards, then skin into empty valleys where the only tracks are yours and a fox's.

Days are long but the vertical is honest: 1,000–1,400m tours to cols facing Ushba, descents through birch glades back to the road, and one big day out towards Ushguli, the towered village at 2,100m that claims to be Europe's highest permanently inhabited place. Snow here is continental and can hide persistent weak layers, so a local IFMGA guide is non-negotiable — happily they cost a fraction of Alpine rates.

Fly to Tbilisi or Kutaisi, then take the long, spectacular road up from Zugdidi (four hours; storms occasionally close it — build in a buffer day). Guesthouses in Mestia serve khachapuri-heavy dinners for a few pounds. About £1,400 for eight days with guiding, half board and transfers.
highlights: Skin tracks with Ushba's double summit filling the skyline
Powder glades under the Tetnuldi lifts
Day tour to the towered village of Ushguli
Mestia's medieval Svan towers in deep snow
Guesthouse suppers of khachapuri and mountain honey
gear: Touring skis with skins and ski crampons
Repair kit — spares are days away

adventures.title: Andermatt Gemsstock Freeride Camp
adventures.description:
The Gemsstock cable car climbs to 2,961m above Andermatt and opens one of the Alps' great freeride mountains: shaded north-facing itineraries that hold cold snow for weeks, with the Felsental and Guspis valleys funnelling 1,500 vertical metres back towards the valley floor. Since the resort linked to Sedrun and Disentis the lift-served scale rivals the big names, but the Gemsstock crowd still thins to a handful of locals by mid-morning.

The skiing is serious — glacial terrain, convex rolls and real avalanche exposure a rope's width from the marked runs — so this is a trip to do with a guide, learning the mountain's classic lines over five focused days. When storms shut the top station, the Nätschen side and the Sedrun valleys keep you moving.

Logistics are the easy part: train from Zurich Airport in under two and a half hours, straight to a village square where the Glacier Express rolls past your café table. Around £950 for five days with shared guiding, a regional pass and B&B lodging — Swiss dinners will test the budget, so self-cater some nights.
highlights: First tram up the Gemsstock on a powder morning
Freeride laps linking Andermatt to Sedrun
Glacier Express watching from the village square
gear: Piste map of the Andermatt-Sedrun link

adventures.title: Araucanía Volcano Ski Safari, Chile
adventures.description:
Spring in Chile's Lakes District means volcano skiing: a week ticking off perfect cones, skinning at dawn on refrozen ash-and-ice and descending 1,500m of buttered corn by lunchtime. Villarrica is the centrepiece — a smoking, actively degassing summit where you transition with sulphur on the wind before one of the great ski descents of the Americas, all the way back towards Pucón's black-sand lake beaches.

Around it you rotate through Llaima, rising over Conguillío's monkey-puzzle forests, wind-scoured Lonquimay, and — if you extend south — Osorno above Lago Llanquihue. The variable nobody controls: SERNAGEOMIN's volcanic alert levels. When Villarrica grumbles, the summit closes and your guide swaps in another peak; that flexibility is why you book a safari rather than a single mountain.

Base yourself in Pucón (fly Santiago to Temuco, then 90 minutes by road), where hot springs and craft beer fill the afternoons. September to November gives the best corn cycles. About £2,200 for eight days with an IFMGA guide, 4x4 transport and B&B lodging.
adventures.location: Villarrica, Llaima and Lonquimay volcanoes, Araucanía
highlights: Summit transition beside Villarrica's steaming crater
Llaima's cone above Conguillío's monkey-puzzle forests
Termas Geométricas hot-spring soak after the ski day
gear: Helmet — volcanic ice is bulletproof at dawn
Light harness for the crater rim
Gas mask or buff for sulphur gusts

adventures.title: Kamchatka Volcano Heli-Ski Expedition
adventures.description:
Kamchatka is the far edge of the skiing world: a peninsula of 300 volcanoes hanging off Russia's Pacific coast, where Mi-8 helicopters the size of buses drop skiers onto smoking cones and the run-outs finish on black-sand beaches with surf breaking behind you. Descents off Avachinsky and Vilyuchinsky top 1,500m; on the coast days you ski literally to the ocean, then eat king crab in the steam of the Paratunka hot springs.

Be honest with yourself about access before you fall in love with this one. There are currently no practical routes for most British travellers — the FCDO advises against travel to Russia, flights route awkwardly via third countries, and many operators have paused their programmes. Treat this as a long-list expedition: research it now, go when the world allows.

When running, trips base near Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky with eight-day packages around £6,500 including the heli hours, guides and full board — weather days are frequent and the Mi-8 group format (up to 16 skiers) is part of the deal. April and May give stable spring snow and volcano summits.
adventures.location: Avachinsky and Vilyuchinsky volcanoes, Kamchatka Peninsula
highlights: Mi-8 drops on the crater rim of Avachinsky
King crab and Paratunka hot springs after the rotors stop
Steller's sea eagles from the helicopter window
gear: Fat touring skis with ski crampons
Avalanche transceiver, shovel, probe and airbag
Boot crampons and ice axe for crater rims

adventures.title: Kaçkar Heliski from Ayder, Black Sea Turkey
adventures.description:
The Kaçkar mountains rise 3,900m out of Turkey's Black Sea coast, and the same humid air that grows the nation's tea plantations dumps a snowpack of near-Japanese depth on their northern flanks. Helicopters lift from the valley around Ayder, a huddle of wooden chalets and hot springs at 1,350m, and drop you into treeline runs that finish above mist-filled gorges — powder skiing with the call to prayer drifting up from Laz villages below.

The Black Sea giveth and taketh: expect roughly a third of your week lost to cloud sitting on the range, which is why operators keep snowcats and ski-touring guides on standby for down days. Terrain suits strong off-piste skiers rather than experts only — the classic runs are rolling 800–1,200m descents rather than spine walls.

Fly Istanbul to Trabzon, then transfer two and a half hours east along the coast. Packages run around £5,200 for seven days with a generous vertical allowance, full board and down-day programme. February to April is the season; add a Rize tea-house crawl before you fly home.
adventures.location: Kaçkar Mountains, Rize Province, Eastern Black Sea
highlights: Heli drops at 3,000m+ above the Fırtına valley
Powder runs ending over mist-filled gorges
Ayder's hot springs after the last lift of the day
Snowcat and touring back-up on cloud days
Laz village suppers of muhlama and mountain honey
gear: Avalanche transceiver, shovel, probe and airbag (operator-provided)
Goggles with storm and sun lenses
Turkish lira in cash for villages

adventures.title: Cedars of Lebanon Ski Touring
adventures.description:
Skinning above the Cedars of God — the last biblical cedar grove, trees older than most nations — you climb towards Qornet es Saouda, at 3,088m the roof of the Levant. From the summit ridge the view is unrepeatable anywhere else on a ski tour: the Qadisha Valley's cliff monasteries 1,500m below on one side, the Mediterranean glittering 25km away on the other. Ski in the morning; drink coffee by the sea in the afternoon. People really do both in a day.

The skiing is honest Middle Eastern mountaineering: wind-worked snow, brilliant spring corn cycles, and a small, warm scene of local guides working out of Bcharré, Khalil Gibran's cliff-hung hometown. Weather swings hard — Levantine storms can drop a metre, then the sun bakes it to velvet in two days.

Fly to Beirut and drive two and a half hours north into the mountains. Check FCDO advice before booking, as the regional picture changes, and go with a Lebanese operator who reads it daily. January to March is the season; about £1,100 for six days with guiding, guesthouse half board and transfers. Bring an appetite — the mezze is a highlight in itself.
adventures.location: Bcharré and Qornet es Saouda, Mount Lebanon Range
highlights: Skin track through the Cedars of God grove
Summit of Qornet es Saouda, 3,088m, roof of the Levant
Qadisha Valley monasteries from the ridge
Mediterranean horizon from your transition point
Mezze nights in Bcharré below Gibran's museum
gear: Swimwear — the sea is an afternoon option

adventures.title: Nazaré Big-Wave Winter, Praia do Norte
adventures.description:
From the lighthouse fort of São Miguel Arcanjo you look straight down into the largest ridden waves on earth. An undersea canyon 5,000 metres deep aims the full North Atlantic at Praia do Norte, and on the right winter day the sea stacks up into 20-metre grey pyramids while jet-skis thread the whitewater like insects. Even as a spectator, the ground-shake of a big set is something you never forget.

Be honest with yourself about the surfing. Tow teams here are professionals with safety drivers and radio protocols; unless you are one of them, this trip is about watching giants from the fort, then paddling proper (and still punchy) waves at Praia do Norte on the small days or around the headland at Praia da Vila. Several operators run big-wave awareness clinics and forecasting workshops in town.

The variable is the forecast itself — giant days come in 48-hour windows between long flat or stormy spells, so build a flexible week from October to March. Nazaré town has abundant winter guesthouses; the funicular links the beach to the clifftop Sítio. Around £900 for a week with accommodation, clinic and hire car; sardines and vinho verde stay mercifully cheap.
highlights: 20-metre sets from the São Miguel Arcanjo fort
The Nazaré Canyon swell forecast coming true
Big-wave safety clinic with a local tow team
Small-day paddle session on Praia do Norte
Funicular up to Sítio for grilled sardines
gear: Gun or step-up board if qualified

adventures.title: Teahupo'o: The Wave at the End of the Road
adventures.description:
The coast road on Tahiti Iti simply stops at PK0, and beyond the marina the island turns to jungle and reef. Half a mile out, over Havae Pass, the heaviest wave on the planet folds below sea level — a lip thicker than the wave is tall, detonating onto coral a metre down. You watch your first set from a taxi-boat in the channel, close enough to feel the compression in your chest, and understand instantly why they call it 'the end of the road'.

This is an EXTREME booking: only experienced reef surfers should paddle out, and even then on the smaller west-swell days. Everyone else surfs the friendlier passes nearby and rides the channel boat when it pumps. The variable that catches people out is swell direction — a rogue west set breaks wide and closes the channel, which is why you hire a local boatman who reads it, not a kayak.

Base in a family pension in Teahupo'o village; book boats through the marina. May to October brings the southern-hemisphere swells. Budget around £1,800 for ten days with pension board, boat shuttles and a guide — Tahiti is expensive, and there is no way around that.
highlights: First light taxi-boat to the Havae Pass channel
Watching a west bora set detonate over the reef
Paddle sessions at the mellower Vairao pass
The PK0 road-end marker and Teahupo'o marina
Poisson cru with the pension family after dark

adventures.title: Mavericks Big-Wave Apprenticeship, Half Moon Bay
adventures.description:
Half a mile off Pillar Point, a reef shaped like a launching ramp turns North Pacific winter swell into Mavericks: 15-to-20-metre faces, 10C water, great white territory, and the wave that defined modern big-wave paddle surfing. This trip is an apprenticeship, not a conquest — a winter week built around a big-wave safety and forecasting clinic, breath-hold and rescue training, and, for genuinely qualified chargers, a shot at the shoulder on a moderate day.

For everyone else the education is total: watching hellmen paddle over the ledge from a charter boat in the channel, debriefing swell models with local watermen, and understanding the harbour culture that polices this wave. The bluff above Pillar Point Harbor gives a distant view; the boat is the real classroom.

Base in Half Moon Bay or El Granada, thirty minutes south of San Francisco. Everything depends on the forecast — the wave breaks properly perhaps a dozen days each winter, so trips are built flexible between November and March. Around £1,500 for the week including clinic, boat time and lodging. The variable that kills plans is fog and northwest wind chop; the variable that kills people is hubris. Train accordingly.
adventures.location: Pillar Point, Half Moon Bay, California
highlights: First boat view of a 15-metre set on the ledge
Pillar Point harbour culture and crab rolls
Bluff-top dawn watch as a giant arrives

adventures.title: Superbank Sand Barrels, Snapper to Kirra
adventures.description:
The Superbank is a man-made miracle: sand pumped across the Tweed River mouth since 2001 accidentally built a two-kilometre pointbreak linking Snapper Rocks, Rainbow Bay, Greenmount and Kirra. On a cyclone swell you can, in theory, ride a spinning sand-bottom barrel from behind the rock at Snapper all the way into Kirra's legendary inside — the longest hollow wave sequence in the world.

In practice, the crowd is the crux. This is the most competitive lineup in Australia, home turf of world champions, and February–April swells bring hundreds to the takeoff zone. Ride the inside runners, surf dawn and dusk, take the scraps with grace, and you will still collect the best sand barrels of your life. Duranbah, over the river training wall, is the pressure valve when the points are maxed or mobbed.

Base in Coolangatta — flat whites, surf clubs and airbnbs a barefoot walk from five world-class waves, with Gold Coast Airport ten minutes away. The variable is sand: the bank shifts with every pumping cycle and cyclone, so some seasons Kirra revives and others it fattens. Ten days self-catered with board hire runs about £800.
highlights: Kirra's inside bowl on a cyclone swell
Duranbah peaks when the points are packed
gear: Backup board for the crowd carnage

adventures.title: Chicama: The Longest Left on Earth
adventures.description:
At Puerto Malabrigo, on Peru's grey desert coast, the left point at Chicama peels for over two kilometres — the longest surfable wave on the planet, protected by Peruvian law as a national heritage break. On a proper south swell you link the sections one after another: Malpaso, Keys, The Point, El Hombre — legs shaking, arms on fire, until the pier finally calls time. Nobody rides it all in one go, but chasing that idea is the whole trip.

The smart logistics are gloriously lazy: surf lodges on the bluff run zodiac shuttles that drop you back at the top of the point, turning a forty-minute walk into a five-minute boat ride and letting you bank ten kilometres of riding in a day. The Humboldt Current keeps the water cold (a 3/2 or 4/3 year-round) and the desert wind blows offshore almost every daylight hour.

Fly Lima to Trujillo, then drive ninety minutes north through sugar-cane flats. The town is tiny and sleepy; lodges provide meals. The variable is swell size — Chicama needs a solid pulse to connect its sections, so April to September is the window. A week with lodge board, zodiac and boards is around £450. Bring a wave-catching machine, not your shortest board.
highlights: Linking Keys to El Hombre in one ride
Zodiac shuttle back to the top of the point
Desert bluffs and endless offshore wind

adventures.title: Waikiki Beachboy Longboarding, Queens
adventures.description:
Surfing was reborn for the modern world at Waikiki, and riding Queens on a longboard remains one of the sport's purest pleasures: a soft, endlessly walling right over deep reef, Diamond Head on your left shoulder, and rides so long you have time to think about your footwork. Canoes, Populars and Paradise spread the neighbouring peaks, outrigger canoes still catch set waves through the lineup, and the beachboy tradition — hire, lessons, easy banter — runs straight back to Duke Kahanamoku, whose statue watches from the sand.

Summer (May–September) south swells bring the classic conditions: waist-to-head-high, warm, and busy — the crowd is part of the culture here, and courtesy earns you waves. Dawn sessions beat both the trade-wind chop and the tourist flotilla.

Stay anywhere in Honolulu's Waikiki district; board lockers and racks rent by the week along Kalakaua Avenue. The variable is simply expectations — this is mellow, communal surfing, not a performance wave. Five days with a modest hotel, board hire and one beachboy lesson runs about £550 before flights; plate lunch and shave ice keep food costs sane.
highlights: Long rights at Queens with Diamond Head views
Dawn glass before the trade winds

adventures.title: Puerto Escondido: The Mexican Pipeline
adventures.description:
Playa Zicatela is the heaviest beach break in the Americas — a deep-water trench that lets southern-hemisphere swell hit the sand at full power, throwing top-to-bottom barrels that have broken more boards than any wave in Mexico. From May to September the 'Mexican Pipeline' delivers days when the paddle-out alone is a trial and the reward is the barrel of your life over a metre of water and a lot of moving sand.

Know your lane. Zicatela proper is for experienced, fit surfers with step-ups and humility; everyone else surfs La Punta at the south end of the bay, a long, forgiving left point with a friendly crowd, or Carrizalillo's cove for small-wave days. Watching the town's bodyboarders and local chargers from the sand at golden hour is half the spectacle.

Puerto has proper infrastructure: fly in via Mexico City or Oaxaca, stay on the Zicatela strip or up in La Punta's sandy lanes, eat tlayudas and fish tacos for pennies. The variable is size — swells jump from head-high to triple-overhead in a day, so bring boards for both and check the bathymetry-driven forecast obsessively. Ten days runs about £750 with a beachfront room.
highlights: Long lefts with the La Punta crowd
Golden-hour spectacle from the black sand
Carrizalillo cove on a small-swell morning
Tlayudas and micheladas on the strip
gear: Spare boards budget or repair cash

adventures.title: Ericeira World Surfing Reserve Week
adventures.description:
Europe's first World Surfing Reserve packs seven named breaks into four kilometres of clifftop coast, and you can walk between most of them before breakfast. Ribeira d'Ilhas is the amphitheatre centrepiece — a long, forgiving right point that hosted world championships — while Coxos, round the next headland, is the best right in continental Europe when the sand and swell align. In between sit Pedra Branca, Reef and Crazy Left for the days you want consequence.

The town itself is the other half of the trip: a whitewashed fishing village of blue-trimmed lanes, grilled fish and pastelarias, an hour's bus from Lisbon. Surf camps and guesthouses are plentiful, but book ahead for September and October when the whole surf world seems to route through.

The catch is wind: the nortada blows out afternoons all summer, so dawn patrols are non-negotiable, and the best combination of clean groundswell and light offshores comes in autumn and spring. A week with a guesthouse room, board hire and a few guided sessions runs about £600 — one of the best-value world-class surf weeks anywhere.
highlights: Dawn patrol at Ribeira d'Ilhas amphitheatre
Watching Coxos reel on a clean groundswell
Clifftop walk linking all seven reserve breaks
Grilled dourada in the old fishing harbour
Day-trip contrast session at Foz do Lizandro

adventures.title: Taghazout Winter Points, Anchor to Boilers
adventures.description:
When winter groundswell trains march out of North Atlantic lows, the argan-covered headlands north of Agadir turn into a right-hand pointbreak conveyor. Anchor Point is the jewel — 500-metre walls wrapping past the old fish-anchor factory that named it — with Killer Point, La Source and Boilers strung up the coast, and Hash Point and Panorama peelers in front of the village for lazier days.

Taghazout itself has grown from hippy fishing village to full surf town: whitewashed lanes stacked with board-repair shacks, tagine cafés and surf-camp roof terraces where you debrief over mint tea as the muezzin sounds. Mornings are offshore off the desert; by afternoon you chase sheltered corners or take the van north to Imsouane's endless bay.

Book a surf camp for the easy version (airport pickup, guiding, half board) or self-cater apartments and hire a van with mates. Agadir airport is 45 minutes. The trap is tide: Anchor's rocks eat boards at low, and the points need mid tide to line up properly, so plan sessions around the push. A week half-board with guiding is about £480 — one of the cheapest quality-wave weeks in this hemisphere.
highlights: Killer Point on a solid winter pulse
Mint tea debriefs on a camp roof terrace
Argan-oil co-op stop on the coast road

adventures.title: Lower Trestles Cobblestone Peaks, San Clemente
adventures.description:
Lower Trestles is the most rippable wave in America: a cobblestone fan at the mouth of San Mateo Creek that bends south swells into flawless, high-performance walls breaking both ways off a single peak. It is where world titles are decided and where average surfers discover their best turns — the wave gives speed for free and asks only that you use it.

The ritual is the walk: park at Cristianitos off the I-5, cross under the railway, and follow the trail through San Onofre State Beach's wetland reserve, board under arm, as the marine layer burns off. Uppers, Middles and Church spread the crowd; old-school San Onofre longboard peelers wait a mile south when you want 1950s California pace.

Summer south swells (May–September) are the season, and dawn is the only quiet shift — by 8am fifty of Orange County's best are trading the peak, and sitting wide means watching. Base in San Clemente, the quintessential surf town with board factories and taco counters on every block. A week with a rental car, motel room and board hire runs about £900. The variable is the crowd's calibre: sets go to those who sit deepest, so bring your paddling fitness.
adventures.location: San Onofre State Beach, San Clemente, California
highlights: Peeling both ways off the Lowers peak
The wetland trail walk-in at dawn
Watching pros dismantle a summer swell

adventures.title: G-Land Jungle Surf Camp, Alas Purwo
adventures.description:
Grajagan — G-Land — is where the surf-camp idea was invented: a string of stilted huts in the teak jungle of Alas Purwo National Park, facing a two-kilometre left reef that catches every pulse of Indian Ocean swell. From the treeline you read the sections like a map: Kong's rolling walls at the top, Money Trees' long mechanical barrels in the middle, and Speedies at the bottom, where the wave drains into its shallowest, hollowest act.

Day one humbles most visitors: the paddle-outs are long, the reef is live coral, and the trade winds that groom the face all dry season also make the inside sections race. Surf it on the morning tide push, rest through the heat, and go again before dusk while macaques raid the camp kitchen and deer graze the clearing.

Access is part of the ritual — fly to Bali, then either speedboat across the strait from Kuta operators or drive via the Ketapang ferry and Banyuwangi. Camps run set packages with meals; book months ahead for June to August. Roughly £950 for eight nights full board. Bring everything you need: the nearest shop is a national park away.
adventures.location: Plengkung, Alas Purwo National Park, East Java
highlights: Money Trees barrels from the camp treehouse tower
Speedies on a draining low-tide push
Macaques and rusa deer in the camp clearing
Speedboat crossing from Bali at dawn
Reef walk to the Plengkung lighthouse
gear: Full tropical first-aid and vinegar kit

adventures.title: Mundaka Rivermouth Left, Basque Country
adventures.description:
When a solid autumn swell meets the sandbar at the mouth of the Oka estuary, Mundaka produces the best rivermouth left in the world: a 400-metre spinning barrel that starts beside the harbour wall and peels along the sand towards Laida beach. You jump off the tiny fishing harbour steps, take three strokes, and you are in one of surfing's genuine cathedrals — with the hilltop church of Santa María above you and the Urdaibai Biosphere Reserve wetlands behind.

It is a fickle masterpiece. The bar is rebuilt every year by winter river floods, the wave only truly breaks from mid to low tide on a west-northwest groundswell, and when it is on, the takeoff zone hosts every good surfer in Euskadi. Bring patience, a fast left-friendly board, and manners.

Stay in Mundaka village itself — pintxo bars, one hotel, several pensiones — or in Gernika ten minutes up the estuary railway. Flat days are for San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, Bilbao's Guggenheim and beach peaks at Laga. October and November are prime; around £550 for a self-catered week with a hire car from Bilbao.
highlights: Pintxos crawl through Mundaka's old square
Flat-day pilgrimage to San Juan de Gaztelugatxe
gear: Compact travel coffin for two boards

adventures.title: Arugam Bay Pointbreak Season, Sri Lanka
adventures.description:
While the southwest coast sleeps under monsoon rain, Sri Lanka's east coast wakes up. From May to September, Arugam Bay's Main Point wraps long sand-bottomed right-handers around the headland — a mellow, walling wave that lets you link a dozen turns before the inside reforms. It is the anchor of a whole coastline of points: Whiskey Point and Peanut Farm for softer peelers, Pottuvil Point for sand-dune rides on the bigger pulses, Okanda far south when you want it empty.

The rhythm is pure surf-town: tuk-tuk dawn missions along red-dirt tracks, rotis and king coconuts between sessions, and lagoon safaris where elephants wade at dusk. The road to Panama and Okanda skirts Kumana National Park — genuinely check for elephants before walking to the beach at dawn.

A-Bay village is backpacker-priced with guesthouses from a few pounds and better boutique options on the point. The catch is the morning glass window: by 11am the cross-shore breeze arrives, so structure your days early. Ten days with guesthouse, tuk-tuk hire and board rental runs about £500 excluding flights. Fly to Colombo, then it is an honest eight-hour drive east.
highlights: Tuk-tuk dawn mission to Peanut Farm
Elephants wading Pottuvil lagoon at dusk
Empty pulse day at Okanda near Kumana
Roti-shop debriefs on the A-Bay strip

adventures.title: Raglan Left Points, Manu Bay to Indicators
adventures.description:
Raglan's black-sand points are the wave that launched a thousand van trips: three connected left-handers — Indicators, Whale Bay and Manu Bay — wrapping down a volcanic coastline under Mount Karioi. On the right southwest swell, Indicators links towards Whale Bay in rides of half a kilometre, walling and workable the whole way, made famous by The Endless Summer and unchanged in spirit since.

Manu Bay is the accessible classic, with its concrete boat-ramp jump-off and a wave that suits everyone from first pointbreak-timers to slashing locals. The town, ten minutes away across the harbour bridge, is New Zealand's surf-culture capital in miniature: wood-fired bakeries, galleries, and Ngarunui Beach's gentle whitewater nursery for absolute beginners.

Swell is remarkably consistent year-round; late summer and autumn (February–June) offer the warmest water and cleanest mornings before winter's power arrives. The catch is wind and tide alignment — the points prefer low-to-mid tide and an easterly — so build slack into your week. Stay at the classic surf lodges above Whale Bay or in town; hire a car in Auckland (two hours). Around £650 for a week with lodge bed and board hire.
highlights: Mount Karioi behind every lineup shot

adventures.title: Tofino Cold-Water Swell, Clayoquot Sound
adventures.description:
Surfing in Tofino means paddling out where temperate rainforest meets the open Pacific: cedar-dark headlands, bald eagles overhead, and beach breaks that work through more tides and winds than seems fair. Cox Bay is the consistent engine room, Chesterman and Long Beach in Pacific Rim National Park Reserve spread the crowds, and the water — 8 to 14C — makes every wave feel earned.

This is Canada's surf town, and it wears the title lightly: float-plane harbour, fish-taco shacks, First Nations culture across Clayoquot Sound, and a community of surfers who treat 5mm rubber as ordinary workwear. September to November brings the sweet spot of lingering warmth and building groundswell. Deep winter is storm-watching season, when lodges sell the spectacle of ten-metre seas from fireside windows.

Fly to Vancouver, hop to Tofino or drive-and-ferry via Nanaimo across Vancouver Island's mountain spine. The thing that catches people out is cold management: without a hood, gloves and booties your session is 40 minutes, with them it is three hours. Wolves and black bears genuinely patrol beaches at dawn — read the signs. A week with lodge, hire car and premium rubber rental runs about £850.
adventures.location: Cox Bay, Tofino, Vancouver Island, British Columbia
highlights: Cox Bay peaks framed by rainforest
Long Beach session in Pacific Rim NP
Fish tacos at the harbour shacks

adventures.title: Margaret River Main Break and The Box
adventures.description:
Three hours south of Perth, the Margaret River region throws raw Indian Ocean power at a coastline of granite and limestone. Main Break at Surfers Point is the amphitheatre — a big-shouldered A-frame that holds triple overhead while spectators watch from the car-park rail — with The Box's square mutant barrel breaking mercilessly close on the northern side and North Point's grinding rights up at Gracetown for the truly committed.

The contrast is the charm: mornings trading heavy water with wetsuited locals, afternoons among vineyards, karri forest and craft breweries. When the main breaks max out, Redgate, Gnarabup and dozens of lesser corners offer options across 130 kilometres of coast — having a car and local knowledge (or a guide for the first days) transforms the trip.

Stay in Margaret River town or Prevelly, five minutes from Surfers Point. The variable is wind and raw swell: this coast rarely goes flat but often goes wild, and autumn (March–June) gives the cleanest marriage of size and grooming. Sharks are part of the local conversation — surf popular breaks and heed beach closures. A week with car hire and guesthouse comes to about £750 before wine purchases.
adventures.location: Surfers Point, Prevelly, Margaret River, Western Australia
highlights: Main Break walls from the Surfers Point rail
The Box unloading on a clean pulse
Vineyard lunch after a dawn session
Karri forest drive down Caves Road

adventures.title: Lagundri Bay Right, Nias Island
adventures.description:
The right-hander at Lagundri Bay is the most photogenic wave in Sumatra: a perfect almond barrel that stands up on the same patch of reef every time, peels for a hundred metres, and delivers you into a deep keyhole channel for the easiest paddle-back in world surfing. Since the 2005 earthquake lifted the reef half a metre, 'The Point' at Sorake breaks harder and hollower than the wave that made it famous in the 1970s.

You stay in a losmen on the point itself — board racks downstairs, the lineup thirty metres from your balcony — while local kids who rip harder than you share the peak. Smaller days offer The Machine and Kiddies Corner inside the bay for a gentler warm-up.

Getting to South Nias takes commitment: fly Medan to Gunungsitoli, then a three-hour drive south to Teluk Dalam and the bay. The variable that catches visitors is the wet-season lull and the crowd factor when a good pulse hits during July and August; June and September offer the best balance. Ten days with losmen board and motorbike hire comes in around £650. Malaria precautions and a solid reef-cut kit are essential kit, not options.
highlights: The Point's almond barrel from your losmen balcony
Keyhole channel paddle-outs with dry hair
Local groms styling on the main peak
Motorbike run to Teluk Dalam market
Sunset reef glow across Lagundri Bay

adventures.title: Pavones: Two-Minute Lefts on Golfo Dulce
adventures.description:
Pavones is a rumour that turns out to be true: when a big southwest swell pushes into the Golfo Dulce, the left point at this end-of-the-road village peels for the best part of a kilometre. Rides are measured in minutes, legs burn out before waves do, and the walk back up the cobblestone shore past the cantina is part of the ritual. It is regularly cited among the two or three longest lefts on the planet.

The flip side is dependency: Pavones needs real swell to wake up, and between pulses it can be lake-flat. Time your trip to the April–September southern-hemisphere season, watch the long-range charts, and treat flat spells as jungle time — scarlet macaws own the shoreline trees, and boat trips cross the gulf to hot springs and dolphin water.

Getting there is a mission: fly to San José, hop to Golfito, then ninety minutes of dirt road around the gulf. The village has simple cabinas, a couple of restaurants and famously little else — book somewhere with a generator and bring cash. Nine days with cabina lodging and transfers runs about £700. When the swell hits, expect every expat regular in the water; the point rewards those who wait their turn.
highlights: A left that peels for nearly a kilometre
Scarlet macaws over the point at dawn
gear: Dry bag for boat and dirt-road transfers

adventures.title: Nosara Longboard Mornings, Playa Guiones
adventures.description:
Playa Guiones catches swell 330 days a year, yet almost never punishes you for showing up: a five-kilometre sweep of jungle-backed sand where consistent, crumbly peaks roll through like a machine set to 'learn'. Dry-season mornings are the magic — glassy, chest-high, offshore until ten — and the lineup spreads wide enough that everyone from first-timer to nose-riding regular finds a peak.

Nosara has matured into the western hemisphere's wellness-surf capital: board rooms in every hotel, yoga shalas in the trees, howler monkeys as your alarm clock. There is no beachfront construction thanks to a maritime protection zone, so you still walk sandy trails through scrub to reach the water. Book surf-and-stay packages at Guiones or cheaper rooms towards Playa Pelada, where a small left reef adds variety.

Fly to Liberia airport, then a two-and-a-half-hour shuttle, the last stretch on dirt. The thing that catches people out is cost — Nosara runs on dollars and wellness pricing, so budget £850 for a week with lessons, board hire and mid-range lodging.
