December to April gives the friendliest conditions; rainy-season afternoons add drama and empty peaks.
highlights: Glassy dawn peaks the full length of Guiones
Howler monkeys in the beach-trail almendros
Sunset nose-riding crowd at high tide
Playa Pelada's blowhole and left reef

adventures.title: Punta de Lobos Left Walls, Pichilemu
adventures.description:
Punta de Lobos is Chile's great left: a lava point south of Pichilemu where the Humboldt Current's endless southwest swell stands up beside two sea stacks — Los Morros — and walls off for 300 metres and more. The entry is pure theatre: climb down the cliff, time the surge off the rock shelf between the stacks, and paddle out into a lineup that holds everything from head-high runners to genuine big-wave days, when a World Surfing Reserve shows its teeth.

Pichilemu, twenty minutes' walk or a short colectivo ride away, is a faded-grand seaside town turned surf hub: wood-smoke restaurants, cabañas among pines, and Infiernillo's punchy beach break in front of town. The water is cold year-round (11–15C) — a 4/3 with boots minimum, hood in winter.

Swell is close to guaranteed; March–May and October–December bring the cleanest long-period pulses with manageable wind. The variable is size management: Lobos triples overnight when a big low arrives, so know your ceiling and respect the local crew, who include some of the world's best big-wave surfers. Fly to Santiago, drive three and a half hours southwest. A week in a cabaña with hire car is about £500.
adventures.location: Punta de Lobos, Pichilemu, O'Higgins Region
highlights: Timing the rock-shelf entry at Los Morros

adventures.title: Hoddevik Fjord Surf, Stadlandet
adventures.description:
Hoddevik is the postcard of Norwegian surfing: a crescent of pale sand wedged between 500-metre mountain walls at the tip of the Stadlandet peninsula, where North Atlantic swell funnels into a bay that looks like a fjord dreamed up by a surf photographer. The beach break peels both ways over sand, friendly enough for improvers on modest days and properly punchy when autumn lows line up. Over the switchback pass, Ervik offers a heavier reef-and-beach alternative facing due northwest.

The experience is as much Norway as surf: sessions ending under alpenglow, sheep watching from the marram grass, and — from late September — genuine chances of aurora over the lineup. Farmhouse surf lodges run guiding, rubber hire and communal dinners.

Fly to Ålesund, then drive four hours of fjord-and-ferry roads, or arrange a lodge transfer. September to November is prime, pairing lingering warmth (11C water) with swell; spring brings crisp clean windows. The variable is the wind funnel — the same mountains that frame the bay accelerate gusts down it, flipping conditions in an hour. Around £800 for six nights half-board with rubber and guiding. Pack for four seasons daily.
highlights: Aurora chance over an evening lineup

adventures.title: Punta Roca Right, La Libertad Coast
adventures.description:
El Salvador built its surf reputation on one wave: Punta Roca, a cobblestone right point at La Libertad that throws long, fast, hollow walls rated the best in Central America. On a solid south swell it links sections for 300 metres, from the sketchy boil at the top through the racetrack middle to an inside that finally lets you breathe. The country hosted world championship surfing here for good reason.

Base yourself twenty minutes west at El Tunco, the black-sand village with the pig-shaped rock, where El Sunzal's soft outside peak gives you a warm-up wave and the strip's pupuserías refuel you for pennies. La Bocana's rivermouth left sits between them when you want a rapid-fire alternative. Everything runs on dawn: by mid-morning the onshore puff arrives and the heat builds towards 33C.

Surf-taxi pickups from El Tunco to Punta Roca are the standard move. The catch is the entry — timing the keyhole between cobblestone sets — and the local hierarchy at the peak, which rewards patience. March to September brings consistent southern swell. About £600 for eight days with guesthouse, surf taxis and board hire; fly into San Salvador, 50 minutes away.
adventures.location: La Libertad and El Tunco, Balsamo Coast
highlights: El Sunzal warm-up peaks at dawn
Pupusas on the El Tunco strip
La Bocana rivermouth left on a pulse
Pelicans gliding the point at sunset

adventures.title: Bundoran Peak Weekend, Donegal Bay
adventures.description:
Bundoran calls itself Ireland's surf capital with a straight face, because The Peak delivers: an A-frame reef in the middle of town that offers a long, workable left and a shorter, barrelling right over flat limestone, all within a stroll of chip shops and pubs with turf fires. Donegal Bay acts as a swell funnel for Atlantic lows, and within twenty minutes' drive you have Tullan Strand's beach peaks for learners, Rossnowlagh's beginner rollers, and heavier reefs like PMPA for those with the skills.

It is the classic long-weekend strike: watch the charts, book late, fly to Knock or Dublin, and score. September to December brings the magic combination of lingering sea warmth (13–14C) and organised groundswell; spring is quieter and cleaner.

The town does surf infrastructure properly — schools, hire, board shapers and surf lodges from £25 a night — and après-surf means live music rather than protein shakes. The variable is wind: The Peak needs a southeasterly quadrant and mid tide, and Irish weather changes hourly, so stay mobile between the bay's corners. A four-day weekend with lodge bed, fuel and hire comes to about £300.
highlights: A-frame sessions at The Peak in town
Turf-fire pub debrief with live music

adventures.title: Thurso East Reef, Caithness Winter
adventures.description:
On the north coast of mainland Scotland, in view of a ruined castle, Thurso East throws one of Europe's best right-hand reef waves: a thick, kelpy flagstone slab that bends Arctic-born swell into long, board-testing barrels. The O'Neill Coldwater Classic made it famous; the 8C water and horizontal sleet keep it honest. On its day — clean groundswell from the north, light southerly offshore — it bears comparison with reefs anywhere on earth.

You suit up in a river-mouth car park with snow blowing over the Pentland Firth, then ride some of the most perfect cold water of your life. Brimms Ness, ten minutes west, offers heavier slabs; Sandside and Melvich give options when Thurso sleeps. Between sessions: castles, distilleries and Britain's most northerly mainland town.

Stay in Thurso itself (guesthouses, a surf-friendly hotel or self-catering). Drive up from Inverness (2.5 hours) with full winter kit — two of everything, because nothing dries. October to March is prime. Around £400 for five days self-catered — the waves are free; the rubber is the investment. The variable is light: December gives you a six-hour surf window, so plan tides carefully.
highlights: Brimms Ness slab session for the brave
Snow flurries over the Pentland Firth
Post-surf dram at a Caithness distillery
gear: Change robe and car heater discipline

adventures.title: Popoyo Offshore Season, Nicaragua
adventures.description:
Nicaragua's party trick is wind: Lake Nicaragua sits behind the coast like a giant fan, blowing offshore over the Emerald Coast up to 300 days a year. At Popoyo that means groomed, feathering walls morning to dusk — a rarity anywhere on earth. The main peak is a punchy A-frame over flat reef that handles from playful to double-overhead, while the Outer Reef beyond turns into a genuine big-wave slab for teams with tow ropes and nerve.

The Guasacate strip behind the beach is barefoot Nicaragua: surf lodges, smoothie shacks and a dirt road that floods in rain, with Playa Santana and beginner-friendly beach peaks a short walk either way. Boat and 4x4 missions reach Lance's Left and Playgrounds when the angle suits.

Fly into Managua and transfer two and a half hours south, or cross overland from Costa Rica. The catch is the midday sun and the reef at low tide — book a lodge with a pool and surf the tide push. Southern swell runs April to October; May–June pairs pumping surf with green hills. Eight days full board at a surf lodge is about £550, one of Central America's best wave-per-pound ratios.
highlights: Outer Reef heaving on a big pulse

adventures.title: Robertsport Point Lefts, Liberia
adventures.description:
Under the green bulk of Cape Mount, where Lake Piso meets the Atlantic, Robertsport hides one of Africa's great pointbreak alignments: five lefts peeling down the cape in sequence — Fisherman's Point the long, perfect headliner, Cassava and Cotton Trees filling the gaps — often with more pelicans than people. This is the frontier story told in the film Sliding Liberia: a town rebuilding through a proud young surf culture.

Expect West Africa logistics, not a resort. Lodging is simple guesthouses and beach camps near the fishing beach; electricity is generator-hours; you bring boards, spares and goodwill (donated equipment goes a long way). The reward is warm, empty, world-class lefts and evenings watching fishing canoes ride the shorebreak home under Cape Mount.

Fly to Monrovia (Roberts International), then it is a two-to-three-hour drive up the coast highway and lakeshore track. Swell runs April to October; May to September is most consistent, accepting rainy-season downpours between sessions. Ten days with guesthouse, driver and food comes to about £600. Carry cash, malaria prophylaxis and patience — all three get used.
highlights: Fisherman's Point lefts under Cape Mount
Surfing with the Robertsport surf club kids
Fishing canoes riding the shorebreak at dusk
Lake Piso lagoon paddle on flat mornings
gear: Two boards plus full spares kit

adventures.title: Hokkaido Snow Surf, Muroran Winter
adventures.description:
Surfing Hokkaido in January is as strange and wonderful as it sounds: paddling out at Itanki Beach in Muroran while snow settles on your board bag, sea smoke curling off 6C water, and a volcanic headland white to the tideline. The Pacific coast around Muroran and Tomakomai catches winter groundswell that wraps clean into the bays, while the northwest monsoon delivers windswell to the Sea of Japan side — a two-coast strategy with mountains in between.

This is the most committed cold-water surfing in Asia, and the reward structure is pure Japan: session, then onsen, then miso ramen, repeat. The local crews are small, hardy and welcoming to travellers who observe lineup etiquette and bow to the car-park elders. Many pair it with Rusutsu powder days.

Fly to New Chitose (Sapporo); Muroran is ninety minutes by car, and a rental with snow tyres is essential. The variable is brutal weather logic — the same low that sends swell also sends blizzards, so flexibility and a good forecast eye decide your week. Around £900 for seven days with guesthouse, car and onsen habit. Rubber matters: 6/5/4 hooded suits, 7mm boots, mitts, and no heroics.
highlights: Post-surf onsen and miso ramen ritual
Two-coast swell chasing with snow tyres

adventures.title: Ngor Right, Dakar Peninsula
adventures.description:
The right-hander off Ngor Island earned its place in surf mythology as the African wave in The Endless Summer, and the pilgrimage still works exactly as it should: a wooden pirogue ferries you across the channel from Ngor beach, you paddle off the island's rocks, and a reeling reef right (with a shorter left on the other side of the peak) delivers you back towards Dakar's skyline. Around the Almadies peninsula — the westernmost tip of Africa — a dozen reefs and beach breaks face every direction, so somewhere is always offshore: Ouakam's dramatic mosque-front peak, Vivier, Club Med and the beach peaks of Yoff.

Dakar wraps the surfing in its own energy: teranga hospitality, thieboudienne lunches, sunset drumming on Ngor beach and a young, growing local surf scene with schools and camps at Ngor and Yoff.

November to March brings consistent North Atlantic groundswell to the peninsula's north side (best for Ngor Right); the boreal summer flips attention to southern-facing beaches. Water sits at a pleasant 20–26C. The catch is urchins and shallow rock — booties on, and time the tide. Fly direct to Dakar; a week with surf-camp lodging, pirogue fares and airport transfer runs about £450.
highlights: Pirogue ride to the Ngor Island lineup
The Endless Summer right on a north pulse
Ouakam's peak below the Divinity Mosque
gear: Shortboard or fish for reef peaks
Shorty or 2mm top for winter mornings

adventures.title: Kalalau Trail on the Nā Pali Coast
adventures.description:
Eleven miles of trail carved into thousand-metre sea cliffs, ending at a beach you can only reach on foot or by kayak. The Kalalau Trail traces Kauai's Nā Pali Coast from Keʻe Beach through a corrugation of jungled valleys — Hanakāpīʻai, Hanakoa — to Kalalau Beach, where you camp under fluted green walls that starred as Jurassic Park's backdrop. The pinch is Crawler's Ledge around mile seven: a narrow catwalk over the Pacific that is fine in the dry and unnerving in rain.

Rain is the real gatekeeper. Streams flash-flood fast enough to strand hikers between valleys for days — if Hanakāpīʻai is brown and pushy, you turn around, no debate. Winter swells also eat the beach and the trail gets greasier the wetter the season.

Overnight camping permits (about US$35 a night) release 90 days out on the Hawaii DLNR site and sell out almost instantly; day access beyond Hanakāpīʻai without one is illegal. Access is via the Hāʻena State Park shuttle or pre-booked parking. Two to three days on trail; budget roughly £220 with permits, shuttle and food, plus whatever Kauai does to your wallet either side.
adventures.location: Nā Pali Coast State Wilderness Park, Kauai, Hawaii
highlights: First sight of Kalalau Beach from Red Hill
Camping beneath the fluted Nā Pali cliffs
Sunset from the sea cave end of Kalalau Beach

adventures.title: Routeburn Track: Fiordland to Mount Aspiring
adventures.description:
Thirty-three kilometres that feel like a highlights reel of the South Island. The Routeburn climbs from red-beech forest at the head of Lake Wakatipu to Harris Saddle, where the moment arrives: you drop your pack, scramble twenty minutes up Conical Hill, and the Hollyford Valley unrolls beneath you all the way to the Tasman Sea. Then it is a balcony traverse high above the valley to Lake Mackenzie, kea wheeling overhead, before the final descent to The Divide in Fiordland.

The booking is the crux. Great Walks season (late October to April) huts are released by DOC each autumn and the Routeburn sells out in hours — set an alarm for the release day or accept shoulder-season conditions, when avalanche paths near Harris Saddle can close the alpine section entirely.

It is a point-to-point walk: most people start at Routeburn Shelter near Glenorchy and finish at The Divide on the Milford road, using a booked shuttle back to Queenstown or Te Anau. Three days, hut bunks around NZ$102–152 a night for visitors; budget roughly £380 with transport. Fitness required is modest; weather discipline is not optional.
adventures.location: Fiordland & Mount Aspiring National Parks, South Island
highlights: Conical Hill view from Harris Saddle to the Tasman Sea
Balcony path above the Hollyford Valley
Lake Mackenzie hut and its mirror-still bay
Routeburn Falls thundering below the flats
Kea encounters on the alpine section

adventures.title: Wonderland Trail Circuit of Mount Rainier
adventures.description:
For ten days you orbit a 4,392m volcano, and the mountain never once looks the same. The Wonderland Trail rings Mount Rainier in roughly 150km of relentless ups and downs — over 6,700m of climbing in total — swinging from old-growth river valleys to flower meadows at Spray Park and the black moraine world of Panhandle Gap, the trail's 2,073m high point. The evening that stays with people is Klapatche Park: sunset firing the glaciers orange above Aurora Lake while you eat dinner on the bluff.

Permits are the battle. Almost all wilderness camps go through the recreation.gov early-access lottery in spring; the remainder are walk-up, which means queueing at a ranger station and taking whatever itinerary is left. Snow lingers on the high sections into late July, and the Panhandle Gap crossing is genuinely hazardous when it is icy.

Most circuits start at Longmire or Sunrise, with food caches posted ahead to ranger stations to split the load. Nearest towns are Ashford and Enumclaw, a couple of hours from Seattle. Self-supported cost is low — think £250–350 for permits, fuel, food and shuttles — the currency here is fitness and planning.
highlights: Sunset over Aurora Lake at Klapatche Park
Spray Park wildflower meadows in August
Suspension bridge over the Tahoma Creek gorge
gear: Microspikes for early-season snow at Panhandle Gap
Food cache buckets posted in advance

adventures.title: Teton Crest Trail
adventures.description:
The Teton Crest is the American skyline walk: roughly 64km along the spine of the range, almost all of it above 2,700m, with the Grand Teton's granite prow appearing and reappearing like a recurring dream. You camp on Death Canyon Shelf — a limestone balcony wide enough for a tent and a thousand-metre view — cross the wildflower amphitheatre of Alaska Basin, and top out on 3,240m Paintbrush Divide before the switchbacks drop you past Lake Solitude into Cascade Canyon.

Two variables catch people: snow and permits. A steep north-facing bank guards Paintbrush Divide well into July and an ice axe is often required kit — check the ranger report, not the weather app. Camping zones inside Grand Teton National Park go to a January lottery on recreation.gov, but a third are held back as walk-ups the day before; flexible parties nearly always get on.

Most hikers ride the Jackson Hole tram from Teton Village to start high, finishing at String Lake. Jackson is the access town, with bear canisters compulsory and moose a genuine trail hazard. Four to five days; around £280 all-in with permits, canister hire and shuttles.
highlights: Alaska Basin wildflowers in late July
Lake Solitude beneath the Cathedral Group
gear: Ice axe for Paintbrush Divide in early season

adventures.title: Kepler Track Circuit, Fiordland
adventures.description:
The Kepler was purpose-built in 1988 to show off everything Fiordland does, and it delivers in a single 60km loop from the lakeshore at Te Anau. Day two is the one you will replay for years: from Luxmore Hut you walk a bare tussock ridgeline for hours, Lake Te Anau a sheet of hammered silver a kilometre below on one side, the Murchison Mountains — last refuge of the takahē — on the other. Kea patrol the emergency shelters; do not turn your back on your lunch.

The alpine crossing is gloriously exposed, and that is also the catch: in a norwester the ridge is no place to be, and parties regularly sit out a day at Luxmore waiting for the cloud to lift. Book the Great Walks season huts the day DOC releases them; Luxmore's 54 bunks vanish first. The caves ten minutes from the hut are worth packing a head torch for.

It is a true local loop — you can walk from Te Anau township or trim the lake sections with the Brod Bay water taxi. Four days, three huts, no shuttle logistics. Roughly £320 including hut fees and a celebratory Te Anau dinner.
highlights: All-day ridgeline traverse above Lake Te Anau
Kea at the alpine emergency shelters
Iris Burn valley and its 80m waterfall
Brod Bay beech forest and lakeshore finish
gear: Hut bookings for Luxmore, Iris Burn and Moturau
Windproof shell for the exposed ridge
Trekking poles for the Iris Burn descent

adventures.title: Tiger Leaping Gorge High Trail
adventures.description:
One of the deepest gorges on Earth, walked on a mule path halfway up its wall. The high trail above the Jinsha River — the young Yangtze — runs from Qiaotou through terraced farms and pine woods with Jade Dragon Snow Mountain's 5,596m glaciated wall filling the sky across the void. The gorge floor lies almost 3,000m below the summits; the famous 28 Bends switchbacks buy you the airiest section, where the path narrows to a ledge and the river is a white thread far beneath your boots.

Guesthouses make it civilised: the Naxi Family, Tea Horse and Halfway House serve cold beer and pumpkin pancakes on terraces built for the view, so you carry a daypack and sleep in beds. The catch-outs are rain and rockfall — the monsoon months (June to August) grease the exposed sections and close the trail after slides — and the descent to the Tiger Leaping Stone itself, a steep, thigh-burning ladder-and-path detour that costs more than it looks.

Stage from Lijiang or Shangri-La, two to three hours by bus, and buy the park entrance ticket at the gate. Two days on trail suits most; three lets you linger. Astonishing value at around £150 including transport, beds, meals and tickets.
highlights: The 28 Bends above the Jinsha River
Jade Dragon Snow Mountain filling the far wall
Sunset from the Halfway House terrace
Descent to the Tiger Leaping Stone rapids
Naxi farm terraces clinging to the gorge
gear: Sun hat for exposed morning climbs
Rain shell outside the dry months
Cash for entrance ticket and guesthouses

adventures.title: Queenstown Adventure Week
adventures.description:
Queenstown invented commercial bungy and never looked back. A week here is a syllabus in adrenaline: the original 43m Kawarau Bridge jump, the 134m Nevis wire strung across a desert canyon, grade IV–V rafting through the Shotover's rock gardens, and a jet boat spinning centimetres from schist walls. Between hits, the town keeps giving — ride the gondola-served Queenstown Bike Park until your forearms quit, then hike Ben Lomond (1,748m) for a summit view over Lake Wakatipu to the Remarkables that explains every postcard.

The honest moment is the Nevis: the pod door opens, the wind comes up through the grate, and eight seconds of freefall recalibrates your sense of what you volunteer for. The variable is weather and demand — high-wind days cancel jumps and January books out, so reserve the marquee activities before you fly.

Queenstown airport is 15 minutes from town; no car needed for the core week. Summer (November to March) gives the full menu and long evenings; winter swaps rafting volume for ski days. Budget about £1,100–1,200 for hostel or budget-hotel beds plus the big-ticket activities — this is not a cheap town, but nothing here is half-hearted.
highlights: Kawarau Bridge, the original commercial bungy
Shotover Canyon rafting and jet boat
Ben Lomond summit above Lake Wakatipu

adventures.title: Tour of Monte Rosa
adventures.description:
The Tour of Monte Rosa circles the second-highest massif in the Alps through two countries and one glacier, and it remains strangely uncrowded next to its Mont Blanc cousin. Over nine days you swing from Zermatt's Matterhorn theatre into Italy's Walser valleys — Gressoney, Alagna, Macugnaga — where wooden houses on stone staddle-stones have faced the Monte Rosa east wall, the biggest mountain face in the Alps, for six centuries. The Colle del Turlo, climbed on a beautifully preserved military mule road, is the quiet masterpiece.

The defining obstacle is the Theodulpass: the classic line between Zermatt and Cervinia crosses the Theodul Glacier at around 3,300m. It is crevassed and requires either a guide, genuine glacier competence, or the honest cop-out of the cable car over the top — decide before you go, not at the moraine.

Stage lodging is mountain huts and village inns, half board almost everywhere, so packs stay light. Access from Zermatt (train from Geneva or Zurich) with escape valves by bus at several cols. Mid-July to mid-September; around £950 for nine days of half-board huts, or £1,600+ with a guide for the glacier day.
highlights: Monte Rosa east face above Macugnaga
Colle del Turlo military mule road
Walser villages of Gressoney and Alagna
Matterhorn sunrise from the Zermatt side
gear: Crampons or microspikes for the glacier day
Guide booking or cable-car plan for Theodulpass
Cash euros and francs for huts

adventures.title: Four Pass Loop, Maroon Bells
adventures.description:
Forty-three kilometres, four passes, every one of them above 3,780m. The Four Pass Loop circles the Maroon Bells — the most photographed mountains in Colorado — via West Maroon, Frigid Air, Trail Rider and Buckskin passes, and between them it stacks more concentrated alpine scenery than routes three times its length: avalanche-combed aspen groves, basins solid with paintbrush and columbine in late July, and the Bells' striped maroon pyramids revolving through every compass bearing.

The two disciplines that make or break it are acclimatisation and clocks. Starting from Aspen at altitude, unacclimatised hikers blow up on West Maroon the first morning; and from midsummer, afternoon thunderstorms arrive with punctual violence, so you crest each pass before noon or you wait a day. Snowfields guard Trail Rider well into July.

Overnight permits for the Maroon Bells–Snowmass Wilderness are booked on recreation.gov, bear canisters are required, and the Maroon Lake trailhead runs on a reservation shuttle from Aspen Highlands. Most parties take four days anticlockwise. Cost on the ground is modest — around £200 with permits, shuttle and food.
highlights: Maroon Bells reflected in Maroon Lake at dawn
Cresting Trail Rider Pass above Snowmass Lake
Four passes over 3,780m in four days

adventures.title: Interlaken Alpine Sampler
adventures.description:
Interlaken sits on a flat green parade ground between two lakes with the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau stacked at the end of the valley, and it has quietly become Europe's most efficient adventure hub. In five days you can paraglide off Beatenberg and land on the Höhematte in the town centre, canyon the polished chutes of the Saxet gorge above Saxeten, raft the glacial Lütschine's grade III–IV snowmelt, and finish with the Schynige Platte to Faulhorn ridge hike, the whole Jungfrau wall lit up across the valley.

The moment that sells it is stepping off the paragliding launch: two strides of running and the lakes swing beneath you, Thun turquoise on one side, Brienz jade on the other. The catch-out is weather churn — föhn wind or a low cloud base cancels flights and canyoning at short notice, so book activities early in your stay and keep the last day free to reshuffle.

Everything is walkable or a train stop apart; no car needed. June to September for the full menu; the Lütschine is snow-fed and properly cold. Budget around £900 for hostel beds and four big activity days — Switzerland charges Swiss prices, but no single ticket disappoints.
highlights: Paraglider landing on the Höhematte in town
Schynige Platte to Faulhorn ridge hike
gear: Half Fare Card or regional travel pass

adventures.title: Moab Desert Multi-Sport Week
adventures.description:
Moab is a small town with an outsized gravitational field: two national parks on its doorstep, a big brown river running through, and more slickrock than anywhere on Earth. The classic week stacks disciplines — a day on the Slickrock Trail's petrified sandstone dunes, where your tyres grip angles that feel impossible; the Whole Enchilada descent from alpine meadows at over 3,300m down to the Colorado River; a raft day through the red walls of Fisher Towers canyon; and a rope day canyoneering a sandstone slot, abseiling into cool shadow while the desert bakes above.

Sunset belongs to Delicate Arch — walk up for the hour when the sandstone goes furnace-orange. The catch-out is heat and timing: June to August is punishing on exposed rock, the Whole Enchilada's top section only melts out from late May, and Arches now runs timed-entry reservations in peak season. Spring and autumn are the sweet spots.

Fly into Grand Junction or drive four hours from Salt Lake City; a car matters here. Bike hire, shuttles, raft and canyoneering guides all book easily in town. Around £850–950 for the week with camping or a budget motel, hire bike and two guided days.
highlights: Whole Enchilada 2,000m descent to the Colorado
gear: Timed-entry reservation for Arches in season

adventures.title: Huemul Circuit above the Southern Ice Field
adventures.description:
The Huemul Circuit is El Chaltén's graduate course. While the crowds queue for Laguna de los Tres, this four-day loop swings south around Cerro Huemul to the one place a trekker can stand and see the Southern Patagonian Ice Field entire: from Paso del Viento the white plain runs to the horizon, cracked like dried paint, with Viedma Glacier calving into its lake below you. Few marked trails anywhere buy a view this expensive for this little technical climbing.

The price is paid in other currencies. Two river crossings are rigged as zip-lines — you clip a harness and pulley to a steel cable and haul yourself across the Río Túnel — and the park office checks you are carrying both before issuing the free permit. Then there is the wind: Paso del Viento and Paso Huemul earn their names, and parties regularly hold camp for a day when the ice field exhales.

Everything stages out of El Chaltén, three hours from El Calafate's airport; harness kits hire cheaply in town. Camps are free and basic. November to March. Budget around £420 self-sufficient including kit hire, or £700+ with a local guide — worth considering, as navigation on the moraine above Lago Viedma is loose in every sense.
adventures.location: Los Glaciares National Park, Santa Cruz, Patagonia
highlights: Southern Patagonian Ice Field from Paso del Viento
Zip-line crossings of the Río Túnel
Fitz Roy skyline on the walk out
gear: Climbing harness with pulley and sling (checked at permit office)
Four-season tent that shrugs off 80km/h gusts
Three days of food with margin

adventures.title: Cape Wrath Trail
adventures.description:
Britain's hardest long walk is not a trail at all: roughly 370km of unmarked, unwaymarked line from Fort William to the lighthouse at Cape Wrath, the northwesternmost point of the British mainland. It threads the roughest country Scotland owns — Knoydart's rough bounds, the sea-loch head at Barrisdale, the sandstone giants of Torridon, the Great Wilderness around Fisherfield's remote six, Assynt's lonely inselbergs — finishing across the empty moor of the Parph to a lighthouse on 100m cliffs.

Every day asks for decisions: rivers rise fast and the crossings at Fisherfield can be impassable after rain; bogs swallow boots; camps and bothies (Shenavall, Kearvaig) replace hotels for days at a stretch. The final sting is logistical — the Kyle of Durness passenger ferry and the MOD's Cape Wrath firing range both control access to the cape, so you check firing times before committing to the last stage.

Most walkers take 14 to 20 days, resupplying at Shiel Bridge, Kinlochewe and Ullapool. May and June bring long days and fewer midges; September trades midges for storms. Budget around £320 in food, ferries and the odd bunkhouse — the trail itself charges in weather, not money.
adventures.location: Northwest Highlands, Fort William to Cape Wrath
highlights: Knoydart and the head of Loch Hourn
Sandwood Bay's mile of empty pink sand
The lighthouse at Cape Wrath itself
gear: Map set and compass (waymarks do not exist)
Waterproof socks or accepted wet feet

imageAttribution.artist: Tom Parnell from Scottish Borders, Scotland

adventures.title: GR221 Dry Stone Route, Mallorca
adventures.description:
Mallorca's mountain spine is nothing like its beach-resort reputation. The GR221 runs the length of the Serra de Tramuntana — a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape — on cobbled pilgrim paths and dry-stone walled terraces built over a thousand years of olive farming. From Port d'Andratx you climb through holm-oak forest to ridge-lines with the Mediterranean glittering on both sides, drop into honey-stone villages like Deià and Sóller for coffee and ensaïmadas, and finish beneath the crags above Pollença.

The walking is civilised but never soft: days regularly top 1,000m of ascent, the limestone is ankle-testing, and in the high section past Cúber reservoir you traverse beneath Puig Major, the island's highest peak. Spring brings wildflowers; July and August bring heat that stops sensible walkers.

The refugis are the catch: the Consell de Mallorca's mountain refuges (Tossals Verds, Muleta, Son Amer) are cheap, excellent and book out months ahead, especially for spring — reserve the moment plans firm up, or mix in village guesthouses. Palma's airport puts the trailhead an hour away by bus. Eight days, around £600 with refuge half-board and a proper Sóller lunch in the middle.
highlights: Ridge walking with sea on both horizons

adventures.title: Kaçkar Traverse: Ayder to Yaylalar
adventures.description:
Turkey's rainiest mountains hide its finest trekking. Above the tea terraces of Rize the Kaçkar rise in a wall of granite that catches every cloud rolling off the Black Sea, and for a week you thread hanging valleys between yayla summer villages — Ayder's hot springs at one end, the stone hamlets of Yaylalar and Olgunlar at the other. The set piece is a pre-dawn push from Dilberdüzü camp to the 3,937m summit of Kaçkar Dağı, with the glacial bowl of Deniz Gölü glittering below you on the way down.

The variable that catches people out is the mist: on most summer days cloud swallows the ridges by late morning, so starts are early and a GPS track matters when the waymarks vanish. Nights split between camps and family-run pensions where dinner is muhlama — molten cheese and cornmeal — after ten hours on your feet.

Fly to Trabzon or Rize–Artvin, then dolmuş via Çamlıhemşin to Ayder. July to September only; snow lingers into early summer. Budget around £700 for a guided week with pension nights, or half that self-sufficient under canvas.
highlights: Deniz Gölü glacial lake below the summit wall
Yayla villages of Yaylalar and Olgunlar
Hot-spring soak at Ayder after the traverse
Cloud-sea sunrises above the Black Sea mist

adventures.title: Sarek Traverse: Kvikkjokk to the Rapa Valley
adventures.description:
Sarek is what the Alps were before the huts arrived: around a hundred glaciers, a cluster of 2,000-metre peaks, and not a single marked trail, bridge or cabin in the core of the park. From the road-end hamlet of Kvikkjokk you walk north into a week of self-reliance — fording braided rivers, reading weather off the Padjelanta plateau, camping wherever the reindeer grass is dry. The reward sits at the far end: the summit of Skierfe, a 700m cliff over the Rapa Valley delta, where the river below plaits itself into jade and silver channels that no photograph makes believable.

Rapadalen itself is Europe's moose stronghold, willow thickets taller than you are, and the fords are the real gatekeepers: after rain the braided rivers feeding the Rapaätno run thigh-deep and fast, and experienced parties build in a waiting day. Mobile coverage is patchy and exits are long.

Access is a sleeper train from Stockholm to Murjek and bus to Kvikkjokk, with the Aktse and Saltoluokta fjällstations bracketing the wild days at either end. Late July to early September, after the melt and before the snows. Roughly £450 in transport, mountain-station nights and food; the solitude comes free.
highlights: Skierfe's 700m cliff over the Rapa delta
Moose in the Rapadalen willow jungles
Midnight-sun light on the Padjelanta plateau

adventures.title: Snow Leopard Vigil at Kibber
adventures.description:
The whistle comes down the valley like a relay — spotter to spotter — and every scope on the ridge swings to the same scree slope. It takes you a full minute to see what they see: a grey cat on grey rock, flowing downhill towards a herd of blue sheep. In late winter the snow leopards of Spiti descend with their prey, and the villages around Kibber, at 4,200 metres, have turned watching them into a quiet local economy of trackers, homestays and radio calls.

This is cold-weather patience hunting. Days are spent glassing from ridgelines above the Parilungbi gorge, often for hours, at minus fifteen; sightings are typically 200–500 metres through optics, occasionally heart-stoppingly closer. Success rates in February–March are remarkably high — most week-long trips connect — with ibex, red fox, bearded vultures and staggering night skies as the supporting cast.

Winter access is the catch: the Manali passes shut, so it is a two-day drive from Shimla through Kinnaur, with an acclimatisation night in Kaza essential before sleeping at Kibber. Homestays are warm-hearted and basic (bucket washes, dry loos). Eight days with transfers, local spotters and full board runs about £1,800–£2,300.
highlights: A snow leopard stalking blue sheep above the Parilungbi gorge
The spotters' whistle-chain when a cat is found
Homestay thukpa nights in Kibber village
Ibex and red fox on the drive to Chicham bridge

adventures.title: Brooks Falls Bear Watch, Katmai
adventures.description:
The floatplane banks over Naknek Lake and there they are before you've even landed: brown bears spaced along the Brooks River like anglers on a beat. In July, when the sockeye run peaks, a dozen or more jostle at the falls themselves — the biggest males stationed on the lip, snatching leaping salmon out of the air a few metres from the viewing platform.

Everything at Brooks Camp is choreographed around the bears: a ranger-led 'bear school' on arrival, boardwalks above the meadows, and platform time limits when the July queues build. September is the connoisseur's month — fewer people, and hulking pre-hibernation bears gorging on carcasses in the lower river.

The booking reality catches people out. Brooks Lodge sells out via lottery around 18 months ahead, and the campground's January lottery fills in minutes; most visitors instead day-trip by floatplane from King Salmon (via Anchorage) or Homer. Weather cancels flights regularly, so build in slack. Budget roughly £2,000–£2,600 for a few days including Alaskan bush flights.
adventures.location: Brooks Camp, Katmai National Park, Alaska
highlights: Bears catching leaping sockeye on the lip of Brooks Falls
Ranger-led bear school before your first boardwalk
Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes day trip

adventures.title: Ranthambhore Lakes and the Fort Tigers
adventures.description:
No tiger reserve on earth has a stage set like this: ruined chhatris and a thousand-year-old hilltop fort above three lakes, banyan roots swallowing palace walls, and tigers that have learned to ignore the audience. When a big male walks the shore of Padam Talao with the fort behind him, you understand why half the famous tiger photographs ever taken came from Ranthambhore.

The machinery takes some patience. Safaris are zone-based — the lake zones (1–5) are the prize — and allocations come via an online lottery-ish scramble on the Rajasthan forest portal 90 days out; agents charge a mark-up to handle it. Choose a six-seat Gypsy over the twenty-seat Canter if you can. October reopening is lush but harder for sightings; February to May the cover burns off and cats come to water.

Sawai Madhopur station is a comfortable train ride from Delhi or Jaipur, and the town runs on tigers — lodges at every budget. Four days with four zone-permitted drives, guide fees and a mid-range lodge is roughly £700–£900. Between drives, walk up to the fort itself: black kites, langurs and one of Rajasthan's great views.
highlights: A tiger on the shore of Padam Talao with the fort behind
Marsh crocodiles hauled out below Malik Talao
The zone lottery drama at dawn in Sawai Madhopur
Sambar bellowing across the lakes at dusk

adventures.title: Lamar Valley Wolf Watch in Winter
adventures.description:
At minus twenty, sound carries. You are out of the van before sunrise, breath freezing to your hood, when the howl starts — one voice, then a ragged chorus rolling across Lamar Valley's blue snow. The spotters lock scopes onto a string of dark shapes trotting a bison trail, and for the next hour you watch a wolf pack do what it has done here since the 1995 reintroduction: test elk, rally, rest, move on.

Winter is the season because wolves stand out against snow and stay low in the valleys. Bison plough drifts with their heads, otters pop through river ice, and a bobcat along the Yellowstone is a genuine possibility. Expect scope views at 400 metres to two kilometres, not close-ups — bring patience and borrow the guides' optics.

Only the northern road (Gardiner to Cooke City) stays open to cars in winter, so base in Gardiner or Silver Gate and fly into Bozeman. Guided wolf weeks run roughly £1,500–£2,200 with lodging; independent watchers can simply pull over where the scopes cluster. Dress for long, still hours in brutal cold.
adventures.location: Lamar Valley, Yellowstone National Park, Montana/Wyoming
highlights: A pack howling across Lamar Valley at first light
Spotting scopes on the Junction Butte wolves
Bison ploughing snow with their heads
Otters and dippers along the ice-fringed Yellowstone
Steaming Mammoth terraces at minus twenty

adventures.title: Leopard Days in Yala Block One
adventures.description:
The jeep rounds a rock outcrop near Patanangala and your tracker taps the roof twice: a leopard is draped along a granite shelf, tail hanging, utterly indifferent to the diesel idle below. Yala's Block 1 holds one of the highest leopard densities on earth, and because these cats grew up as top predator — no lions, no hyenas — they walk the tracks in daylight like they own them.

Between cat sightings the park delivers constantly: elephants at the waterholes, painted storks and crocodiles in the lagoons, sloth bears snuffling palu fruit in June, and peacocks displaying on every second termite mound. The honest downside is company — a good sighting can draw a scrum of jeeps. Go at first light, ask your driver to work the quieter blocks, or add a day in adjacent Kumana.

Base yourself in Tissamaharama, 30 minutes from the Palatupana gate; safaris run roughly 5.30am and 2.30pm. The park usually closes for several weeks around September–October drought. Four days with a private jeep, tracker and guesthouse comes to around £600–£700.
highlights: A leopard draped over the rocks at Patanangala
Elephants and painted storks at the waterholes
Sloth bear snuffling palu fruit in June
Dawn queue at Palatupana gate breaking into open scrub
Curd and treacle back in Tissamaharama

adventures.title: Spirit Bear Search, Great Bear Rainforest
adventures.description:
Somewhere on this mossed-over salmon stream, a black bear that isn't black is fishing. The Kermode or 'spirit' bear — a white-coated genetic morph found almost nowhere else on earth — is the reason you are standing in the rain in Kitasoo/Xai'xais territory, watching your guide read fresh tracks in the estuary mud. When one finally materialises between the cedars, pale against the green dark, it feels less like wildlife watching than folklore made flesh.

Trips run from Klemtu, a First Nations village on Swindle Island, out of the community-owned Spirit Bear Lodge — boat days threading fjords where humpbacks lunge-feed, then quiet hours at viewing stands on the salmon rivers. Roughly one bear in ten here carries the white gene, so manage expectations: black bears, coastal wolves and whales are near-certain; the white bear is a gift, most likely during the September–early October salmon run.

Getting in is part of it: fly Vancouver to Bella Bella and transfer by boat, or take the inside-passage ferry. It rains — properly — so bring full rubber. Four to five nights all-inclusive from Klemtu runs £3,000–£3,800, and books out a year ahead.
adventures.location: Klemtu, Great Bear Rainforest, British Columbia
highlights: A white Kermode bear fishing a salmon stream
First Nations guides reading tracks on the estuary
Old-growth cedars a thousand years old
Big House stories back in Klemtu
gear: soft duffel for floatplane and boat

adventures.title: Corcovado Wild Coast on Foot
adventures.description:
National Geographic once called the Osa Peninsula the most biologically intense place on earth, and a dawn walk out of Sirena station makes the case: a Baird's tapir asleep in the shade behind the ranger buildings, scarlet macaws shrieking through the beach almonds, spider monkeys overhead and fresh puma tracks stitched along the tideline. Corcovado is Central America's last big block of Pacific lowland rainforest, and it is walked, not driven.

The rules shape the trip: entry only with a licensed local guide, daily visitor caps, and permits that sell out weeks ahead in the December–April dry season. Most people boat in from Drake Bay (spinner dolphins en route are a bonus) or approach from Puerto Jiménez via Carate; an overnight in the Sirena dormitory doubles your wildlife hours. The variable that flattens visitors is heat — 90 per cent humidity by 8am — so starts are pre-dawn, water is carried in litres, and the midday hours belong to the hammock.

Four days from Drake Bay with guide, permits, boats, dorm night and meals runs about £600–£800. Swimming at river mouths is off the menu: bull sharks and crocodiles patrol them.
highlights: Baird's tapir asleep behind Sirena station
Scarlet macaws in the beach almonds
All four Costa Rican monkey species in one morning
Fresh puma tracks on the tideline
Spinner dolphins on the boat in from Drake Bay

adventures.title: Odzala Lowland Gorilla Immersion
adventures.description:
Mountain gorillas get the headlines; Odzala is the harder, wilder other half of the story. Deep in the Congo Basin's second-largest rainforest block, trackers read bent marantaca stems to bring you — masked, silent, sweating — into the presence of a habituated western lowland gorilla family: a silverback stripping stems while youngsters somersault through the understorey. Sightlines are short in this thicket, which makes the encounters feel less like viewing and more like being admitted.

The classic circuit links three camps: Ngaga for the gorillas, Lango for waist-deep bai walks among forest buffalo and grey parrots, Mboko for kayaking the Lekoli past forest elephants. Wildlife here is genuinely wild — this is expedition-flavoured safari, not the Mara.

Be clear-eyed about logistics: access is by light aircraft charter from Brazzaville, departures are fixed-date, and the all-in land cost for a week runs £6,500–£8,500 per person. June to September is the drier window. Yellow fever certificate and malaria prophylaxis are non-negotiable, and a respiratory mask is required within range of the gorillas.
highlights: An hour with a habituated lowland gorilla family at Ngaga
Waist-deep bai walk among forest buffalo at Lango
Kayaking the Lekoli past forest elephants
Grey parrot flocks wheeling over the saline clearings
Charter flight over unbroken rainforest from Brazzaville

imageAttribution.artist: Thomas Breuer / Wildlife Conservation Society (PLoS Biology)

adventures.title: Tala Meadows Tiger Watch, Bandhavgarh
adventures.description:
Chital alarm calls ricochet across the meadow, langurs explode into the sal canopy, and your naturalist kills the engine: somewhere between you and the ramparts of Bandhavgarh Fort, a tiger is moving. Minutes later she steps onto the track — a resident tigress on her morning beat, padding past the open Gypsy close enough that you hear her feet on the dust. Bandhavgarh carries one of India's densest tiger populations, and the Tala zone's mosaic of meadows, cliffs and 2,000-year-old cave inscriptions is the classic stage.

Safaris run in two blocks, roughly 6am and 3pm, each needing a separate permit tied to your passport — book on the Madhya Pradesh forest portal as soon as the 120-day window opens, and be picky about zones. April and May are ferociously hot but give the best sighting odds as cats stick to waterholes; November to February is kinder and greener.

Fly to Jabalpur (four hours' drive) or take the train to Umaria. Five days with six safaris, naturalist, park fees and a decent lodge comes to about £900–£1,100.
highlights: A tigress crossing the meadows below Bandhavgarh Fort
Chital alarm calls pinpointing a moving cat
Vultures wheeling off the fort cliffs
Sal forest dawn from an open Gypsy
Cave inscriptions two thousand years old inside the park
gear: layered neutral clothing for cold dawns and hot noons

adventures.title: Chimpanzee Habituation Days, Kibale
adventures.description:
The pant-hoots start somewhere off to your left, ricochet through the fig canopy, and suddenly the forest is moving: black shapes swinging overhead, a big male barrelling down a trunk to drum on a buttress root two metres from your boots. Kibale protects East Africa's greatest density of primates, and its habituated chimp communities near Kanyanchu give the most reliable close encounters on the continent.

The standard trek buys you one hour with the apes; the Chimpanzee Habituation Experience puts you alongside researchers from the 6am nest-leaving to late afternoon — exhausting, muddy and unforgettable. Chimps travel fast on the ground, so expect sweaty scrambles through vines rather than a stroll. Between treks, walk the Bigodi wetland for great blue turacos and red colobus, and swim-gaze at the Fort Portal crater lakes.

Permits (around £160 standard, £230 habituation) book through the Uganda Wildlife Authority and sell out in the December–February and June–September dry seasons. Fort Portal, five hours' drive from Entebbe, is the base. Four days with permits, guiding and mid-range lodges runs to about £1,000–£1,200, and pairs naturally with gorillas in Bwindi.
highlights: Dawn-to-dusk habituation day with the Kanyanchu chimps
Pant-hoots ricocheting through the fig canopy
Twelve other primate species, red colobus included
Great blue turacos on the Bigodi wetland walk
Fort Portal crater lakes at sunset

adventures.title: Cristalino Canopy Towers, Southern Amazon
adventures.description:
You climb the 50-metre steel tower in the dark, and as the forest exhales its first mist the canopy spreads at your feet: macaws crossing in pairs, a channel-billed toucan yelping from an emergent kapok, and — if the guides' radio crackle is right — a harpy eagle hunched on a distant snag. Cristalino is the southern Amazon at its richest, a private reserve beside a state park on a blackwater river so clear it looks like poured glass.

Days alternate boat drifts for giant otters and tapir with slow trail walks for white-whiskered spider monkeys, curl-crested aracaris and poison-dart frogs. The catch is expectation: this is dense rainforest, not the Serengeti, and wildlife is earned in fragments — a good guide and quiet feet matter more than luck.

Fly Cuiabá to Alta Floresta, then a short drive and boat transfer upriver. The lodge is comfortable but remote; budget around £350–£400 a night full board with guiding, and come in the June–October dry season when trails are open and the clay licks are busy.
adventures.location: Cristalino State Park, Alta Floresta, Mato Grosso
highlights: Dawn above the canopy from the 50-metre observation tower
Giant otters and tapir on a blackwater boat drift
White-whiskered spider monkeys on the Figueira trail
Harpy eagle watch from the Serra viewpoint
Night walk for tarantulas and tree frogs

adventures.title: Monarch Winter Roosts of Michoacán
adventures.description:
You smell the fir forest before you hear it, and you hear it before you understand it: a low rush, like distant surf, that turns out to be wings. Every winter, hundreds of millions of monarch butterflies funnel out of North America into a few hectares of oyamel fir on the Michoacán–México state border, bending whole branches under their massed weight. When the sun breaks through and a roost erupts into orange blizzard, grown adults cry. It is that kind of place.

The visit itself is a half-day mountain hike: from the El Rosario gate you climb — on foot or by hired horse — to around 3,200 metres, where mandatory local ejido guides walk you quietly to the colony ropeline. Sierra Chincua, over the ridge, is the calmer second sanctuary. The altitude and near-freezing dawns surprise people who packed for 'Mexico'; bring proper layers and take the climb slowly.

Base in the old mining town of Angangueo or day-trip from Mexico City or Morelia (about three hours). The season runs late November to March, peaking January–February, and colonies shift location within the reserve year to year. Go midweek, arrive before the 1pm cloud, and budget around £300–£450 for a guided three-day trip.
highlights: Oyamel firs bowed under millions of monarchs
The roar of wings when sun hits a roost
Horseback climb from the El Rosario gate
Hot gorditas from the trailhead comedores
gear: cash for ejido guides and horses

adventures.title: Chitwan Rhino Country by Canoe and Foot
adventures.description:
Nepal means mountains to most people, but drop 3,000 metres to the Terai and a different country appears: sal forest and elephant grass, mist on the Rapti river, and a greater one-horned rhino grazing the far bank like a leftover from deeper time. Chitwan's rhinos — nearly 700 of them — anchor Asia's best-value big-mammal safari, with gharial crocodiles, sloth bears, wild elephants and a rising tiger population in the supporting cast.

What sets Chitwan apart is how you move: drifting silently past mugger crocodiles in a dugout canoe, then continuing on foot with two guides who brief you, entirely seriously, on what to do if a rhino charges (find a big tree). Jeep drives cover more ground, but the canoe-and-walk mornings are the memory you keep. Tharu villages fringe the park, and their stick-dance evenings and home kitchens are worth a night of anyone's time.

Sauraha is the classic base — a 5–6 hour drive or short flight (to Bharatpur) from Kathmandu — while Meghauli on the quieter western side suits those avoiding crowds. October to March is cool and clear; March's grass-cutting opens up visibility. Four days with guides, park fees, canoe and lodge runs £350–£550.
highlights: One-horned rhino grazing through dawn mist
Dugout canoe drift past gharials on the Rapti
The straight-faced rhino-charge briefing before your first walk
Bengal florican displaying over the grasslands

adventures.title: The Gathering at Minneriya Tank
adventures.description:
By late August the ancient Minneriya reservoir has shrunk to a silver puddle ringed by sweet new grass, and the elephants come. Two hundred, sometimes three hundred, drift out of the dry-zone jungle each afternoon — the largest recurring meeting of Asian elephants anywhere. You sit in an open jeep a respectful distance off and watch matriarchs marshal calves, young bulls spar, and the whole grey assembly graze its way towards sunset with Sigiriya's rock fortress smudged on the horizon.

The Gathering follows water, not the calendar: in some years the herds shift to neighbouring Kaudulla or Hurulu Eco Park, so let your driver chase the elephants rather than the park name — permits work the same way. Afternoon (3–6pm) is when the herds are out; expect other jeeps, and insist your driver keeps distance rather than crowding.

Base in Habarana or Sigiriya in the cultural triangle, four to five hours from Colombo, and fold the safari into a Sigiriya–Polonnaruwa loop. Three days with jeep hire, park fees and a guesthouse runs to around £300–£400.
adventures.location: Minneriya National Park, North Central Province
highlights: Three hundred elephants on the receding tank bed
Calves shielded inside the herd at sunset
Sigiriya rock fortress on the horizon
Fish eagles and pelicans working the shallows

adventures.title: Zakouma Dry-Season Spectacle
adventures.description:
By March the Salamat floodplains have burned down to a handful of pans, and everything that walks or flies in south-eastern Chad converges on them. Five hundred elephants — a herd that survived the poaching wars and is growing again under African Parks' watch — mass at Rigueik alongside thousands of black-crowned cranes, quelea clouds that move like smoke, Kordofan giraffe, roan, tiang and unbothered lions. It is the closest thing left to the Africa of the nineteenth-century journals.

Zakouma runs on a short, hard season: roughly December to April, before the rains close every track. Days are open-vehicle drives and walks with rangers; nights are spent listening to lions from an open-fronted room at Tinga Camp or, if you can get one of the handful of places, under the stars at Camp Nomade. Heat is the variable that catches people — by April it passes 40°C daily, which is exactly why the wildlife concentrates.

Access is a charter from N'Djamena arranged with your camp booking. This is a remote, high-commitment trip: budget £3,500–£6,000 land cost for six days depending on camp, and book close to a year ahead — the whole season sells out.
highlights: Five hundred elephants massed at Rigueik pan
Black-crowned cranes in their thousands at dawn
Kordofan giraffe necks above the acacia
Ranger patrol briefing with African Parks
Sleeping under the stars at Camp Nomade
gear: light down layer for Harmattan nights

adventures.title: Kangaroo Island Wildlife Circuit
adventures.description:
Kangaroo Island is what mainland Australia looked like before foxes and rabbits: sea lions dozing in heaps on a sugar-white beach, koalas wedged into manna gums beside the road, echidnas trundling across tracks in broad daylight. A five-day self-drive loops the lot, from the Seal Bay boardwalk — where a guide walks you onto the sand among wild Australian sea lions — to Remarkable Rocks glowing orange at sunset and the fur-seal surge pools under Admirals Arch.

The island is bigger than people expect (150 kilometres end to end), and the best wildlife happens at dawn and dusk, which is exactly when locals tell you not to drive — kangaroos own the roads after dark. The answer is to stay put in each corner: a night or two near Flinders Chase in the west, the rest around Kingscote or American River. The 2020 bushfires burned half the island; the regrowth, and the wildlife's rebound, is now part of the story.

Get there by SeaLink ferry from Cape Jervis to Penneshaw (45 minutes) or fly Adelaide–Kingscote. Five days with hire car, ferry, park passes and comfortable stays comes to roughly £700–£850 per person.
highlights: Walking the Seal Bay beach among wild sea lions
Koalas in the manna gums on the Hanson Bay road
Fur seals surging under Admirals Arch
Echidnas crossing the Flinders Chase tracks
gear: windproof jacket for the Southern Ocean coast

adventures.title: Kaziranga Rhino Floodplains
adventures.description:
Morning mist lifts off the elephant grass and the floodplain reveals its census: greater one-horned rhinos grazing like armoured lawnmowers, wild water buffalo with two-metre horn spans, swamp deer in herds the guidebooks said no longer existed. Kaziranga holds roughly two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinos on a strip of Brahmaputra floodplain, and from an open jeep in the central range you can have a dozen in view at once.

It is also, quietly, one of Asia's best all-round wildlife parks: the highest tiger density in India (seen rarely, in grass this tall), hog deer, smooth-coated otters, and winter wetlands stacked with pelicans and Pallas's fish eagles. Add a morning at nearby Hollongapar sanctuary for hoolock gibbons whooping through the canopy.

Fly to Jorhat (two hours) or Guwahati (four and a half) and base at Kohora village on the park's southern edge. The park closes entirely for the monsoon, roughly May to October, when the Brahmaputra drowns the grasslands; November to April is the season, February–March the sweet spot. Four days with jeep safaris, fees and a lodge runs to about £600–£750.
highlights: One-horned rhinos grazing the dawn mist
Wild water buffalo on the Brahmaputra floodplain
Pallas's fish eagles over the winter beels
Tea-garden breakfasts on the Kohora road

adventures.title: Selvaggio Blu: Sardinia's Wild Blue
adventures.description:
The Selvaggio Blu is routinely called Italy's toughest trek, though it is really a climbing journey that follows a coastline. From the limestone prow of Pedra Longa the route traces the Golfo di Orosei north along goat-herders' ledges and juniper-branch stairways built by charcoal burners, linking coves that no road has ever reached. Days involve scrambling to about grade IV, a dozen abseils — the longest around 45m, some free-hanging above turquoise water — and navigation through maquis where the 'path' is a memory shared between guides.

The logistics are half the adventure. There is no water on route, so guides arrange boat drops of supplies into the calas ahead of you; you sleep under the stars at Cala Goloritzé's arch or in caves above Cala Sisine, and a support boat is also the only exit if weather turns. Ropework is genuinely required — this is a trip to do guided unless your party can rig and retrieve abseils quickly and confidently.

Stage from Baunei or Santa Maria Navarrese on Sardinia's east coast (Cagliari or Olbia airports). April to June and September to October avoid the killing heat. Guided traverses run about £850–1,000 including boat support.
highlights: Bivouac at Cala Goloritzé's limestone arch
Juniper-stair ledges of the charcoal burners
Boat-dropped supply caches in roadless calas
Swimming at Cala Sisine after the ropes
gear: Bivvy bag (no huts, no tents needed)

adventures.title: El Mirador Jungle Trek
adventures.description:
Somewhere north of the last road in Guatemala's Petén, five days' walk into the Maya Biosphere Reserve, a forested hill resolves into La Danta — by volume one of the largest pyramids ever built, its summit poking through the canopy of a city that fell twelve centuries before the Spanish arrived. The trek to El Mirador starts in the village of Carmelita, whose community cooperative runs the trips: local guides, mules or horses carrying water and food, hammocks or tents slung at old chiclero camps where spider monkeys crash through the branches overhead.

The walking itself is flat but honest — 40km of jungle track each way, thick with mud early in the season and airless by mid-morning — and that is the variable: go in the December–April dry season, start each day at dawn, and let the mules do the carrying. The reward is a Manhattan-sized ruined city — and sunset from La Danta's platform with howler monkeys roaring below — almost entirely to yourselves.

Stage from Flores (flights from Guatemala City), two bumpy hours from Carmelita. Book the cooperative directly or through Flores agencies. Five to six days, roughly £350–420 including guide, mules, food and camps.
highlights: Sunset from the summit of La Danta pyramid
The lost city of El Mirador emerging from canopy
Howler and spider monkeys over the camps
Chiclero jungle camps with the Carmelita cooperative
Jaguar tracks on the morning trail
gear: Hammock with bug net or inner tent
Two pairs of socks per day in dry bags

adventures.title: Iberá Marshes Rewilding Safari
adventures.description:
The causeway into Colonia Carlos Pellegrini doubles as a game drive: capybara families graze the verges, caimans line the lagoon edge like parked cars, and marsh deer stand belly-deep among floating gardens of water hyacinth. The Iberá wetlands — 13,000 square kilometres of them — are South America's quiet answer to the Pantanal, and thanks to the Tompkins-founded rewilding programme they are getting wilder by the year: giant anteaters, pampas deer, macaws and, since 2021, jaguars again breeding on San Alonso island.

Days here are gentle and close-range: boat safaris nosing into the reedbeds, horseback rides with local gauchos, night drives picking out lamplit caiman eyes and maned-wolf shapes on the road. Birders tally 350-plus species without trying. Posadas in the village are estancia-style, all home cooking and siesta courtyards.

The catch is the access road: 120 kilometres of dirt from Mercedes that rain turns to impassable clay — build in a buffer day. Reach Mercedes by overnight bus from Buenos Aires or fly to Corrientes and drive. Five days full board with excursions runs £700–£1,000; spring and autumn dodge the fiercest heat.
highlights: Capybara families grazing the Carlos Pellegrini causeway
Marsh deer belly-deep in floating gardens
Lamplit caiman eyes on the night drive
News from the jaguar reintroduction on San Alonso
Gaucho horseback ride into the palm savanna

adventures.title: Hornstrandir Traverse: Hesteyri to Hornvík
adventures.description:
The Westfjords' abandoned peninsula is Iceland with the volume turned down and the wildness turned up. Hornstrandir lost its last permanent residents in the 1950s; today there are no roads, no shops, no phone signal — just derelict farmsteads, whale bones on black beaches, and Arctic foxes so unhunted they trot up to inspect your bootlaces. The traverse from the ghost settlement at Hesteyri crosses low passes between fjords to Hornvík bay, beneath Hornbjarg: a 534m sea cliff shaped like a breaking wave, screaming with guillemots and puffins all summer.

Everything here is ferry-fed. Boats from Ísafjörður drop and collect hikers on a published summer schedule, and a missed pickup means days of waiting — so you build a buffer day in, and you treat the captain's weather word as law. Fog can erase the passes, river mouths shift, and camping is only permitted at designated sites, all gloriously basic.

The season is short and precise: mid-June to mid-August, when the boats run and the snow has gone. Stage from Ísafjörður (flights from Reykjavík), hire camping gas in town, and carry every meal. Around £380 including ferries and campsites.
highlights: Hornbjarg cliff rearing 534m from the sea
Puffin and guillemot colonies at Hornvík
Ferry ride out of Ísafjörður between fjord walls

adventures.title: Long Range Traverse, Gros Morne
adventures.description:
There is no trail on the Long Range Traverse. A boat drops you at the head of Western Brook Pond — a landlocked fjord walled by 600m cliffs — and you climb a steep gully onto the plateau, where for four or five days you navigate tundra, tarns and head-high tuckamore thickets by map, compass and judgement. Caribou drift across the barrens, moose crash out of spruce hollows, and from the rim you look straight down the fjord you sailed up on day one.

Parks Canada treats this as a serious undertaking: numbers are capped, you must pass a navigation briefing (and quiz) at the visitor centre before your backcountry permit is issued, and you carry a loaned emergency beacon. Fog is the true examiner — the plateau is featureless in cloud, and parties who trust their legs over their compass end up walled out above the wrong gully.

Stage from Rocky Harbour or Cow Head on Newfoundland's west coast; Deer Lake is the nearest airport. The boat across the pond and the permit must both be booked ahead for July to September. Around £380 including permit, boat and campsites — plus a rest day in your plan for weather, which you will probably use.
highlights: Boat ride up Western Brook Pond fjord to the trailhead
The gully climb onto the Long Range plateau
Caribou herds on the tundra barrens
Cliff-edge camp above Ten Mile Pond
gear: Map, compass and the skills to use both

adventures.title: Ruta 40 del Norte: Salta, Cachi and Cafayate
adventures.description:
Argentina's Ruta 40 is famous for Patagonia, but its high-desert northern reaches out of Salta are the connoisseur's section: a compact loop through polychrome rock, colonial adobe villages and the world's highest serious wine country, most of it above 1,600 m.

Head south through the Quebrada de las Conchas, where the road threads red sandstone past the Garganta del Diablo and the natural Amphitheatre, to Cafayate and its torrontés bodegas. Then pick up RN40 proper through Angastaco and the Quebrada de las Flechas — the moment of the trip, a moonscape of grey rock blades tilted at the sky with the gravel road slaloming between them. Continue to sleepy Molinos and whitewashed Cachi, and return to Salta over the 3,348 m Piedra del Molino on the Cuesta del Obispo's great earthen ramp, through the cactus forests of Los Cardones national park.

The variables: the Cafayate–Cachi stretch is ripio (gravel), so hire something with clearance; summer storms from December to March wash out fords; and the altitude sneaks up on you at viewpoints. Eight days from Salta runs about £1,100 per person in bodega stays and empanada money.
highlights: Quebrada de las Flechas rock blades
Cuesta del Obispo and Piedra del Molino pass
Cardón cactus forest in Los Cardones
gear: Full-size spare checked before leaving Salta
Sun hat and lip balm for altitude

adventures.title: Last Lions of Gir
adventures.description:
The world's only wild Asiatic lions live in one dry teak forest in Gujarat, and seeing them feels different from Africa: a lioness and grown cubs sprawled on the sandy bed of the Hiran river, shorter-maned, slighter, and sharing their forest with Maldhari buffalo herders who walk these tracks daily. From a few hundred animals a century ago the population has climbed steadily — a conservation recovery you can sit in an open Gypsy and watch.

Drives run at dawn and mid-afternoon from Sasan Gir village, and the permit is the crux: slots are capped and released online 90 days ahead, selling out around weekends and Indian holidays instantly. If you miss out, the Devalia interpretation zone offers a fallback sighting, but the real forest is the point. Beyond lions there are leopards, chowsingha, chinkara and 300-odd bird species.

December to March is dry, bright and comfortable; April and May are scorching but excellent for sightings; the park closes mid-June to mid-October for the monsoon. Fly to Rajkot or Diu, then drive two to three hours. Three days with permits, Gypsy hire, guide and a lodge costs roughly £500–£650.
highlights: A lioness and cubs on the Hiran riverbed
Maldhari herders sharing the forest with lions
Pre-dawn permit scramble at Sasan Gir
Chowsingha and chinkara in the teak scrub
Somnath temple on the drive in

adventures.title: Browning Wall Cold-Water Colour, God's Pocket
adventures.description:
Nobody believes cold water can out-colour the tropics until they see Browning Wall: a sheer face in Queen Charlotte Strait carpeted edge to edge in crimson strawberry anemones, white plumose towers and basket stars, with not a bare inch of rock in fifty metres. Giant Pacific octopus den in the crevices, wolf eels lean out for a look, and Steller sea lions strafe your safety stop like torpedoes with attitude. Surface intervals come with humpbacks, and some weeks orcas.

You stay at the God's Pocket wilderness lodge on Hurst Island or run boats out of Port Hardy at the top of Vancouver Island. Either way this is drysuit diving in 7-10°C water with genuine current, and slack-tide timing decides the day's schedule — your skipper's tide tables are the real itinerary.

Get to Port Hardy by the five-hour drive up-island from Nanaimo or a short flight from Vancouver. Late summer into autumn brings the clearest water once the plankton blooms fade. A week at the lodge with boat dives runs about £2,300; bring your own undersuit and thick dry gloves.
adventures.location: Browning Pass, Queen Charlotte Strait, British Columbia
highlights: Browning Wall's unbroken carpet of strawberry anemones
Steller sea lions buzzing the safety stop
Humpbacks and orcas on surface intervals

adventures.title: Painted Monasteries of Bucovina and Maramureș
adventures.description:
In the far north of Romania, entire churches wear their theology on the outside: Voroneț's west wall carries a Last Judgement on a blue so distinctive it has its own name, Sucevița's Ladder of Divine Ascent shows angels and demons contesting every rung, and Moldovița's siege of Constantinople turns Ottoman history into fresco propaganda — all painted in the 1500s and still vivid after five centuries of weather.

This eight-day drive loops from Cluj or Suceava through two of Europe's most intact rural worlds. In Bucovina you visit the great painted monasteries (Voroneț, Sucevița, Moldovița, Humor) and the black-pottery village of Marginea; over the Prislop Pass, Maramureș answers with its UNESCO wooden churches at Bârsana, Ieud and Poienile Izei, hand-carved gates taller than houses, hay meadows cut by scythe, and the Merry Cemetery at Săpânța, where painted oak crosses tell each villager's life in cheerfully blunt verse.

Stay in family guesthouses — dinner is whatever the garden produced, plus horincă plum brandy you cannot politely refuse twice. Roads are slow; budget driving time generously. May to September is the season. About £800–£1,000 for eight days with car hire.
highlights: Sucevița's Ladder of Divine Ascent fresco
Wooden churches of Bârsana and Ieud
Guesthouse dinners and horincă in Maramureș
gear: lei cash for guesthouses and entry fees

adventures.title: Kang Yatse II above the Markha Valley
adventures.description:
Kang Yatse II is the summit that turns Ladakhi trekkers into mountaineers. The 6,250 m western top of the twin-headed massif rises straight off the Nimaling plain at the head of the Markha Valley, and its northwest face is a single sweeping snow slope — steep enough to demand crampons, axe and a rope, forgiving enough to be many people's first 6,000er.

The approach is half the point: a week walking the Markha Valley through Hemis National Park, sleeping in whitewashed villages and parachute-tent teahouses, crossing rivers below ruined forts while blue sheep watch from the scree. From high camp at 5,200 m the climb starts at 2 a.m.; six hours later the Zanskar range is a frozen ocean below you and, on the clearest mornings, the Karakoram giants crowd the northern horizon.

July to September is the window — Ladakh sits in the monsoon's rain shadow while the rest of the Himalaya drips. Trips run 9 to 12 days out of Leh — fly from Delhi and spend two nights acclimatising at 3,500 m first; hurrying is what fells people here. A guided climb with permits, ponies and full camping runs about £1,400. Kang Yatse I is far more serious; check which head your itinerary names.
adventures.location: Markha Valley, Hemis National Park, Ladakh
highlights: A week's approach through the Markha Valley villages
High camp on the Nimaling plain at 5,200 m
The single great snow ramp of the northwest face
Karakoram skyline from the 6,250 m summit
Blue sheep and golden marmots in Hemis National Park

adventures.title: Pelican Waters of the Danube Delta
adventures.description:
Where the Danube finally gives up, 2,860 kilometres from the Black Forest, it dissolves into Europe's greatest wetland: 4,000 square kilometres of reedbeds, willow-lined channels and lakes that hold the continent's largest white pelican colonies and its rarest breeder, the Dalmatian pelican. From a small boat at dawn you watch fishing flotillas of pelicans herd shoals in synchronised horseshoes while pygmy cormorants, rollers and bee-eaters cross overhead — 300-plus species use the delta, and in May and June it simply thrums.

Life here moves at boat speed. Base in Tulcea for a night, then push down-channel to the Lipovan fishing villages — Mila 23, Crisan, or Sfântu Gheorghe at the river's mouth — for pensiune stays built on fish soup and home wine. Guided small-boat days work the back channels that big hotel-boats cannot enter; kayaks get quieter still.

June mosquitoes are legendary — cover up and bring serious repellent — and wind can cancel small-boat days on the open lakes, so keep the itinerary loose. Access is a flight to Bucharest, then four hours by road to Tulcea. Five days with boats, guide, full-board pensiunes and transfers runs around £500–£700.
adventures.location: Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve, Tulcea County
highlights: White pelican flotillas herding fish on Fortuna Lake
Dalmatian pelicans — Europe's rarest — at close range
Rollers and bee-eaters over the reed channels
Sunset run home along the Sulina channel

adventures.title: Tasmanian Trail: Devonport to Dover
adventures.description:
The Tasmanian Trail runs 480km down the middle of the island from the ferry ramp at Devonport to the fishing port of Dover in the far south — a multi-use route of forestry roads, fire trails and quiet farm lanes that most Tasmanians have never heard of — precisely its appeal. You ride under Mount Roland's dolerite ramparts near Sheffield, climb onto the Central Plateau's lake country, cross the Derwent at New Norfolk, and finish among Huon Valley apple orchards with the D'Entrecasteaux Channel ahead.

This is self-reliant touring rather than groomed trail: navigation apps are essential, some sections cross private land with gates to leave as found, and resupply towns are a day apart. The variable that catches people out is Tasmanian weather doing all four seasons in an afternoon — the plateau can snow in January.

The Spirit of Tasmania ferry from Geelong delivers you and your bike to the start. Eight days at around 60km/day suits a loaded gravel bike or hardtail. Camp at designated sites and showgrounds, with pub beds in Bothwell and New Norfolk breaking it up. Buy the Tasmanian Trail guidebook — sales fund the route. Budget around £700 all in.
highlights: Mount Roland looming over Sheffield's mural streets
Highland lakes country on the Central Plateau
Crossing the Derwent at New Norfolk
Rolling into Dover on the D'Entrecasteaux Channel
gear: Gravel bike or hardtail with 45mm+ tyres
GPX tracks plus the official guidebook

adventures.title: Busua Beach Break Week, Ghana
adventures.description:
Busua is West Africa's easiest surf gateway: a wide, palm-lined bay in Ghana's Western Region where warm, forgiving beach-break peaks roll in all year and the country's first surf shops and schools — grown from the local community — will have you standing in a session or two. At the west end, Black Mamba point adds a proper left when swell picks up, and a short canoe or drive around the headland brings you to Dixcove's fishing harbour and further empty corners.

The town runs on juice bars, beach football and highlife music; homestays and simple beach lodges cost little, and the surf community welcomes visitors who muck in. Beginners and cruisy intermediates both score daily, and hire fees visibly support local instructors.

Fly to Accra, then it is a four-to-five-hour drive west via Takoradi (public transport works; private transfer is easier with boards). March to August brings the most consistent southern swell; rainy-season showers pass quickly. The variable is water quality after heavy rain near the lagoon mouth — surf the main bay peaks. A week with lodge, meals and daily lessons is about £350, among the best-value surf weeks anywhere.
highlights: First green-wave rides on the main bay peaks
Black Mamba left when the swell pulses
Canoe hop to Dixcove fishing harbour
Beach football with the surf-school crew
Highlife nights at the juice bars
gear: Small gifts for the surf club

adventures.title: Jatbula Trail: Katherine Gorge to Leliyn
adventures.description:
The Jatbula follows a songline of the Jawoyn people for 62km across the top of the Arnhem Land escarpment, and it has solved the problem that ruins most tropical treks: heat with nowhere to cool off. Here, every single day ends at water — the plunge pool below Biddlecombe Cascades, the pandanus-lined channels of Crystal Falls, the midnight-green pool at 17 Mile Falls, and finally the tiered swimming lagoons of Leliyn (Edith Falls). You walk in the morning, swim all afternoon, and fall asleep to frogs arguing in the paperbarks.
