In between comes the quiet astonishment: rock-art galleries in the Amphitheatre's rainforest pocket and whistling kites riding the thermals. The trail is one-direction only, walker numbers are capped, and bookings open about a year out and vanish quickly for the June–August window.

The catch-outs are heat discipline — you start at first light and carry more water than feels reasonable between pools — and the season itself: outside May to September the creeks flood and the trail closes. Stage from Katherine, 30 minutes away, with a boat drop across the river to start. Roughly £300 in permits, camp fees and transfers.
highlights: Crystal Falls camp on the escarpment edge
Ferry crossing from Katherine Gorge to start
Finish in the tiered pools of Leliyn (Edith Falls)
gear: Trail booking confirmation (opens a year ahead)

adventures.title: Quttinirpaaq: Ellesmere Island Expedition
adventures.description:
Quttinirpaaq means "top of the world", and the name is literal: Canada's second-largest national park sits at 82 degrees north, closer to the Pole than to any city. Your Twin Otter drops onto the gravel strip at Tanquary Fiord and leaves, and for twelve days the only humans in an area the size of Switzerland are your team. You trek beneath Gull Glacier, ford braided meltwater rivers, and walk valleys where muskox and Peary caribou never learned to fear people — Arctic wolves sometimes trot into camp out of sheer curiosity.

The thermal oasis around Lake Hazen, the largest lake entirely north of the Arctic Circle, is the surprise: microclimate warmth, wildflowers, 24-hour daylight. The variable that catches people out is the fly-in logistics — everything hinges on charter weather from Resolute, and a two-day delay either side is normal, so build slack into your plans.

This is expedition travel at expedition prices: Kenn Borek charters from Resolute Bay dominate the roughly £22,000 land cost, and guided departures run a handful of times each July. Register with Parks Canada and train with a loaded pack — you carry your safety with you.
adventures.location: Quttinirpaaq National Park, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut
highlights: Landing by Twin Otter on the Tanquary Fiord gravel airstrip
Trekking beneath Gull Glacier at 82 degrees north
Muskox and Peary caribou in the Lake Hazen thermal oasis
Curious Arctic wolves with no fear of humans
24-hour daylight across an empty quarter the size of Switzerland
gear: Expedition tent rated for katabatic winds

adventures.title: Voss Adventure Week
adventures.description:
Voss calls itself the adventure capital of Norway and then spends all summer proving it. The town sits on a lake between Bergen and the fjords, and a five-day sampler runs the gamut: rafting the Raundalselvi's grade III–V snowmelt, paragliding from Hanguren above the lake, a canyoning day of slides and jumps in granite chutes, and — this being the home town of Norwegian skydiving — a tandem jump or a session in the wind tunnel where the national team trains. A finishing day kayaking the UNESCO-listed Nærøyfjord from Gudvangen, beneath kilometre-high walls, lands the point gently.

The moment that stays is the Raundalselvi: glacier-cold water, big bouncing wave trains, and cliffs the road never reaches. The variable is water level — snowmelt peaks in June and rapids get portaged or upgraded with flow — and weather can cancel flying days, so keep the schedule loose.

Everything books through operators in town, and the Bergen–Oslo railway stops literally in the middle of it (an hour from Bergen). Late June's Ekstremsportveko festival doubles the town's pulse if you can get a bed. Around £850 for hostel nights and four activity days.
highlights: Ekstremsportveko festival energy in late June
gear: Thermal base layers for glacial rivers
Rail tickets on the Bergen line

adventures.title: North Sea Coast: Hook of Holland to Skagen
adventures.description:
Follow the North Sea Cycle Route (EuroVelo 12) up the continent's edge: roughly 1,300km from Hook of Holland to Skagen at Denmark's tip, where the North Sea and Kattegat visibly collide over the Grenen sandbar. This is dune-and-dyke touring at its purest — the Netherlands' immaculate fietspaden through the Kennemerland dunes, the surreal 32km ruler-line of the Afsluitdijk, East Frisia's sheep-cropped sea dykes, and Jutland's heathered west coast where the path runs through marram grass metres from the surf.

It is technically easy and logistically frictionless: campsites and hostels every 20km, bakeries on schedule, and trains at every escape point. The variable that catches people out is wind. The prevailing south-westerly is a tailwind northbound — ride it that way — but a stiff northerly can turn a 100km dyke day into a grovel, and there is no shelter on a dyke.

Fourteen days at around 95km/day suits a loaded tourer. Train to Rotterdam starts it cleanly; from Skagen, rails run home via Hamburg. Budget around £1,300 mixing campsites, hostels and harbour-town splurges on herring and pastries. June and July give 17-hour days.
adventures.location: North Sea coast, Netherlands to Jutland
highlights: Dune paths through Nationaal Park Zuid-Kennemerland
Sea-dyke riding past East Frisian harbours
The Rømø causeway into Danish Wadden country
Standing on Grenen where two seas meet
gear: Touring bike with dynamo hub lighting

adventures.title: Kosciuszko Main Range Spring Ski Tour
adventures.description:
Australia has real backcountry skiing, and the Main Range is where it lives: a rolling alpine crest above the tree line where you can link Mount Twynam, Carruthers Peak and the country's rooftop, 2,228m Mount Kosciuszko, on skis. Watsons Crags fall away to the west in genuinely steep chutes, and the Blue Lake cirque holds snow — and occasionally water ice — well into spring.

Start from Guthega or Charlotte Pass, crossing the infant Snowy River on snow bridges, and camp or day-tour depending on ambition. The range is featureless when cloud drops, and rime-plastered gales arrive with little warning even in September — carry navigation you trust and treat the forecast as gospel. Snow depth also swings wildly between seasons, so book late once the cover is known.

Base in Jindabyne (two hours from Canberra airport), buy your Kosciuszko National Park pass, and go with a guide unless you are competent in whiteout navigation. August to October gives the classic corn window. About £700 for four days guided with lodging — or a fraction of that self-sufficient.
adventures.location: Main Range, Kosciuszko National Park, New South Wales
highlights: Watsons Crags chutes above the Sentinel ridgeline
Blue Lake cirque under spring rime
Snow-bridge crossing of the infant Snowy River
Sunset colours across the Ramshead Range
gear: Map, compass and GPS for whiteouts
Goggles plus spare lens for rime storms

adventures.title: Chichibu 34 Kannon Pilgrimage on Foot
adventures.description:
Japan's most walkable pilgrimage is not Shikoku — it is this 100km loop through the low mountains of Chichibu, ninety minutes from Ikebukuro on the Seibu line. Thirty-four temples dedicated to Kannon, goddess of mercy, thread through persimmon orchards, cedar plantations and the town's back streets. You carry a nokyocho stamp book and collect hand-brushed calligraphy at each temple office; the rhythm of bell, bow and stamp becomes the trip.

The moment: climbing the ladder-steep steps to temple 31, Kannon-in, where the hall is tucked under a rock overhang, and hearing nothing but water. Most walkers take four to six days, staying in ryokan and business hotels in Chichibu town and finishing at Suisen-ji, temple 34, in the hills near Mitsumine-guchi.

Spring brings the shibazakura moss-phlox fields; November the fire festival build-up and blazing maples. The catch is temple office hours — stamps stop at 4pm sharp (winter 5pm closures vary), so plan stages backwards from the last office. Budget around £450–£550 for five days including trains from Tokyo.
highlights: Cliff-hung Kannon-in (temple 31) under its rock overhang
Finishing the loop at Suisen-ji, temple 34
Shibazakura moss-phlox carpets at Hitsujiyama Park in spring
gear: comfortable trainers or light walking shoes
cash for temple stamps (500 yen each)
IC transit card for Seibu line

adventures.title: Río Baker Packraft Descent
adventures.description:
The Baker is Chile's biggest river by volume, and it looks the part: an impossible glacial turquoise, fed from Lago Bertrand and ultimately the Northern Patagonian Ice Field, surging through lenga forest and bare granite. Over seven days you descend it by packraft, portaging the unrunnable cataracts and riding the friendly wave trains between them, camping above water so blue it photographs like a lie.

The image everyone carries home is the Neff confluence, where the silt-grey Río Neff slams into the Baker's turquoise and the two colours run side by side, unmixed, below a thundering cascade. Downstream the valley opens to Caleta Tortel, a roadless village of cypress boardwalks where the river braids into fjord country — as good a finish line as paddling owns.

The access town is Cochrane, a day's bus from Balmaceda airport; guided descents with rafts, drysuits and support vehicle run around £2,300. The variables are Patagonian: wind arrives without appointment and can pin boats to the bank for an afternoon, and the water hovers near 8C, so a swim is serious even on easy sections. December to March gives settled weather; November trades stability for empty campsites.
highlights: The unmixed turquoise-and-grey confluence of the Baker and Neff
Packrafting beneath the Carretera Austral's remotest stretch
Wave trains of Chile's highest-volume river
Finishing at Caleta Tortel's cypress boardwalks
Camping under Patagonian granite and lenga forest
gear: Drysuit — the Baker runs at about 8C
Throw bag and carabiners for portage lowers
Dry bags sized for a week of food
